# Clean Code Rulebook for Coding Agents

## How to read this file

Every bullet is an enforceable rule. `**Bold**` is the rule name; the text after it is the
rule and, where present, its condition or exception. Numbered lists are ordered mechanics -
execute the steps in order. `// BAD` / `// GOOD` snippets are the minimum needed to make a
rule unambiguous. Where two rules conflict, the stated condition on each decides which applies.
Nothing here is optional background; there is no narrative to skip.

# BOOK 1 - Clean Code (Robert C. Martin)

## Clean Code: Ch1 Clean Code

### There Will Be Code

- **Code never goes away** - Never assume code will be replaced by models, requirements, or generation from specifications; code is the detail of the requirements, and specifying requirements precisely enough for a machine to execute is programming.
- **Higher abstraction does not remove rigor** - Expect language abstraction levels and the number of domain-specific languages to keep rising, but treat every such specification as code that must still be rigorous, accurate, formal, and detailed enough for a machine to execute.
- **Requirements are executable-grade** - Treat well-specified requirements as being as formal as code, usable as executable tests of that code.
- **Precision is never eliminated** - Tools may parse and assemble requirements into formal structures, but necessary precision cannot be removed, so there will always be code.

### Bad Code

- **Good code matters** - Treat "good code matters" as a robust premise, not a fragile one; bad code has killed shipping products and companies by making the codebase unmanageable as features are added.
- **Wading is the symptom** - Recognize "wading" (slogging through tangled, senseless code hunting for a clue about what is going on) as the diagnostic sign of bad code.
- **Never trade cleanliness for speed** - Never write a mess because you are rushed, tired, behind on a backlog, or afraid of a boss's reaction; a "working mess" is not acceptable output.
- **LeBlanc's law** - Later equals never. Never defer cleanup to a later day, because that day does not come.

### The Total Cost of Owning a Mess

- **Slowdown is near-universal and fast** - Assume that after more than two or three years of programming you have already been significantly slowed down by messy code, yours and other people's, and that the degree of slowdown can be significant: over the span of a year or two, a team that was moving very fast at the start of a project can find itself moving at a snail's pace.
- **Mess compounds to a standstill** - Expect a mess to make every change break two or three other parts of the code, so no change is trivial and every addition requires understanding the existing tangles, twists, and knots in order to add more of them.
- **Productivity decays asymptotically to zero** - As the mess builds, team productivity continues to decrease, approaching zero asymptotically, and past some point the mess cannot be cleaned up at all.
- **Adding staff accelerates the decay** - Never expect added staff to restore productivity in a messy codebase: new staff do not know the design intent, cannot tell a change that matches it from one that thwarts it, and under pressure to raise productivity make more messes, driving productivity further toward zero.

#### The Grand Redesign in the Sky

- **Redesign is not an escape** - Never treat a grand redesign as the remedy for a mess. The redesign team must reproduce everything the old system does while keeping pace with the changes still being made to it, because management will not retire the old system until parity is reached.
  - Expect the failure shape: a tiger team of only the best and brightest is staffed onto the greenfield rewrite while everyone else is left maintaining the current system, putting the two teams into a race.
- **Redesign races run for years** - Expect this race to last a very long time (observed: 10 years), by which time the original redesign team is gone and the current members demand that the new system be redesigned because it is a mess.
- **Cleanliness is professional survival** - Treat time spent keeping code clean not merely as cost-effective but as a matter of professional survival.

#### Attitude

- **Recognize the symptoms of a grave mess** - Treat these as all too common signs: wading through a mess so grave that it takes weeks to do what should have taken hours, and what should have been a one-line change made instead in hundreds of different modules.
- **Own the rot** - Never blame changed requirements, tight schedules, managers, customers, or marketing for code rot; the fault is the programmer's, and blaming others is unprofessional.
  - Managers and marketers depend on us for the information behind their promises and commitments; tell them what you think even when they do not ask.
  - Users depend on us to validate how requirements fit the system; project managers depend on us to help work out the schedule. We are complicit in planning and share responsibility for failures, especially failures caused by bad code.
- **Defend the code as they defend the schedule** - Most managers want the truth, even when they do not act like it, and want good code even when they are obsessing about the schedule; defending schedule and requirements with passion is their job, defending the code with equal passion is yours.
  - Do not accept "if I don't do what my manager says, I'll be fired" as a reason to comply: probably you will not be.
- **Refuse orders that create risk you understand better than the requester** - Never bend to the will of managers who do not understand the risk of making messes, exactly as a doctor must refuse a patient's demand to skip pre-surgical hand-washing to save time; the professional with the knowledge of the risk must refuse.

#### The Primal Conundrum

- **Messes never buy a deadline** - Never make a mess to meet a deadline. The mess slows you down instantly and forces you to miss the deadline. The conundrum is that developers who know previous messes slow them down still will not take the time to go fast.
- **Clean is the only fast** - The only way to go fast, and the only way to make the deadline, is to keep the code as clean as possible at all times.

#### The Art of Clean Code?

- **Recognition is not ability** - Do not assume that recognizing dirty code means you can write clean code; writing it requires the disciplined use of a myriad of little techniques applied through an acquired sense of cleanliness.
- **Code-sense is the key skill** - Cultivate "code-sense": it tells you whether code is good or bad and shows the strategy for transforming bad code into clean code. Without it you can see a mess but have no idea what to do; with it you see options and variations, choose the best variation, and plot a sequence of behavior-preserving transformations from here to there.

### What Is Clean Code?

- **Elegant and efficient (Stroustrup)** - Keep logic straightforward so it is hard for bugs to hide; keep dependencies minimal to ease maintenance; make error handling complete according to an articulated strategy; keep performance close to optimal so nobody is tempted to mess up the code with unprincipled optimizations. Clean code does one thing well.
  - Elegant means pleasingly graceful and stylish, pleasingly ingenious and simple; clean code is pleasing to read.
  - Treat wasted cycles as inelegant.
- **Bad code tempts the mess to grow** - Assume that when others change bad code they tend to make it worse; one broken window starts the process toward decay (broken-windows metaphor), so never leave the first broken window.
- **Attention to detail** - Never gloss over details. Abbreviated error handling, memory leaks, race conditions, and inconsistent naming are all instances of the same failure; clean code exhibits close attention to detail.
- **Focus, single-mindedness** - Never let a unit do too much, have muddled intent, or carry ambiguity of purpose. Each function, each class, each module must expose a single-minded attitude that remains entirely undistracted and unpolluted by surrounding details.
- **Reads like well-written prose (Booch)** - Keep code simple and direct; never obscure the designer's intent; fill it with crisp abstractions and straightforward lines of control.
  - Crisp means briskly decisive and matter-of-fact, without hesitation or unnecessary detail; code must be matter-of-fact rather than speculative, must contain only what is necessary, and must make readers perceive that you were decisive.
  - Clean code should clearly expose the tensions in the problem, build them to a climax, and resolve them in an obvious solution.
- **Enhanceable by others (Big Dave Thomas)** - Clean code can be read and enhanced by a developer other than its original author. Easy to read and easy to change are different properties; deliver both.
  - It has unit and acceptance tests.
  - It has meaningful names.
  - It provides one way rather than many ways to do one thing.
  - It has minimal dependencies, which are explicitly defined, and provides a clear and minimal API.
  - It is literate (Knuth's literate programming): composed in a form readable by humans, because depending on the language not all necessary information can be expressed clearly in code alone.
- **No tests means not clean** - Code without tests is not clean, no matter how elegant, readable, or accessible it is. Treat Test Driven Development as one of the most fundamental disciplines.
- **Smaller is better** - Prefer small code to large code; prefer minimal everything.
- **Care (Feathers)** - Clean code always looks like it was written by someone who cares: there is nothing obvious you can do to make it better, and attempted improvements lead you back to what is already there. Care is the one overarching quality that leads to all the others: take the time to keep code simple and orderly and to pay appropriate attention to details.

#### Beck's Rules of Simple Code (Jeffries), in priority order

1. Runs all the tests.
2. Contains no duplication.
3. Expresses all the design ideas that are in the system.
4. Minimizes the number of entities such as classes, methods, functions, and the like.

- **Attack duplication first** - Focus mostly on duplication. When the same thing is done over and over, treat it as a sign that an idea in your mind is not well represented in the code; identify that idea and express it more clearly.
- **Iterate on names** - Include meaningful names in expressiveness and expect to change the names of things several times before settling; with modern tooling renaming is inexpensive, so renaming is never a reason to keep a poor name.
- **One thing per object and per method** - Check whether an object or method is doing more than one thing. If it is an object, it probably needs to be broken into two or more objects. If it is a method, always apply the Extract Method refactoring, yielding one method that says more clearly what it does plus submethods saying how it is done.
- **Build simple abstractions early** - When you notice a recurring generic element (for example "find things in a collection" across a database of records, a hash map, or an array), wrap the particular implementation in a more abstract method or class.
  - Implement the simplest thing now (say a hash map); because all references go through the abstraction, the implementation can change at any time. This lets you go forward quickly while preserving the ability to change later.
  - The abstraction also reveals what is really going on and keeps you from implementing arbitrary collection behavior when a few simple ways of finding what you want are all that is needed.
- **The summary formula** - Reduced duplication, high expressiveness, and early building of simple abstractions: no duplication, one thing, expressiveness, tiny abstractions.
- **No surprises (Cunningham)** - Use expectation-matching as the test of clean code: each routine you read should turn out to be pretty much what you expected, obvious, simple, compelling, requiring little effort, with each module setting the stage for the next and telling you how the next will be written.
- **Make the language look made for the problem** - Code is beautiful when it makes the language look like it was made for the problem. It is never the language that makes programs appear simple; it is the programmer who makes the language appear simple, so the responsibility is yours.

### Schools of Thought

- **These rules are stated as absolutes** - Apply these rules as absolutes within their school of thought (the Object Mentor School of Clean Code), while knowing that no school is absolutely right and other schools and masters have equal claim to professionalism; learn from them as well.
  - Rightness within a school does not invalidate the teachings of a different school.
- **Expect controversy** - Some recommendations here are controversial and you may violently disagree with some; final authority is not claimed. The recommendations were nonetheless learned through decades of experience and repeated trial and error, so whether you agree or disagree, see and respect the point of view rather than dismissing it.

### We Are Authors

- **Write for readers** - You are an author with readers who will judge your effort; authors are responsible for communicating well with their readers.
- **Reading-to-writing ratio is well over 10:1** - Optimize for reading even when it makes the writing harder, because old code is constantly read as part of writing new code.
- **Easy to read is easy to write** - You cannot write code if you cannot read the surrounding code, so making code easy to read actually makes it easier to write. If you want to go fast and get done quickly, make the code easy to read.

### The Boy Scout Rule

- **Leave the campground cleaner than you found it** - Writing code well once is not enough; take an active role in preventing degradation over time.
- **Check in cleaner than you checked out** - If every check-in is a little cleaner than the checkout, the code cannot rot.
- **Cleanups may be tiny** - The cleanup does not have to be big: change one variable name for the better, break up one function that is a little too large, eliminate one small bit of duplication, clean up one composite if statement.
- **Continuous improvement is intrinsic to professionalism** - Treat a codebase that gets better as time passes as the only professional option.

### Prequel and Principles

- **Named design principles** - Apply the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP), the Open Closed Principle (OCP), and the Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP), among other principles of object-oriented design.

### Conclusion

- **Practice is required** - Tools, techniques, thought processes, heuristics, disciplines, and worked examples of bad code transformed into good code cannot by themselves give you code-sense; acquiring it from them requires practice.

## Clean Code: Ch2 Meaningful Names

### Use Intention-Revealing Names

- **Answer the big questions in the name** - the name of a variable, function, or class must tell why it exists, what it does, and how it is used.
- **A name needing a comment is a failed name** - if a name requires a comment, the name does not reveal its intent; rename instead of commenting.
- **Encode the measured quantity and its unit** - `int d; // elapsed time in days` reveals nothing; use `elapsedTimeInDays`, `daysSinceCreation`, `daysSinceModification`, `fileAgeInDays`.
- **Rename as soon as a better name is found** - choosing good names takes time but saves more than it takes; intention-revealing names make code much easier both to understand and to change.
- **Attack implicity, not complexity** - unreadable code is usually not complex; it is implicit, meaning the degree to which context is not explicit in the code itself. The bad version of a function can have the exact same number of operators, constants, and nesting levels as the good version and still be unreadable.
- **Make the implicit questions answerable from the text** - for any expression, the reader must not have to know out-of-band answers to: what kinds of things are in this collection; what is the significance of a given subscript; what is the significance of a literal value; how would I use the returned value.
- **Name the domain concepts, then hide magic numbers behind an intention-revealing predicate**

```java
// BAD
public List getThem() {
  List list1 = new ArrayList();
  for (int[] x : theList)
    if (x[0] == 4) list1.add(x);
  return list1;
}

// GOOD
public List getFlaggedCells() {
  List flaggedCells = new ArrayList();
  for (Cell cell : gameBoard)
    if (cell.isFlagged()) flaggedCells.add(cell);
  return flaggedCells;
}
```

  - Intermediate step, also valid: rename `theList` to `gameBoard`, `x` to `cell`, and replace `x[0] == 4` with `cell[STATUS_VALUE] == FLAGGED`.
  - Final step: replace the array of ints with a class exposing `isFlagged()`.

### Avoid Disinformation

- **Never leave false clues that obscure meaning** - avoid words whose entrenched meanings vary from your intended meaning.
- **Never reuse names with entrenched foreign meanings** - `hp`, `aix`, `sco` are poor variable names because they name Unix platforms or variants, even when `hp` looks like a good abbreviation for hypotenuse.
- **Never encode a container type you are not using** - do not call a grouping of accounts `accountList` unless it actually is a `List`; `accountGroup`, `bunchOfAccounts`, or plain `accounts` is better. Even when the container *is* a `List`, it is probably better not to encode the container type into the name at all.
- **Beware names that vary in small ways** - `XYZControllerForEfficientHandlingOfStrings` versus `XYZControllerForEfficientStorageOfStrings` have frightfully similar shapes. Spelling similar concepts similarly is information; using inconsistent spellings is disinformation.
- **Make names for very similar things sort together alphabetically, with very obvious differences** - with automatic code completion, developers pick an object by name without seeing your copious comments or the list of methods supplied by that class.
- **Never use lower-case `l` or uppercase `O` as variable names, especially together** - they look almost entirely like the constants one and zero. `int a = l; if ( O == l ) a = O1; else l = 01;` is unreadable. Solve it by renaming, not by mandating a special font, which becomes oral tradition or an extra work product passed to all future developers.

### Make Meaningful Distinctions

- **Never rename arbitrarily just to satisfy the compiler** - do not misspell one of two clashing names; that produces the situation where correcting a spelling error makes the code stop compiling. Never create `klass` because `class` was taken.
- **If names must differ, they must mean something different** - adding number series or noise words satisfies the compiler and nothing else.
- **Never use number-series naming** - `a1, a2, .. aN` is the opposite of intentional naming; such names are not disinformative, they are noninformative and give no clue to the author's intention. In `copyChars(char a1[], char a2[])`, use `source` and `destination`.
- **Never use noise words to distinguish** - `Info` and `Data` are indistinct noise words like `a`, `an`, and `the`. `Product`/`ProductInfo`/`ProductData`, `Customer`/`CustomerObject`, `getActiveAccount()`/`getActiveAccounts()`/`getActiveAccountInfo()` are all failures: the reader cannot know which to call.
  - Exception: prefix conventions like `a` and `the` are acceptable so long as they make a meaningful distinction, for example `a` for all local variables and `the` for all function arguments. The failure is naming a variable `theZork` only because `zork` already exists.
  - Caveat on that exception: this `a`/`the` practice was used in C++ but has been given up, because modern IDEs make it unnecessary.
- **Never let a name state its own kind** - the word `variable` should never appear in a variable name; the word `table` should never appear in a table name. `NameString` is no better than `Name`; if a `Name` could be a floating point number, that breaks the disinformation rule.
- **In the absence of specific conventions, treat these as identical** - `moneyAmount`/`money`, `customerInfo`/`customer`, `accountData`/`account`, `theMessage`/`message`. Distinguish names so the reader knows what the differences offer.

### Use Pronounceable Names

- **Make every name pronounceable** - if you cannot pronounce it, you cannot discuss it; programming is a social activity and unpronounceable names force new developers into made-up words instead of proper English terms.
- **Replace compressed vowel-less encodings with words**

```java
// BAD
class DtaRcrd102 {
  private Date genymdhms;
  private Date modymdhms;
  private final String pszqint = "102";
}

// GOOD
class Customer {
  private Date generationTimestamp;
  private Date modificationTimestamp;
  private final String recordId = "102";
}
```

### Use Searchable Names

- **Never leave a value that must be grepped as a bare literal** - `MAX_CLASSES_PER_STUDENT` is easy to grep; the number `7` turns up in file names, other constant definitions, and expressions using the value with different intent. A long numeric literal is worse: a transposed digit creates a bug that simultaneously evades the programmer's search.
- **Never name a searchable variable `e`** - it is the most common letter in English and shows up in every passage of text in every program.
- **Prefer the searchable name** - longer names trump shorter names, and any searchable name trumps a constant in code.
- **Restrict single-letter names to local variables inside short methods** - use a single-letter name only as a local variable inside a short method; this restriction is a personal preference, not an absolute.
- **The length of a name should correspond to the size of its scope [N5]** - if a variable or constant might be seen or used in multiple places, it is imperative to give it a search-friendly name.
- **Accept a longer function as the price of named constants**

```cpp
// BAD
for (int j=0; j<34; j++) { s += (t[j]*4)/5; }

// GOOD
int realDaysPerIdealDay = 4;
const int WORK_DAYS_PER_WEEK = 5;
int sum = 0;
for (int j=0; j < NUMBER_OF_TASKS; j++) {
  int realTaskDays = taskEstimate[j] * realDaysPerIdealDay;
  int realTaskWeeks = (realdays / WORK_DAYS_PER_WEEK);
  sum += realTaskWeeks;
}
```

  - `sum` is not a particularly useful name but at least it is searchable; finding `WORK_DAYS_PER_WEEK` beats finding every use of `5` and filtering to the intended meaning.

### Avoid Encodings

- **Avoid encoding type or scope information into names** - we have enough encodings to deal with without adding more; it adds an extra burden of deciphering, it hardly seems reasonable to require each new employee to learn another encoding "language" on top of the (usually considerable) body of code, it is an unnecessary mental burden when trying to solve a problem, and encoded names are seldom pronounceable and are easy to mis-type.

#### Hungarian Notation

- **Never use Hungarian Notation (HN) or any other type encoding in modern languages** - HN was justified only in the Windows C API era when the compiler did not check types and everything was an integer handle, long pointer, void pointer, or one of several "string" implementations; modern type systems, compilers, editors that detect type errors before compiling, and small classes with short functions remove the need.
- **Know the failure modes of type encoding** - it makes the name or type of a variable, function, or class harder to change, makes the code harder to read, and creates the possibility that the encoding system will mislead the reader: `PhoneNumber phoneString; // name not changed when type changed!`
- **Historical exception only** - encodings were violated out of necessity and with regret in name-length-challenged languages: Fortran forced the first letter to code the type; early BASIC allowed only a letter plus one digit.

#### Member Prefixes

- **Do not prefix member variables with `m_` anymore** - you no longer need to: classes and functions should be small enough that you do not need them, and you should be using an editing environment that highlights or colorizes members to make them distinct.

```java
// BAD
public class Part {
  private String m_dsc; // The textual description
  void setName(String name) { m_dsc = name; }
}

// GOOD
public class Part {
  String description;
  void setDescription(String description) { this.description = description; }
}
```

  - Readers quickly learn to ignore a prefix or suffix and see only the meaningful part; prefixes become unseen clutter and a marker of older code.

#### Interfaces and Implementations

- **Prefer to leave interfaces unadorned; if you must encode either the interface or the implementation, encode the implementation** - interfaces and implementations are sometimes a special case for encodings, for example an ABSTRACT FACTORY interface for creating shapes implemented by a concrete class. The preceding `I`, so common in today's legacy wads, is a distraction at best and too much information at worst; users should not be told they are being handed an interface, only that it is a `ShapeFactory`. `ShapeFactoryImp`, or even the hideous `CShapeFactory`, is preferable to `IShapeFactory`.

### Avoid Mental Mapping

- **Never force the reader to mentally translate your names into names they already know** - this arises from choosing neither problem domain terms nor solution domain terms.
- **A single-letter name is a placeholder the reader must map to the concept** - it is a poor choice in most contexts.
  - Exception: a loop counter may be named `i`, `j`, or `k` (never `l`) if its scope is very small and no other names can conflict, because those names are traditional for loop counters.
- **Never choose a letter name because the earlier letters are taken** - there is no worse reason for the name `c` than that `a` and `b` were already taken.
- **Clarity is king** - do not demonstrate mental juggling ability, such as remembering that `r` is the lower-cased url with host and scheme removed. The professional writes code others can understand.

### Class Names

- **Give classes and objects noun or noun phrase names** - `Customer`, `WikiPage`, `Account`, `AddressParser`.
- **Do not name a class with a verb** - a class name should not be a verb.
- **Keep noise words out of class names** - avoid `Manager`, `Processor`, `Data`, or `Info` in a class name.

### Method Names

- **Give methods verb or verb phrase names** - `postPayment`, `deletePage`, `save`.
- **Name accessors, mutators, and predicates for their value, prefixed `get`, `set`, `is` per the javabean standard** - `employee.getName()`, `customer.setName("mike")`, `paycheck.isPosted()`.
- **When constructors are overloaded, use static factory methods with names that describe the arguments** - `Complex.FromRealNumber(23.0)` is generally better than `new Complex(23.0)`. Consider enforcing their use by making the corresponding constructors private.

### Don't Be Cute

- **Never use clever, cute, or joke names** - they are memorable only to people who share the author's sense of humor, and only while they remember the joke. `DeleteItems`, not `HolyHandGrenade`.
- **Never use colloquialisms or slang** - do not use `whack()` to mean `kill()`; do not use culture-dependent jokes like `eatMyShorts()` to mean `abort()`.
- **Choose clarity over entertainment value** - say what you mean, mean what you say.

### Pick One Word per Concept

- **Pick one word for one abstract concept and stick with it** - `fetch`, `retrieve`, and `get` as equivalent methods of different classes is confusing; the reader ends up having to remember which company, group, or individual wrote each class, or browse headers and previous code samples.
- **Function names must stand alone and be consistent** - context-sensitive completion lists in modern IDEs do not give the comments you wrote around function names and parameter lists, and you are lucky if they give parameter names from declarations.
- **Never mix interchangeable role words in one code base** - a `controller`, a `manager`, and a `driver` together is confusing; the difference between `DeviceManager` and `ProtocolController` is undefined, and differing names lead the reader to expect differing types as well as differing classes.
- **Keep one consistent lexicon across the code base** - a consistent lexicon is a great boon to the programmers who must use your code.

### Don't Pun

- **Avoid using the same word for two purposes** - using the same term for two different ideas is essentially a pun.
- **Same-named methods must be semantically equivalent** - many classes with an `add` method is fine as long as their parameter lists and return values are semantically equivalent.
  - Failure case: if existing `add` methods create a new value by adding or concatenating two existing values, a new method that puts its single parameter into a collection must not be called `add`; use `insert` or `append`. Calling it `add` for "consistency" is a pun.
- **The author is responsible for being clear** - code should be a quick skim, not an intense study; follow the popular paperback model, not the academic model where the scholar digs the meaning out of the paper.

### Use Solution Domain Names

- **Use computer science terms, algorithm names, pattern names, and math terms freely** - readers will be programmers. `AccountVisitor` means a great deal to a programmer who knows the VISITOR pattern; every programmer knows what a `JobQueue` is.
- **It is not wise to draw every name from the problem domain** - coworkers should not have to run back and forth to the customer asking what each name means when they already know the concept by another name. For technical things, technical names are usually the most appropriate course.

### Use Problem Domain Names

- **When there is no "programmer-eese" for what you are doing, take the name from the problem domain** - then the maintaining programmer can ask a domain expert what it means.
- **Separate solution and problem domain concepts** - code that has more to do with problem domain concepts should have names drawn from the problem domain; this separation is part of the job of a good programmer and designer.

### Add Meaningful Context

- **Place names in context by enclosing them in well-named classes, functions, or namespaces** - few names are meaningful in and of themselves.
- **Use a prefix only as a last resort, when all else fails** - `firstName`, `lastName`, `street`, `houseNumber`, `city`, `state`, `zipcode` read as an address together, but `state` alone does not; `addrFirstName`, `addrLastName`, `addrState` at least tell the reader the variables are part of a larger structure. The better solution is a class named `Address`, so even the compiler knows the variables belong to a bigger concept.
- **When a function's variables need inferred context, extract a class whose fields they become** - apply this when the function name provides only part of the context and the algorithm provides the rest, so the variables' meanings are opaque until the whole function has been read, the function is a bit too long, and the variables are used throughout.

```java
// BAD - variables with unclear context
private void printGuessStatistics(char candidate, int count) {
  String number; String verb; String pluralModifier;
  if (count == 0) { number = "no"; verb = "are"; pluralModifier = "s"; }
  else if (count == 1) { number = "1"; verb = "is"; pluralModifier = ""; }
  else { number = Integer.toString(count); verb = "are"; pluralModifier = "s"; }
  print(String.format("There %s %s %s%s", verb, number, candidate, pluralModifier));
}
```

  1. Create a `GuessStatisticsMessage` class and make `number`, `verb`, and `pluralModifier` fields of it, giving them a definite context.
  2. With context established, break the algorithm into many smaller functions: a `make(candidate, count)` that calls `createPluralDependentMessageParts(count)` then formats, and a dedicated method per branch (`thereAreNoLetters()`, `thereIsOneLetter()`, `thereAreManyLetters(count)`) replacing the inline `if/else if/else` chain that assigned all three variables.

### Don't Add Gratuitous Context

- **Do not prefix every class in an application with the application's initials** - in "Gas Station Deluxe", prefixing classes with `GSD` is a bad idea and works against your tools: typing `G` and pressing completion yields a mile-long list of every class in the system.
- **Do not bake a module or app name into a reusable concept's name** - `GSDAccountAddress` for a mailing address class is wrong; ten of its seventeen characters are redundant or irrelevant, and the name does not fit when the customer contact application needs a mailing address.
- **Add no more context to a name than is necessary** - shorter names are generally better than longer ones, so long as they are clear. (Condition boundary: this applies to trimming redundant context; longer names trump shorter names when a name must be findable or might be seen or used in multiple places.)
- **Name instances and classes at different specificity** - `accountAddress` and `customerAddress` are fine names for instances of class `Address` but could be poor names for classes. `Address` is a fine name for a class; to differentiate MAC addresses, port addresses, and Web addresses, consider `PostalAddress`, `MAC`, and `URI`. More precise names are the point of all naming.

### Final Words

- **Rename freely; do not let fear of others' objection stop you** - renaming is a code improvement like any other, and refactoring tools resolve these problems in someone else's code.
- **Judge code by whether it reads like paragraphs and sentences, or at least like tables and data structures** - a sentence is not always the best way to display data. Do not rely on memorizing class and method names; use modern tools for those details.
- **Good naming requires good descriptive skills and a shared cultural background** - it is a teaching issue, not a technical, business, or management issue.

## Clean Code: Ch3 Functions

### Small!

- **First rule of functions** - functions should be small. The second rule of functions is that they should be smaller than that. No research is offered as justification; it comes from long trial and error.
- **Hard line limits** - lines should not be 150 characters long; functions should not be 100 lines long; functions should hardly ever be 20 lines long.
- **Target size** - aim for functions of two, three, or four lines, each transparently obvious, each telling a story, each leading to the next in a compelling order.
- **Extract until intent is visible** - when a function is long and contains duplicated code, odd strings, inobvious data types, and mixed abstraction levels, repair it with a few simple method extractions, some renaming, and a little restructuring; that usually captures its intent in about nine lines, and a nine-line version should usually be shortened further, to about three.

### Blocks and Indenting

- **One-line blocks** - blocks within `if`, `else`, `while` and similar statements should be one line long, and that line should probably be a function call. This keeps the enclosing function small and adds documentary value because the called function has a descriptive name.
- **Indent level at most one or two** - functions should not be large enough to hold nested structures, so the indent level of a function should not be greater than one or two.

### Do One Thing

- **FUNCTIONS SHOULD DO ONE THING. THEY SHOULD DO IT WELL. THEY SHOULD DO IT ONLY.** - this advice has appeared in one form or another for 30 years or more.
- **Definition of "one thing"** - if a function does only those steps that are one level below the stated name of the function, then the function is doing one thing. The reason we write functions is to decompose a larger concept (the function's name) into a set of steps at the next level of abstraction.
- **TO paragraph test** - describe the function as a brief "TO" paragraph: "TO RenderPageWithSetupsAndTeardowns, we check to see whether the page is a test page and if so, we include the setups and teardowns. In either case we render the page in HTML." Several apparent "things" at one level below the name still count as one thing.
- **Extractability test [G34]** - a function is doing more than one thing if you can extract another function from it with a name that is not merely a restatement of its implementation. Extracting an `if` into `includeSetupsAndTeardownsIfTestPage` restates the code without changing the level of abstraction, so it proves nothing.

```java
// GOOD - one thing: steps are all one level below the name
public static String renderPageWithSetupsAndTeardowns(
    PageData pageData, boolean isSuite) throws Exception {
  if (isTestPage(pageData))
    includeSetupAndTeardownPages(pageData, isSuite);
  return pageData.getHtml();
}
```

### Sections within Functions

- **No sections** - do not divide a function into sections; a function that can be divided into sections, such as declarations, initializations, and the main algorithm (for example a sieve), is an obvious symptom of doing more than one thing. Functions that do one thing cannot be reasonably divided into sections.

### One Level of Abstraction per Function

- **Single abstraction level** - make sure all statements within a function are at the same level of abstraction. Mixing high-level concepts (`getHtml()`), intermediate ones (`PathParser.render(pagePath)`), and remarkably low-level ones (`.append("\n")`) in one function is always confusing.
- **Failure mode** - readers cannot tell whether an expression is an essential concept or a detail; and, like broken windows, once details are mixed with essential concepts, more and more details tend to accrete within the function.

### Reading Code from Top to Bottom: The Stepdown Rule

- **The Stepdown Rule** - code should read like a top-down narrative: every function is followed by those at the next level of abstraction, so the program can be read descending one level of abstraction at a time down the list of functions.
- **Read as TO paragraphs** - each function is a TO paragraph describing the current level of abstraction and referencing subsequent TO paragraphs at the next level down ("To include the setups and teardowns, we include setups, then the test page content, then the teardowns. To include the setups, we include the suite setup if this is a suite, then the regular setup. ...").
- **Hard but essential** - programmers find it very difficult to write functions that stay at a single level of abstraction; it is the key to keeping functions short and making sure they do one thing.

### Switch Statements

- **Switch statements always do N things** - it is hard to make a small switch statement (this includes if/else chains); even a two-case switch is larger than a single block or function should be, and by their nature switch statements do N things.
- **Bury and never repeat; rule for switch statements [G23]** - since switch statements cannot always be avoided, ensure each one is buried in a low-level class and is never repeated; do this with polymorphism. A switch statement can be tolerated if it appears only once, is used to create polymorphic objects, and is hidden behind an inheritance relationship so the rest of the system can't see it. Every circumstance is unique and there are times when one or more parts of that rule are violated.
- **Type-switch defects** - a `switch (e.type)` dispatch function is large and grows as new types are added, clearly does more than one thing, violates the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) because there is more than one reason for it to change, violates the Open Closed Principle (OCP) because it must change whenever new types are added, and worst of all, an unlimited number of other functions (`isPayday`, `deliverPay`, ...) will share the same deleterious structure.
- **Solution** - bury the switch in the basement of an ABSTRACT FACTORY and never let anyone see it; the factory uses the switch to create the appropriate derivative instances, and the various functions are dispatched polymorphically through the abstract interface.

```java
// BAD
public Money calculatePay(Employee e) throws InvalidEmployeeType {
  switch (e.type) {
    case COMMISSIONED: return calculateCommissionedPay(e);
    case HOURLY:       return calculateHourlyPay(e);
    case SALARIED:     return calculateSalariedPay(e);
    default: throw new InvalidEmployeeType(e.type);
  }
}
// GOOD - abstract Employee with isPayday/calculatePay/deliverPay;
// the only switch lives in EmployeeFactoryImpl.makeEmployee(EmployeeRecord r)
// and returns new CommissionedEmployee(r) / HourlyEmployee(r) / SalariedEmployee(r).
```

### Use Descriptive Names

- **Name says what the function does** - choose a name that describes what the function does, and give private methods equally descriptive names. It is hard to overestimate the value of good names.
- **Ward's principle** - "You know you are working on clean code when each routine turns out to be pretty much what you expected." Half the battle is choosing good names for small functions that do one thing.
- **Small functions are easier to name** - the smaller and more focused a function is, the easier it is to choose a descriptive name.
- **Long names are fine** - don't be afraid to make a name long. A long descriptive name is better than a short enigmatic name, and better than a long descriptive comment.
- **Multi-word convention** - use a naming convention that allows multiple words to be easily read in function names, then use those words to say what the function does.
- **Spend time on names** - try several different names and read the code with each in place; use IDE rename support to experiment until the name is as descriptive as possible. Hunting for a good name commonly results in a favorable restructuring of the code and clarifies the design in your mind.
- **Be consistent** - use the same phrases, nouns, and verbs across a module's function names (`includeSetupAndTeardownPages`, `includeSetupPages`, `includeSuiteSetupPage`, `includeSetupPage`) so the sequence tells a story and missing counterparts become conspicuous.

### Function Arguments

- **Argument count ranking** - the ideal number of arguments is zero (niladic); next one input argument (monadic), which is the next best thing to no arguments; followed closely by two (dyadic). Three (triadic) should be avoided where possible. More than three (polyadic) requires very special justification, and then shouldn't be used anyway.
- **Why arguments are hard** - they take a lot of conceptual power; the reader must interpret them each time they appear, and an argument is often at a different level of abstraction than the function name, forcing knowledge of an unimportant detail. Prefer making such a value an instance variable: `includeSetupPage()` is easier to understand than `includeSetupPageInto(newPageContent)`.
- **Testing cost** - argument combinations multiply test cases. Zero arguments is trivial to test, one is not too hard, two is more challenging, and with more than two, testing every combination of appropriate values can be daunting.

### Common Monadic Forms

- **Two expected monadic forms** - either ask a question about the argument (`boolean fileExists("MyFile")`), or operate on the argument, transforming it into something else and returning it (`InputStream fileOpen("MyFile")`). Choose names that make the distinction clear and always use the two forms in a consistent context.
- **Event form** - a less common but useful monadic form is an event: an input argument, no output argument, where the call is interpreted as an event that alters system state, e.g. `void passwordAttemptFailedNtimes(int attempts)`. Use this form with care; it must be very clear to the reader that this is an event, so choose names and contexts carefully.
- **Avoid other monadic forms** - try to avoid any monadic function that does not follow one of these forms, e.g. `void includeSetupPageInto(StringBuffer pageText)`; using an output argument instead of a return value for a transformation is confusing.
- **Transformations return their result** - if a function transforms its input argument, the transformation should appear as the return value. `StringBuffer transform(StringBuffer in)` is better than `void transform(StringBuffer out)` even if the first implementation simply returns the input argument, because it still follows the form of a transformation.

### Flag Arguments

- **Never pass a boolean flag** - flag arguments are ugly; passing a boolean into a function is a truly terrible practice. It immediately complicates the signature and loudly proclaims that the function does more than one thing: one thing if the flag is true and another if false.
- **Split instead** - split the function into two, e.g. `renderForSuite()` and `renderForSingleTest()`, rather than `render(true)`.
  - Exception: a flag may be kept when the callers already pass it in and you are deliberately limiting the scope of the refactoring to the function and below; even then, a call like `render(true)` is plain confusing to the reader, and splitting the function into two remains the right fix.
  - Do not rely on tooling to compensate: mousing over the call and seeing `render(boolean isSuite)` helps a little, but not that much.

### Dyadic Functions

- **Dyads cost more than monads** - `writeField(name)` is easier to understand than `writeField(outputStream, name)`; the second requires a short pause until the reader learns to ignore the first parameter, and we should never ignore any part of code because the parts we ignore are where the bugs will hide.
- **When two arguments are appropriate** - when the two arguments are ordered components of a single value, e.g. `Point p = new Point(0,0)`; Cartesian points naturally take two arguments and `new Point(0)` would be surprising. Arguments like `outputStream` and `name` have neither natural cohesion nor natural ordering.
- **Ordering conventions are a hazard** - even obvious dyads like `assertEquals(expected, actual)` are problematic because the two arguments have no natural ordering; the expected/actual ordering is a convention that requires practice to learn.
- **Convert dyads to monads where possible** - dyads aren't evil and you will have to write them, but be aware of the cost and use available mechanisms to reduce them:
  - make the method a member of one argument's class, e.g. `outputStream.writeField(name)`;
  - make the argument a member variable of the current class so it need not be passed;
  - extract a new class (e.g. `FieldWriter`) that takes the `outputStream` in its constructor and has a `write` method.

### Triads

- **Think very carefully before creating a triad** - triads are significantly harder to understand than dyads; the issues of ordering, pausing, and ignoring are more than doubled.
- **Insidious triad** - `assertEquals(message, expected, actual)` causes a double-take on every reading, and the reader learns to ignore the message.
- **Tolerable triad** - `assertEquals(1.0, amount, .001)` still requires a double-take, but one worth taking, because it is always good to be reminded that equality of floating point values is a relative thing.

### Argument Objects

- **Wrap argument groups into objects** - when a function seems to need more than two or three arguments, some of those arguments likely ought to be wrapped into a class of their own: prefer `Circle makeCircle(Point center, double radius)` over `Circle makeCircle(double x, double y, double radius)`.
- **This is not cheating** - when groups of variables are passed together, they are likely part of a concept that deserves a name of its own.

### Argument Lists

- **Variadic args count as one argument** - if variable arguments are all treated identically they are equivalent to a single argument of type `List`, so `public String format(String format, Object... args)` is dyadic and all the same rules apply.
- **Cap variadic signatures at triad** - functions taking variable arguments can be monads, dyads, or even triads (`void monad(Integer... args)`, `void dyad(String name, Integer... args)`, `void triad(String name, int count, Integer... args)`), but it would be a mistake to give them more arguments than that.

### Verbs and Keywords

- **Verb/noun pair for monads** - the function and its argument should form a good verb/noun pair: `write(name)` is evocative; `writeField(name)` is better because it tells us the "name" thing is a "field".
- **Keyword form** - encode the names of the arguments into the function name; `assertEquals` might be better written as `assertExpectedEqualsActual(expected, actual)`, which strongly mitigates the problem of having to remember argument ordering.

### Have No Side Effects

- **Side effects are lies** - a function that promises one thing while making hidden changes to its own class's variables, its parameters, or system globals commits a devious and damaging mistruth that often results in strange temporal couplings and order dependencies.
- **Side effect failure mode** - a `checkPassword(userName, password)` that also calls `Session.initialize()` means a caller who believes the name risks erasing existing session data merely by validating a user.
- **Temporal coupling** - a hidden side effect means the function can only be called at certain times; called out of order, data may be inadvertently lost. If you must have a temporal coupling, make it clear in the name of the function (e.g. `checkPasswordAndInitializeSession`), though such a name certainly violates "Do one thing."

### Output Arguments

- **Avoid output arguments in general** - output arguments are harder to understand than input arguments, because readers expect information to go in through arguments and out through the return value, so output arguments cause a double-take. `appendFooter(s)` forces the reader to ask whether `s` is input or output; anything that forces you to check the function signature is equivalent to a double-take, a cognitive break that should be avoided.
- **Change the owning object's state** - if your function must change the state of something, have it change the state of its owning object: `report.appendFooter()` instead of `appendFooter(report)`. Output arguments were sometimes necessary before object oriented programming, but much of the need disappears in OO languages because `this` is intended to act as an output argument.

### Command Query Separation

- **Do something or answer something, not both** - a function should either change the state of an object or return information about that object. Doing both often leads to confusion.
- **Failure mode** - `public boolean set(String attribute, String value)` produces `if (set("username", "unclebob"))...`, which reads ambiguously because it is unclear whether "set" is a verb or an adjective; renaming to `setAndCheckIfExists` does not much help the readability of the `if` statement.
- **Real fix** - separate the command from the query so the ambiguity cannot occur:

```java
// GOOD
if (attributeExists("username")) {
  setAttribute("username", "unclebob");
  ...
}
```

### Prefer Exceptions to Returning Error Codes

- **Error codes violate command query separation** - returning error codes from command functions is a subtle violation of command query separation because it promotes commands being used as expressions in the predicates of `if` statements, e.g. `if (deletePage(page) == E_OK)`.
- **Failure mode** - error codes avoid verb/adjective confusion but lead to deeply nested structures, because the caller must deal with the error immediately.
- **Use exceptions** - with exceptions, the error processing code can be separated from the happy path code and simplified:

```java
// GOOD
try {
  deletePage(page);
  registry.deleteReference(page.name);
  configKeys.deleteKey(page.name.makeKey());
} catch (Exception e) {
  logger.log(e.getMessage());
}
```

### Extract Try/Catch Blocks

- **Extract try and catch bodies into their own functions** - try/catch blocks are ugly in their own right; they confuse the structure of the code and mix error processing with normal processing. Extraction leaves one function that is all about error processing (easy to understand and then ignore) and another that is all about the real process, with error handling ignorable.

```java
// GOOD
public void delete(Page page) {
  try { deletePageAndAllReferences(page); }
  catch (Exception e) { logError(e); }
}
private void deletePageAndAllReferences(Page page) throws Exception { ... }
private void logError(Exception e) { logger.log(e.getMessage()); }
```

### Error Handling Is One Thing

- **A function that handles errors should do nothing else** - error handling is one thing, and functions do one thing. This implies that if the keyword `try` exists in a function, it should be the very first word in the function, and there should be nothing after the `catch`/`finally` blocks.

### The Error.java Dependency Magnet

- **Error enums are dependency magnets** - returning error codes usually implies a class or enum defining all error codes (`enum Error { OK, INVALID, NO_SUCH, LOCKED, OUT_OF_RESOURCES, WAITING_FOR_EVENT; }`); many other classes must import and use it, so when it changes all of them must be recompiled and redeployed.
- **Resulting failure mode** - the negative pressure means programmers reuse old error codes rather than add new ones, to avoid rebuilding and redeploying everything.
- **Exceptions avoid this** - new exceptions are derivatives of the exception class and can be added without forcing any recompilation or redeployment. This is an example of the Open Closed Principle (OCP).

### Don't Repeat Yourself

- **Eliminate duplication (the DRY principle)** - duplication bloats the code, so hunt it down and remove it. An algorithm repeated four times (for example once each for the SetUp, SuiteSetUp, TearDown and SuiteTearDown cases) requires four-fold modification should the algorithm ever have to change, and is a four-fold opportunity for an error of omission; remedy it by extracting the repeated algorithm into a single method (such as one `include` method), which enhances the readability of the whole module.
- **Duplication hides** - duplicated instances may be intermixed with other code and not uniformly duplicated, which makes them hard to spot.
- **Duplication may be the root of all evil in software** - many principles and practices exist to control or eliminate it: Codd's database normal forms eliminate duplication in data; object-oriented programming concentrates otherwise redundant code into base classes; structured programming, Aspect Oriented Programming, and Component Oriented Programming are all in part strategies for eliminating duplication.

### Structured Programming

- **Dijkstra's rules** - every function, and every block within a function, should have one entry and one exit: only one `return` statement in a function, no `break` or `continue` statements in a loop, and never, ever, any `goto` statements.
- **When the rules do not pay** - those rules serve little benefit when functions are very small; they provide significant benefit only in larger functions. If you keep your functions small, the occasional multiple `return`, `break`, or `continue` does no harm and can sometimes be more expressive than the single-entry, single-exit rule.
- **goto is the exception** - `goto` only makes sense in large functions, so it should be avoided.

### How Do You Write Functions Like This?

1. Get the first draft down even though it comes out long and complicated, with lots of indenting and nested loops, long argument lists, arbitrary names, and duplicated code.
2. Have a suite of unit tests covering every one of those clumsy lines of code.
3. Massage and refine: split out functions, change names, eliminate duplication.
4. Shrink the methods and reorder them.
5. Break out whole classes when needed, all the while keeping the tests passing.

- **No one writes clean functions on the first pass** - do not expect to write functions this way to start.

### Conclusion

- **Functions are verbs, classes are nouns** - every system is built from a domain-specific language designed by the programmers to describe that system; functions are the verbs of that language and classes are the nouns. This is not the old notion of taking nouns and verbs from a requirements document as a first guess at classes and functions.
- **Design the language, not just the program** - think of systems as stories to be told rather than programs to be written, and use the facilities of the language to construct a richer, more expressive language for telling that story; part of that language is the hierarchy of functions describing every action in the system.
- **Write to tell the story** - mechanics that make functions short, well named, and nicely organized are not the end in themselves; the real goal is to tell the story of the system, so the functions you write must fit cleanly together into a clear and precise language that helps that telling.

## Clean Code: Ch4 Comments

### Core stance on comments

- **Treat every comment as a failure** - comments are always failures: a comment exists only to compensate for a failure to express intent in code. We must have them because we cannot always figure out how to express ourselves without them, but their use is never a cause for celebration; when you feel the need to write one, first try to turn the tables and express it in code instead.
- **Never rely on comments staying true** - comments lie: not always and not intentionally, but too often. The older a comment is, and the farther away it is from the code it describes, the more likely it is to be just plain wrong, because programmers cannot realistically maintain them while code moves, splits, and recombines.
  - Failure mode: unrelated declarations get interposed between a constant and its explanatory comment, orphaning the comment far from what it described.
- **Inaccurate comments are far worse than no comments at all** - they delude and mislead, set expectations that will never be fulfilled, and lay down old rules that need not or should not be followed any longer.
- **Treat code as the only source of truth** - truth can only be found in one place: the code. Only the code can truly tell you what it does; it is the only source of truly accurate information.
- **Minimize comments deliberately** - though comments are sometimes necessary, expend significant energy to reduce their number.
  - Programmers should be disciplined enough to keep comments in a high state of repair, relevance, and accuracy, but spend that energy instead on making the code so clear and expressive that it does not need the comments in the first place.
- **Do not comment bad code, clean it** - bad code is one of the most common motivations for writing comments; clear and expressive code with few comments is far superior to cluttered and complex code with lots of comments. Spend the time cleaning the mess, not explaining it.
- **Explain yourself in code** - in many cases it is simply a matter of creating a function that says the same thing as the comment you wanted to write; it takes only a few seconds of thought to explain most intent in code.

```java
// BAD
// Check to see if the employee is eligible for full benefits
if ((employee.flags & HOURLY_FLAG) && (employee.age > 65))

// GOOD
if (employee.isEligibleForFullBenefits())
```

### Good Comments

- **The only truly good comment is the comment you found a way not to write** - some comments are necessary or beneficial, but reach for any of the permitted comment categories only after you have tried and failed to make the comment unnecessary.
- **Legal Comments** - copyright and authorship statements at the start of each source file are necessary and reasonable when corporate coding standards require them.
  - Keep them out of the way; collapsing them in the IDE stops them acting as clutter.
  - Never let them become contracts or legal tomes; where possible refer to a standard license or external document instead of putting all terms and conditions into the comment.
- **Informative Comments** - a comment may supply basic information such as the meaning of a return value or the format a regular expression matches.
  - Prefer conveying that information in the function name where possible (for example rename `responderInstance` to `responderBeingTested`, making the comment redundant).
  - Prefer moving the logic into a dedicated class (for example a date/time format converter) so the comment becomes superfluous.
- **Explanation of Intent** - a comment is justified when it records the intent behind a decision rather than the implementation, so a reader knows what the author was trying to do even if they disagree with the solution.

```java
// GOOD
return 1; // we are greater because we are the right type.
```

- **Clarification** - a comment translating the meaning of an obscure argument or return value into something readable can be useful when the value is part of the standard library or in code you cannot alter.
  - In general it is better to find a way to make that argument or return value clear in its own right.
  - There is a substantial risk that a clarifying comment is itself incorrect and hard to verify; before writing one, take care that there is no better way, and then take even more care that it is accurate.
- **Warning of Consequences** - use a comment to warn other programmers about a consequence, such as why a test is disabled or why an object must be created per use.
  - When a factory must return a fresh instance because the type is not thread safe (for example `SimpleDateFormat`), state that in a comment; it prevents an overly eager programmer from introducing a static initializer in the name of efficiency.
  - For disabled tests, prefer the mechanism the framework provides: `@Ignore("Takes too long to run")` rather than the pre-JUnit-4 convention of prefixing the method name with an underscore.
- **TODO Comments** - `//TODO` notes are sometimes reasonable: work the programmer thinks should be done but cannot do now (deleting a deprecated feature, asking someone to look at a problem or suggest a better name, a change dependent on a planned event), and they can explain why a function has a degenerate implementation and what its future should be.
  - A TODO is never an excuse to leave bad code in the system.
  - Scan through TODOs regularly and eliminate the ones you can; do not let code become littered with them. Good IDEs can locate them all, so they are unlikely to get lost.
- **Amplification** - a comment may amplify the importance of something that would otherwise seem inconsequential (for example that a `trim()` call is essential because leading spaces would cause the item to be recognized as another list).
- **Javadocs in Public APIs** - if you are writing a public API, write good javadocs for it, while keeping the rest of these comment rules in mind: javadocs can be just as misleading, nonlocal, and dishonest as any other comment.

### Bad Comments

- **Assume most comments are bad** - most comments are crutches or excuses for poor code, or justifications for insufficient decisions, amounting to little more than the programmer talking to himself.
- **Mumbling** - never plop in a comment just because you feel you should or because the process requires it; if you decide to write a comment, spend the time necessary to make it the best comment you can write.
  - Any comment that forces you to look in another module for its meaning has failed to communicate and is not worth the bits it consumes. Example failure: `// No properties files means all defaults are loaded` in an empty catch block leaves the reader unable to tell who loads the defaults or when.
- **Redundant Comments** - delete comments that are not more informative than the code, do not justify the code, do not provide intent or rationale, and are not easier to read than the code.
  - Such a comment can take longer to read than the code itself, is less precise than the code, and entices the reader to accept that lack of precision in lieu of true understanding.
  - Reject the legion of redundant javadocs on self-describing fields; they only clutter and obscure and serve no documentary purpose at all.
- **Misleading Comments** - never let a comment be imprecise enough to be inaccurate; a slightly wrong comment sends the next programmer into a debugging session over behavior they were promised.
  - Concrete failure: a header saying a method "returns when this.closed is true" when in fact it returns if `this.closed` is already true, otherwise waits for a blind timeout and then throws; a caller expects prompt return and instead debugs slow code.
- **Mandated Comments** - never adopt a rule that every function must have a javadoc or every variable must have a comment; such rules clutter code, propagate lies, and lend to general confusion and disorganization.
  - Required-javadoc abominations list every `@param` with a restatement of its name, add nothing, obfuscate the code, and create the potential for lies and misdirection.
- **Journal Comments** - remove journal/log comments accumulated at the start of a module recording every edit; the historic reason (no source code control system) is gone, and these long journals are now just clutter. They should be completely removed.
- **Noise Comments** - delete comments that restate the obvious and provide no new information, such as `/** Default constructor. */`, `/** The day of the month. */` on `dayOfMonth`, or a `getDayOfMonth()` javadoc whose `@return` repeats the method name.
  - Noise comments train readers to skip over them, and they eventually begin to lie as the code around them changes.
  - When a comment expresses frustration (venting, "Give me a break!"), treat the frustration as a signal to improve the structure of the code: extract the offending try/catch block into a separate named function (for example `addExceptionAndCloseResponse(e)`) instead of commenting.
  - An empty catch block whose comment explains why the exception is ignored (`// normal. someone stopped the request.`) can be appropriate; a venting comment in another catch block of the same function is pure noise.
  - Replace the temptation to create noise with the determination to clean your code.
- **Scary Noise** - redundant noisy javadocs written out of a misplaced desire to provide documentation are also a source of copy-paste errors (for example two different fields both documented `/** The version. */`); if authors are not paying attention when comments are written or pasted, readers cannot be expected to profit from them.
- **Don't Use a Comment When You Can Use a Function or a Variable** - refactor by extracting explanatory names rather than commenting the expression.

```java
// BAD
// does the module from the global list depend on the
// subsystem we are part of?
if (smodule.getDependSubsystems().contains(subSysMod.getSubSystem()))

// GOOD
ArrayList moduleDependees = smodule.getDependSubsystems();
String ourSubSystem = subSysMod.getSubSystem();
if (moduleDependees.contains(ourSubSystem))
```

  - If you wrote the comment first and then the code, refactor afterward so that the comment can be removed.
- **Position Markers** - banners such as `// Actions //////////////////////////////` are generally clutter that should be eliminated, especially the noisy train of slashes at the end.
  - There are rare times when gathering certain functions beneath a banner makes sense; use banners very sparingly and only when the benefit is significant, because overused banners fall into the background noise and are ignored.
- **Closing Brace Comments** - do not annotate closing braces (`} //while`, `} // try`, `} //catch`, `} //main`); this may make sense for long functions with deeply nested structures, but it only clutters the small, encapsulated functions we prefer. If you find yourself wanting to mark closing braces, shorten your functions instead.
- **Attributions and Bylines** - never add bylines such as `/* Added by Rick */`; source code control systems remember who added what and when, and bylines stay around for years getting less accurate and relevant even though they seem useful for knowing who to talk to.
- **Commented-Out Code** - never comment out code; just delete it. Source code control systems remember it for you and it will not be lost.
  - Failure mode: others will not have the courage to delete commented-out code because they assume it is there for a reason and is too important to delete, so it gathers like dregs, leaving nobody able to say whether the lines matter, were reminders, or are years-old cruft.
  - The practice was only useful back in the sixties, before good source code control existed.
- **HTML Comments** - never adorn source comments with HTML; it makes them hard to read in the one place where they should be easy to read, the editor/IDE. If a tool such as Javadoc extracts comments into a Web page, adding the HTML is that tool's responsibility, not the programmer's.
- **Nonlocal Information** - if you must write a comment, make sure it describes the code it appears near; never offer systemwide information in a local comment.
  - Failure mode: a setter's javadoc documenting a default port value that the function has no control over; there is no guarantee the comment is updated when the distant default changes.
- **Too Much Information** - never put historical discussions or irrelevant detail into comments; a reader of a base64 encode/decode test needs nothing beyond the RFC number, not the transcribed RFC prose about 24-bit groups and bit ordering.
- **Inobvious Connection** - the connection between a comment and the code it describes must be obvious; a reader should be able to look at both and understand what the comment is talking about. It is a pity when a comment needs its own explanation.
  - Failure example: a comment about "an extra 200 bytes for header info" plus "filter bytes" over `new byte[((width + 1) * height * 3) + 200]` leaves the reader unable to tell whether filter bytes explain the `+1`, the `*3`, both, or the 200.
- **Function Headers** - prefer a well-chosen name over a comment header for a small function that does one thing, because that name is usually the better of the two; short functions do not need much description.
- **Javadocs in Nonpublic Code** - javadocs are anathema to code not intended for public consumption; generating javadoc pages for internal classes and functions is not generally useful, and the extra formality amounts to little more than cruft and distraction.

### Worked example: GeneratePrimes to PrimeGenerator

- **Reduce comments by extracting named functions** - replace a single commented, sectioned function with small functions whose names carry what the comments said (for example `uncrossIntegersUpTo`, `crossOutMultiples`, `crossOutMultiplesOf`, `determineIterationLimit`, `notCrossed`, `putUncrossedIntegersIntoResult`, `numberOfUncrossedIntegers`); after that split the module keeps only two comments, both explanatory in nature.
- **Delete comments an extraction makes redundant** - delete the inline markers that the split obsoletes, such as `// declarations`, `// size of array`, `// initialize array to true`, `// get rid of known non-primes`, `// sieve`, `// if i is uncrossed, cross its multiples.`, `// multiple is not prime`, `// how many primes are there?`, `// bump count.`, `// if prime`, `// move the primes into the result`, `// return the primes`, `// the only valid case`, `// maxValue < 2`, and `// return null array if bad input.`; they all disappear once the code is split into well-named functions and guard clauses.
- **Strip author, version, and encyclopedia content from headers** - remove `@author`, `@version`, and encyclopedic background (such as a biography of the algorithm's namesake) from a class header; retain only a short statement of what the class generates and the algorithm's steps.
- **Keep a comment that explains a rationale no name can express** - a comment explaining why the square root of the array size is the loop limit (every multiple in the array has a prime factor less than or equal to that root) is almost certainly necessary, because no simple variable name and no different coding structure makes that point clear.
- **Question an optimization that costs readers' time** - before keeping an optimization that needs an explanatory comment, weigh its cost: a square-root iteration limit may be a conceit, because calculating the square root could take more time than it saves and it may not be worth the time and effort everyone else will expend to understand it.
- **Contradiction retained on a class-header comment that summarizes the algorithm** - both statements stand, unreconciled. Statement 1 (the general rule): delete a comment that restates the code, and it is easy to argue such a header is redundant because it reads very much like the function it summarizes. Statement 2: "Still, I think the comment serves to ease the reader into the algorithm, so I'm inclined to leave it." Condition for each: apply the deletion rule when a comment merely restates the code; keep such a header on the sole ground that it eases the reader into the algorithm.

## Clean Code: Ch5 Formatting

### The Purpose of Formatting

- **Format deliberately** - take care that code is nicely formatted; choose a set of simple rules that govern the format of your code, then apply those rules consistently.
- **Treat formatting as communication, not religion** - code formatting is too important to ignore and too important to treat religiously; communication is the professional developer's first order of business, ahead of "getting it working".
- **Optimize for readability over today's functionality** - functionality has a good chance of changing in the next release, but readability affects every change ever made; coding style and readability set precedents that continue to affect maintainability and extensibility long after the original code has been changed beyond recognition; your style and discipline survives even though your code does not.

### Vertical Formatting: File Size

- **Keep source files small** - it is possible to build significant systems (FitNesse is close to 50,000 lines) out of files that are typically 200 lines long, with an upper limit of 500. This should not be a hard and fast rule, but it should be considered very desirable. Small files are usually easier to understand than large files.
  - Calibration from seven projects (Junit, FitNesse, testNG, Time and Money, JDepend, Ant, Tomcat): FitNesse's average file is about 65 lines, about one-third of its files are between 40 and 100+ lines, its largest file is about 400 lines and its smallest is 6 lines.
  - Junit, FitNesse, and Time and Money are composed of relatively small files: none over 500 lines, most under 200 lines. Tomcat and Ant have some files several thousand lines long, and close to half are over 200 lines.
- **In Java, file size tracks class size** - treat the file-size guidance as coupled to class size.

### The Newspaper Metaphor

- **Structure a source file like a newspaper article** - read top to bottom: name, then high-level concepts, then increasing detail.
  - The name should be simple but explanatory, and by itself sufficient to tell the reader whether they are in the right module.
  - The topmost parts of the source file provide the high-level concepts and algorithms.
  - Detail increases as you move downward, until at the end you find the lowest-level functions and details.
- **Keep most modules very small** - a newspaper is composed of many articles, most very small, some a bit larger, very few as long as a full page; a single long disorganized agglomeration of facts would not be read.

### Vertical Openness Between Concepts

- **Separate each complete thought with a blank line** - nearly all code is read left to right and top to bottom: each line represents an expression or clause and each group of lines represents a complete thought; blank lines belong between the package declaration, the imports, and each function.
- **Rely on the blank line as a visual cue** - the eye is drawn to the first line following a blank line; removing blank lines has a remarkably obscuring effect and makes the code look like a muddle when you unfocus your eyes.

```java
// GOOD
package fitnesse.wikitext.widgets;

import java.util.regex.*;

public class BoldWidget extends ParentWidget {
  public static final String REGEXP = "'''.+?'''";

  public BoldWidget(ParentWidget parent, String text) throws Exception {
    ...
  }

  public String render() throws Exception {
    ...
  }
}
```

### Vertical Density

- **Keep tightly related lines vertically dense** - openness separates concepts, density implies close association; lines of code that are tightly related should appear vertically dense.
- **Do not let useless comments break vertical density** - comment blocks inserted between two instance variables break their close association and force much more eye and head motion; a class with two variables and a method should fit in an "eye-full".

```java
// BAD
public class ReporterConfig {
  /** The class name of the reporter listener */
  private String m_className;

  /** The properties of the reporter listener */
  private List m_properties = new ArrayList();

// GOOD
public class ReporterConfig {
  private String m_className;
  private List m_properties = new ArrayList();
```

### Vertical Distance

- **Keep closely related concepts vertically close [G10]** - readers should not have to hop around through source files and classes hunting for pieces, or chase up the inheritance chain for a definition.
- **Never separate closely related concepts into different files without a very good reason** - the vertical-closeness rule cannot work across files. This is one of the reasons protected variables should be avoided.
- **Scale vertical separation to mutual importance** - for concepts closely related enough to belong in the same source file, their vertical separation should measure how important each is to the understandability of the other.

#### Variable Declarations

- **Declare variables close to their usage** - declare every variable as close to its usage as possible.
- **Put local variables at the top of the function** - this works because functions are very short.
- **Declare loop control variables in the loop statement** - usually declare a loop's control variable within the loop statement itself.
- **Declare a variable at the top of a block or just before a loop only in rare cases** - the one acceptable case is a variable inside a long-ish function.
- **Declare instance variables at the top of the class** - in a well-designed class they are used by many, if not all, methods, so this does not increase their vertical distance.
  - The Java convention is top of the class; the C++ "scissors rule" put them at the bottom. Follow the top-of-class convention.
  - The important thing is that instance variables live in one well-known place that everybody knows to look at.
  - Failure mode: instance variables declared halfway down the class body (as in JUnit 4.3.1's TestSuite) can only be found by stumbling across them by accident.

#### Dependent Functions
