- **Apply the entire body of knowledge about good software design during the refactoring step** - increase cohesion, decrease coupling, separate concerns, modularize system concerns, shrink functions and classes, choose better names.
- **Apply the final three rules of simple design during refactoring** - eliminate duplication, ensure expressiveness, and minimize the number of classes and methods.

### No Duplication

- **Treat duplication as the primary enemy of a well-designed system** - it represents additional work, additional risk, and additional unnecessary complexity.
- **Recognize duplication in all its forms**
  - Lines of code that look exactly alike.
  - Lines of code that are merely similar: massage them to look even more alike so they can be more easily refactored.
  - Duplication of implementation: two methods computing overlapping facts independently.
- **Remove duplicate implementation by defining one method in terms of another**

  ```java
  // BAD - isEmpty tracks its own boolean, size tracks a counter
  // GOOD
  boolean isEmpty() { return 0 == size(); }
  ```

- **Eliminate duplication even in just a few lines of code** - creating a clean system requires the will to do this.
- **Extract the shared tail/body of near-identical methods into a private method** - example: `scaleToOneDimension` and `rotate` both ended with `image.dispose(); System.gc(); image = newImage;`; extracting `replaceImage(RenderedOp newImage)` removed the duplication and left each public method holding only its own logic.
- **Use tiny-scale extraction as a detector for SRP violations** - as you extract commonality at a very tiny level you start to recognize violations of SRP, so you may move the newly extracted method to another class, which elevates its visibility; someone else may then further abstract it and reuse it in a different context. This "reuse in the small" can cause system complexity to shrink dramatically, and understanding reuse in the small is essential to achieving reuse in the large.
- **Use the TEMPLATE METHOD pattern to remove higher-level duplication** - when two methods run largely the same algorithm and differ only in one step that varies by type, hoist the algorithm into a base-class method and leave the varying step abstract.

  ```java
  // GOOD - TEMPLATE METHOD
  abstract public class VacationPolicy {
    public void accrueVacation() {
      calculateBaseVacationHours();
      alterForLegalMinimums();
      applyToPayroll();
    }
    private void calculateBaseVacationHours() { /* ... */ }
    abstract protected void alterForLegalMinimums();
    private void applyToPayroll() { /* ... */ }
  }
  // USVacationPolicy / EUVacationPolicy override alterForLegalMinimums() only
  ```

  - The subclasses fill in the "hole" in the algorithm, supplying only the bits of information that are not duplicated.

### Expressive

- **Code should clearly express the intent of its author** - the majority of the cost of a software project is in long-term maintenance; to minimize the potential for defects as change is introduced, it is critical to be able to understand what a system does. As systems become more complex they take more time to understand and offer ever greater opportunity for misunderstanding. The clearer the author makes the code, the less time others spend understanding it, which reduces defects and shrinks maintenance cost.
- **Do not assume your own understanding transfers** - it is easy to write code you understand because at the time of writing you are deep in an understanding of the problem; other maintainers will not have that depth.
- **Express intent by choosing good names** - you should be able to hear a class or function name and not be surprised when you discover its responsibilities.
- **Express intent by keeping functions and classes small** - small classes and functions are usually easy to name, easy to write, and easy to understand.
- **Express intent by using standard nomenclature** - design patterns are largely about communication and expressiveness; using standard pattern names such as COMMAND or VISITOR in the names of the classes implementing those patterns succinctly describes your design to other developers.
- **Write expressive unit tests** - a primary goal of tests is to act as documentation by example; a reader of the tests should get a quick understanding of what a class is all about.
- **The most important way to be expressive is to try** - do not get code working and move on to the next problem without sufficient thought about making it easy for the next person to read. Spend a little time with each function and class: choose better names, split large functions into smaller functions, take care of what you created. Care is a precious resource.

### Minimal Classes and Methods

- **Keep function and class counts low** - keep the overall system small while also keeping functions and classes small; even elimination of duplication, code expressiveness, and the SRP can be taken too far, and in an effort to make classes and methods small you can create too many tiny classes and methods.
- **Resist pointless dogmatism, which is a common cause of high class and method counts** - reject rules such as a coding standard insisting on an interface for each and every class, or insistence that fields and behavior must always be separated into data classes and behavior classes. Adopt a more pragmatic approach.
- **Minimizing the number of classes and methods is the lowest priority of the four rules of Simple Design** - although keeping class and function count low is important, it is more important to have tests, eliminate duplication, and express yourself.

### Emergence: conclusion

- **Simple practices do not replace experience** - but following the practice of simple design does encourage and enable adherence to good principles and patterns that otherwise take years to learn.

## Clean Code: Ch13 Concurrency

### Why Concurrency

- **Treat concurrency as a decoupling strategy** - use it to decouple *what* gets done from *when* it gets done; in single-threaded code what and when are so strongly coupled that whole-application state can be read off a stack backtrace.
- **Expect structural change, not just throughput change** - decoupling what from when can dramatically improve both the throughput and the structure of an application; a decoupled system looks like many little collaborating computers rather than one big main loop, which can make it easier to understand and offers powerful ways to separate concerns.
- **Adopt concurrency for response-time and throughput constraints that single-threaded code cannot meet** - valid drivers include:
  - A single-threaded aggregator that hits Web sites in turn, finishing one before starting the next, whose daily run must complete in under 24 hours but grows past 24 hours as sites are added; most of that time is waiting at Web sockets for I/O.
  - A system needing only one second per user that queues users, so response time grows with user count; no user wants to get in line behind 150 others.
  - A system that can only give a complete solution after processing all data sets, where each data set can be processed on a different computer in parallel.

### Myths and Misconceptions - reject these

- **"Concurrency always improves performance" is false** - concurrency can sometimes improve performance, but only when there is a lot of wait time that can be shared between multiple threads or multiple processors, and neither situation is trivial.
- **"Design does not change when writing concurrent programs" is false** - the design of a concurrent algorithm can be remarkably different from a single-threaded design, decoupling what from when usually has a huge effect on system structure, and concurrency often requires a fundamental change in design strategy.
- **"Understanding concurrency issues is not important when working inside a container" is false** - the decoupling provided by Web/EJB containers is far less than perfect, so you had better know just what your container is doing and how to guard against concurrent update and deadlock; servlet programmers must still be very aware and very careful to make their concurrent programs correct.
- **Budget for concurrency overhead** - concurrency incurs overhead both in performance and in additional code to write.
- **Assume correct concurrency is complex even for simple problems.**

### Challenges

- **Never trust concurrent code because it looks correct** - writing clean concurrent programs is hard, very hard; it is much easier to write single-threaded code, and it is easy to write multithreaded code that looks fine on the surface but is broken at a deeper level, working fine until the system is placed under stress.
- **Treat even a one-line read-modify-write as unsafe** - `return ++lastIdUsed;` shared by two threads has three possible outcomes, including both threads getting the same value and the field advancing only once.

  ```java
  // BAD - unsafe under sharing
  public class X {
    private int lastIdUsed;
    public int getNextId() { return ++lastIdUsed; }
  }
  ```

  - With `lastIdUsed` starting at 42 and two threads calling `getNextId()`: (43, 44, field 44), (44, 43, field 44), or (43, 43, field 43).
  - The third result occurs when the two threads step on each other, because many possible paths run through that one line and some generate incorrect results.
- **Assume an enormous number of execution interleavings** - working from the generated byte-code alone there are 12,870 possible execution paths for two threads executing a `getNextId` method whose body is `return ++lastIdUsed;`; changing `lastIdUsed` from `int` to `long` raises it to 2,704,156. Most paths give valid results; the problem is that some don't.
  - To really answer how many paths there are you must understand what the Just-In-Time Compiler does with the generated byte-code and what the Java memory model considers to be atomic.

### Concurrency Defense Principles

#### Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)

- **First and foremost, follow SRP: keep your concurrency-related code separate from other code** - SRP states a given method/class/component should have a single reason to change, and concurrency design is complex enough to be a reason to change in its own right; break the system into POJOs that separate thread-aware code from thread-ignorant code.
  - Concurrency-related code has its own life cycle of development, change, and tuning.
  - Concurrency-related code has its own challenges, different from and often more difficult than nonconcurrency-related code.
  - The number of ways miswritten concurrency-based code can fail makes it challenging enough without the added burden of surrounding application code.
- **Never embed concurrency implementation details directly into other production code** - this is all too common and it violates SRP.

#### Corollary: Limit the Scope of Data

- **Take data encapsulation to heart; severely limit the access of any data that may be shared, and keep the amount of shared objects and the scope of the sharing as narrow as possible** - use `synchronized` to protect a critical section that touches a shared object, and restrict the number of such critical sections.
- **Minimize the number of places shared data can be updated** - the more places, the more likely that:
  - You will forget to protect one or more of them, effectively breaking all code that modifies that shared data.
  - There will be duplication of effort to make sure everything is guarded (a violation of DRY).
  - It will be difficult to determine the source of failures, which are already hard enough to find.

#### Corollary: Use Copies of Data

- **Avoid sharing data in the first place** - where possible copy objects and treat them as read-only, or copy objects, collect results from multiple threads into the copies, then merge the results in a single thread.
- **Do not reject copying on object-creation cost without measuring** - it is worth experimenting to find out whether cost is in fact a problem; if using copies lets the code avoid synchronizing, the savings from avoiding the intrinsic lock will likely make up for the additional creation and garbage collection overhead.

#### Corollary: Threads Should Be as Independent as Possible

- **Attempt to partition data into independent subsets that can be operated on by independent threads, possibly in different processors** - write each thread so it exists in its own world, sharing no data with any other thread.
- **Take all data for one request from an unshared source and store it in local variables** - then each thread behaves as if it were the only thread in the world with no synchronization requirements. `HttpServlet` subclasses receive all information as parameters to `doGet`/`doPost`; so long as the servlet uses only local variables there is no chance of synchronization problems.
- **Still expect shared resources** - most applications using servlets eventually run into shared resources such as database connections.

### Know Your Library

- **Review the concurrency classes available to you** - in Java, become familiar with `java.util.concurrent`, `java.util.concurrent.atomic`, and `java.util.concurrent.locks`.
- **Use the provided thread-safe collections.**
- **Use the executor framework for executing unrelated tasks.**
- **Use nonblocking solutions when possible.**
- **Remember several library classes are not thread safe.**
- **Start with `ConcurrentHashMap` if Java 5 is the deployment environment** - the collections in `java.util.concurrent` are safe for multithreaded situations and perform well; `ConcurrentHashMap` performs better than `HashMap` in nearly all situations, allows simultaneous concurrent reads and writes, and has methods supporting common composite operations that are otherwise not thread safe.

### Know Your Execution Models - definitions to use exactly

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| ReentrantLock | A lock that can be acquired in one method and released in another. |
| Semaphore | An implementation of the classic semaphore, a lock with a count. |
| CountDownLatch | A lock that waits for a number of events before releasing all threads waiting on it, so all threads get a fair chance of starting at about the same time. |
| Bound Resources | Resources of a fixed size or number used in a concurrent environment, e.g. database connections and fixed-size read/write buffers. |
| Mutual Exclusion | Only one thread can access shared data or a shared resource at a time. |
| Starvation | One thread or a group of threads is prohibited from proceeding for an excessively long time or forever, e.g. always letting fast-running threads through first starves longer-running threads if the fast ones never end. |
| Deadlock | Two or more threads waiting for each other to finish, each holding a resource the other requires, so neither can finish. |
| Livelock | Threads in lockstep, each trying to work but finding another "in the way"; due to resonance they keep trying to make progress but cannot for an excessively long time, or forever. |
| Critical section | Any section of code that must be protected from simultaneous use for the program to be correct. |

- **Learn your library and these three basic algorithms (Producer-Consumer, Readers-Writers, Dining Philosophers) and understand their solutions** - most concurrent problems you will likely encounter will be some variation of these three; study these algorithms and write solutions using them on your own, and understand how the features offered by your library support solving problems similar to them, so that when you come across concurrent problems you are more prepared to solve them.
- **Producer-Consumer** - one or more producer threads create work and place it in a buffer or queue; one or more consumer threads acquire and complete it.
  - The queue between producers and consumers is a bound resource: producers must wait for free space before writing, consumers must wait until there is something to consume.
  - Coordination is by signaling: producers write and signal that the queue is no longer empty; consumers read and signal that the queue is no longer full. Both potentially wait to be notified when they can continue.
- **Readers-Writers** - a shared resource that primarily serves readers but is occasionally updated by writers makes throughput the issue.
  - Emphasizing throughput can cause starvation and accumulation of stale information; allowing updates can impact throughput.
  - Writers tend to block many readers for a long period, causing throughput issues.
  - Making writers wait until there are no readers starves writers if there are continuous readers; giving frequent writers priority makes throughput suffer.
  - The challenge is to balance the needs of both readers and writers to satisfy correct operation, provide reasonable throughput, and avoid starvation, while avoiding concurrent update issues.
- **Dining Philosophers** - philosophers around a circular table each need the two forks beside them to eat, and must wait if a neighbor holds one; replace philosophers with threads and forks with resources. Systems whose processes compete this way can experience deadlock, livelock, throughput and efficiency degradation unless carefully designed.

### Beware Dependencies Between Synchronized Methods

- **Avoid using more than one method on a shared object** - dependencies between synchronized methods cause subtle bugs; `synchronized` protects an individual method, so if there is more than one synchronized method on the same shared class your system may be written incorrectly.
- **When you must use more than one method on a shared object, use one of exactly three fixes:**
  - **Client-Based Locking** - have the client lock the server before calling the first method and make sure the lock's extent includes the code calling the last method.
  - **Server-Based Locking** - within the server create a method that locks the server, calls all the methods, then unlocks; have the client call that new method.
  - **Adapted Server** - create an intermediary that performs the locking; this is server-based locking for the case where the original server cannot be changed.

### Keep Synchronized Sections Small

- **Keep your synchronized sections as small as possible** - all sections guarded by the same lock are guaranteed to have only one thread executing through them at a time, but locks are expensive: they create delays and add overhead, so do not litter code with `synchronized` statements.
- **Design for as few critical sections as possible, but never leave a critical section unguarded.**
- **Never enlarge a critical section to reduce the count of critical sections** - extending synchronization beyond the minimal critical section increases contention and degrades performance.

### Writing Correct Shut-Down Code Is Hard

- **Think about shut-down early and get it working early** - it is going to take longer than you expect; review existing algorithms because this is probably harder than you think.
- **Expect deadlock in shutdown paths, with threads waiting for a signal to continue that never comes** - known failure shapes:
  - A parent spawns children and waits for all to finish before releasing resources; if one child deadlocks the parent waits forever and the system never shuts down.
  - A producer/consumer child pair: the producer receives the shutdown signal and quickly shuts down, while the consumer is blocked waiting for a message from the producer and cannot receive the shutdown signal, so it never finishes and the parent never finishes either.
- **Budget much of your time for getting graceful shutdown correct** - a system meant to stay live forever is different from one that shuts down gracefully, and these situations are not at all uncommon.

### Testing Threaded Code

- **Write tests that have the potential to expose problems and run them frequently, with different programmatic configurations, system configurations, and load** - proving code correct is impractical and testing does not guarantee correctness, but good testing can minimize risk.
- **If tests ever fail, track down the failure; never ignore a failure just because the tests pass on a subsequent run.**
- **Treat spurious failures as candidate threading issues** - threaded code causes things to fail that "simply cannot fail"; concurrency bugs usually aren't repeatable and may exhibit symptoms once in a thousand, or a million, executions, so they are often ignored as one-offs instead of the true defects they are.
  - Never write a concurrency bug off as a one-off. Do not ignore system failures as one-offs. Assume one-offs do not exist. The longer they are ignored, the more code is built on top of a potentially faulty approach.
  - Issues that do not crop up early get written off as a one-time occurrence, and these so-called one-offs typically only happen under load or at seemingly random times.
- **Get your nonthreaded code working first** - make sure code works outside its use in threads, generally by creating POJOs called by your threads that are not thread aware and can be tested outside the threaded environment. Place as much of the system in such POJOs as possible.
  - Do not try to chase down nonthreading bugs and threading bugs at the same time.
- **Make your threaded code pluggable** - write concurrency-supporting code so it can run in several configurations:
  - One thread, several threads, and a count varied as it executes.
  - Threaded code interacting with something that can be either real or a test double.
  - Execution with test doubles that run quickly, slowly, and variably.
  - Tests configurable to run for a number of iterations.
- **Make your threaded code tunable** - getting the right balance of threads typically requires trial and error, so find ways early to time performance under different configurations and allow the thread count to be easily tuned. Consider allowing it to change while the system is running, and consider self-tuning based on throughput and system utilization.
- **Run with more threads than processors or cores** - do this to encourage task swapping; the more frequently your tasks swap, the more likely you will encounter code that is missing a critical section or causes deadlock.
- **Run your threaded code on all target platforms early and often, in many configurations, repeatedly and continuously** - different operating systems have different threading policies and multithreaded code behaves differently in different environments; run your tests in every potential deployment environment.
  - Observed case: tests written to demonstrate failure conditions, developed under OS X and presented on Windows XP under a VM, did not fail as frequently on XP even though the code under test was known to be incorrect in all cases.
  - The Java threading model does not guarantee preemptive threading; modern OSes support it so you get it "for free", but the JVM does not guarantee it.

#### Instrument Your Code to Try and Force Failures

- **Assume flaws in concurrent code hide** - simple tests often do not expose them, they hide during normal processing, and may show up once every few hours, days, or weeks. Only a very few of the many thousands of possible pathways through a vulnerable section actually fail, so the probability of taking a failing pathway can be startlingly low, making detection and debugging very difficult.
- **Force different orderings by instrumenting the code** - add calls to `Object.wait()`, `Object.sleep()`, `Object.yield()`, and `Object.priority()`; each affects execution order and increases the odds of detecting a flaw. It is better when broken code fails as early and as often as possible.
- **Never blame the instrumentation for a new failure** - if the code breaks after you add a call to `yield()`, the code was already broken and the call merely made the failure evident. (Strictly, because the JVM does not guarantee preemptive threading, a particular algorithm might always work on an OS that does not preempt threads, and the reverse is also possible for different reasons.)
- **Invest in instrumentation early, by hand or by automated technology** - the two instrumentation options are hand-coded and automated, and taking the time to instrument greatly improves your chances of finding erroneous code.
- **Hand-coded: insert `wait()`, `sleep()`, `yield()`, `priority()` calls by hand** - appropriate when testing a particularly thorny piece of code.

  ```java
  public synchronized String nextUrlOrNull() {
    if (hasNext()) {
      String url = urlGenerator.next();
      Thread.yield(); // inserted for testing
      updateHasNext();
      return url;
    }
    return null;
  }
  ```

  - Problems with the hand-coded approach: you must manually find appropriate places; you do not know where to put the call or which kind of call to use; leaving such code in production unnecessarily slows the code down; it is a shotgun approach that may or may not find flaws, and indeed the odds aren't with you.
  - Require instrumentation that runs during testing but not in production, and that lets you easily mix up configurations between runs to increase the chances of finding errors in the aggregate; hand-coded instrumentation does not meet this requirement.
- **Divide the system into POJOs that know nothing of threading plus classes that control threading** - this makes it easier to find appropriate places to instrument, and lets you create many different test jigs that invoke the POJOs under different regimes of `sleep`, `yield`, and so on.
- **Automated: instrument programmatically with an Aspect-Oriented Framework, CGLIB, or ASM** - use jiggling strategies to ferret out errors.

  ```java
  public class ThreadJigglePoint {
    public static void jiggle() { }
  }
  ```

  - Call `ThreadJigglePoint.jiggle()` at various places in the code, then use a simple aspect that randomly selects among doing nothing, sleeping, or yielding.
  - Or give `ThreadJigglePoint` two implementations: one whose `jiggle` does nothing, used in production; one that generates a random number to choose between sleeping, yielding, or just falling through.
  - Run the tests a thousand times with random jiggling; you may root out some flaws, and if the tests pass you can at least say you have done due diligence. Though a bit simplistic, this is a reasonable option in lieu of a more sophisticated tool.
  - `ConTest` (IBM) does something similar with quite a bit more sophistication.
  - The point is to jiggle the code so threads run in different orderings at different times; well-written tests plus jiggling dramatically increase the chance of finding errors.

### Conclusion - rules to apply whenever writing concurrent code

- **Write clean concurrent code with rigor or else face subtle and infrequent failures** - code that is simple to follow can become nightmarish when multiple threads and shared data get into the mix.
- **Keep thread-aware code small and focused, and when testing it, test only it and nothing else.**
- **Know the possible sources of concurrency issues** - multiple threads operating on shared data, or using a common resource pool. Boundary cases such as shutting down cleanly or finishing the iteration of a loop can be especially thorny.
- **Learn how to find regions of code that must be locked and lock them; do not lock regions that do not need to be locked** - this requires a deep understanding of whether something is or is not shared.
- **Avoid calling one locked section from another.**
- **Change the design of objects with shared data to accommodate clients rather than forcing clients to manage shared state.**
- **Rely on testability from the Three Laws of TDD to get plug-ability** - testability implies some level of plug-ability, which provides the support needed to run code in a wider range of configurations.
- **Run thread-based code as long as possible before putting it into production.**

## Clean Code: Ch14 Successive Refinement (Args worked example)

### Target design: the Args utility

- **Constructor parses, accessors query** - construct with a schema/format string plus the raw `String[] args`; if the constructor returns without throwing, the command line was parsed and the instance is ready to be queried. Never require callers to run a separate parse step or check a validity flag.
- **Typed accessors by name** - expose `getBoolean(char)`, `getString(char)`, `getInt(char)`, `getDouble(char)`, `getStringArray(char)`, `has(char)`, `cardinality()` (count of arguments found), `usage()` (`"-[" + schema + "]"`, or `""` for an empty schema), and `nextArgument()` (index of the first non-flag argument); each getter returns the argument's true type, keyed by its name.
- **Stop parsing at the first non-flag argument** - while iterating the argument list, parse a token only if it starts with `-`; on the first token that does not, push the iterator back one position and break, so the caller can pick up the remainder from `nextArgument()`.
- **One exception type from the module** - report every problem, whether in the format string or in the command-line arguments, by throwing the module's own single exception (`ArgsException`), and expose a human-readable description through `errorMessage()`.
- **Schema element encoding** - a schema is comma-separated elements; the leading char is the argument id, the tail selects the marshaler:

| Schema tail | Type | Marshaler |
|---|---|---|
| (empty) | boolean | `BooleanArgumentMarshaler` |
| `*` | String | `StringArgumentMarshaler` |
| `#` | integer | `IntegerArgumentMarshaler` |
| `##` | double | `DoubleArgumentMarshaler` |
| `[*]` | String array | `StringArrayArgumentMarshaler` |
| anything else | error | throw `INVALID_ARGUMENT_FORMAT` |

- **Validate the argument id** - if the element id is not `Character.isLetter`, throw `INVALID_ARGUMENT_NAME`.
- **Error codes are an enum on the exception** - `OK, INVALID_ARGUMENT_FORMAT, UNEXPECTED_ARGUMENT, INVALID_ARGUMENT_NAME, MISSING_STRING, MISSING_INTEGER, INVALID_INTEGER, MISSING_DOUBLE, INVALID_DOUBLE`, with one message format per code:

| ErrorCode | Message |
|---|---|
| `UNEXPECTED_ARGUMENT` | `Argument -%c unexpected.` |
| `MISSING_STRING` | `Could not find string parameter for -%c.` |
| `INVALID_INTEGER` | `Argument -%c expects an integer but was '%s'.` |
| `MISSING_INTEGER` | `Could not find integer parameter for -%c.` |
| `INVALID_DOUBLE` | `Argument -%c expects a double but was '%s'.` |
| `MISSING_DOUBLE` | `Could not find double parameter for -%c.` |
| `INVALID_ARGUMENT_NAME` | `'%c' is not a valid argument name.` |
| `INVALID_ARGUMENT_FORMAT` | `'%s' is not a valid argument format.` |
| `OK` | `TILT: Should not get here.` |

- **Unknown argument character is an error** - if no marshaler is registered for the character, throw `UNEXPECTED_ARGUMENT` carrying that character; otherwise record the character in `argsFound` and delegate to the marshaler.
- **Attach the failing argument id at the boundary** - when a marshaler's `set` throws, catch it, call `e.setErrorArgumentId(argChar)`, and rethrow, so the low-level marshaler need not know the argument name.

### Properties of the finished code that must be emulated

- **Readable top to bottom** - structure the module so it reads from top to bottom without a lot of jumping around or looking ahead; the only thing a reader must look ahead for is the definition of the central abstraction (`ArgumentMarshaler`), deliberately left out of the class.
- **Each new derivative replicates one pattern** - once one marshaler derivative exists, write each remaining derivative (double, String array) by simply replicating that same pattern.
- **Pay explicit attention to three things** - when you re-read code you have just written, pay explicit attention to the way things are named, the size of the functions, and the formatting of the code.
- **New variants must be trivial to add** - it must be obvious how to add a new argument type, and the addition must require only: a new `ArgumentMarshaler` derivative, a new `getXXX` function, a new case in `parseSchemaElement`, and probably a new `ErrorCode` plus error message. If adding a variant costs more, the structure is wrong.
- **Bury type-specific failures in the derivative** - keep `NumberFormatException` and its kin inside `IntegerArgumentMarshaler`/`DoubleArgumentMarshaler`; do not let them surface in the parsing algorithm.
- **Marshaler interface stays minimal** - keep the abstraction down to `void set(Iterator currentArgument) throws ArgsException;` and, where a typed getter is used, give each derivative a static `getValue(ArgumentMarshaler am)` that null-checks, `instanceof`-checks, and returns the type's default (`false`, `""`, `0`) otherwise.
- **Static typing costs words** - expect a remarkable amount of code to flesh out even a simple concept in a statically typed language like Java, because the type system requires a lot of words; the same program in Ruby, Python, or Smalltalk is much smaller. A Ruby rewrite of this argument-parsing module was 1/7th the size and had a subtly better structure.

### Successive refinement: the core discipline

- **Write dirty, then clean it** - programming is a craft more than a science: to write clean code you must first write dirty code and then clean it. Do not expect to write clean and elegant programs in one pass; treat the first version as a rough draft and produce successive drafts until the structure is right.
- **Never ship the draft** - it is not enough for code to work, because code that works is often badly broken. Do not treat "it works" as done and move on, leaving the working program in whatever state it happened to reach. Programmers who satisfy themselves with merely working code are behaving unprofessionally; that is professional suicide, and it is exactly how others will judge code you leave in rough-draft form.

### Detecting a rough draft

- **Daunting instance-variable count** - a long list of instance variables at the top of the class (`schema`, `args`, `valid`, `unexpectedArguments`, three type-keyed maps, `argsFound`, `currentArgument`, `errorArgumentId`, `errorParameter`, `errorCode`) is a primary indicator of a festering pile.
- **Odd magic strings** - sentinel strings like `"TILT"` used as an initial value are a smell.
- **Parallel type-keyed maps** - one `HashMap` per supported type (`booleanArgs`, `stringArgs`, `intArgs`) plus `HashSet`/`TreeSet` bookkeeping is duplication that grows linearly with each new type.
- **try-catch-catch blocks that set flags** - `catch` blocks that assign `valid = false`, `errorArgumentId`, `errorParameter`, and `errorCode` before throwing a bare exception scatter error state across the class.
- **Null-defaulting helpers are temporary scaffolding** - private `falseIfNull`, `zeroIfNull`, `blankIfNull` helpers exist only to paper over null map lookups; once the null check moves to the abstraction they are irrelevant and useless, and must be deleted rather than kept.
- **Validity flag plus swallowed exception** - treat a `valid` field with an `isValid()` query, together with a `parse()` that catches and discards the module's own `ArgsException`, as a smell; keep neither, because the constructor must either throw or leave an instance ready to be queried.
- **Good names and crude structure are not enough** - reasonable function and variable names plus a crude structure can still be a mess; do not let them reassure you.
- **Watch the growth rate, not the current state** - a first version can be compact, simple, and easy to understand and still contain the seeds of a festering pile: a Boolean-only argument parser read cleanly, yet adding just two argument types (String and integer) had a massively negative impact, converting reasonably maintainable code into code expected to become riddled with bugs and warts. Judge a structure by what the next two features will do to it.
  - The two types went in one at a time. After String the code was "starting to get out of hand", still not horrible, a pile but not festering yet. It took the third type, integer, to get the pile really fermenting and festering. Do not read "still not horrible" as permission to add the next one.

### When to stop adding features

- **Stop when the next features would leave an unfixable mess** - when at least two more variants are still to be added and you know they would make things much worse, stop adding features and start refactoring; bulldozing forward would probably get them working but leave behind a mess too large to fix. If the structure is ever going to be maintainable, now is the time to fix it.
- **Find the repeated change sites** - diagnose the mess by naming the places every new variant must touch. In an argument parser each argument type required new code in three major places: (1) parsing its schema element to select the map for that type, (2) parsing the command-line strings and converting to its true type, (3) a `getXXX` method to return it as its true type.
- **Many types with similar methods means a class** - when several types all need the same set of methods, extract an abstraction (for an argument parser, `ArgumentMarshaler`) rather than adding another branch per type.

### On incrementalism

- **Never make massive structural changes at once** - one of the best ways to ruin a program is to make massive changes to its structure in the name of improvement; some programs never recover, because it is very hard to get the program working the same way it worked before the "improvement".
- **Keep the system running at all times** - under TDD you are not allowed to make a change that breaks the system; every change must keep the system working as it worked before.
- **Require a runnable regression suite first** - you need a suite of automated tests you can run on a whim that verifies the behavior of the system is unchanged. Build unit tests (JUnit) and acceptance tests (FitNesse wiki pages) while writing the draft, so the refactoring is possible later.
- **Many very tiny changes** - proceed by a large number of very tiny changes, each moving the structure toward the target concept and each keeping the system working. The full separation of the marshaler abstraction took about 30 tiny steps with tests passing between each; one sub-goal alone took ten steps, passing all tests after each.
- **Start with a change that cannot break anything** - add the skeleton of the new abstraction at the end of the existing pile first, then make the simplest modification that would break as little as possible.
- **Fix a broken test before the next change** - when a test breaks, get it passing again before continuing. Incrementalism demands you get it working quickly before making any other changes.
- **Unchanged failures are evidence of no new damage** - after removing code you believe is now useless, if the tests still fail in exactly the same way, you can be confident you have not introduced new errors.
- **Refactoring moves things back and forth** - putting things in so you can take them out again is common in refactoring; the smallness of the steps plus the need to keep tests running means you move things around a lot. Refactoring is like solving a Rubik's cube: lots of little steps to achieve a large goal, each step enabling the next.
- **Run every suite, not your favorite one** - run all suites after each change, not only the one you habitually run: a `ClassCastException` case was missed because the FitNesse acceptance tests asserted that `getBoolean` on a non-boolean argument returns `false` while the unit tests did not, and only the unit tests were being run. Add a unit test that invokes all the acceptance tests so this class of surprise cannot recur.
- **Expect the first refactoring pass to disappoint** - after a full pass the structure may be only a bit better: all the instance variables still at the top, a horrible type-case still in the dispatch function, the set functions still really ugly, and the error processing untouched. Keep going; do not read a partial improvement as done.

### Refactoring mechanics: migrating to the marshaler abstraction

1. Append the skeleton of the new abstraction (base class plus one empty derivative per existing type) to the existing file.
2. Change one type's map to hold the abstraction, and fix the statements that break. Expect the breakage to be exactly in the three known places: the parse, the set, and the get for that type.
3. Repair the resulting null path where the value used to be null-defaulted: delete the now-irrelevant `falseIfNull`-style helper, hoist the marshaler into a local variable, and null-check the marshaler instead of the value.
4. Repeat step 2-3 for each remaining type, one type at a time, putting all marshalling implementation in the base class first.
5. Once all marshalling behavior is in the base class, push behavior down into the derivatives one member at a time. This is what allows the program's shape to change gradually while everything keeps running.
6. Deploy `set` first: add an `abstract set` to the base, implement it in one derivative, replace the call site, run tests, then delete the superseded base method.
7. Deploy `get` next. Deploying `get` functions is always ugly because the return type has to be `Object` and the caller must cast. To keep compiling, first add a concrete `get()` returning `null` to the base, then make it abstract and implement it in the derivative.
8. When both `set` and `get` are deployed to a derivative, delete the old typed accessor from the base, move the value field down into the derivative, and make it private.
9. Do the integer/double types last: they are more complicated because parsing can throw, but the result is better because the parse exception ends up buried in the derivative.
10. Replace the parallel type maps with one generic map: do not delete the old maps, add the new map, then change methods one by one to use it. Delete each old map only when its last use is gone.
11. Replace `containsKey` type tests with `instanceof` tests on the marshaler from the generic map, then hoist the repeated `marshalers.get` into a single local, then inline the now-trivial `isXxxArg` predicates because there is no good reason left for them.
12. Inline any function the migration has hollowed out. The three `parseXxxSchemaElement` methods were inlined into `parseSchemaElement` because they did not do much anymore.
13. Pull the scattered error-flag assignments up into the single dispatch function (`setArgument`) so the branch chain contains no error handling.
14. Turn the abstract base into an interface once it declares only `set` and `get` and holds no fields.

- **Placeholder parameters are acceptable when the sibling needs them** - give the abstract `set` a parameter that one derivative ignores when the other derivatives will use it and you intend to deploy all implementations through a single abstract method.
- **Get the error condition out of an if-else chain before deleting the chain** - you cannot eliminate the chain while it also carries error handling.

### Eliminating the type-case

- **Remove type-case switches [G23]** - a chain of `instanceof` tests dispatching to type-specific setters must be replaced by a single polymorphic call.

```java
// BAD - type-case in the dispatcher
if (m instanceof BooleanArgumentMarshaler) setBooleanArg(m);
else if (m instanceof StringArgumentMarshaler) setStringArg(m);
else if (m instanceof IntegerArgumentMarshaler) setIntArg(m);
else return false;

// GOOD
try { m.set(currentArgument); return true; }
catch (ArgsException e) { e.setErrorArgumentId(argChar); throw e; }
```

- **Do not add arguments to enable a move [F1]** - never widen a function's parameter list just to make it movable into a derivative: moving `setIntArg` down would have required passing both `args` and `currentArg` as function arguments, which is dirty. Prefer passing one argument instead of two: convert the array to a `List` and pass an `Iterator` down to the `set` functions.
- **Restore compilation with empty stubs when adding an abstract method** - adding `abstract void set(Iterator currentArgument)` to the base breaks every derivative at once; give each derivative an empty implementation immediately, keep the old abstract method alongside it, then move the real bodies in and switch the call sites one derivative at a time.
- **Shorten redundant local names [N5]** - shorten a local whose name merely repeats its type (`argumentMarshaller` is badly redundant and clutters the function) to a short form such as `am` when the scope is small and the type is obvious.
- **Delete crufty leftovers** - after the polymorphic `set(Iterator)` exists, delete the now-empty `set(String)` overloads and any other functions the migration made vestigial.

### Adding a new type after the refactoring

1. Write the failing test for the new type first (`testSimpleDoublePresent`), asserting the parsed value, `cardinality()`, and `has()`; compare doubles with an explicit tolerance (`assertEquals(42.3, args.getDouble('x'), .001)`).
2. Clean up the schema parsing code and add detection of the new tail (`##`).
3. Write the new derivative (`DoubleArgumentMarshaler`) implementing the interface.
4. Add the new `ErrorCode` values it forces.
5. Add the new `getXXX` accessor.
6. Add a test for the invalid-value error path (`testInvalidDouble`) and the message it must produce.
7. Add a test for the missing-value error path (`testMissingDouble`).

- **Write the completeness test even when it already passes** - write the test even when you expect it to pass on the first run, as `testMissingDouble` did, simply for completeness. Do not skip a case just because the code already handles it.
- **Test each error code's message directly** - keep a separate test per `ErrorCode` asserting the exact `errorMessage()` string, including the error argument id and error parameter.
- **Test the schema-level failures too** - cover empty schema with no arguments (`cardinality()` is 0), empty schema with one argument, empty schema with multiple unexpected arguments (the reported error argument id is the first one), a non-letter schema name (`"*"`), an invalid argument format (`"f~"`), spaces in the format (`"x, y"` with `-xy` yields cardinality 2), and present/missing/invalid for every type.
- **Assert the code, the id and the parameter, not just the throw** - in each failure test call `fail()` after the constructor, then in the catch assert `getErrorCode()`, `getErrorArgumentId()`, and, where the value caused the failure, `getErrorParameter()`.

### Separating the exception module

- **Move error machinery out of the working class** - ugly exception code that does not belong in the class should be merged into a single exception class in its own module. Do this and the only exception thrown by the module is its own.
- **Do not throw exceptions that do not belong to you** - stop throwing a borrowed exception type (`java.text.ParseException`) from your module's API.
- **A new module attracts the related cruft** - moving the exception into its own module provides a natural and obvious place for the miscellaneous error-support code, and pulling that code out is what keeps cleaning the original module going forward.
- **Expect deletions to dominate** - in a successful refactoring the majority of the changes to the original class are deletions; code moves out to the new modules, and each derivative moves into its own file.
- **Partitioning is most of good design** - much of good software design is simply about partitioning: creating appropriate places to put different kinds of code. This separation of concerns makes code much simpler to understand and maintain.
- **SRP on error formatting** - keep error message formatting out of the working class: putting it into an `Args`-style argument processor is clearly a violation of the SRP, because that class should be about the processing of arguments, not about the format of the error messages.
  - Caveat: putting the formatting into `ArgsException` is frankly a compromise. Users who do not like the supplied messages will have to write their own, but the convenience of having canned error messages already prepared is not insignificant.

### Conclusion

- **Bad code is the worst project risk** - nothing has a more profound and long-term degrading effect upon a development project than bad code. Bad schedules can be redone, bad requirements can be redefined, bad team dynamics can be repaired, but bad code rots and ferments into an inexorable weight that drags the team down.
- **Cleanup cost grows with rot** - bad code can be cleaned up, but it is very expensive: as code rots the modules insinuate themselves into each other, creating hidden and tangled dependencies, and finding and breaking old dependencies is a long and arduous task.
- **Clean immediately** - a mess made this morning is easy to clean up this afternoon; a mess made five minutes ago is very easy to clean up right now. Continuously keep code as clean and simple as it can be, and never let the rot get started.

## Clean Code: Ch15 JUnit Internals + Ch16 Refactoring SerialDate

### Baseline obligations for any module you touch

- **Boy Scout Rule** - leave every module cleaner than you found it, even when the original authors did an excellent job. No module is immune from improvement, and each of us has the responsibility to leave the code a little better than we found it.
- **Work from tests, not from claims of quality** - before critiquing or changing a module, read its test cases; they define the requirements of the module in depth better than prose explanation does. While reading them, critique the structure of the tests themselves: could they be simpler or more obvious?
- **Measure coverage with a tool before refactoring [T2]** - run a code coverage analysis and read the number rather than trusting a passing suite; Clover reported only 91 of 185 executable statements (~50 percent) executed for one suite whose tests all passed, a coverage map like a patchwork quilt of unexecuted gobs of code. 100 percent covered (every line, every `if` statement, every `for` loop executed) is what justifies confidence that the code works and that your refactoring is safe.
- **Never accept unexplainable names** - reject cryptic member and local names (`ctxt`, `s1`, `s2`, `pfx`, `sfx`) and reject a version that inlines all loops into one function; the target is code that is nicely partitioned, reasonably expressive, and simple in structure.

### ComparisonCompactor refactoring, in order applied

1. **Delete scope-encoding prefixes on member variables [N6]** - remove the `f` prefix (`fExpected` -> `expected`). Today's environments make this kind of scope encoding redundant.
2. **Encapsulate an unencapsulated conditional [G28]** - extract a predicate whose name explains the condition, so intent is clear.
   ```java
   // BAD
   if (expected == null || actual == null || areStringsEqual())
   // GOOD
   if (shouldNotCompact())
   ```
3. **Never give a local variable the same name as a member variable [N4]** - `this.expected` / `this.actual` notation is a symptom; the locals represent something else, so name them unambiguously (`compactExpected`, `compactActual`).
4. **Prefer positives to negatives [G29]** - negatives are slightly harder to understand than positives; invert the sense of the conditional (`shouldNotCompact` -> `canBeCompacted`).
5. **Rename a function that hides a side effect [N7]** - `compact` might not compact (the error check can short-circuit it) and it returns a formatted message rather than just the compacted strings, so the honest name is `formatCompactedComparison`. Check that the name reads well together with the argument list.
6. **One responsibility per function name [G30]** - the `format...` function must do all the formatting and the `compact...` function must do nothing but compacting. Split accordingly; extract `compactExpectedAndActual`.
   - Accept that this promoted `compactExpected` and `compactActual` to member variables.
7. **Use consistent conventions inside one function [G11]** - do not mix lines that return values with lines that mutate hidden state; make `findCommonPrefix` / `findCommonSuffix` return their values so all four lines read the same way.
8. **Name variables accurately [N1]** - rename members to say what they are (they are indices: `prefixIndex`, `suffixIndex`).
9. **Expose hidden temporal coupling [G31]** - `findCommonSuffix` depends on `prefixIndex` having been computed by `findCommonPrefix`; calling them out of order means a difficult debugging session. First attempt: pass `prefixIndex` in as an argument.
10. **Do not enforce ordering with an arbitrary argument [G32]** - a passed-in `prefixIndex` establishes the ordering but does nothing to explain the need for it, so another programmer may undo it. Better: rename `findCommonSuffix` to `findCommonPrefixAndSuffix` and have it call `findCommonPrefix` before doing anything else. That establishes the temporal nature far more dramatically.
11. **Clean the newly ugly function immediately** - when a rename or merge leaves a function ugly, extract from it in the same pass; here `charFromEnd(String s, int i)` and `suffixOverlapsPrefix(int suffixLength)` came out of `findCommonPrefixAndSuffix`.
12. **Make lengths zero based to kill scattered `+1`s [G33]** - `suffixIndex` was really a suffix length but 1 based, which is why `computeCommonSuffix` was full of `+1`s. Convert to a true zero-based `suffixLength`; the `+1`s become a single `-1` inside `charFromEnd`, and two `<=` operators inside `suffixOverlapsPrefix`, where each makes perfect sense. Renaming `suffixIndex` to `suffixLength` greatly enhances readability.
    - "index" and "length" are synonymous for the prefix, but use "length" for consistency.
13. **Treat "the fix makes an old operator wrong" as a bug signal** - when a change of basis says you should flip an existing operator (zero-basing forced `if (suffixLength > 0)` toward `>=`) and the flipped form makes no sense while the original form only now makes sense, stop and analyze, because the original was probably a bug. Here it turned out to be not quite a bug: after the change the `if` prevents a zero length suffix from being appended, whereas before the change it was nonfunctional because `suffixIndex` could never be less than one.
14. **Delete conditionals you can prove extraneous, then simplify [G9]** - when a guard looks as though it can never change the result, comment it out and run the tests; if they pass, remove it and let the function simply compose its fragments. Both `if`s in `compactString` went this way.
    ```java
    // GOOD
    private String compactString(String source) {
      return computeCommonPrefix() + DELTA_START +
        source.substring(prefixLength, source.length() - suffixLength) +
        DELTA_END + computeCommonSuffix();
    }
    ```
15. **Compose from named fragment functions** - build the result by appending named fragments to a `StringBuilder`, each fragment a one-expression private method; the final `compact` appends `startingEllipsis()`, `startingContext()`, `DELTA_START`, `delta(s)`, `DELTA_END`, `endingContext()`, `endingEllipsis()`.
16. **Separate analysis functions from synthesis functions** - put all analysis functions first and all synthesis functions last, topologically sorted so the definition of each function appears just after it is used.

- **Expect to reverse your own earlier refactorings** - the final version inlined several previously extracted methods back into `formatCompactedComparison` and re-inverted the `shouldNotBeCompacted` expression. This is typical: often one refactoring leads to another that leads to the undoing of the first. Refactoring is an iterative process full of trial and error, inevitably converging on something worthy of a professional.

### Order of work

- **First make it work, then make it right** - get full test coverage and fix behavior first; only then restructure.
- **Walk the class from top to bottom** - improve it in declaration order as you go, then make one more pass over the whole class to see how well it flows.
- **Run the whole suite after every single change** - run all of the surrounding project's unit tests, not just the class's own tests, after each change.
- **Review other people's code as a professional act** - critique is not malice or arrogance; it is how we learn, and we should welcome it when done for us.

### First, Make It Work: tests and bug hunting

- **Passing tests do not mean tested [T1]** - do not conclude a class is tested because its suite passes; run a "Find Usages" search on each method, because a method nothing calls (`monthCodeToQuarter` [F4]) is never tested.
- **You cannot refactor what you cannot cover** - to completely understand and refactor a class, first write your own suite of completely independent unit tests. The new suite reached 170 of 185 executable statements (92 percent) even with some tests commented out.
- **Commit intended behavior as commented-out tests** - tests that fail because they describe behavior the class should have stay in the file, commented out, and are made to pass as refactoring proceeds.
- **Write tests for obvious behavior [G2]** - if behavior seems obvious (a code-to-string lookup should not be case sensitive), test it even if the program was not designed for it. Writing such tests is trivial [T3]; here making them pass was just switching two comparisons to `equalsIgnoreCase`.
- **Leave a test commented out when the requirement itself is genuinely unclear** - the "tues" and "thurs" abbreviation tests stayed commented out because it is not clear those abbreviations ought to be supported.
- **Wrong answers are wrong however small [G3],[T1]** - `getFollowingDayOfWeek` returned December 25th, 2004 as the Saturday following December 25th, 2004 (the answer is January 1st, 2005).
- **Suspect boundary conditions first [T5]** - when a "next" or "following" query answers with its own starting value, check the comparison operators before anything else; the `getFollowingDayOfWeek` defect was a typical boundary condition error, repaired by one comparison operator:
  ```java
  // GOOD
  if (baseDOW >= targetWeekday) {
  ```
- **Read the change history for bug clusters [T6]** - the history showed earlier "bug" fixes in `getPreviousDayOfWeek`, `getFollowingDayOfWeek`, and `getNearestDayOfWeek`; those are exactly the functions still broken. Add many more test cases wherever initial cases fail.
- **Read the pattern of failures, not just the count [T7]** - inspect which cases you had to comment out, because that pattern is revealing: all failures were "nearest day is in the future", pointing again at a boundary condition error [T5].
- **Read the pattern of coverage as evidence [T8]** - a line that never executes proves its guarding `if` is always false. Here `adjust` was always negative so it could never be `>= 4`; the algorithm was simply wrong. Replacement:
  ```java
  int delta = targetDOW - base.getDayOfWeek();
  int positiveDelta = delta + 7;
  int adjust = positiveDelta % 7;
  if (adjust > 3)
    adjust -= 7;
  return SerialDate.addDays(adjust, base);
  ```
- **Throw, do not return error strings** - signal a bad argument by throwing `IllegalArgumentException` instead of returning an error string; `weekInMonthToString` and `relativeToString` were made correct this way.

### Then Make It Right: comments and imports

- **Delete change-history comments [C1]** - source code control tools do this for us now; a change log in the source is a leftover from the 1960s. Copyrights and license text must stay for legal reasons.
- **Shorten long import lists with wildcard imports [J1]** - e.g. `java.text.*` and `java.util.*`.
- **Do not mix languages in one source file [G1]** - a Javadoc containing Java, English, Javadoc, and html is four languages; with that many in use it is hard to keep things straight, and the source's visible layout is lost when Javadoc is generated. Prefer wrapping the whole comment as preformatted so the formatting apparent in the source is preserved in the Javadoc.
- **Delete redundant comments [C2]** - redundant comments are just places to collect lies and misinformation.
- **Delete comments whose names already say it [C3]** - delete a comment that adds nothing over the name of the thing it documents, such as a comment describing a constant table whose name is already sufficient.
- **Delete Javadocs that do not add to the method signature [C3],[G12]** - they are clutter; and after a signature change (returning an enum, throwing `IllegalArgumentException` instead of returning `-1`) such a comment is actually wrong [C2].
- **Fix or shorten an out-of-date opening comment [C2]** - do not leave a class comment that is long out of date.
- **Delete repeated explanatory comments** - repetition in comments is not necessary.

### Then Make It Right: naming and abstraction level

- **Names must be descriptive of the concept, not of a marketing term [N1]** - "serial number" has more to do with product identification markers than dates; the value is a relative offset, so "ordinal" is the descriptive term.
- **A class name must not imply an implementation [N2]** - `SerialDate` is an abstract class; there is no need to imply anything about the implementation, and good reason to hide it. That name is at the wrong level of abstraction. `Date` is the honest name, but too many library classes are called `Date` and `Day` is also heavily used, so `DayDate` was the compromise.
- **Rename to remove ambiguity about mutation [N4],[G20]** - `date.addDays(7)` deceives the reader into thinking the object changed; `oldDate.plusDays(5)` used as `DayDate date = oldDate.plusDays(5);` reads as returning a new instance, and the bare statement `date.plusDays(5);` does not read fluidly enough to be accepted as a mutation. Use `plusDays` / `plusMonths`, not `addDays` / `addMonths`.
- **Prefer established mathematical nomenclature [N3]** - `INCLUDE_NONE`, `INCLUDE_FIRST`, `INCLUDE_SECOND`, `INCLUDE_BOTH` became a `DateInterval` enum with `CLOSED`, `CLOSED_LEFT`, `CLOSED_RIGHT`, `OPEN`, matching "open interval", "half-open interval", "closed interval".
- **Rename until the name communicates what is returned [N1]** - `compare` actually returns the difference in days since the argument, so it became `daysSince`; `toSerial` became `toOrdinal` and finally `getOrdinalDay`; `getYYY` became `getYear`; `createInstance` became `makeDate`; `Month.make` became `Month.fromInt` (applied to all enums); `getMonths` was renamed to be more self-descriptive.
- **Accept that chosen names may be debated** - the point of converting constants to enums is that the names and types are now easy to change [J3]: values are passed as symbols instead of integers, an IDE rename covers every use, and no stray `-1` or `2` or poorly described `int` argument can be missed.

### Then Make It Right: constants, enums, and Java-specific rules

- **Never inherit from a class just to get its constants [J2]** - inheriting from a constants class to avoid writing `MonthConstants.January` is an old Java trick and a bad idea; the constants should be an enum.
- **Turn related integer constants into enums [J3]** - month constants, day constants, week-in-month constants, interval constants, and search-direction constants all become enums with a private index, a `fromInt`, a `toInt()` accessor, and behavior methods.
  - `Month` with `JANUARY(1)` .. `DECEMBER(12)`, a `fromInt` that throws `IllegalArgumentException("Invalid month index " + monthIndex)`, plus `quarter()` returning `1 + (index-1)/3`, `toString()` and `toShortString()` off `DateFormatSymbols`, a private `matches(String)` that compares case-insensitively against both, and a `parse(String)` that trims, tries `matches`, then falls back to parsing an int, then throws `IllegalArgumentException("Invalid month " + s)`.
  - `Day` with `MONDAY(Calendar.MONDAY)` .. `SUNDAY(Calendar.SUNDAY)`, plus `make`, `toString` returning the weekday name, and a `parse(String)` that trims and compares case-insensitively against both the short and the long weekday names before throwing `IllegalArgumentException`.
  - `WeekInMonth` with `FIRST(1), SECOND(2), THIRD(3), FOURTH(4), LAST(0)`.
  - `WeekdayRange` with `LAST`, `NEXT`, `NEAREST`.
- **Enums delete whole categories of validation code [G5]** - once every month parameter is a `Month`, `isValidMonthCode` and all month-code error checking (as in `monthCodeToQuarter`) can be deleted. Budget for the ripple: this change took an hour across the class and all its users.
- **Move an enum to its own source file once it grows [G13]** - and because the concept does not depend on the owning class. Do the same for every sibling enum for consistency [G11],[G12].
- **Replace a `switch` with polymorphic enum bodies [G23]** - `isInRange`'s switch moved into the `DateInterval` enum as an abstract method implemented per enumerator.
  ```java
  public enum DateInterval {
    OPEN { public boolean isIn(int d, int left, int right) { return d > left && d < right; } },
    CLOSED_LEFT { public boolean isIn(int d, int left, int right) { return d >= left && d < right; } },
    CLOSED_RIGHT { public boolean isIn(int d, int left, int right) { return d > left && d <= right; } },
    CLOSED { public boolean isIn(int d, int left, int right) { return d >= left && d <= right; } };
    public abstract boolean isIn(int d, int left, int right);
  }
  ```
- **Eliminate magic numbers [G25]** - replace a literal `1` with `Month.JANUARY.toInt()` or `Day.SUNDAY.toInt()` as appropriate.
- **Prefer automatic control of `serialVersionUID` [G4]** - deleting the declaration lets the compiler generate a new one on every change, producing an `InvalidClassException` with a clear-cut cause, which is preferable to debugging the odd behavior that ensues when someone forgets to update a manual ID; a forgotten ID gives an undefined and possibly silent failure mode.
  - Contradiction preserved: all the documents recommend manual control of this variable, and reviewers contend that in an open source framework it is better to assert manual control over the serial ID so that minor changes do not invalidate old serialized dates, which is a fair point. Apply manual control when cross-version deserialization of published data matters; apply automatic control otherwise. The real moral is that you should not expect to deserialize across versions.
- **Do not spread `final` across arguments and variable declarations [G12]** - in this refactoring all such `final` keywords were deleted as clutter adding no real value; the errors `final` might catch are already caught by the unit tests you write. Contradiction preserved: conventional advice (Simmons) is to "spread final all over your code"; Martin explicitly disagrees, allowing a few good uses such as the occasional final constant.

### Then Make It Right: placement, dead code, duplication

- **Delete unused code [G9]** - unused tables (`AGGREGATE_DAYS_TO_END_OF_MONTH`, `LEAP_YEAR_AGGREGATE_DAYS_TO_END_OF_MONTH`), an unused `description` field together with its accessor and mutator, and functions made irrelevant by a refactoring (`isValidMonthCode`, `isValidWeekdayCode`) all get deleted.
- **Delete degenerate default constructors [G12]** - the compiler generates them.
- **Collapse a pair where one function's only caller is its twin [G9],[G12],[F4]** - when one overload is called only by its twin, collapse the two into one function and simplify it; the two `getMonths` overloads collapsed into one, vastly simplified.
- **Never pass a flag argument, especially one that only selects output format [G15]** - the `monthCodeToString` twin-with-a-flag pattern is a bad idea; rename, simplify, restructure, and move the behavior to the type that owns it.
- **Make tables private and expose them through a function [G8]** - `LAST_DAY_OF_MONTH` had no good reason to be public since a static `lastDayOfMonth` provides the same data.
- **Push members down to the only class that uses them [G6]** - `EARLIEST_DATE_ORDINAL` / `LATEST_DATE_ORDINAL`, `MINIMUM_YEAR_SUPPORTED` / `MAXIMUM_YEAR_SUPPORTED`, and `leapYearCount` were used only by the concrete derivative, so they belong there, not in the abstract base.
- **Move data close to where it is used [G10]** - when only one implementation actually exists, move a shared-looking table next to its single user (`AGGREGATE_DAYS_TO_END_OF_PRECEDING_MONTH`, and likewise the leap-year aggregate table).
  - Tradeoff preserved: the counter-argument is that the table is not specific to any particular implementation [G6]. Resolve it on consistency [G11] (to be consistent the table becomes private and would then need an exposing function like `julianDateOfLastDayOfMonth`, which nobody seems to need) and on reversibility (the table can be moved back to the base class easily if a new implementation needs it).
- **Move a method to the class whose data it uses (FEATURE ENVY) [G14],[G17]** - `monthCodeToQuarter` became `Month.quarter()`; `stringToWeekdayCode` became `Day.parse`; `weekdayCodeToString` became `Day.toString`; `monthCodeToString` and `stringToMonthCode` moved into `Month`; the `LAST_DAY_OF_MONTH` array moved into `Month`.
  - An instance method that takes an argument of its own type envies its own class [G14]; make it a true instance method (`getEndOfCurrentMonth(DayDate)` -> `getEndOfMonth()`).
- **Do not leave a method static when it operates on the object's variables [G18]** - `addDays`, `addMonths`, `addYears`, `getPreviousDayOfWeek`, `getFollowingDayOfWeek` all became instance methods.
- **Never let a base class know about its derivatives [G7]** - `addDays` -> `createInstance` created a concrete `SpreadsheetDate` from inside the abstract base. Fix with the ABSTRACT FACTORY pattern.
  - Create `DayDateFactory` holding a static default instance (`new SpreadsheetDateFactory()`), a `setInstance` to swap it at any time, `protected abstract _makeDate(...)` / `_getMinimumYear()` / `_getMaximumYear()` methods, and public static `makeDate(...)` / `getMinimumYear()` / `getMaximumYear()` that delegate to them.
  - This is how a user of an abstract class gets implementation-dependent information (minimum and maximum dates) without polluting the abstract class itself.
  - Static methods that delegate to abstract methods are a useful combination of the SINGLETON, DECORATOR, and ABSTRACT FACTORY patterns.
- **Pull an abstract method up when its implementation depends on nothing in the derivative [G6]** - `toDate`, `compare`, `isInRange`, and six further abstract methods were implemented once in the base instead of per derivative; a method that is inappropriately abstract is a defect.
  - Exception: leave a method abstract when it genuinely varies by implementation (`getOrdinalDay`, `getYYYY`, `getMonth`, `getDayOfMonth` are nicely abstract).
- **Never leave a logical dependency without a physical one [G22]** - `getDayOfWeek` had no physical dependency on the derivative but implicitly depended on the day of the week of ordinal day 0. Introduce an abstract method that names the dependency (`getDayOfWeekForOrdinalZero`, returning `Day.SATURDAY` in `SpreadsheetDate`) and implement the generic part in the base [G6]: keep the implementation-dependent portion as small as possible.
  ```java
  public Day getDayOfWeek() {
    Day startingDay = getDayOfWeekForOrdinalZero();
    int startingOffset = startingDay.index - Day.SUNDAY.index;
    return Day.make((getOrdinalDay() + startingOffset) % 7 + 1);
  }
  ```
- **Eliminate duplicate implementations [G5]** - merge duplicate `if` statements inside a loop with `||`; delete a duplicate instance method that shadows a static one; extract a shared helper (`correctLastDayOfMonth`) out of the duplication between `plusYears` and `plusMonths`, which made all three methods much clearer.
- **Move helpers with no home into a utility class [G6]** - the static `dateFormatSymbols` field and the static `getMonthNames`, `isLeapYear`, `lastDayOfMonth` methods moved into a new `DateUtil` class.
- **Put abstract methods at the top of the class [G24]** - declare the abstract methods above the concrete members.

### Then Make It Right: making algorithms expressive

- **Make a condition expressive by naming its parts [G16]** - use explaining boolean locals rather than one dense expression.
  ```java
  // GOOD
  public static boolean isLeapYear(int year) {
    boolean fourth = year % 4 == 0;
    boolean hundredth = year % 100 == 0;
    boolean fourHundredth = year % 400 == 0;
    return fourth && (!hundredth || fourHundredth);
  }
  ```
- **Use EXPLAINING TEMPORARY VARIABLES on complicated algorithms [G19]** - applied to `addMonths`/`plusMonths` (`thisMonthAsOrdinal`, `resultMonthAsOrdinal`, `resultYear`, `resultMonth`, `lastDayOfResultMonth`, `resultDay`), `plusYears`, `getPreviousDayOfWeek`, `getFollowingDayOfWeek`, and `getNearestDayOfWeek`.
- **Simplify by first understanding what is really going on [G21]** - working but complicated code should be re-derived, not patched.
  ```java
  // GOOD
  public DayDate getNearestDayOfWeek(final Day targetDay) {
    int offsetToThisWeeksTarget = targetDay.index - getDayOfWeek().index;
    int offsetToFutureTarget = (offsetToThisWeeksTarget + 7) % 7;
    int offsetToPreviousTarget = offsetToFutureTarget - 7;
    if (offsetToFutureTarget > 3)
      return plusDays(offsetToPreviousTarget);
    else
      return plusDays(offsetToFutureTarget);
  }
  ```
- **Make sibling algorithms follow one pattern [G11]** - once `getPreviousDayOfWeek` and `getFollowingDayOfWeek` shared a shape (`offsetToTarget`, adjust by 7, `plusDays`), `getNearestDayOfWeek` was rewritten to match; an earlier fix that does not match the current pattern is itself a defect to correct.
- **Write the missing tests when a pulled-up method has none** - after pulling an implementation up into the base class, check whether it has tests and write them if it does not; `compare`/`daysSince` had none.

### Then Make It Right: the deletion chain, and its lesson

1. Move a method that really belongs to an enum onto that enum, using the IDE's refactoring tools.
2. Rename it to `toString`.
3. Change it from a static method to an instance method. All tests still pass.
4. Delete the method entirely; the failing asserts show exactly who depended on it.
5. Change those asserts to use the enumerator names, because every enumerator's `toString` already returns its name; the refactoring tool guarantees all previous callers now resolve to `toString`.

- **Check the caller list before investing in a refactoring** - after all that, the only users of `weekInMonthToString` were the tests just modified, so both the function and those tests were deleted. Applying the lesson once learned, `relativeToString` was confirmed to have no non-test callers and was deleted with its tests immediately.

### Interpreting coverage after shrinking a class

- **A falling coverage percentage can mean success** - before treating a coverage drop as a regression, compare the executable statement counts: coverage dropped to 84.9 percent (45 of 53 executable statements) not because less functionality is tested but because the class shrank so much that the few uncovered lines carry greater weight.
- **Leave trivial lines untested when they are genuinely trivial** - you may leave an uncovered line untested when it is trivial enough that it is not worth testing.

### Outcome to aim for

- **Every refactoring pass should deliver all of these** - increased test coverage, fixed bugs, clarified code, and shrunken code, so the next person finds it easier to deal with than you did and can clean it a bit further.

## Clean Code: Ch17 Smells and Heuristics

### Comments

- **C1: Inappropriate Information** - Never put information in a comment that belongs in another record-keeping system (source code control, issue tracking). Change histories just clutter source files with volumes of historical, uninteresting text. In general, meta-data such as authors, last-modified-date, SPR number, and so on should not appear in comments. Reserve comments for technical notes about the code and design.
- **C2: Obsolete Comment** - A comment that has gotten old, irrelevant, and incorrect is obsolete. Comments get old quickly; it is best not to write a comment that will become obsolete. On finding an obsolete comment, update it or delete it as quickly as possible, because obsolete comments migrate away from the code they described and become floating islands of irrelevance and misdirection.
- **C3: Redundant Comment** - Delete any comment that describes something that adequately describes itself. Comments should say things the code cannot say for itself.
  - `i++; // increment i` is redundant.
  - A Javadoc that says nothing more than (or even less than) the function signature is redundant:

```java
// BAD
/**
 * @param sellRequest
 * @return
 * @throws ManagedComponentException
 */
public SellResponse beginSellItem(SellRequest sellRequest)
    throws ManagedComponentException
```

- **C4: Poorly Written Comment** - A comment worth writing is worth writing well. Choose words carefully, use correct grammar and punctuation, don't ramble, don't state the obvious, be brief.
- **C5: Commented-Out Code** - When you see commented-out code, delete it. Do not suffer commented-out code to survive. The source code control system still remembers it; anyone who really needs it can check out a previous version. Commented-out code is an abomination: it rots, calling functions that no longer exist, using variables whose names changed, and following conventions that are long obsolete; it pollutes the modules that contain it and distracts the people who try to read it, and nobody deletes it because everyone assumes someone else needs it or has plans for it.

### Environment

- **E1: Build Requires More Than One Step** - Building a project must be a single trivial operation. You should be able to check out the system with one simple command and then issue one other simple command to build it. Never require checking out many little pieces from source control, a sequence of arcane commands, context-dependent scripts, or hunting for extra JARs, XML files, and other artifacts.

```sh
svn get mySystem
cd mySystem
ant all
```

- **E2: Tests Require More Than One Step** - You must be able to run all the unit tests with just one command. Best case: one button click in the IDE. Worst case: a single simple shell command. Running all tests must be quick, easy, and obvious.

### Functions

- **F1: Too Many Arguments** - Keep the argument count small. No argument is best, followed by one, two, and three. More than three is very questionable and should be avoided with prejudice.
- **F2: Output Arguments** - Do not use output arguments; they are counterintuitive because readers expect arguments to be inputs, not outputs. If your function must change the state of something, have it change the state of the object it is called on.
- **F3: Flag Arguments** - Eliminate boolean arguments; they loudly declare that the function does more than one thing and are confusing.
- **F4: Dead Function** - Discard methods that are never called. Keeping dead code around is wasteful; do not be afraid to delete the function, because source code control still remembers it.

### General

- **G1: Multiple Languages in One Source File** - The ideal is for a source file to contain one, and only one, language. Realistically more than one will be needed, but take pains to minimize both the number and the extent of extra languages in a source file.
