Mixing Java, XML, HTML, YAML, JavaDoc, English, JavaScript, tag library syntax and so forth in one file is confusing at best and carelessly sloppy at worst.
- **G2: Obvious Behavior Is Unimplemented** - Following "The Principle of Least Surprise" (also "The Principle of Least Astonishment"), any function or class must implement the behaviors another programmer could reasonably expect. Example: `Day day = DayDate.StringToDay(String dayName)` must translate `"Monday"` to `Day.MONDAY`, must translate common abbreviations, and must ignore case. When obvious behavior is missing, readers can no longer trust their intuition about function names and must fall back on reading the details of the code.
- **G3: Incorrect Behavior at the Boundaries** - Do not rely on intuition that code works; there is no replacement for due diligence. Look for every boundary condition, corner case, quirk, and exception, and write a test for each one.
- **G4: Overridden Safeties** - Never override safeties casually; it is risky. Exerting manual control over `serialVersionUID` may be necessary but is always risky. Turning off compiler warnings (or all warnings) may get the build to succeed at the risk of endless debugging sessions. Turning off failing tests and telling yourself you'll get them to pass later is as bad as pretending your credit cards are free money.
- **G5: Duplication** - Find and eliminate duplication wherever you can; this is one of the most important rules of all. Known as the DRY principle (Don't Repeat Yourself); Kent Beck's Extreme Programming names it "Once, and only once"; Ron Jeffries ranks it second, just below getting all the tests to pass. Every duplication is a missed opportunity for abstraction, and folding it into an abstraction raises the abstraction level and increases the vocabulary of your design.
  - Clumps of identical copy-pasted code: replace with simple methods.
  - A `switch`/`case` or `if`/`else` chain that appears again and again in various modules, always testing the same set of conditions: replace with polymorphism.
  - Modules with similar algorithms that do not share similar lines of code: this is still duplication; address it with the TEMPLATE METHOD or STRATEGY pattern.
  - Most design patterns of the last fifteen years, the Codd Normal Forms, OO itself, and structured programming are all strategies for eliminating duplication.
- **G6: Code at Wrong Level of Abstraction** - Separate higher level general concepts from lower level detailed concepts, and make the separation complete. All lower level concepts belong in derivatives; all higher level concepts belong in the base class. Constants, variables, or utility functions that pertain only to the detailed implementation must not be present in the base class; the base class should know nothing about them. This applies equally to source files, components, and modules: never mix lower and higher level concepts in one container.
  - Example: `double percentFull()` on a general `Stack` interface is at the wrong level of abstraction, because some implementations cannot know how full they are; move it to a derivative interface such as `BoundedStack`.
  - Do not "fix" it by returning zero for a boundless stack: that is telling a lie, since no stack is truly boundless and you cannot prevent an `OutOfMemoryException` by checking `stack.percentFull() < 50.0`. You cannot lie or fake your way out of a misplaced abstraction, and there is no quick fix when you get it wrong.
- **G7: Base Classes Depending on Their Derivatives** - In general, base classes should know nothing about their derivatives; a base class mentioning derivative names is suspect, because the point of partitioning is to make higher level base concepts independent of lower level derivative concepts.
  - Exception: when the number of derivatives is strictly fixed and the base class selects between them (common in finite state machine implementations). In that case derivatives and base are strongly coupled and always deploy together in the same jar file.
  - In the general case, deploy derivatives and bases in different jar files and keep the base jars ignorant of derivative jar contents, so modified components can be redeployed without redeploying the base components.
- **G8: Too Much Information** - Keep interfaces very tight and very small; limit what you expose to keep coupling low. Well-defined modules have very small interfaces that let you do a lot with a little; poorly defined modules have wide and deep interfaces requiring many gestures for simple things, so coupling is high.
  - The fewer methods a class has, the better. The fewer variables a function knows about, the better. The fewer instance variables a class has, the better.
  - Hide your data, your utility functions, your constants, and your temporaries. Don't create classes with lots of methods or lots of instance variables. Don't create lots of protected variables and functions for your subclasses.
- **G9: Dead Code** - Delete code that isn't executed. It hides in `if` bodies checking impossible conditions, `catch` blocks of `try` blocks that never throw, uncalled utility methods, and `switch`/`case` conditions that never occur. Dead code is not updated when designs change: it still compiles but no longer follows newer conventions or rules, and the older it is the worse it smells.
- **G10: Vertical Separation** - Define variables and functions close to where they are used.
  - Declare local variables just above their first usage, with a small vertical scope; never hundreds of lines distant from their usages.
  - Define private functions just below their first usage, so finding a private function is a matter of scanning downward from the first usage, even though they belong to the scope of the whole class.
- **G11: Inconsistency** - If you do something a certain way, do all similar things in the same way (principle of least surprise). Choose conventions carefully and keep following them. If you name a variable `response` for an `HttpServletResponse` in one function, use that same name in the other functions that use `HttpServletResponse`. If you name a method `processVerificationRequest`, name the sibling methods `processDeletionRequest` and so on.
- **G12: Clutter** - Remove clutter: default constructors with no implementation, unused variables, uncalled functions, comments that add no information. Keep source files clean, well organized, and free of clutter.
- **G13: Artificial Coupling** - Never artificially couple things that don't depend on each other. An artificial coupling is a coupling between two modules that serves no direct purpose, resulting from putting a variable, constant, or function in a temporarily convenient though inappropriate location; this is lazy and careless.
  - General enums must not be contained within more specific classes, because that forces the whole application to know about those specific classes. Same for general purpose static functions declared in specific classes.
  - Take the time to figure out where functions, constants, and variables ought to be declared instead of tossing them into the most convenient place at hand.
- **G14: Feature Envy** - Methods of a class should be interested in the variables and functions of the class they belong to, not those of other classes. A method that uses accessors and mutators of another object to manipulate that object's data envies the scope of that other class. Eliminate Feature Envy, all else being equal, because it exposes the internals of one class to another.

```java
// BAD - calculateWeeklyPay envies HourlyEmployee
public class HourlyPayCalculator {
  public Money calculateWeeklyPay(HourlyEmployee e) {
    int tenthRate = e.getTenthRate().getPennies();
    int tenthsWorked = e.getTenthsWorked();
    int straightTime = Math.min(400, tenthsWorked);
    int overTime = Math.max(0, tenthsWorked - straightTime);
    return new Money(straightTime * tenthRate
        + (int)Math.round(overTime * tenthRate * 1.5));
  }
}
```

  - Exception: Feature Envy is sometimes a necessary evil. An `HourlyEmployeeReport.reportHours()` that reads `employee.getName()` and `employee.getTenthsWorked()` to build a format string envies `HourlyEmployee`, but moving the report format string into `HourlyEmployee` would violate the Single Responsibility Principle, the Open Closed Principle, and the Common Closure Principle, and would couple `HourlyEmployee` to the report format, exposing it to changes in that format.
- **G15: Selector Arguments** - Never pass a selector argument to choose behavior; prefer many functions over passing some code into a function to select behavior. Selector arguments need not be boolean: enums, integers, or any other type used to select behavior count. Each selector argument combines many functions into one, its purpose is difficult to remember, and it is a lazy way to avoid splitting a large function into several smaller ones. A dangling `false` at the end of a call is unreadable: nobody can recall what `calculateWeeklyPay(false)` means.

```java
// GOOD - split instead of a boolean selector
public int straightPay() {
  return getTenthsWorked() * getTenthRate();
}
public int overTimePay() {
  int overTimeTenths = Math.max(0, getTenthsWorked() - 400);
  return straightPay() + overTimeBonus(overTimeTenths);
}
private int overTimeBonus(int overTimeTenths) {
  return (int) Math.round(0.5 * getTenthRate() * overTimeTenths);
}
```

- **G16: Obscured Intent** - Make code as expressive as possible; take the time to make intent visible. Run-on expressions, Hungarian notation, and magic numbers all obscure the author's intent. Code like `m_otCalc()` returning `iThsWkd * iThsRte + (int) Math.round(0.5 * iThsRte * Math.max(0, iThsWkd - 400))` is small and dense yet virtually impenetrable.
- **G17: Misplaced Responsibility** - Place code where a reader would naturally expect it to be (principle of least surprise). The `PI` constant goes where the trig functions are declared; the `OVERTIME_RATE` constant is declared in `HourlyPayCalculator`. Do not put functionality in a location that is convenient for you but not intuitive to the reader.
  - One way to decide is to look at function names: between a report module's `getTotalHours` and a timecard module's `saveTimeCard`, the name that implies calculating a total should own the calculation.
  - Exception: there are sometimes performance reasons to calculate a total as time cards are accepted rather than when the report is printed. That is fine, but the function names must reflect it, for example a `computeRunningTotalOfHours` function in the timecard module.
- **G18: Inappropriate Static** - Prefer nonstatic methods to static methods; when in doubt, make the function nonstatic. Only make a function static if there is no chance you'll want it to behave polymorphically.
  - `Math.max(double a, double b)` is a good static method: it does not operate on a single instance, all its data comes from its two arguments, and there is almost no chance we'd want it polymorphic.
  - `HourlyPayCalculator.calculatePay(employee, overtimeRate)` should not be static: there is a reasonable chance we'll want several algorithms (`OvertimeHourlyPayCalculator`, `StraightTimeHourlyPayCalculator`), so it should be a nonstatic member function of `Employee`.
- **G19: Use Explanatory Variables** - Break calculations up into intermediate values held in variables with meaningful names. It is hard to overdo this: more explanatory variables are generally better than fewer, and an opaque module can suddenly become transparent from this alone.

```java
// GOOD
String key = match.group(1);
String value = match.group(2);
headers.put(key.toLowerCase(), value);
```

- **G20: Function Names Should Say What They Do** - Name functions so the call site alone tells you what happens; if you have to look at the implementation or documentation to know what a function does, find a better name or rearrange the functionality into functions with better names. `date.add(5)` is ambiguous (days? weeks? hours? mutating or not?). If it adds five days and mutates, call it `addDaysTo` or `increaseByDays`; if it returns a new date and leaves the instance alone, call it `daysLater` or `daysSince`.
- **G21: Understand the Algorithm** - Before considering yourself done with a function, make sure you understand how it works; passing all the tests is not good enough, you must know the solution is correct. Getting something to work by plugging in enough `if` statements and flags is an acceptable exploration technique, but it is not sufficient to leave the quotation marks around "work". The best way to gain this understanding is often to refactor the function into something so clean and expressive that it is obvious how it works. Being unsure whether an algorithm is appropriate for the job is often a fact of life; being unsure what your code does is just laziness.
- **G22: Make Logical Dependencies Physical** - If one module depends on another, make the dependency physical, not just logical. The dependent module must not make assumptions about the module it depends on; it must explicitly ask that module for all the information it depends on.
  - Example: `HourlyReporter` holding `private final int PAGE_SIZE = 55` is a misplaced responsibility (G17) that makes `HourlyReporter` assume it knows the page size, and assume `HourlyReportFormatter` can deal with a page size of 55; if some formatter implementation could not, there would be an error. Physicalize it by adding `getMaxPageSize()` to `HourlyReportFormatter` and calling it instead of using the constant.
- **G23: Prefer Polymorphism to If/Else or Switch/Case** - Consider polymorphism before using a `switch`. Most people use `switch` because it is the obvious brute force solution, not because it is right, and cases where functions are more volatile than types are relatively rare, so every `switch` statement should be suspect.
  - "ONE SWITCH" rule: there may be no more than one `switch` statement for a given type of selection, and the cases in that `switch` must create polymorphic objects that take the place of other such `switch` statements in the rest of the system.
  - Qualifier: `switch` statements are probably appropriate in the parts of the system where adding new functions is more likely than adding new types.
- **G24: Follow Standard Conventions** - Every team should follow a coding standard based on common industry norms, specifying where to declare instance variables, how to name classes, methods, and variables, where to put braces, and so on. The team should not need a document to describe these conventions, because their code provides the examples. Everyone on the team must follow them; each member must be mature enough to realize it doesn't matter a whit where you put your braces so long as you all agree.
- **G25: Replace Magic Numbers with Named Constants** - In general it is a bad idea to have raw numbers in code; hide them behind well-named constants. Hide 86,400 behind `SECONDS_PER_DAY`; hide 55 lines per page behind `LINES_PER_PAGE`.
  - Exception: some constants are so easy to recognize that they need no named constant, so long as they are used in conjunction with very self-explanatory code. `feetWalked/5280.0` (5280 is so well known and unique that readers recognize it standing alone), `hourlyRate * 8`, and `radius * Math.PI * 2` need no `FEET_PER_MILE`, `WORK_HOURS_PER_DAY`, or `TWO`; the `TWO` case is absurd. Some formulae are simply better written with raw numbers. `WORK_HOURS_PER_DAY` is quibbleable because laws or conventions might change, but the formula reads so nicely with the 8 in it that you should be reluctant to add 17 extra characters to the readers' burden.
  - Counter-exception: constants like `3.141592653589793` are well known and recognizable, but the chance for error is too great to leave them raw, because readers see the digits, assume pi, and fail to scrutinize them; and we don't want people using 3.14, 3.14159, 3.142, and so forth. Use `Math.PI`.
  - "Magic Number" applies to any token whose value is not self-describing, not only numbers. In `assertEquals(7777, Employee.find("John Doe").employeeNumber())` both `7777` and `"John Doe"` are magic numbers; write `assertEquals(HOURLY_EMPLOYEE_ID, Employee.find(HOURLY_EMPLOYEE_NAME).employeeNumber())`.
- **G26: Be Precise** - When you make a decision in your code, make it precisely; know why you made it and how you will deal with any exceptions. Ambiguities and imprecision in code result from disagreements or laziness and should be eliminated.
  - Expecting the first match to be the only match to a query is probably naive; if you query for what you think is the only record, check that there aren't others.
  - Using floating point numbers to represent currency is almost criminal; use integers (or better, a `Money` class that uses integers) and deal with rounding appropriately.
  - Avoiding locks and/or transaction management because you don't think concurrent update is likely is lazy at best; if concurrent update is possible, implement some kind of locking mechanism.
  - Declaring a variable to be an `ArrayList` when a `List` will do is overly constraining; making all variables protected by default is not constraining enough.
  - If you call a function that might return null, check for null.
- **G27: Structure over Convention** - Enforce design decisions with structure over convention. Naming conventions are good but inferior to structures that force compliance: `switch`/`case` with nicely named enumerations is inferior to base classes with abstract methods, because nothing forces every `switch` to be written the same way, while base classes do enforce that concrete classes implement all abstract methods.
- **G28: Encapsulate Conditionals** - Extract functions that explain the intent of a conditional. Prefer `if (shouldBeDeleted(timer))` over `if (timer.hasExpired() && !timer.isRecurrent())`.
- **G29: Avoid Negative Conditionals** - Express conditionals as positives when possible, since negatives are harder to understand. Prefer `if (buffer.shouldCompact())` over `if (!buffer.shouldNotCompact())`.
- **G30: Functions Should Do One Thing** - Convert functions with multiple sections performing a series of operations into many smaller functions, each of which does one thing.

```java
// BAD - loops, checks payday, and pays
public void pay() {
  for (Employee e : employees)
    if (e.isPayday()) {
      Money pay = e.calculatePay();
      e.deliverPay(pay);
    }
}
// GOOD
public void pay() {
  for (Employee e : employees) payIfNecessary(e);
}
private void payIfNecessary(Employee e) {
  if (e.isPayday()) calculateAndDeliverPay(e);
}
private void calculateAndDeliverPay(Employee e) {
  Money pay = e.calculatePay();
  e.deliverPay(pay);
}
```

- **G31: Hidden Temporal Couplings** - Temporal couplings are often necessary, but never hide the coupling. Structure the arguments of your functions so the order in which they must be called is obvious: create a bucket brigade where each function produces a result the next function needs, so there is no reasonable way to call them out of order.

```java
// BAD - order is required but not enforced
public void dive(String reason) {
  saturateGradient();
  reticulateSplines();       // may throw UnsaturatedGradientException if called first
  diveForMoog(reason);
}
// GOOD
public void dive(String reason) {
  Gradient gradient = saturateGradient();
  List splines = reticulateSplines(gradient);
  diveForMoog(splines, reason);
}
```

  - This does increase the syntactic complexity of the functions, and that is acceptable: the extra syntactic complexity exposes the true temporal complexity of the situation.
  - Leave instance variables in place if private methods in the class need them, and still pass the arguments to make the temporal coupling explicit.
- **G32: Don't Be Arbitrary** - Have a reason for the way you structure code, and make sure that reason is communicated by the structure. If a structure appears arbitrary, others will feel empowered to change it; if it appears consistently throughout the system, others will use and preserve it. Public classes that are not utilities of some other class must not be scoped inside another class; the convention is to make them public at the top level of their package.
- **G33: Encapsulate Boundary Conditions** - Put the processing for boundary conditions in one place; don't let them leak all over the code, and don't scatter swarms of `+1`s and `-1`s. If `level + 1` appears twice, encapsulate it in a variable such as `int nextLevel = level + 1;` and use that.
- **G34: Functions Should Descend Only One Level of Abstraction** - All statements within a function must be written at the same level of abstraction, one level below the operation described by the function's name. This may be the hardest of these heuristics to interpret and follow, because humans are far too good at seamlessly mixing levels of abstraction.
  - Example transformation: a `render()` that built an HR tag by appending HTML syntax into a `StringBuffer` mixed the notion "a horizontal rule has a size" with the syntax of the HR tag. Refactoring to `new HtmlTag("hr")` plus `hr.addAttribute("size", hrSize(extraDashes))` moved all HTML syntax into `HtmlTag`, and the `size` field was renamed to `extraDashes` to reflect its true purpose (the number of extra dashes).
  - Making that change caught a latent defect: the hand-built code omitted the closing slash required by XHTML, which `HtmlTag` had long since handled.
  - Separating levels of abstraction is one of the most important functions of refactoring and one of the hardest to do well. A first attempt that merely creates separation and gets tests to pass can still mix levels (constructing the HR tag versus interpreting and formatting the size variable). Expect that breaking a function along lines of abstraction uncovers new lines of abstraction obscured by the previous structure.
- **G35: Keep Configurable Data at High Levels** - If a constant such as a default or configuration value is known and expected at a high level of abstraction, never bury it in a low-level function; expose it as an argument to that low-level function, called from the high level. Declare defaults (for example `DEFAULT_PATH = "."`, `DEFAULT_ROOT = "FitNesseRoot"`, `DEFAULT_PORT = 80`, `DEFAULT_VERSION_DAYS = 14`) at the top of the arguments class, parse the command line in the very first executable line, and pass values down. Then you never have to hunt in low levels for statements like `if (arguments.port == 0) // use 80 by default`. The lower levels of the application do not own the values of these constants.
- **G36: Avoid Transitive Navigation** - Do not let a module know much about its collaborators: if A collaborates with B and B collaborates with C, modules that use A must not know about C. Never write `a.getB().getC().doSomething();`. This is sometimes called the Law of Demeter; the Pragmatic Programmers call it "Writing Shy Code". Modules must know only about their immediate collaborators and not the navigation map of the whole system. If many modules use `a.getB().getC()`, interposing a Q between B and C means finding and converting every instance to `a.getB().getQ().getC()`, which is how architectures become rigid. Require immediate collaborators to offer all the services you need so you can simply say `myCollaborator.doSomething()`.

### Java

- **J1: Avoid Long Import Lists by Using Wildcards** - If you use two or more classes from a package, import the whole package with `import package.*;`. Long lists of imports are daunting; do not clutter the top of a module with 80 lines of imports.
  - Specific imports are hard dependencies; wildcard imports are not. A specifically imported class must exist, whereas a wildcard import merely adds the package to the name search path, so no true dependency is created and modules stay less coupled.
  - Rare useful case for specific imports: in legacy code, walking the list of specific imports to find the true qualified names of classes you need mocks and stubs for. Even then it's better to import wildcards, since most modern IDEs convert wildcard imports to specific imports with a single command.
  - Wildcard imports can cause name conflicts and ambiguities: two same-named classes in different packages must be specifically imported or at least specifically qualified when used. This is a nuisance but rare enough that wildcard imports are still generally better.
- **J2: Don't Inherit Constants** - Never put constants in an interface and gain access to them by inheriting that interface (for example `abstract class Employee implements PayrollConstants`); this hides the constants at the top of the inheritance hierarchy. Do not use inheritance as a way to cheat the scoping rules of the language. Use a static import instead: `import static PayrollConstants.*;`.
- **J3: Constants versus Enums** - Use enums (available since Java 5); stop using the old trick of `public static final int`. The meaning of ints can get lost; the meaning of enums cannot, because they belong to a named enumeration. Study the enum syntax carefully: enums can have methods and fields, which makes them far more expressive and flexible than ints (for example `enum HourlyPayGrade` with `public abstract double rate();` overridden per constant: `APPRENTICE` 1.0, `LEUTENANT_JOURNEYMAN` 1.2, `JOURNEYMAN` 1.5, `MASTER` 2.0).

### Names

- **N1: Choose Descriptive Names** - Don't be too quick to choose a name; make sure it is descriptive, and frequently reevaluate the appropriateness of names you chose, because meanings tend to drift as software evolves. Names in software are 90 percent of what makes software readable; they are too important to treat carelessly. Well-chosen names overload the structure of the code with description and set readers' expectations about what the other functions in the module do, so that reading a function like `isStrike` yields "pretty much what you expected".
  - Rename hodge-podge symbols and magic numbers to intent-revealing names (`x()` to `score()`, `q` to `score`, `z` to `frame`, `kk` to `frameNumber`, `l` to `rolls`), and replace inline `== 10` tests and index arithmetic with named functions (`isStrike`, `isSpare`, `nextTwoBallsForStrike`, `nextBallForSpare`, `twoBallsInFrame`). The algorithm then becomes immediately inferable from the names alone, and `isStrike` contains exactly the expected `rolls[frame] == 10`.
- **N2: Choose Names at the Appropriate Level of Abstraction** - Don't pick names that communicate implementation; choose names that reflect the level of abstraction of the class or function you are working in. Each pass over your code will likely find a variable named at too low a level; change it when you find it, because making code readable requires a dedication to continuous improvement. Example: a `Modem` interface with `dial(String phoneNumber)` and `getConnectedPhoneNumber()` is at the wrong level once modems can be hard wired or connected by sending a port number to a switch over USB; use `connect(String connectionLocator)` and `getConnectedLocator()`, which make no commitment about phone numbers and still serve phone numbers or any other connection strategy.
- **N3: Use Standard Nomenclature Where Possible** - Base names on existing convention or usage. If you use the DECORATOR pattern, use the word `Decorator` in the names of the decorating classes (for example `AutoHangupModemDecorator`). Follow language conventions such as naming object-to-string conversions `toString` rather than inventing your own. Teams often invent their own standard system of names for a project, which Eric Evans calls a ubiquitous language; use its terms extensively in code. The more you use names overloaded with special meanings relevant to your project, the easier it is for readers to know what your code is talking about.
- **N4: Unambiguous Names** - Choose names that make the workings of a function or variable unambiguous. `doRename()` says nothing beyond broad vague terms, made worse by containing a function named `renamePage`; rename it `renamePageAndOptionallyAllReferences`. A long name is acceptable when its explanatory value outweighs the length, for example when it is called from only one place in the module.
- **N5: Use Long Names for Long Scopes** - Relate the length of a name to the length of its scope: very short variable names for tiny scopes, longer names for big scopes. Names like `i` and `j` are just fine if their scope is five lines long.

## Clean Code: Appendix A Concurrency II

### Concurrent Update and the Memory Model

- **Never assume `++` is atomic** - pre- and post-increment compile to multiple byte-code instructions (e.g. GETFIELD, add, PUTFIELD), so a thread can be preempted mid-sequence.
  - Failure mode: thread 1 executes up to GETFIELD (holding 42 on the operand stack) and is interrupted; thread 2 runs the whole method and gets 43; thread 1 resumes, adds one to its stale 42, stores 43 and returns 43. One increment is silently lost.
  - Making the accessor/incrementer method `synchronized` fixes this specific problem.
- **Understand the memory model well enough to tell what is and is not safe** - intimate byte-code expertise is not required, but this level of memory-model knowledge is.
- **Know these three things for every concurrent program** - where there are shared objects/values; the code that can cause concurrent read/update issues; how to guard such concurrent issues from happening.

### Knowing Your Library: Executor Framework

- **Use the Executor framework instead of hand-rolled threading** - if you are creating threads and are not using a thread pool, or are using a hand-written one, consider `java.util.concurrent`'s Executor (introduced in Java 5). It makes code cleaner, easier to follow, and smaller.
- **Rely on what Executor gives you** - it pools threads, resizes automatically, recreates threads if necessary, and supports futures.
- **Use `Callable` when the task must return a value** - Executor works with both `Runnable` and `Callable`; a `Callable` is like a `Runnable` but returns a result, a common need in multithreaded solutions.
- **Use a future to overlap independent operations** - submit the long operation, do local processing, then call `get()`, which blocks until the future completes.

```java
// GOOD
Callable makeExternalCall = new Callable() {
  public String call() throws Exception { /* make external request */ }
};
Future result = executorService.submit(makeExternalCall);
String partialResult = doSomeLocalProcessing();
return result.get() + partialResult;
```

### Knowing Your Library: Nonblocking Solutions

- **Prefer the atomic classes over `synchronized` for single-value updates** - `AtomicBoolean`, `AtomicInteger`, `AtomicReference` and several more exist for exactly this case.

```java
// BAD
public class ObjectWithValue {
  private int value;
  public void synchronized incrementValue() { ++value; }
  public int getValue() { return value; }
}

// GOOD
public class ObjectWithValue {
  private AtomicInteger value = new AtomicInteger(0);
  public void incrementValue() { value.incrementAndGet(); }
  public int getValue() { return value.get(); }
}
```

- **Expect the nonblocking version to win on performance** - even though it uses an object instead of a primitive and sends `incrementAndGet()` instead of `++`, it will nearly always beat the synchronized version; sometimes only slightly faster, but cases where it is slower are virtually nonexistent.
- **Understand Compare and Swap (CAS)** - modern processors provide an atomic CAS operation; it is analogous to optimistic locking in databases, whereas the `synchronized` version is analogous to pessimistic locking.
  - CAS verifies the variable still holds its last known value; if so it changes it, if not another thread got in the way, so the attempting method sees the change did not happen and retries.
  - Logical shape: loop reading `currentValue` and retry while `currentValue != compareAndSwap(currentValue, newValue)`.
- **Know why locks cost more** - `synchronized` always acquires a lock even when no second thread is trying to update the same value; intrinsic locks have improved from version to version but are still costly. Nonblocking code assumes contention is rare, detects collisions, and retries, which is almost always less costly than acquiring a lock even in moderate to high contention.

### Knowing Your Library: Nonthread-Safe Classes

- **Treat these as inherently not thread safe** - `SimpleDateFormat`, database connections, containers in `java.util`, servlets.
- **Never treat a sequence of thread-safe calls as thread safe** - some collection classes have individual thread-safe methods, but any operation involving more than one method call is not thread safe.
  - Failure mode: `if(!hashTable.containsKey(someKey)) hashTable.put(someKey, new SomeValue());` - another thread can add the value between `containsKey` and `put`.
- **Fix a multi-call race with one of three options**
  - Client-based locking: lock the `HashTable` first and make sure every other user of it does the same, e.g. wrap the check-then-put in `synchronized(map) { ... }`.
  - Server-based locking: wrap the `HashTable` in its own object exposing a different API and put the check-then-put inside a single `synchronized putIfAbsent(K key, V value)` method, using an ADAPTER.
  - Use the thread-safe collections: `ConcurrentHashMap` with `map.putIfAbsent(key, value)`; the collections in `java.util.concurrent` provide operations like `putIfAbsent()` precisely to accommodate such compound operations.

### Dependencies Between Methods Can Break Concurrent Code

- **Never let a client depend on two synchronized methods of a shared object** - synchronizing each method individually does not protect a client that calls two of them, because one call can have a side effect that invalidates the result of the other.
  - Failure mode with an iterator whose `hasNext()`/`next()`/`getNextValue()` are all `synchronized`: thread 1 gets `hasNext() == true`, is preempted; thread 2 gets `true`, calls `next()`, which as a side effect makes `hasNext()` false; thread 1 resumes still believing `hasNext()` is true, calls `next()`, and runs past the end of the iterator.
  - This fault only manifests during the final iteration, so it is subtle, appears long after a system is in production, and is hard to track down.
  - The `Iterator` interface is inherently not thread-safe; it was never designed for use by multiple threads.
- **Choose deliberately among the three options** - tolerate the failure; solve it by changing the client (client-based locking); solve it by changing the server, which additionally changes the client (server-based locking).

#### Tolerate the Failure

- **Only tolerate a failure when you can set things up so it causes no harm** - for example the client catches the exception and cleans up. This is a bit sloppy, rather like cleaning up memory leaks by rebooting at midnight.

#### Client-Based Locking

- **If you must use client-based locking, every client must take the lock** - each client introduces its own `synchronized` block around the whole compound operation.

```java
// GOOD (client-based locking)
while (true) {
  int nextValue;
  synchronized (iterator) {
    if (!iterator.hasNext()) break;
    nextValue = iterator.next();
  }
  doSometingWith(nextValue);
}
```

- **Know the two costs of client-based locking** - the per-client lock duplication violates the DRY principle, and the strategy is risky because every programmer using the server must remember to lock before use and unlock when done; one forgotten lock among hundreds of call sites produces intermittent, near-unfindable corruption.
- **Accept client-based locking only when forced** - it might be necessary if the code uses non-thread-safe third-party tools.

#### Server-Based Locking

- **In general you should prefer server-based locking** - move the compound operation into the server and change the API to be multithread aware; the client then does a null check instead of calling `hasNext()` and `next()`.

```java
// GOOD (server-based locking)
public synchronized Integer getNextOrNull() {
  if (nextValue < 100000) return nextValue++;
  else return null;
}
```

- **Reasons to prefer server-based locking**
  - It reduces repeated code: clients use the object without writing additional locking code.
  - It allows better performance: you can swap a thread-safe server for a non-thread-safe one in a single-threaded deployment and avoid all overhead.
  - It reduces the possibility of error: all it takes is one programmer forgetting to lock properly.
  - It enforces a single policy: the policy lives in one place, the server, not in many clients.
  - It reduces the scope of the shared variables: the client is unaware of them or how they are locked, so when things break there are fewer places to look.
- **When you do not own the server code** - use an ADAPTER to change the API and add locking (a wrapper whose `synchronized getNextOrNull()` calls the unsafe `hasNext()`/`next()` pair), or better yet use the thread-safe collections with extended interfaces.

### Increasing Throughput

- **Share the iterator, not the worker** - one synchronized producer (e.g. a `PageIterator` handing out page contents by URL) can be shared among many threads, each using its own instance of the non-shared worker (e.g. its own `PageReader`) to read and parse.
  - Release the per-request resource in a `finally` block inside the worker (`method.releaseConnection()`), and handle the exception rather than letting it escape.
- **Keep the synchronized block as small as possible** - it should contain just the critical section deep inside the shared object. It is always better to synchronize as little as possible as opposed to synchronizing as much as possible.
- **Compute throughput before threading** - with I/O time to retrieve a page averaging 1 second, processing time to parse averaging .5 seconds, I/O requiring 0 percent of the CPU and processing requiring 100 percent:
  - Single thread: total execution time for N pages is 1.5 seconds * N; 13 pages takes about 19.5 seconds.
  - Three threads: process-bound parsing overlaps with I/O-bound reading, so in an idealized world the processor is fully utilized, each one-second read overlaps two parses, giving two pages per second - three times the single-threaded throughput.
- **Only parallelize when order and independence allow it** - the multithreaded gain assumes pages can be retrieved in any order and processed independently.

### Deadlock

- **Treat deadlock as a design problem, not a debugging problem** - it happens in the field, takes weeks to solve, and adding debug statements typically changes the code enough that the deadlock moves to a different situation and takes months to recur. Never leave debugging output in as the "fix" just because the problem "disappeared."
- **Four conditions are required for deadlock; all four must hold** - Mutual exclusion, Lock & wait, No preemption, Circular wait. Break any one of these conditions and deadlock is not possible.
  - **Mutual exclusion** - multiple threads need the same resources, and those resources cannot be used by multiple threads at the same time and are limited in number. Examples: a database connection, a file open for write, a record lock, a semaphore.
  - **Lock & wait** - once a thread acquires a resource, it will not release it until it has acquired all the other resources it requires and has completed its work.
  - **No preemption** - one thread cannot take resources away from another; the only way another thread gets a held resource is for the holder to release it.
  - **Circular wait** - also called the deadly embrace: T1 holds R1 and needs R2 while T2 holds R2 and needs R1.
- **Canonical deadlock scenario to recognize** - two finite pools (10 database connections, 10 MQ connections to a master repository) and two operations that acquire them in opposite orders (create: master repository then database; update: database then master repository). Ten create threads take all database connections, ten update threads take all master repository connections, each waits on the other, and the system never recovers.

#### Breaking Mutual Exclusion

- **Sidestep mutual exclusion where you can** - use resources that allow simultaneous use, for example `AtomicInteger`; increase the number of resources so it equals or exceeds the number of competing threads; check that all your resources are free before seizing any.
- **Expect sidestepping mutual exclusion to often be impossible** - most resources are limited in number and do not allow simultaneous use, and it is not uncommon for the identity of the second resource to be predicated on the results of operating on the first.

#### Breaking Lock & Wait

- **Refuse to wait** - check each resource before you seize it, and release all resources and start over if you run into one that is busy.
- **Know the two failure modes that refusing to wait introduces**
  - Starvation: one thread keeps being unable to acquire the resources it needs, perhaps because it needs a unique combination that seldom all become available. Results in low CPU utilization.
  - Livelock: several threads get into lockstep, each acquiring one resource then releasing one resource over and over. Especially likely with simplistic CPU scheduling algorithms (embedded devices, simplistic hand-written thread balancing algorithms). Results in high and useless CPU utilization.
- **Use refusing to wait as the fallback strategy** - both of its failure modes cause poor throughput, but it is better than nothing and can almost always be implemented if all else fails.

#### Breaking Preemption

- **Let threads take resources away from other threads** - usually via a simple request mechanism: when a thread finds a resource busy, it asks the owner to release it; if the owner is itself waiting for another resource, it releases them all and starts over.
- **Weigh the preemption tradeoff before choosing it** - a thread is allowed to wait for a resource, which decreases the number of startovers, but managing all those requests can be tricky.

#### Breaking Circular Wait

- **Prefer a global ordering of resource acquisition** - this is the most common approach to preventing deadlock; for most systems it requires no more than a simple convention agreed to by all parties. If all threads agree on a global ordering of resources and allocate in that order, deadlock is impossible.
- **Know the two problems a global acquisition ordering can cause**
  - The order of acquisition might not correspond to the order of use, so a resource acquired at the start might not be used until the end, locking resources longer than strictly necessary.
  - Sometimes you cannot impose an order: if the ID of the second resource comes from an operation performed on the first, ordering is not feasible.
- **There is no free deadlock strategy** - some lead to starvation, others make heavy use of the CPU and reduce responsiveness. TANSTAAFL (there ain't no such thing as a free lunch).
- **Isolate the thread-related part of your solution** - doing so allows tuning and experimentation and is a powerful way to gain the insights needed to determine the best strategies.

### Testing Multithreaded Code

- **Write a test that proves the concurrency bug exists** - to prove that an unsynchronized `takeNextId() { return nextId++; }` is broken:
  1. Remember the current value of `nextId`.
  2. Create two threads, both of which call `takeNextId()` once.
  3. Verify that `nextId` is two more than what you started with.
  4. Run this until you demonstrate that `nextId` was only incremented by one instead of two.
  - Mechanics: hold the shared instance in a `final` local so an anonymous inner `Runnable` can use it; in each loop pass record the starting value and set the expected result to two more than it; start both threads then `join()` both before reading the ending value; `return`, which passes the test, the moment the ending value differs from the expected result, because the goal was to prove brokenness; call `fail("Should have exposed a threading issue but it did not.")` after the loop, meaning either the code is not broken or you did not run enough iterations.
- **Know that a loop-until-failure concurrency test is unreliable, and by how much** - the loop count is a balancing act between demonstrating failure and taking too long.
  - At 50,000 iterations the vast majority of runs will not detect the problem.
  - Detecting it truly requires over one million iterations; in ten executions with a loop count of 1,000,000 the problem occurred only once.
  - Reliable failures probably need an iteration count well over one hundred million.
  - A count tuned to fail reliably on one machine will probably have to be retuned for another machine, operating system, or JVM version.
- **Monte Carlo Testing** - make tests flexible so they can be tuned, then run them over and over, say on a test server, randomly changing the tuning values. If the tests ever fail, the code is broken. Start writing those tests early so a continuous integration server starts running them soon, and carefully log the conditions under which a test failed.
- **Run the test on every one of the target deployment platforms** - repeatedly, continuously. The longer the tests run without failure, the more likely either the production code is correct or the tests are not adequate to expose problems.
- **Run the tests on a machine with varying loads** - simulate loads close to a production environment if you can.
- **Expect a poor chance of finding threading problems even with Monte Carlo testing, every target platform and varying loads** - the most insidious problems have such a small cross section that they only occur once in a billion opportunities; such problems are the terror of complex systems.

#### Tool Support for Testing Thread-Based Code

- **Instrument code to make non-thread-safe failures more likely** - IBM's ConTest instruments classes to make it more likely that non-thread-safe code fails.
- **Procedure for using ConTest**
  1. Write tests and production code, including tests specifically designed to simulate multiple users under varying loads.
  2. Instrument test and production code with ConTest.
  3. Run the tests.
- **Expect instrumentation to expose the failure far sooner** - success rate went from roughly one failure in ten million iterations to roughly one failure in thirty iterations; observed loop values across runs after instrumentation: 13, 23, 0, 54, 16, 14, 6, 69, 107, 49, 2. Instrumented classes fail much earlier and with much greater reliability.

### Full Code Examples: Client/Server

- **Shut a server loop down with a `volatile` flag** - declare `volatile boolean keepProcessing = true`, loop `while (keepProcessing)` around `serverSocket.accept()`, and have `stopProcessing()` set the flag false and close the server socket.
- **Set a socket timeout** - construct the server with a millisecond timeout applied via `serverSocket.setSoTimeout(millisecondsTimeout)`.
- **Do not print stack traces for `SocketException`** - the accept-loop handler prints the stack trace only when the exception is not a `SocketException`.
- **Close sockets in dedicated close-ignoring-exception helpers** - one per socket type; null-check, `close()` inside `try`, and swallow `IOException` on close.
- **Guard against a null socket** - `process(socket)` returns immediately if the socket is null.
- **Keep message framing in one utility** - a single `MessageUtils` with `sendMessage(Socket, String)` (get `OutputStream`, wrap in `ObjectOutputStream`, `writeUTF`, `flush`) and `getMessage(Socket)` (get `InputStream`, wrap in `ObjectInputStream`, `readUTF`).
- **Convert the nonthreaded server to a threaded one by changing only `process`** - take the socket as `final`, move the existing body into an anonymous `Runnable`, then create and start a `Thread` with it. No other change to the server is required.

```java
// GOOD
void process(final Socket socket) {
  if (socket == null) return;
  Runnable clientHandler = new Runnable() {
    public void run() { /* existing per-client body */ }
  };
  Thread clientConnection = new Thread(clientHandler);
  clientConnection.start();
}
```

# BOOK 2 - Refactoring, 2nd Edition (Martin Fowler)

## Refactoring: Ch1 Refactoring: A First Example

### When to refactor at all

- **Refactor first, then add the feature** - when you have to add a feature to a program but the code is not structured in a convenient way, first refactor the program to make it easy to add the feature, then add the feature. If the program lacks structure, it is usually easier to add structure to the program first, and then make the change you need.
- **Let required change drive refactoring** - it is the changes you actually have to make that drive the need to perform refactoring. If the code works and doesn't ever need to change, it's perfectly fine to leave it alone; it would be nice to improve it, but unless someone needs to understand it, it isn't causing real harm.
  - As soon as someone does need to understand how that code works and struggles to follow it, you have to do something about it.
- **Short code may need no structure** - a very short program does not require any deep structure to be comprehensible, so leaving it as it is can be tolerable. Judge structure against the size and change rate the code will actually have (imagine the same program at hundreds of lines long, where a single inline function is hard to understand), not against aesthetics.
- **Structure is not aesthetics, it is change cost** - a poorly designed system is hard to change because it is difficult to figure out what to change and how the changes will interact with existing code; if it is hard to figure out what to change, there is a good chance you will make mistakes and introduce bugs.
- **Copy-and-paste rule** - if you are writing a program that will never change again, copy-and-paste is fine. If it's a long-lived program, then duplication is a menace: any change to the shared logic forces you to update both copies and ensure they are updated consistently.
  - When a function must support a second output format, do not wrap a conditional around every statement that adds a string to the result; that adds a host of complexity to the function. Do not take the other common option either - copying the whole function and changing the copy to emit the other format sets up all sorts of problems for the future.
  - As the rules grow in complexity it gets harder to figure out where to make the changes and harder to make them without a mistake.
- **Expect the requirement to change again** - assume whatever scheme the users come up with, they will change it again within six months; feature requests come not as single spies but in battalions. Structure for that.
- **Camping rule** - always leave the code base healthier than when you found it. It will never be perfect, but it should be better.
- **Balance refactoring against features** - strike a balance between all the refactorings you could do and adding new features; most people underprioritize refactoring, but there still is a balance.
- **The test of good code** - the true test of good code is how easy it is to change it. Code should be obvious: when someone needs to make a change, they should be able to find the code to be changed easily and to make the change quickly without introducing any errors. Pay attention to what is getting between the team and that ideal, then refactor to get closer to it.

### Definitions

- **Refactoring (noun)** - a change made to the internal structure of software to make it easier to understand and cheaper to modify without changing its observable behavior.
- **Refactoring (verb)** - to restructure software by applying a series of refactorings without changing its observable behavior. A couple of hours of refactoring means applying a few dozen individual refactorings.
- **Refactoring is not "any code cleanup"** - refactoring is applying small behavior-preserving steps and making a big change by stringing together a sequence of those behavior-preserving steps. Each individual refactoring is either pretty small, or built out of steps that are.
- **"Compile" means whatever makes the code executable** - in JavaScript that may mean nothing, or moving code to an output directory and/or running a processor such as Babel.

### The first step: tests

- **Never start refactoring without a solid suite of tests** - before you start refactoring, make sure you have a solid suite of tests for that section of code. The tests are essential because even refactorings structured to avoid most opportunities for introducing bugs are executed by a fallible human; the larger the program, the more likely a change breaks something inadvertently.
- **Tests must be self-checking** - it is vital to make tests self-checking. They either go green (all output identical to reference values) or red (a list of the failures, i.e. the lines that turned out differently). Without self-checking you spend time hand-checking values, which slows you down. Modern testing frameworks provide all the features needed to write and run self-checking tests, so there is no excuse.
- **Make tests trivially runnable and fast** - set the tests up in a testing framework so they run with a single keystroke and take only a few seconds; you will run them very often.
- **Test by comparing to hand-checked reference output** - for a function returning a string, build a few inputs (invoices with several performances of various play kinds), generate the outputs, and string-compare against reference strings you have hand-checked.
- **Tests are a bug detector against your own mistakes** - by writing what you want twice, in the code and in the test, you must make the mistake consistently in both places to fool the detector. Building tests costs time but repays it with considerable interest through less debugging.
- **Add tests at the seam you create** - when a refactoring produces an intermediate data structure, add tests that probe that intermediate data structure; then you can ignore the downstream formatting code so long as you produce the same output data.

### The rhythm: compile-test-commit

- **Test after every refactoring, however simple** - immediately compile and test after each change, however simple that change was. Small changes plus testing after each change is the essence of the refactoring process. Then, when you make a mistake, you only have a small change to consider to spot the error. Do it at every opportunity even when it gets tedious; skipping it gives mistakes the chance to bite you, and if you try to do too much, a mistake forces a tricky debugging episode that can take a long time.
- **Commit after each successful refactoring** - use a version control system that allows private commits (git, mercurial); commit after each successful refactoring so you can easily get back to a working state. Squash changes into more significant commits before pushing to a shared repository.
- **On a red test you cannot immediately explain, revert** - if a test fails during a refactoring and you can't immediately see and fix the problem, revert to the last good commit and redo what you just did with smaller steps. This only works because you commit so frequently.
- **When it gets hard, take shorter steps** - whenever things get difficult, the first reaction is to take shorter steps; small steps are the key to moving quickly, particularly with difficult code.
- **Each step must leave the code working** - every step leaves the code in a working state that compiles and passes its tests. You go faster when you take tiny steps, the code is never broken, and you compose those small steps into substantial changes.
- **Do renames one at a time** - even when you have several renames planned and they look trivial together, perform them individually with a compile-test-commit after each.
- **Use an automated refactoring when the tooling has one** - Extract Function is a common refactoring to automate; reach for the IDE key sequence where robust support exists. Where it does not (JavaScript at time of writing), do it manually and be careful with locally scoped variables.
- **A bare compile after moving code catches only syntax errors** - compiling after copying a function into its new context will catch syntax errors in the new function but little more than that; it is still a useful step, and it is not a substitute for the test run.

### Understanding and naming

- **Move insight out of your head into the code** - understanding held in your head is a notoriously volatile form of storage. When you conclude what a chunk of code does, persist that conclusion by turning the chunk into its own function named after what it does, so you never have to figure it out again.
- **The positive feedback loop** - read the code, gain some insight, and use refactoring to move that insight from your head back into the code; clearer code is easier to understand, leading to deeper insights.
- **Decomposition only pays if names are good** - breaking a large function into smaller ones only adds value if the names are good; with good names you don't have to read the function body to see what it does.
- **Name now, rename later** - it's hard to get names right the first time, so use the best name you can think of for the moment and don't hesitate to rename later. It often takes a second pass through the code to realize what the best name really is.
- **Never be afraid to change names to improve clarity** - good code should clearly communicate what it is doing and variable names are key. With good find-and-replace tools it is usually not difficult; testing, and static typing where the language supports it, will highlight any occurrences you miss. With automated refactoring tools it is trivial to rename even widely used functions.
- **Always name a function's return value `result`** - a coding standard so the role of the variable is always known.
- **Name a parameter after its type with an indefinite article** - `aPerformance`, `aPlay`, `aNumber`. In a dynamically typed language such as JavaScript it is useful to keep track of types this way. Use a role-specific name instead only when there is specific role information to capture.
- **Pick the name that highlights the salient fact, and keep it short in-scope** - reject a name that does not convey enough of what the function does, and reject one that is too long-winded for the scope it is used in. For a currency-formatting function used inside a string template in a small scope, `format` conveys too little and `formatAsUSD` is too long-winded, so name it `usd` because formatting a currency amount is the thing to highlight.
- **Use a deliberate throwaway name to break a name collision** - when the best name for an extracted function is already taken by the variable you are about to delete, extract with a random placeholder name (e.g. `appleSauce`), compile-test-commit, inline the variable, then rename the function properly with another compile-test-commit.
- **Delete comments that the extraction made redundant or wrong** - after extracting, remove the unnecessary comment; check for comments that are downright misleading (a `// add extra credit for every ten comedy attendees` comment sitting over `Math.floor(audience / 5)`).

### Local variables and temporaries

- **Remove local variables before doing extractions** - the great benefit of removing local variables is that it makes extractions much easier because there is less local scope to deal with; usually take out local variables before doing any extractions.
- **Temporary variables encourage long routines** - temps are only useful within their own routine, so they encourage long, complex routines. Replace them.
- **For a loop accumulator, shadow and return** - an accumulator updated on each pass of the loop cannot simply be passed in: initialize a shadow of it inside the extracted function and return it, with the caller doing `acc += extracted(...)`.
- **Recompute derived values instead of passing them** - a variable computed from the loop variable need not be a parameter at all; recalculate it inside the callee via a query function.
- **Replace a function-valued temp with a declared function** - when a temp holds a function value, replace it with a declared function. (This refactoring has no catalog name: it is simple to do and relatively rare.)
- **Nest extracted functions inside the container when the language allows** - when extracting a helper used only by its container in a language with nested functions such as JavaScript, extract it as a nested function; then you don't have to pass data that is already inside the containing function's scope, which is one less issue to deal with.

### Performance

- **Ignore performance while refactoring, most of the time** - repeating a lookup three times instead of once, or rerunning a loop, usually has a negligible effect; the performance of software usually depends on just a few parts of the code, and changes anywhere else don't make an appreciable difference.
- **Do not trust performance intuition** - most programmers, even experienced ones, are poor judges of how code actually performs; intuitions are broken by clever compilers, modern caching techniques, and the like. If you timed such a change before and after, you would probably not notice any significant change in speed, and that is usually the case.
- **"Mostly" isn't "alwaysly"** - sometimes a refactoring will have a significant performance implication. Even then, usually go ahead and do it, because it is much easier to tune the performance of well-factored code.
- **If a refactoring slows things down, finish refactoring first, then tune** - performance tuning afterwards may lead to reversing some of the earlier refactoring, but most of the time the refactoring enables a more effective tuning enhancement instead, giving code that is both clearer and faster.

### Data and structure

- **Treat data as immutable as much as you can** - mutable state quickly becomes something rotten. When enriching a record, copy it first rather than modifying the data passed into the function (`const result = Object.assign({}, aPerformance)`, a shallow copy).
- **Follow the host language's idiom even when you'd prefer a helper** - `Object.assign({}, x)` is so baked into JavaScript usage that a hand-written copy function would look out of place.
- **Store money as integer cents** - it avoids the dangers of storing fractional monetary values as floats while still allowing arithmetic operators; the formatting function must therefore do the division by 100, so the division is not duplicated at each call site.
- **Pass an explicit parameter rather than relying on enclosing scope** - when a function you have moved or extracted needs a data structure that is already within its scope at the new location, prefer passing that data structure to it as an explicit parameter instead of reading it from the enclosing scope.
- **Move a shared helper up to the level that all users can reach** - as soon as a second caller outside the helper's current container needs it, move the helper up to the level (top level if necessary) where every user can reach it.
- **Accept more lines in exchange for modularity** - decomposing a function into named functions produces more code than you started with (44 lines became 70, not counting the second renderer), mostly due to the extra wrapping involved in putting things in functions. If all else is equal, more code is bad, but rarely is all else equal: the extra code breaks the logic into identifiable parts, separating calculation from layout, and allows a second output format with no duplication of the calculations. Brevity is the soul of wit, but clarity is the soul of evolvable software.

### Named refactorings

#### Extract Function

- **Inverse** - Inline Function.

```js
// BAD
let thisAmount = 0;
switch (play.type) { /* ...charge rules... */ }
// GOOD
let thisAmount = amountFor(perf, play);
function amountFor(perf, play) { let thisAmount = 0; /* ...rules... */ return thisAmount; }
```

- **Motivation** - apply when you can identify a chunk of code that separates one part of the overall behavior, and you can name it after what it does; this persists your understanding of the chunk into the code. Extract when the containing function is long enough that a single inline function is hard to understand.
- **Mechanics as applied**
  1. Identify the chunk that is one coherent piece of behavior (a switch statement sitting in the middle of a loop body is a typical first candidate).
  2. Look in the fragment for any variables that will no longer be in scope once the code is extracted into its own function, and classify each as used-but-not-modified or modified.
  3. Pass in as parameters the variables that are used but not modified.
  4. With exactly one modified variable, return it and bring its initialization inside the extracted code. (With more than one modified variable, more care is needed.)
  5. Name the new function after what it does.
  6. Replace the original chunk with a call that populates the original variable.
  7. Compile and test.
  8. Commit.
  9. Look at what you just extracted for quick and easy clarifications - rename the internal variables and the parameters - each with its own compile-test-commit.

#### Inline Variable

- **Inverse** - Extract Variable.

```js
// BAD
const play = playFor(perf);
result += `${play.name}`;
// GOOD
result += `${playFor(perf).name}`;
```

- **Motivation** - apply when a temp is set from an expression or call and is not updated again; removing it removes locally scoped names that complicate later extractions. Also the final step that removes a variable after its computation has been extracted into a query function.
- **Mechanics as applied**
  1. Ensure the variable's right-hand side has already been extracted into a function (so the inlined expression is a single call).
  2. Replace every reference to the variable with the call.
  3. Delete the variable declaration.
  4. Compile, test, commit.

#### Replace Temp with Query

```js
// BAD
const play = plays[perf.playID];   // temp used across the loop body
// GOOD
function playFor(aPerformance) { return plays[aPerformance.playID]; }
```

- **Motivation** - apply to get rid of temporaries that create locally scoped names complicating extraction; especially worthwhile before breaking down a long function. Accept the extra recomputation.
- **Mechanics as applied**
  1. Extract the right-hand side of the assignment into a query function.
  2. Compile, test, commit.
  3. Apply Inline Variable to remove the temp, so every use calls the query.
  4. Compile, test, commit.
- **For an accumulator temp built up inside a loop, apply this four-step sequence** - each step followed by compile, test, and commit:
  1. Split Loop to isolate the accumulation.
  2. Slide Statements to bring the initializing code next to the accumulation.
  3. Extract Function to create a function for calculating the total.
  4. Inline Variable to remove the variable completely.

#### Change Function Declaration

- **Motivation** - apply to rename a function or to add/remove a parameter, including removing a parameter that the callee can now compute for itself.
- **Mechanics as applied (removing a parameter, in two steps)**
  1. Inside the callee, replace every use of the parameter with the new query call, leaving the parameter in place.
  2. Compile, test, commit.
  3. Delete the parameter from the declaration and from every call site.
  4. Compile, test, commit.

#### Split Loop

```js
// BAD
for (let perf of invoice.performances) { volumeCredits += ...; result += ...; totalAmount += ...; }
// GOOD
for (let perf of invoice.performances) { result += ...; totalAmount += ...; }
for (let perf of invoice.performances) { volumeCredits += volumeCreditsFor(perf); }
```

- **Motivation** - apply to separate one accumulation from everything else in the loop body, so that accumulation can then be extracted and the variable removed. Ignore the intuition that repeating a loop is costly.
- **Mechanics as applied**
  1. Duplicate the loop header.
  2. Leave only the statements for the one concern in each copy.
  3. Compile, test, commit.

#### Slide Statements

- **Motivation** - apply to gather together everything that touches one variable, in particular to bring a declaration/initialization next to the loop that updates it; this makes Replace Temp with Query possible.
- **Mechanics as applied**
  1. Move the declaration down so it sits immediately before the loop that uses it.
  2. Compile, test, commit.

#### Replace Loop with Pipeline

```js
// BAD
let result = 0;
for (let perf of data.performances) { result += perf.amount; }
return result;
// GOOD
return data.performances.reduce((total, p) => total + p.amount, 0);
```

- **Motivation** - apply to an accumulation loop over a collection once the loop body is a pure accumulation of a field.
- **Mechanics as applied** - rewrite the loop as a `reduce` with the seed value; compile, test, commit.

#### Split Phase

```js
// BEFORE: statement() interleaves calculation and text layout
// AFTER:  statement(invoice, plays) -> renderPlainText(createStatementData(invoice, plays))
```

- **Motivation** - apply to divide logic into a phase that calculates the data and a phase that renders it, where the first phase creates an intermediate data structure that it passes to the second. Apply when you need a second renderer (text and HTML) using the same calculations and refuse to copy the calculation code.
- **Mechanics as applied**
  1. Apply Extract Function to the code that makes up the second phase, taking its nested functions with it into a new top-level function.
  2. Compile, test, commit.
  3. Create an empty object to act as the intermediate data structure and pass it in as an extra argument to the second-phase function.
  4. Compile, test, commit.
  5. Examine each remaining argument of the second-phase function; move the data it supplies into the intermediate structure one field at a time, updating the renderer to read `data.x`, and delete the argument once nothing uses it. Compile-test-commit after each field. The target state is that all the calculation code sits in the first phase and the renderer operates solely on data passed to it through the `data` parameter.
  6. Where the renderer needs derived data, enrich each element record: first `map` over the collection with an enrich function that only copies the record, compile-test-commit, then add one derived field per step by applying Move Function to the calculating function and switching the renderer to the new field. Compile-test-commit after each.
  7. Move the aggregate totals into the intermediate structure last, passing the structure to them as an explicit parameter.
  8. Extract all the first-phase code into its own function.
  9. Compile, test, commit.
  10. Move that function to its own file, renaming its returned variable to the `result` convention, and import it.
  11. Compile, test, commit. Only now write the second renderer.

#### Move Function

- **Motivation** - apply when a function belongs in a different context (for example, into a class that hosts the calculations). Casual moves between nested functions need no ceremony; step through the full refactoring when the change of context is deeper.
- **Mechanics as applied**
  1. Copy the logic over to its new context.
  2. Adjust the code to fit its new home (`aPerformance` becomes `this.performance`, `playFor(aPerformance)` becomes `this.play`).
  3. Compile to check for compile-time errors (this catches syntax errors and little more).
  4. Turn the original function into a delegating function that calls the new one.
  5. Compile, test, commit, to confirm the code works in its new home.
  6. Apply Inline Function to make callers call the new function directly.
  7. Compile, test, commit.
  8. Repeat the whole process for each further function being moved.

#### Inline Function

- **Inverse** - Extract Function.
- **Motivation** - apply as the final step of Move Function: once the original function is only delegating, replace the call to the delegating function with a direct call to the moved function (for example `result.amount = calculator.amount;`), then compile-test-commit.

#### Replace Constructor with Factory Function

```js
// BAD
const calculator = new PerformanceCalculator(aPerformance, aPlay);
// GOOD
const calculator = createPerformanceCalculator(aPerformance, aPlay);
function createPerformanceCalculator(aPerformance, aPlay) { return new PerformanceCalculator(aPerformance, aPlay); }
```

- **Motivation** - required before subclassing in JavaScript because JavaScript constructors can't return subclasses; the creation function selects which subclass to return.
- **Mechanics as applied**
  1. Add a factory function that only forwards to the constructor.
  2. Change callers to use the factory function.
  3. Compile, test, commit.
  4. Add the subclass selection inside the factory once subclasses exist.

#### Replace Type Code with Subclasses

- **Motivation** - apply to create the inheritance structure that Replace Conditional with Polymorphism requires; you cannot replace the conditional until a class hierarchy hosts the varying behavior.
- **Mechanics as applied**
  1. Create a class to host the functions that vary by type code, holding the subject and its type record (`this.performance`, `this.play`).
  2. Move the varying functions into that class (Move Function).
  3. Apply Replace Constructor with Factory Function.
  4. Create empty subclasses, one per type code (`TragedyCalculator`, `ComedyCalculator`).
  5. Switch on the type code in the factory to return the right subclass; keep a `default` branch that throws `unknown type: ${aPlay.type}`.
  6. Compile, test, commit.

#### Replace Conditional with Polymorphism

```js
// BAD
get amount() { switch (this.play.type) { case "tragedy": ... case "comedy": ... default: throw ... } }
// GOOD
class TragedyCalculator extends PerformanceCalculator { get amount() { /* tragedy rules */ } }
class ComedyCalculator  extends PerformanceCalculator { get amount() { /* comedy rules */ } }
```

- **Motivation** - apply when conditional logic keys off a type and that type plays a central role in the choice of calculations; conditional logic like this tends to decay as further modifications are made unless it is reinforced by more structural elements of the programming language.
  - There are various ways to introduce structure that makes the type explicit; type polymorphism is one natural approach, not the only one. Judge it against the situation.
  - The more functions there are that depend on the same type of polymorphism, the more useful this approach becomes: for example, the conditional lookup moves out of two functions (an amount calculation `amountFor` and a volume-credits calculation `volumeCreditsFor`) into a single creation function.
  - Prefer it when most future changes will be to this code; adding a new kind then requires only writing a new subclass and adding it to the creation function.
  - The code will increase in size; the benefit is that the calculations for each kind are grouped together.
- **Mechanics as applied**
  1. With the hierarchy in place, push one case of the conditional down into its subclass as an overriding method. Just having the method in the subclass is enough to override the superclass conditional.
  2. Optionally (paranoid check) replace that case in the superclass conditional with an explicit `throw` so you learn immediately if it is still reached. Throwing a bare string rather than a proper error object is acceptable only because this throw will live for a couple more minutes. Alternatively remove the case and let the `default` branch throw.
  3. Compile, test, commit.
  4. Move the next case down the same way. Compile, test, commit.
  5. When all cases are gone, do not simply delete the superclass method: leave a tombstone that throws `new Error('subclass responsibility')`.
- **Keep the common case as a superclass default** - when most kinds share one behavior and only some introduce a variation, leave the common case on the superclass and let the variations override it, calling `super` to extend rather than replace.

```js
// GOOD
class PerformanceCalculator { get volumeCredits() { return Math.max(this.performance.audience - 30, 0); } }
class ComedyCalculator extends PerformanceCalculator {
  get volumeCredits() { return super.volumeCredits + Math.floor(this.performance.audience / 5); }
}
```

- **Moving non-varying data into the calculator is optional but preferred** - moving data that does not vary polymorphically (such as the type record itself) into the calculator class is strictly not needed, but prefer to move it anyway, because keeping all the data transforms in one place makes the code clearer.
- **Choosing between returning the calculator and populating an intermediate structure** - where getters look like regular data access, as in JavaScript, the creation function can return the calculator itself instead of populating an intermediate data structure. Decide by who is using the downstream data structure; an intermediate data structure hides the decision to use a polymorphic calculator.

### Worked-example structure (what the three stages demonstrate)

- **Stage 1 - decompose the original function into nested functions** - extract each calculation, remove every local variable and temp, and rename to convention. Aim for a top-level entry function of seven lines that only lays out the printing, with all calculation logic in a handful of supporting functions; this makes each individual calculation and the overall flow easier to understand.
- **Stage 2 - apply Split Phase to separate calculation from printing** - produce a calculation function in its own file (`createStatementData`) plus a renderer (`renderPlainText`), and only then write the second output format (`htmlStatement` calling `renderHtml`), with no duplication of the calculations.
- **Stage 3 - introduce a polymorphic calculator for the calculation logic** - a base calculator class (`PerformanceCalculator`) with one subclass per type code (`TragedyCalculator`, `ComedyCalculator`), selected by a creation function (`createPerformanceCalculator`).
- **The charging and credit rules a polymorphic split of this kind encodes**

| Play type | Base amount | Audience surcharge | Per-head | Volume credits |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| tragedy | 40000 | +1000 per attendee over 30 | none | max(audience - 30, 0) |
| comedy | 30000 | +10000 + 500 per attendee over 20 | +300 per attendee | max(audience - 30, 0) + floor(audience / 5) |
| unknown | throw `unknown type: ${type}` | | | |

## Refactoring: Ch2 Principles in Refactoring

### Definition and Scope

- **Refactor in small steps only** - every refactoring is a small step or a combination of small steps, so the code never spends much time in a broken state and you can stop at any moment even if you have not finished.
  - If someone says their code was broken for a couple of days while they were refactoring, you can be pretty sure they were not refactoring.
  - Tiny steps let you go faster because they compose well and because you spend no time debugging - even when a single bigger step "would do".
