- **Distinguish refactoring from restructuring** - "restructuring" is any kind of reorganizing or cleaning up of a code base; refactoring is one particular kind of restructuring. Do not call arbitrary restructuring "refactoring".
- **Preserve observable behavior, not exact behavior** - "observable behavior" is deliberately loose: overall the code must do the same things it did before. It need not work exactly the same.
  - Extract Function alters the call stack, so performance characteristics might change; that is acceptable.
  - Module interfaces often do change, via refactorings such as Change Function Declaration and Move Function.
  - Any bug you notice during refactoring should still be present after refactoring. You may fix latent bugs that nobody has observed yet.
- **Separate refactoring from performance optimization by purpose** - both carry out code manipulations that do not change the overall functionality, but refactoring is always done to make the code "easier to understand and cheaper to modify" (which might speed things up or slow them down), while with performance optimization you only care about speeding up the program and are prepared to end up with code that is harder to work with if you really need that improvement.

### The Two Hats

- **Wear exactly one hat at a time** - divide your time between two distinct activities, adding functionality and refactoring, and always be aware of which hat you are wearing.
  - Adding functionality hat: do not change existing code; only add new capabilities. Measure progress by adding tests and getting them to work.
  - Refactoring hat: add no functionality; only restructure. Add no tests, unless you find a case missed earlier. Change tests only when you must accommodate an interface change.
- **Swap hats frequently** - swapping several times in ten minutes is normal and correct: try to add a capability, notice restructuring would make it easier, refactor, swap back, add the capability, refactor again when the new code reads awkwardly.

### Why Refactor

- **Refactoring is no "silver bullet"** - it is not the cure for all software ills; it is a valuable tool that can and should be used for several distinct purposes.
- **Refactor to stop design decay** - without refactoring the internal design decays as people change code for short-term goals without full comprehension of the architecture; the loss of structure is cumulative, because the harder the design is to see, the harder it is to preserve and the faster it decays further.
- **Eliminate duplicated code as the primary design improvement** - poorly designed code takes more code to do the same things, often literally doing the same thing in several places. The goal is not a smaller footprint (that effect is rarely significant); it is that the more code there is, the harder it is to modify correctly. Say everything once and only once - that is the essence of good design.
- **Optimize for the future human reader, not the compiler** - it does not matter if the computer takes a few more cycles; it matters greatly if a change takes a programmer a week instead of an hour. Refactor to make code better communicate its purpose.
- **Put everything you must remember into the code** - do not rely on remembering things about code you wrote; encode understanding so it does not have to be recalled.
- **Refactor to find bugs** - refactoring forces deep understanding of what the code does and puts that understanding back into the code; clarifying structure exposes the assumptions you made, to the point where bugs become unavoidable to spot.
- **Refactor to program faster** - this is the point that all other benefits reduce to. A good internal design makes it easy to find where to change, good modularity means understanding only a small subset of the code base, clear code means fewer introduced bugs and easier debugging.
  - Design Stamina Hypothesis: putting effort into good internal design increases the stamina of the software effort, allowing you to go faster for longer. It is a hypothesis, not proven.
  - Symptoms of the alternative: each new feature takes longer, bugs crop up that take even longer to fix, the code base becomes patches covering patches requiring archaeology, and developers wish for a blank slate.
- **Do not require design to be complete before coding** - the design can be formed and improved over time as needs change; since good up-front design is very difficult, refactoring is vital to achieving rapid functionality.

### When to Refactor

- **Refactor every hour you program** - refactoring is not a separate activity from programming, any more than you set aside time to write if statements. Do not put refactoring on the plan; most refactoring happens while doing other things.
- **Rule of Three** - the first time you do something, just do it. The second time you do something similar, you wince at the duplication but do the duplicate thing anyway. The third time you do something similar, you refactor. ("Three strikes, then you refactor.")
- **Refactor when you hit ugly code AND when the code is excellent** - it is a common error to treat refactoring as only fixing past mistakes or cleaning ugly code. Every piece of code embodies tradeoffs (how much to parameterize, where to draw lines between functions) that were correct for yesterday's features and may be wrong for today's. Clean code is easier to refactor when those tradeoffs must change.
- **Do not treat software as ever "done"** - often the fastest way to add a feature is to change existing code to make the addition easy; the changes in existing code can be greater than the new code.
  - "for each desired change, make the change easy (warning: this may be hard), then make the easy change".

#### Preparatory Refactoring

- **Refactor just before adding a feature** - the best time. If a function does almost all you need but has literal values that conflict, do not copy it and change the values; use Parameterize Function, then call it with the parameters you need.
  - Copy-paste creates duplication you must later find and change in both spots, and does not help with the next variation.
- **Refactor after locating a bug's cause, before fixing it** - unify the copied bits of code causing the error, or separate update logic from queries to remove the tangling that caused it. This increases the chance the bug stays fixed and reduces the chance of new ones in the same crevices.

#### Comprehension Refactoring

- **Whenever you have to think to understand code, ask whether refactoring can make that understanding immediately apparent** - triggers include awkwardly structured conditional logic and badly named functions that cost minutes to decode.
- **Move the understanding out of your head into the code** - your head is a poor record of details; code preserves it longer and makes it visible to colleagues. Then test that understanding by running the software to see if it still works.
- **Start with small details** - rename variables once you know what they are; chop a long function into smaller parts. As the code gets clearer, design-level insights appear that you could not have visualized in your head. Dismissing comprehension refactoring as fiddling means never seeing the opportunities hidden behind the confusion.

#### Litter-Pickup Refactoring

- **When the code is understandable but done badly, clean it with a time tradeoff in mind** - convoluted logic, or nearly identical functions replaceable by one parameterized function.
  - If it is easy to change, do it right away.
  - If it is a bit more effort, note it and fix it when the immediate task is done.
  - If it will take hours and there are more urgent things, still make it a little bit better.
- **Always leave the code better than you found it** - a little better each pass gets it fixed over time, and because refactoring never breaks the code, a job may take months while the code is never broken part way through.

#### Planned and Opportunistic Refactoring

- **Prefer opportunistic refactoring** - preparatory, comprehension and litter-pickup refactoring are all opportunistic, done as part of adding a feature or fixing a bug. Most refactoring effort should be the unremarkable, opportunistic kind.
- **Planned refactoring is not always wrong, but should be rare** - a team that has neglected refactoring often needs dedicated time, and a week spent refactoring now can repay itself over the next couple of months; even with regular refactoring a problem area can grow to need concerted effort.
- **Do not treat "separate refactoring commits from feature commits" as a principle** - the claimed advantage is independent review and approval, but refactorings are often closely interwoven with new features, separating them is not worth the time, and it can remove the context that justifies the refactoring. Each team should experiment; it is only worthwhile if it makes life easier.

#### Long-Term Refactoring

- **Most refactoring finishes in minutes to hours; for the rare multi-week efforts, be reluctant to have a team do dedicated refactoring** - examples: replacing an existing library with a new one, pulling a section of code out into a component shared with another team, fixing a nasty mess of dependencies that had been allowed to build up.
- **Agree to move the problem gradually over weeks** - whenever anyone goes near code in the refactoring zone, they move it a little in the agreed direction. This works because each small change leaves everything in a still-working state.
- **Branch By Abstraction for library replacement** - introduce a new abstraction that can act as an interface to either library; once calling code uses the abstraction, switching libraries is much easier.

#### Refactoring in a Code Review

- **Do regular code reviews** - they spread knowledge, pass experience from senior to junior developers, help more people understand more aspects of a large system, and are very important for writing clear code, because code that looks clear to its author may not be clear to the team.
- **Refactor during the review instead of only imagining the suggestion** - implement ideas then and there where they are easy; seeing the code with the suggestion in place produces a second level of ideas you would never have reached otherwise, and yields concrete implemented results rather than only suggestions.
- **Have the original author present at the review** - the common pull request model, where a reviewer looks at code without the original author, does not work too well; the author provides context and can fully appreciate the reviewers' intentions.
  - Best results: sit one-on-one with the original author, go through the code, and refactor as you go.
  - The logical conclusion of this style is pair programming: continuous code review embedded in programming.

#### Talking to Management

- **Never schedule weeks of pure refactoring as a way to explain refactoring** - refactoring has become a dirty word in places, with managers and customers believing it is either correcting errors made earlier or work that yields no valuable features. Scheduled weeks of pure refactoring exacerbate that, especially when what is really being done is not refactoring but less careful restructuring that causes breakages in the code base.
- **Justify refactoring economically, never morally** - the most dangerous trap is justifying refactoring in terms of "clean code", "good engineering practice", or similar moral reasons. The point is purely economic: we refactor because it makes us faster to add features and faster to fix bugs. Keep that in front of your own mind and in all communication.
- **With a technically savvy manager who understands the design stamina hypothesis, justify it openly** - such managers should encourage regular refactoring and watch for signs a team is not doing enough. Teams doing too much refactoring happens, but is much rarer than teams not doing enough.
- **With managers or customers who lack the technical awareness to see how code base health affects productivity: don't tell** - developers are professionals paid for expertise in delivering capabilities fast; a schedule-driven manager wants the fastest way, and how you do it is your responsibility. Refactoring first is faster both for adding a function whose design does not suit the change and for understanding software to fix a bug.
- **Beware self-inflicted suppression** - developers often squelch their own refactoring even when leadership favors it. A tech lead must show team members that they value improving code base health, and must mentor the less experienced heavily, because the judgment of when to refactor takes years to build.

#### When NOT to Refactor

- **Do not refactor a mess you do not need to modify** - ugly code you can treat as an API may remain ugly; refactoring only pays off when you need to understand how it works.
- **Do not refactor when rewriting is easier** - a tricky decision; often you cannot tell how easy refactoring is until you have spent some time trying. This requires judgment and experience and cannot be reduced to simple advice.
- **Skip a large-scale refactoring when the feature is very small** - a genuine tradeoff and a judgment call that cannot easily be described or quantified.
  - More inclined to refactor: preparatory refactoring that makes the new feature easier; ugliness you have already run into a couple of times.
  - More inclined not to refactor: code you rarely touch, so the inconvenience cost is seldom felt.
  - Delay when unsure what improvement to make - or try something as an experiment to see if it makes things better.
- **Assume too little rather than too much** - industry evidence is that too little refactoring is far more prevalent than too much; most people should refactor more often. You may be unable to judge the productivity difference between a healthy and a sickly code base because you have never experienced a healthy one, and the power that comes from easily combining existing parts into new configurations to quickly enable complicated new features.
  - The perception of refactoring as slowing down new features is still common and is perhaps the biggest barrier to people doing enough refactoring; the whole purpose of refactoring is to make us program faster, producing more value with less effort.

### Problems with Refactoring

#### Code Ownership

- **When you own all callers, change declaration and callers in one change** - apply Change Function Declaration to the declaration and all call sites together.
- **When callers are outside your ownership, use Rename Function and keep the old declaration as a pass-through to the new one** - this applies when the calling code belongs to another team whose repository you cannot write to, or the function is a published interface (an interface used by clients independent of those who declare it) where you cannot even tell if or how much it is used.
  - This complicates the interface, and that is the price of not breaking clients.
  - You may mark the old interface deprecated and retire it in time, but sometimes you must retain it forever.
  - Ownership boundaries do not prevent refactoring; they impose limitations.
- **Recommended against: fine-grained strong code ownership** - a single programmer owning and being the only one allowed to change a piece of code causes gyrations to maintain interfaces when going into the code base and editing would be far easier.
- **Prefer team ownership** - anyone in the team can modify the team's code even if someone else wrote it. Individual responsibility for an area should mean monitoring changes to it, not blocking them by default.
- **Consider an open-source-like model across teams** - people from other teams change a branch of your code and send the commit to be approved. This lets one team change the clients of their own functions and delete the old declarations once their commits to those clients are accepted. It is often a good compromise between strong code ownership and chaotic changes in large systems.

#### Branches

- **Prefer Continuous Integration (CI), also known as Trunk-Based Development: every team member integrates with mainline at least once per day** - this prevents branches diverging and greatly reduces merge complexity.
  - Distinguish merging from integration: merging mainline into your branch is one-way (only your branch changes); integrating is two-way - pull mainline changes into your branch, then push the result back into mainline, changing both.
  - CI is not free: you must use practices that keep the mainline healthy, learn to break large features into smaller chunks, and use feature toggles (aka feature flags) to switch off in-process features that cannot be broken down.
  - The dominant reason to favor CI is not merge simplicity but that it is far more compatible with refactoring.
- **Long feature branches and refactoring are mutually destructive** - refactorings make lots of little changes all over the code base, which are particularly prone to semantic merge conflicts such as renaming a widely used function. Feature-branching teams commonly find refactoring so exacerbates merge problems that they stop refactoring.
- **Merge difficulty grows exponentially with branch length** - integrating branches that are four weeks old is more than twice as hard as branches a couple of weeks old. Many people therefore argue for keeping feature branches short, perhaps just a couple of days; keep them even shorter than that.
  - **Frequently merging or rebasing from mainline into your branch does not solve this** - it reduces the pain but not the problem when several people are working on individual feature branches, because you do not see another person's changes until they integrate with mainline, and only then must you merge them into your feature branch, which may mean considerable work.
  - Feature-branch advocates claim it keeps the mainline clear of in-process code, provides a clear version history of feature additions, and allows features to be reverted easily should they cause problems; weigh those claims against the cost feature branches impose on refactoring.
- **Version control tools cannot save you from semantic conflicts** - modern tools merge program text well but are blind to code semantics: if you rename a function and someone else adds a call to the old name on their branch, the text merges cleanly and the code fails.
- **Feature branches are not banned** - if sufficiently short their problems are much reduced, and CI users usually also use branches but integrate them with mainline each day. They may be the right technique for open source projects with infrequent commits from programmers you do not know well. In a full-time development team the cost they impose on refactoring is excessive.
- **Even without full CI, integrate as frequently as possible** - there is objective evidence that teams using CI are more effective in software delivery.

#### Testing

- **In most cases, to refactor you need self-testing code** - a comprehensive test suite that runs quickly enough that you are not deterred from running it frequently.
  - When a test fails, look only at the change made since the tests last ran correctly - with frequent runs that is only a few lines, which makes the bug easy to find.
  - Mistakes are not a problem provided you catch them quickly; each refactoring is a small change, so if something breaks there is only a small change to inspect, and failing that you revert version control to the last working version.
  - Self-testing code also makes adding new features much safer.
  - Without self-testing code, the worry that refactoring risks introducing bugs is a reasonable one.
- **Exception: with good automated refactorings, you can refactor without running tests, provided you only use refactorings that are safely automated** - this removes a lot of nice refactorings from the menu but still leaves enough for useful benefit. Self-testing code is still preferable; treat this as an option in the toolkit. The self-testing-code requirement holds for manual refactoring; trusting the tool holds only for the subset of provably safe automated refactorings.
- **A refactoring style limited to provably safe refactorings requires carefully following the steps and is language-specific** - teams using it have done useful refactoring on large code bases with poor test coverage.
- **Self-testing code is the mechanism that catches semantic integration conflicts** - it is closely associated with Continuous Integration, is a component of Extreme Programming, and is a key part of Continuous Delivery.

#### Legacy Code

- **Use refactoring as a tool to understand a legacy system** - legacy code is often complex, frequently comes with poor tests, and is written by someone else; rename functions with misleading names so they make sense, and smooth out awkward programming constructs.
- **Never assume a big legacy system with no tests can be safely refactored into clarity** - you cannot. The lack of tests is the guarding dragon.
- **Add tests, knowing it is often much trickier than it sounds** - a system is usually only easy to put under test if it was designed with testing in mind, in which case it would already have tests.
- **Get the system under test by finding seams in the program where you can insert tests** - creating those seams involves refactoring, which is much more dangerous because it is done without tests, but is a necessary risk to make progress. Safe automated refactorings are a godsend here.
- **Do not try to refactor a complicated legacy mess into beautiful code all at once, even when you do have tests** - tackle it in relevant pieces, making each section you pass through a little bit better.
- **In a large system, do more refactoring in the areas you visit frequently** - frequent visits give a bigger payoff for making code easier to understand.
- **Write self-testing code from the start** - there is no shortcut out of a hole this deep.

#### Databases

- **Combine schema and access-code changes with data migration scripts that compose** - this is evolutionary database design and database refactoring; the composition of small migrations handles large changes.
- **To rename a field (column)** - as in Change Function Declaration, find the original declaration of the structure and all callers and change them in a single change; additionally write a small hunk of code that transforms any data using the old field to the new one, and store it in version control together with the declaration and access-routine changes. To migrate between two versions of the database, run all migration scripts that exist between the current copy and the desired version.
- **Keep each database change small yet complete** - the system must still run after applying the migration. Small changes are easy to write and can be strung into a sequence that significantly changes structure and stored data.
- **Unlike regular refactorings, database changes are often best separated over multiple releases to production** - this makes any change that causes a production problem easy to reverse.
- **Parallel change (also called expand-contract) sequence for renaming a field:**
  1. Commit the new database field but do not use it.
  2. Set up updates so they write both the old and new fields at once.
  3. Gradually move the readers over to the new field.
  4. Once all readers have moved and a little time has passed for bugs to show themselves, remove the now-unused old field.

### Refactoring, Architecture, and Yagni

- **Do not fix architecture before coding** - refactoring lets you significantly alter the architecture of software that has been running in production for years. The biggest issue with finishing architecture first is that it assumes requirements can be understood early on, which experience shows is often, even usually, unachievable: people only understand what they need once they have used the software.
- **Do not add flexibility mechanisms speculatively** - parameters added to handle anticipated circumstances are mechanisms, not a free lunch. They complicate the function for the one case it is used in right now; if you miss a parameter the existing parameterization makes adding more harder; and flexibility mechanisms are often wrong, because either the needs did not change as expected or the mechanism design was faulty. Most of the time they actually slow down your ability to react to change.
- **Build software that solves only the currently understood needs, but design it excellently for those needs** - then refactor the architecture as understanding of users' needs changes. This is simple design, incremental design, or yagni (originally an acronym for "you aren't going to need it").
  - Freely include mechanisms that do not increase complexity, such as small, well-named functions.
  - Any flexibility that complicates the software has to prove itself before inclusion.
  - If callers do not have different values for a parameter, do not add it to the parameter list. Parameterize Function is an easy refactoring to apply when the need arrives.
- **Estimate how hard the later refactoring would be** - only if it would be substantially harder to refactor later should you consider adding a flexibility mechanism now.
- **Yagni does not remove architectural thinking** - it is a different style of incorporating architecture and design into development, and it is not credible without the foundation of refactoring. Some refactoring changes are difficult and some preparatory thinking saves time; the balance has shifted toward dealing with issues later when they are better understood. This is the discipline of evolutionary architecture.

### Refactoring and the Wider Software Development Process

- **Refactoring's effectiveness is tied to the other practices the team uses** - its early adoption was as part of Extreme Programming (XP), whose practices are relatively unusual and interdependent: continuous integration, self-testing code, and refactoring (the latter two woven into test-driven development).
- **A team cannot really be agile without being capable and enthusiastic refactorers** - most "agile" projects only use the name; many aspects of the process must align to make refactoring a regular part of the work.
- **First foundation: self-testing code** - a suite of automated tests you can run and be confident that if you made a programming error, some test will fail.
- **Second foundation: Continuous Integration** - so each member can refactor when they need to without interfering with others' work; refactorings are shared quickly, nobody builds new work on interfaces being removed, and refactorings that will cause a problem for someone else's work are discovered quickly. Self-testing code is also a key element of CI, so there is a strong synergy between the three practices of self-testing code, continuous integration, and refactoring.
- **Refactoring and yagni reinforce each other in both directions** - refactoring and its prerequisites are a foundation for yagni, and yagni makes refactoring easier because a simple system is easier to change than one with lots of speculative flexibility.
- **With the trio in place, add Continuous Delivery to keep software always releasable** - this enables releasing many times a day, and even when that is not needed it reduces risk and lets releases be scheduled to satisfy business needs rather than technological constraints.

### Refactoring and Performance

- **Do not ignore performance in favor of design purity or in hope of faster hardware** - software has been rejected for being too slow, and faster machines merely move the goalposts.
- **The secret to fast software, in all but hard real-time contexts, is to write tunable software first and then tune it for sufficient speed** - refactoring can certainly make software slower in the short term, but it makes the software more amenable to performance tuning, so you end up well ahead.
- **Three approaches to writing fast software:**

| Approach | How it works | When to use |
|---|---|---|
| Time budgeting | As you decompose the design, give each component a budget for resources - time and footprint. The component must not exceed its budget, though a mechanism for exchanging budgeted resources is allowed. | Hard real-time systems where late data is always bad data (e.g. heart pacemakers). Inappropriate for other kinds of systems such as corporate information systems. |
| Constant attention | Every programmer, all the time, does whatever she can to keep performance high. | Common and intuitively attractive, but it does not work very well: the improvements are spread all around the program, each made with a narrow perspective of program behavior and often a misunderstanding of how compiler, runtime and hardware behave, and they make the program harder to work with, which slows development without usually making the software quicker. |
| Well-factored plus deliberate optimization exercise | Build the program well-factored, paying no attention to performance until a deliberate optimization exercise, then follow the profiler-driven process. | The default for all but hard real-time systems. |

- **In most programs most of the time is spent in a small fraction of the code** - optimizing all the code equally wastes 90 percent of the work on code that is not run much, plus all the time lost to reduced clarity.
- **Profiler-driven optimization process:**
  1. Run the program under a profiler that reports where it consumes time and space, to find the small part of the program where the hot spots lie.
  2. Focus on those hot spots, using the same optimizations the constant-attention approach would use, but with much more effect for less work.
  3. Make the changes in small steps, as in refactoring.
  4. After each step, compile, test, and rerun the profiler.
  5. If performance has not improved, back out the change.
  6. Continue finding and removing hot spots until performance satisfies your users.
- **Measure performance; never speculate** - even if you know exactly what is going on in your system, measure. Nine times out of ten what you learn will not be that you were right. Speculating about the cause and sketching designs for improvements before measuring produces no good at all.
- **A well-factored program helps optimization in two ways** - it lets you add functionality more quickly, which buys time to spend on performance tuning (with profiling ensuring that time goes to the right place); and it gives finer granularity for performance analysis, because the profiler leads you to smaller, easier-to-tune parts and clearer code shows your options and which tuning will work.
- **A clarity-motivated refactoring can itself be the optimization** - one case: half the time was spent creating date instances that all had the same couple of values and were almost all going through a string conversion with no external inputs involved, purely for typing convenience; most were used to build date ranges, and most of those ranges were empty. Extracting the "range that ends before it starts is empty" convention into a factory method for empty date ranges (a clarity change) then allowed returning a single constant empty date range instead of creating one every time. That doubled the speed of the system and took about five minutes.

### Automated Refactorings

- **Text manipulation is a crude automation and cannot be trusted without rerunning tests** - search/replace to change a name, or simple code reorganizing for Extract Variable. It is a handy first step, and editor macros are worth using when more sophisticated refactorings are unavailable.
- **Do not assume equal tool support** - actual automated-refactoring capabilities vary a fair bit, partly because of the tool and partly because of the limits of what automated refactoring can do in a given language.
- **Proper refactoring tools operate on the syntax tree, not the text** - manipulating the syntax tree is much more reliable at preserving what the code does; the tool must also figure out how to rerender the code as text in the editor view.
- **Many refactorings are made much safer in a statically typed language** - with `addClient` on both a `Salesman` and a `Server` class, a tool without static typing cannot tell which call sites are intended for the salesman; it can only list call sites for manual selection, which makes it a nonsafe refactoring that forces you to rerun the tests. With static typing the tool resolves the method to the correct class, so the equivalent Rename Function can be completely safe and automatic.
- **Tools go further, and this is a compelling reason to use an IDE over a text editor** - renaming a variable can prompt for changes to comments using that name; Extract Function can spot code duplicating the new function's body and offer to replace it with a call.
- **Run the test suite every so often even with mostly safe automated refactorings** - there are edge cases where tools slip up; less mature tools struggle with reflective calls such as `Method.invoke` in Java (more mature tools handle this quite well). Refactoring with a mix of automated and manual refactorings naturally produces frequent enough test runs.
  - Exception: for a menu-driven rename in a mature Java IDE, confidence in the tool can be sufficient not to bother running the test suite.
- **Language Servers** - when you prefer a text editor to an IDE, use a language server: software that forms a syntax tree and presents an API to text editors, supporting many editors with commands for sophisticated code analysis and refactoring; it is the route to syntax-tree power without abandoning a preferred text editor.

### Deciding When: Smells

- **Knowing how to refactor is not knowing when** - deciding when to start refactoring and when to stop is just as important as the mechanics.
- **Use smells, not vague programming aesthetics** - certain structures in code suggest, sometimes scream for, the possibility of refactoring.
- **Do not expect precise criteria for when a refactoring is overdue** - no set of metrics rivals informed human intuition. Smells indicate that there is trouble that can be solved by a refactoring; you must develop your own sense of how many instance variables or how many lines of code in a method are too many.
- **"If it stinks, change it."** - once you can name a smell in code you are working in, change that code.

## Refactoring: Ch3 Bad Smells in Code + Ch4 Building Tests + Ch5 Introducing the Catalog

### How to use the smell catalog

- **Diagnose by smell, then look up the remedy** - identify what you are smelling, then apply the refactorings listed for that smell to see whether they help.
- **Accept an inexact match** - you may not find the exact smell you detect; the closest smell should still point you in the right direction.

### Mysterious Name

- **Names must be mundane and clear** - put a lot of thought into naming functions, modules, variables, and classes so they clearly communicate what they do and how to use them. Code is not a detective novel.
- **Rename freely** - naming is one of the two hard things in programming, so the most common refactorings are the renames: Change Function Declaration (to rename a function), Rename Variable, and Rename Field. Do not skip a rename thinking it is not worth the trouble; a good name saves hours of puzzled incomprehension later.
- **Treat an unnameable thing as a design defect** - when you cannot think of a good name for something, that is often a sign of a deeper design malaise; puzzling over a tricky name often leads to significant simplifications.

### Duplicated Code

- **Unify the same code structure wherever it appears in more than one place** - duplication forces you to read every copy carefully to spot differences, and to find and change every copy when the logic changes.
- **Same expression in two methods of the same class** - Extract Function and invoke it from both places.
- **Similar but not identical code** - use Slide Statements first to bring the similar items together so they are easy to extract.
- **Duplicate fragments in subclasses of a common base class** - use Pull Up Method to avoid one subclass calling another.

### Long Function

- **Prefer short functions** - the programs that live best and longest are those with short functions; all the payoffs of indirection (explanation, sharing, choosing) are supported by small functions.
- **Be aggressive about decomposing functions** - the longer a function is, the more difficult it is to understand. Modern languages have pretty much eliminated in-process call overhead; the remaining overhead is for the reader, who must switch context to see what the function does. A development environment that jumps between a call and its declaration, or shows both at once, helps, but the real key is good naming: with a good function name you mostly do not need to look at its body.
- **Whenever you feel the need to comment something, write a function instead** - name it after the intention of the code rather than the way it works. Do this on a group of lines or even a single line, and do it even if the call is longer than the code it replaces, provided the name explains the purpose.
- **The criterion is semantic distance, not length** - what matters is the distance between what the method does and how it does it.
- **Ninety-nine percent of the time, shortening a function means Extract Function** - find parts that go nicely together and make a new function.
- **Too many parameters and temps block extraction** - if extracting forces you to pass so many parameters that the result is scarcely more readable than the original:
  - Use Replace Temp with Query to eliminate temps.
  - Slim long parameter lists with Introduce Parameter Object and Preserve Whole Object.
  - If temps and parameters still remain, get out the heavy artillery: Replace Function with Command.
- **Find extraction clumps by looking for comments** - a block with a comment saying what it does can be replaced by a method named after the comment; even a single line is worth extracting if it needs explanation.
- **Conditionals and loops signal extractions**
  - Use Decompose Conditional on conditional expressions.
  - Turn the legs of a big switch statement into single function calls with Extract Function.
  - If more than one switch statement switches on the same condition, apply Replace Conditional with Polymorphism.
  - Extract the loop and the code within the loop into its own method. If the extracted loop is hard to name, it is probably doing two different things: use Split Loop to break out the separate tasks.

### Long Parameter List

- **Do not pass in everything a function needs just to avoid global data** - global data quickly becomes evil, but long parameter lists are confusing in their own right.
- **One parameter obtainable from another** - use Replace Parameter with Query to remove the second parameter.
- **Many values pulled out of one data structure** - use Preserve Whole Object to pass the original data structure instead.
- **Parameters that always fit together** - combine them with Introduce Parameter Object.
- **A parameter used as a flag to dispatch different behavior** - use Remove Flag Argument.
- **Multiple functions sharing several parameter values** - use Combine Functions into Class to capture those common values as fields; in functional terms this creates a set of partially applied functions.

### Global Data

- **Treat global data as one of the most pungent smells** - it can be modified from anywhere with no mechanism to discover which code touched it, producing spooky action at a distance and bugs that are very hard to locate. Global variables are the obvious form; class variables and singletons have the same problem.
- **Encapsulate Variable is always the first move** - apply it whenever data is open to contamination by any part of the program; once wrapped by a function you can see where it is modified and control access.
- **Then shrink the scope** - move the variable inside a class or module where only that module's code can see it.
- **Mutable global data is especially nasty** - global data guaranteed never to change after program start is relatively safe, but only if the language can enforce that guarantee.
- **Dose matters (Paracelsus's maxim: the difference between a poison and something benign is the dose)** - you can get away with small doses of global data, but it gets exponentially harder to deal with the more you have. Keep even little bits encapsulated.

### Mutable Data

- **Limit the risks of unrestricted data updates** - updating data here can break another part of the software that expected something different, a failure that is particularly hard to spot when it only happens under rare conditions. Functional programming avoids this entirely by never changing data and returning a new copy on every update; in mutable languages apply the following.
- **Encapsulate Variable** - ensure all updates occur through narrow functions that are easier to monitor and evolve.
- **A variable updated to store different things** - use Split Variable to keep them separate and avoid the risky update.
- **Separate side-effect-free code from updating code** - use Slide Statements and Extract Function to move logic out of the code that processes the update.
- **In APIs, use Separate Query from Modifier** - so callers need not call code with side effects unless they really need to.
- **Use Remove Setting Method as soon as you can** - just trying to find clients of a setter helps spot opportunities to reduce a variable's scope.
- **Mutable data that can be calculated elsewhere is particularly pungent and unnecessary** - apply Replace Derived Variable with Query.
- **Risk grows with scope** - mutable data is not a big problem for a variable scoped to a couple of lines. Use Combine Functions into Class or Combine Functions into Transform to limit how much code needs to update a variable.
- **A variable holding data with internal structure** - it is usually better to replace the entire structure than to modify it in place: use Change Reference to Value.

### Divergent Change

- **Structure software so that one change means jumping to a single clear point in the system** - when you cannot do this you are smelling either divergent change or shotgun surgery.
- **One module changed in different ways for different reasons is divergent change** - the signal is "I have to change these three functions every time I get a new database; these four functions every time there is a new financial instrument." Separate contexts belong in separate modules so a change to one context requires understanding only that context.
- **Expect to discover context boundaries late** - boundaries are usually unclear early in a program and continue to shift as capabilities change; you often only see divergent change after adding a few databases or instruments.
- **If the two aspects naturally form a sequence (get data from the database, then apply financial processing)** - use Split Phase to separate them with a clear data structure between them.
- **If there is more back-and-forth in the calls** - create appropriate modules and use Move Function to divide the processing up.
- **If single functions mix both types of processing** - use Extract Function to separate them before moving.
- **If the modules are classes** - Extract Class formalizes the split.

### Shotgun Surgery

- **Many little edits to many different classes for one change is shotgun surgery** - the opposite of divergent change; scattered changes are hard to find and easy to miss.
- **Consolidate the change** - use Move Function and Move Field to put all the changes into a single module.
- **A bunch of functions operating on similar data** - Combine Functions into Class.
- **Functions transforming or enriching a data structure** - Combine Functions into Transform.
- **Split Phase** - often useful for shotgun surgery when the common functions can combine their output for a consuming phase of logic.
- **Use inlining as an intermediate step** - Inline Function or Inline Class to pull together poorly separated logic. You will end up with a Long Method or Large Class, then use extractions to break it into more sensible pieces. Do not be afraid of creating something large as an intermediate step to reorganization.

### Feature Envy

- **Maximize interaction inside a module and minimize interaction between modules** - Feature Envy is a function in one module spending more time communicating with functions or data in another module than within its own (classically, invoking half-a-dozen getters on another object to compute a value).
- **The function wants to be with the data** - use Move Function to get it there.
- **When only part of a function is envious** - Extract Function on the jealous bit, then Move Function on the extract.
- **When a function uses features of several modules** - the heuristic is to determine which module has most of the data and put the function with that data; Extract Function to break the function into pieces that go to different places.
- **Exceptions: patterns that deliberately break this rule** - Strategy and Visitor (Gang of Four) and Kent Beck's Self Delegation. Use these to combat the divergent change smell; they isolate the small amount of behavior that needs overriding at the cost of further indirection.
- **Fundamental rule of thumb: put things together that change together** - data and the behavior referencing that data usually change together, but there are exceptions; when they occur, move the behavior to keep changes in one place.

### Data Clumps

- **The same three or four data items appearing together in many places must find a home together** - as fields in a couple of classes and as parameters in many method signatures.
  1. Look for where the clumps appear as fields; use Extract Class on the fields to turn the clump into an object.
  2. Then turn to method signatures and slim them with Introduce Parameter Object or Preserve Whole Object.
- **Do not worry about clumps that use only some of the fields of the new object** - as long as you replace two or more fields with the new object, you come out ahead.
- **The deletion test** - consider deleting one of the data values; if the others then make no sense, you have an object dying to be born.
- **Create a class, not a simple record structure** - a class lets you then look for feature envy, which suggests behavior to move into the new class; this removes duplication and accelerates future development.

### Primitive Obsession

- **Create your own fundamental domain types** - money, coordinates, ranges. Otherwise you get monetary amounts treated as plain numbers, physical quantities that ignore units (adding inches to millimeters), and lots of `if (a < upper && a > lower)`.
- **Do not represent a domain concept as a string** - strings are particularly common carriers of this odor, so common that people call such variables "stringly typed"; a telephone number is more than just a collection of characters, and if nothing else a proper type can carry consistent display logic for when it needs to be displayed in a user interface.
- **Replace Primitive with Object** - apply it to move to meaningful types.
- **If the primitive is a type code controlling conditional behavior** - use Replace Type Code with Subclasses followed by Replace Conditional with Polymorphism.
- **Groups of primitives that commonly appear together are data clumps** - civilize them with Extract Class and Introduce Parameter Object.

### Repeated Switches

- **The smell is the repeated switch, not the switch** - the same conditional switching logic (a switch/case statement or a cascade of if/else statements) appearing in different places. Whenever you add a clause you must find and update all the switches.
- **Replace Conditional with Polymorphism** - apply it to duplicated switching logic.
- **Do not treat every conditional as a defect** - never be unconditionally opposed to the conditional. Object-oriented evangelists argue that any switch statement you see is begging for Replace Conditional with Polymorphism, and some argue all conditional logic should be replaced with polymorphism; do not accept that. A single switch statement is not the simple red flag it was fifteen years ago; polymorphism is more widespread now and many languages support switch forms based on more than a primitive code. (The first edition's smell was named "switch statements" because in the late 90s polymorphism was underappreciated.)

### Loops

- **Replace loops with pipelines** - use Replace Loop with Pipeline now that first-class functions are widely supported. Pipeline operations such as `filter` and `map` let you quickly see which elements are included in the processing and what is done with them.

### Lazy Element

- **Delete structure that is not earning its keep** - a function named the same as its body code reads, or a class that is essentially one simple function (whether it never grew as expected, or was downsized by refactoring).
- **Remedies** - use Inline Function or Inline Class; with inheritance, use Collapse Hierarchy.

### Speculative Generality

- **Remove hooks and special cases added for things that are not required** - "I think we'll need the ability to do this someday" produces machinery that is harder to understand and maintain. If the machinery were being used it would be worth it; if it is not, get rid of it.
- **Abstract classes that are not doing much** - Collapse Hierarchy.
- **Unnecessary delegation** - Inline Function and Inline Class.
- **Unused or unneeded parameters** - Change Function Declaration to remove them; they often get tossed in for future variations that never come to pass.
- **When the only users of a function or class are test cases** - that is speculative generality: delete the test case and apply Remove Dead Code.

### Temporary Field

- **A field set only in certain circumstances is a smell** - you expect an object to need all of its fields, so such code is difficult to understand.
- **Remedies**
  - Extract Class to create a home for the orphan variables.
  - Move Function to put all the code that concerns those fields into the new class.
  - Introduce Special Case to create an alternative class for when the variables aren't valid, which may also eliminate conditional code.

### Message Chains

- **A client asking one object for another, then asking that for another, and so on, couples the client to the structure of the navigation** - any change to the intermediate relationships forces the client to change. It appears as a long line of getThis methods or a sequence of temps.
- **Hide Delegate** - the move to use on a message chain; apply it at any of various points in the chain, but doing it to every object in the chain often turns every intermediate object into a middle man.
- **Often a better alternative** - see what the resulting object is used for; use Extract Function on the code that uses it, then Move Function to push it down the chain.
- **If several clients of one object in the chain want to navigate the rest of the way** - add a method to do that.
- **Do not treat any method chain as a terrible thing** - apply calm, reasoned moderation.

### Middle Man

- **Delegation is good until it goes too far** - encapsulation (hiding internal details) often comes with delegation, and callers should not need to know how a responsibility is fulfilled internally. The smell is a class whose interface has half its methods delegating to another class.
- **Remove Middle Man** - apply it and talk to the object that really knows what is going on.
- **If only a few methods aren't doing much** - Inline Function to inline them into the caller.
- **If there is additional behavior** - Replace Superclass with Delegate or Replace Subclass with Delegate to fold the middle man into the real object, letting you extend behavior without chasing all that delegation.

### Insider Trading

- **Keep inter-module data trading to a minimum and above board** - some trade must occur to make things work, but excess trading increases coupling.
- **Modules that whisper to each other** - use Move Function and Move Field to reduce the need to chat.
- **Modules with common interests** - create a third module to hold the commonality, or use Hide Delegate to make another module act as intermediary.
- **Inheritance leads to collusion** - subclasses always know more about their parents than the parents would like. When it is time to leave home, apply Replace Subclass with Delegate or Replace Superclass with Delegate.

### Large Class

- **Too many fields means the class is trying to do too much** - and where there are too many fields, duplicated code cannot be far behind.
- **Extract Class to bundle variables that belong together** - choose variables that make sense in one component; for example "depositAmount" and "depositCurrency" belong together. Common prefixes or suffixes across a subset of variables suggest a component.
- **If the component makes sense with inheritance** - Extract Superclass or Replace Type Code with Subclasses (which is essentially extracting a subclass) are often easier.
- **If the class does not use all its fields all the time** - you may be able to do these extractions many times.
- **Too much code is also a breeding ground for duplicated code, chaos, and death** - the simplest solution is to eliminate redundancy within the class itself: five hundred-line methods with lots of code in common may become five ten-line methods plus another ten two-line methods extracted from the original.
- **Use clients to find the split** - look at whether clients use a subset of the class's features; each subset is a possible separate class. Break out a useful subset with Extract Class, Extract Superclass, or Replace Type Code with Subclasses.

### Alternative Classes with Different Interfaces

- **Make substitutable classes present the same interface** - substitution only works if interfaces match.
  - Use Change Function Declaration to make functions match up.
  - Keep using Move Function to move behavior into classes until the protocols match.
  - If this leads to duplication, use Extract Superclass.

### Data Class

- **Classes with only fields plus getters and setters are dumb data holders** - and are often manipulated in far too much detail by other classes.
- **Public fields** - immediately apply Encapsulate Record.
- **Any field that should not be changed** - Remove Setting Method.
- **Move behavior into the data class** - find where the getters and setters are used by other classes and use Move Function; if you cannot move a whole function, use Extract Function to create a function that can be moved.
- **Exception: a result record from a distinct function invocation** - for example the intermediate data structure produced by Split Phase. Its key characteristic is that it is immutable (at least in practice). Immutable fields don't need to be encapsulated, and information derived from immutable data can be represented as fields rather than getting methods.

### Refused Bequest

- **The traditional remedy, applied only when needed** - the traditional story is that a subclass not wanting or needing what it inherits means the hierarchy is wrong: create a new sibling class and use Push Down Method and Push Down Field to push all unused code to the sibling, so the parent holds only what is common. The traditional advice also says all superclasses should be abstract.
- **Do not apply the traditional advice all the time** - subclassing to reuse a bit of behavior is a perfectly good way of doing business, and there is a smell but usually it isn't a strong one. Follow the traditional advice only if the refused bequest is causing confusion and problems. Nine times out of ten this smell is too faint to be worth cleaning.
- **The smell is much stronger when a subclass reuses behavior but refuses the superclass's interface** - refusing implementations is acceptable; refusing interface is not. In that case do not fiddle with the hierarchy: gut it with Replace Subclass with Delegate or Replace Superclass with Delegate.

### Comments

- **Comments are not a bad smell; they are a sweet smell** - but they are often used as a deodorant, and thickly commented code frequently is commented because the code is bad.
- **Use comments as a pointer to bad code** - remove the bad smells by refactoring first; afterwards the comments are often superfluous.
- **Refactor instead of commenting** - when you feel the need to write a comment, first try to refactor the code so that any comment becomes superfluous.
  - Comment explaining what a block of code does - Extract Function.
  - Method already extracted but still needs a comment to explain what it does - Change Function Declaration to rename it.
  - Comment stating rules about the required state of the system - Introduce Assertion.
- **Good times to use a comment** - when you don't know what to do; to indicate areas in which you aren't sure; to explain why you did something, which helps future modifiers, especially forgetful ones.

### The Value of Self-Testing Code

- **Refactoring requires tests** - to refactor properly you need a solid suite of tests to spot inevitable mistakes. Even with automated refactoring tools, many refactorings still need checking via a test suite. If you want to refactor, you have to write tests. Writing good tests increases your effectiveness as a programmer even without refactoring.
- **Most programming time is spent debugging, not writing code** - fixing a bug is usually quick; finding it is the nightmare, and a fix can introduce another bug you notice only much later.
- **Classes should contain their own tests** - incorporate tests into the code base together with the production code.
- **Make sure all tests are fully automatic and that they check their own results** - the test compares expected output embedded in the test code against actual output and prints only pass/fail; never require a human to read console output and judge it.
- **A suite of tests is a powerful bug detector that decapitates the time it takes to find bugs** - running tests frequently means only a few minutes of work separates you from the bug's source, so it is fresh in your mind. Bugs that would take an hour or more to find take a couple of minutes at most.
- **Add tests immediately after writing a bit of function** - do not wait for the end of an increment.
- **Manual tests are gut-wrenchingly boring; automatic tests can be fun to write** - the extra code is worth it, though this only becomes obvious after experiencing the speed-up.
- **One of the most useful times to write tests is before you start programming** - writing the test first asks what needs to be done to add the function, concentrates you on the interface rather than the implementation, and gives a clear point at which you are done coding: when the test works.
- **Test-Driven Development (TDD)** - short cycles of writing a failing test, writing the code to make that test work, and refactoring to make the result as clean as possible. This test-code-refactor cycle should occur many times per hour. Warmly recommended.
- **Make untested code self-testing before refactoring it** - if you must refactor code that has no tests, make the code self-testing first.
- **Separate business logic from UI, persistence, and external service interaction** - once business logic gets at all complicated, separate it so you can reason about it and test it more easily. Start self-testing with the easiest case: code that involves none of those three.
- **Parse strings at the boundary** - setters that will be called with strings from UI fields must parse the numbers (`parseInt`) so the values can be used reliably in calculations.
- **Do not refactor an ugly construct before it is covered** - e.g. a setter that updates derived data in another object is a refactoring target, but you have to write the tests before you can refactor it.

### A First Test

- **Structure of a test** - a test framework groups a suite of tests in a `describe` block; each test is an `it` block. A simple test has two steps: set up the fixture (the data and objects needed), then verify some characteristic of that fixture.
- **Descriptive strings** - put in just enough to identify which test is which when you get failures. (Some write a full explanatory sentence; others leave them empty, arguing the sentence duplicates the code like a comment.)
- **Always make sure a test will fail when it should** - see every test fail at least once when you write it. The preferred way is to temporarily inject a fault into the production code, confirm the failure is reported where you injected it, then revert the fault.

```js
// temporary injected fault to prove the test can fail
get shortfall() {
  return this._demand - this.totalProduction * 2;
}
// framework reports: AssertionError: expected -20 to equal 5
```

- **Demand simple, immediate feedback** - a good framework reports how many tests ran, which failed, and for each failure the expected and actual values.
- **Run tests frequently** - run those exercising the code you are working on at least every few minutes; run all tests at least daily.
- **Never refactor on a red bar** - do not refactor while the test suite has a failing test. "Revert to green" means undo recent changes and go back to the last all-passing state, usually via a recent version-control checkpoint.
- **Graphical test runners are nice but not essential** - the key point is that you can quickly see if all tests are OK; text feedback bound to a single key is enough.
- **Assertion style is a preference, not a rule** - `assert.equal(asia.shortfall, 5)` ("assert" style) and `expect(asia.shortfall).equal(5)` ("expect" style) are both acceptable.

### Add Another Test

- **Test what the class should do, not every public method** - look at all the things the class should do and test each one for any conditions that might cause the class to fail.
- **Testing should be risk-driven** - the goal is to find bugs now or in the future. Do not test accessors that just read and write a field; they are so simple that a bug is unlikely.
- **It is better to write and run incomplete tests than not to run complete tests** - trying to write too many tests usually leads to not writing enough, and risks leaving you discouraged and writing none; there is a law of diminishing returns in testing. Beware rules that ensure you have tested every combination of everything: they are worth a look, but do not let them get to you. Focus on the areas you are most worried about going wrong: concentrate on where the risk is, looking at where the code becomes complex and considering a function's likely areas of error.
- **Pattern for adding tests to existing code that is believed to be working** - write the test with a placeholder for the expected value, replace the placeholder with the value the code actually produces, inject a fault to see the test fail, then revert the fault.
- **Be as suspicious of duplication in test code as in regular code** - factor common setup to a common place.
- **Never hoist a mutable fixture into the enclosing scope** - a shared fixture causes tests to interact, giving intermittent failures that depend on test execution order. In JavaScript `const` only makes the reference constant, not the object's content. That nondeterminism means long, difficult debugging at best and collapse of confidence in the tests at worst.

```js
// BAD - shared fixture in the describe scope
describe('province', function() {
  const asia = new Province(sampleProvinceData()); // DON'T DO THIS
  it('shortfall', function() { expect(asia.shortfall).equal(5); });
});

// GOOD - fresh fixture per test
describe('province', function() {
  let asia;
  beforeEach(function() { asia = new Province(sampleProvinceData()); });
  it('shortfall', function() { expect(asia.shortfall).equal(5); });
  it('profit',    function() { expect(asia.profit).equal(230); });
});
```

- **Build a fresh fixture before each test** - `beforeEach` clears and re-creates the fixture, keeping tests isolated.
- **Exception for speed** - most of the time fresh fixtures are not noticeably slower. If it is a genuine problem, consider a shared fixture but be really careful that no test ever changes it; a shared fixture is also acceptable if it is truly immutable. The reflex should still be a fresh fixture, because the debugging cost of a shared-fixture mistake is high.
- **Put setup in `beforeEach` rather than inside each `it` block** - a common standard fixture lets you become familiar with it and see the various characteristics to test; the presence of `beforeEach` signals to the reader that all tests in that `describe` block start from the same base data.

### Modifying the Fixture

- **Test complicated update behavior; skip simple setters** - simple setters have little chance of being the source of a bug, but a setter with complicated behavior (e.g. one that adjusts a derived total held on another object) is worth a test that exercises it and then verifies every derived value it touches - for a production-plan fixture, setting a producer's production to 20 must give shortfall -6 and profit 292.
- **Follow the standard test phase pattern** - take the initial standard fixture from `beforeEach`, exercise it, then verify it did what it should have. Known variously as setup-exercise-verify, given-when-then, or arrange-act-assert. Sometimes all steps are inside the test; sometimes common early phases move into standard setup routines like `beforeEach`.
- **Teardown is the implicit fourth phase** - it removes the fixture between tests so tests don't interact. Doing all setup in `beforeEach` lets the framework tear down implicitly. Occasionally an explicit teardown matters, particularly for a fixture you must share between tests because it is slow to create.
- **As a general rule, have only a single verify statement in each `it` clause** - the test fails on the first verification failure, which can hide useful information when you are figuring out why a test broke.
  - Exception: two verifications closely enough connected may share one test; you can separate them into separate `it` clauses later.

### Probing the Boundaries

- **Do not stop at the "happy path"** - also throw tests at the boundaries of normal conditions to see what happens when things might go wrong; think of the boundary conditions under which things might go wrong and concentrate your tests there.
- **Play the part of an enemy to your code** - actively think about how you can break it.
- **Boundary cases to probe**
  - Any collection: what happens when it is empty (e.g. a province with `producers: []` gives shortfall 30 and profit 0).
  - Numbers: probe zero (zero demand gives shortfall -25, profit 0).
  - Numbers: probe negatives (demand -1 gives shortfall -26, profit -10).
  - String inputs from UI fields constrained to numbers: they can still be blank, so test that blank input behaves as intended (empty-string demand yields NaN shortfall and NaN profit).
  - Wrong-typed input where a collection is expected - e.g. a string such as `producers: ""` in place of an array, in a test that verifies shortfall 0.
- **Use boundary tests to interrogate the domain** - a negative demand producing a negative profit raises the question whether minimum demand should be zero, and whether the setter should raise an error or coerce to zero. Writing such tests helps you think about how the code ought to react.
- **Distinguish failure from error** - a failure is a verify step whose actual value is outside the expected bounds; an error is an exception raised during an earlier phase (e.g. setup), typically unanticipated by the code's authors (for example a message like `doc.producers.forEach is not a function`). Many frameworks separate the two; Mocha reports both as failures.
- **Deciding how to respond to an unanticipated error**
  - Add handling that raises a more meaningful error message, or set the value to a safe default such as an empty array with perhaps a log message.
  - There may be valid reasons to leave it as is: if the input object comes from a trusted source such as another part of the same code base, lots of validation checks between modules can duplicate checks done elsewhere and cause more trouble than they are worth.
  - If the input comes from an external source such as a JSON-encoded request, validation checks are needed and should be tested.
- **When writing tests before refactoring, discard tests of non-observable behavior** - refactoring preserves observable behavior; an error like an unanticipated type exception is outside the bounds of observable, so a refactoring changing that response need not concern you.
- **If a bad input could let bad data run around the program and cause a hard-to-debug failure, use Introduce Assertion to fail fast** - do not add tests to catch such assertion failures; assertions are themselves a form of test.
- **Don't let the fear that testing can't catch all bugs stop you from writing tests that catch most bugs** - you cannot prove a program has no bugs by testing, but that does not affect testing's ability to speed up programming.
- **Expect to grow the suite while refactoring** - always start refactoring with a test suite, but invariably add to it as you go; your tests will not find every bug, and as you refactor you understand the program better and thus find more bugs.

### Much More Than This

- **Unit tests are the backbone of self-testing code** - designed to operate on a small area of the code and run fast; most tests in such a system are unit tests. Other kinds focus on integration between components, exercise multiple levels of the software together, or look for performance issues.
- **Architectures are rightly judged on their testability** - testing is a first-class concern of any decent software developer, not the responsibility of a separate group.
- **Testing is an iterative activity** - you won't get tests right the first time. Continuously work the test suite as much as the main code: add tests with new features, and also review existing tests for clarity, refactor them for understandability, and ask whether you have the right tests.
- **When you get a bug report, start by writing a unit test that exposes the bug** - only after you have the test do you fix the bug; the test keeps the bug dead. Then ask whether that bug and its test reveal other gaps in the suite.
- **Do not use test coverage as a measure of how much testing is enough** - coverage analysis is only good for identifying untested areas of the code, not for assessing the quality of a test suite.
- **The best measure of a good enough test suite is subjective: how confident are you that if someone introduces a defect into the code, some test will fail?** - this cannot be objectively analyzed and does not account for false confidence, but if you can refactor and be pretty sure you introduced no bug because tests come back green, the tests are good enough.
- **Over-testing exists but is vanishingly rare compared to under-testing** - the sign is spending more time changing the tests than the code under test and feeling the tests are slowing you down.

### Format of the Refactorings

- **Each catalog refactoring has five parts, in this order**
  1. **Name** - important for building a vocabulary of refactorings; common aliases are also listed.
  2. **Sketch** - a short code example of the transformation, to help you find a refactoring quickly and remind you what it is if you have met it before; it is not meant to explain what the refactoring is or how to do it.
  3. **Motivation** - why the refactoring should be done, and the circumstances in which it should not be done.
  4. **Mechanics** - a concise, terse, step-by-step description of how to carry it out, usually without explanations of why the steps are that way; use it as a lookup and as a checklist, since the steps include references to special cases that are easy to forget.
  5. **Examples** - a very simple use illustrating how it works; read the example the first time you do a refactoring. Some very simple refactorings have no example.
- **Emphasize the safe way: take very small steps and test after every one** - larger steps are acceptable in practice, but if you run into a bug, back out the last step and take the smaller steps. The trickier the situation, the smaller the steps.
- **The listed mechanics are not the only way** - they work pretty well most of the time; varying them with practice is fine, as long as you keep the steps small.
- **Each refactoring's examples illustrate only that one refactoring** - in most cases problems remain in the code at the end, and fixing them requires other refactorings. Where refactorings often go together, an example may be carried from one to another; otherwise each refactoring is self-contained because the catalog's primary role is reference.

### The Choice of Refactorings

- **The catalog is not complete** - it collects the refactorings that are both commonly used and worthwhile to name and describe (interesting mechanics that build general refactoring skill, or a strong effect on improving design).
- **Some refactorings are omitted as too small and straightforward** - e.g. Slide Statements was omitted in the first edition despite frequent use, and added in this edition.
- **Every refactoring has a logical inverse, but not every inverse is written up** - inverses that are rarely used or trivially similar to other refactorings are omitted; for example the inverse of Encapsulate Variable is rarely done and easy to perform.

### First Set of Refactorings

- **Learn this set first** - these are the refactorings most useful to learn first.
  - Extract Function and Extract Variable - the most common refactorings; their inverses Inline Function and Inline Variable are used just as frequently.
  - Change Function Declaration - change function names, and add or remove a function's arguments. Extraction is all about giving names, and names need changing as you learn.
  - Rename Variable - relies on Encapsulate Variable.
  - Introduce Parameter Object - combine a common clump of arguments into a single object when changing function arguments.
  - Combine Functions into Class - group functions, together with the data they operate on, into a class.
  - Combine Functions into Transform - combine functions into a transform; particularly handy with read-only data.
  - Split Phase - form modules into distinct processing phases, a step further in scale.
- **Group functions into higher-level modules once they are named** - forming and naming functions are essential low-level refactorings, but once created, group functions into higher-level modules.

## Refactoring: Ch6 A First Set of Refactorings

### Extract Function

formerly: Extract Method. inverse of: Inline Function.

```js
// BEFORE
function printOwing(invoice) {
  printBanner();
  let outstanding = calculateOutstanding();
  //print details
  console.log(`name: ${invoice.customer}`);
  console.log(`amount: ${outstanding}`);
}
// AFTER
function printOwing(invoice) {
  printBanner();
  let outstanding = calculateOutstanding();
  printDetails(outstanding);
  function printDetails(outstanding) { /* ... */ }
}
```

- **Extract on intention/implementation separation, not on length or reuse** - if you have to spend effort looking at a fragment and figuring out what it is doing, extract it and name the function after the "what"; then the purpose leaps out on rereading and most of the time you need not care how the function fulfills it. The separation between intention and implementation is the criterion that makes most sense, rather than the length guideline ("functions should be no larger than fit on a screen") or the reuse guideline ("any code used more than once should be put in its own function, but code only used once should be left inline"). "Function" here also means a method in an object-oriented language, or any kind of procedure or subroutine.
- **Write very small functions** - typically only a few lines long; any function with more than half-a-dozen lines of code starts to smell; single-line functions are normal.
- **Extract even when the name is longer than the body** - size is irrelevant when the distance between intention and implementation is big (e.g. Smalltalk's `highlight` whose whole implementation was a call to `reverse`).
- **Do not reject short functions for function-call performance cost** - that is very rare now; optimizing compilers often work better with shorter functions, which can be cached more easily. Follow the general guidelines on performance optimization instead.
- **Small functions only work if the names are good** - pay explicit attention to naming; this takes practice.
- **Use an existing leading comment as the name source** - a fragment that starts with a comment saying what it does gives you the name of the extracted function; delete the comment once the name says it.
- **Name by what it does, never by how it does it.**
- **Extract even a single function call if the new name reveals intent better** - but if you cannot come up with a more meaningful name, that is a sign you should not extract this code.
- **Extraction is reversible and cheap** - you need not find the best name immediately; a good name often only appears while working with the extraction. It is OK to extract, work with it, realize it is not helping, and inline it back; as long as you learned something the time was not wasted.

#### Mechanics

1. Create a new function and name it after the intent of the function (name it by what it does, not by how it does it).
   - If the language supports nested functions, nest the extracted function inside the source function. That reduces the out-of-scope variables to deal with in the next steps; you can always use Move Function later.
2. Copy the extracted code from the source function into the new target function.
3. Scan the extracted code for references to any variables that are local in scope to the source function and will not be in scope for the extracted function. Pass them as parameters.
   - Extracting into a nested function of the source function avoids these problems entirely.
   - Usually these are local variables and parameters of the source function. The most general approach is to pass all such parameters in as arguments.
   - Variables that are used but not assigned to cause no difficulty.
   - If a variable is only used inside the extracted code but is declared outside, move the declaration into the extracted code.
   - Variables that are assigned to need more care if passed by value. If there is only one, treat the extracted code as a query and assign the result to that variable.
   - If too many local variables are being assigned by the extracted code, it is better to abandon the extraction at this point; consider other refactorings such as Split Variable or Replace Temp with Query to simplify variable usage, and revisit the extraction later.
4. Compile after all variables are dealt with.
   - Useful if the language environment does compile-time checks; it often finds variables not dealt with properly.
5. Replace the extracted code in the source function with a call to the target function.
6. Test.
7. Look for other code that is the same or similar to the code just extracted, and consider using Replace Inline Code with Function Call to call the new function.
   - Some refactoring tools do this directly; otherwise run quick searches for duplicate code elsewhere.
