- **With more complex data structures, interference is much harder to be sure of, so rely on tests** - slide, run tests, see if things break. If coverage is good, be happy; if tests are not reliable, be more wary, or more likely improve the tests for the code you are working on.
- **The most important consequence of a test failure after a slide is to use smaller slides** - instead of ten lines, pick five, or slide up to the line you reckon is dangerous. It may also mean the slide is not worth it and something else must be worked on first.
- **Sliding across a conditional boundary** - sliding a fragment out of a conditional removes duplicate logic; sliding a fragment into a conditional means repeating it in every leg.

```js
// BEFORE: same statement in both legs
if (availableResources.length === 0) { result = createResource(); allocatedResources.push(result); }
else { result = availableResources.pop(); allocatedResources.push(result); }
// AFTER: slid out, one statement
if (availableResources.length === 0) { result = createResource(); }
else { result = availableResources.pop(); }
allocatedResources.push(result);
```

- **Swap Statement is the single-statement special case of Slide Statements** - it moves adjacent fragments but only works with single-statement fragments. Move one statement at a time only when a larger slide is giving difficulty; with messier code, smaller slides end up being easier.

#### Split Loop

```js
// BAD: one loop, two calculations
for (const p of people) { averageAge += p.age; totalSalary += p.salary; }
// GOOD: one loop per calculation
for (const p of people) { totalSalary += p.salary; }
for (const p of people) { averageAge += p.age; }
```

- **Split a loop that does two different things** - otherwise every modification to the loop requires understanding both things; splitting means you only need to understand the behavior you are modifying.
- **Splitting makes the loop easier to use** - a loop calculating a single value can just return that value, whereas loops doing many things must return structures or populate local variables.
- **Follow Split Loop with Extract Function on each loop** - this is the usual sequence, and the point of Split Loop is what it sets up next rather than what it does on its own.
- **Do not reject the split because the loop now executes twice** - separate refactoring from optimization. Once the code is clear, optimize; if loop traversal is a bottleneck it is easy to slam the loops back together. Iteration through even a large list is rarely a bottleneck, and splitting often enables other, more powerful optimizations.

Mechanics:

1. Copy the loop.
2. Identify and eliminate duplicate side effects.
   - Anything in the loop with no side effects can be left in both copies for now.
3. Test.
4. When done, consider Extract Function on each loop.

- **Slide each split loop next to its own initialization and result handling before extracting** - use Slide Statements to reorganize the code after the split.
- **Consider Replace Loop with Pipeline and Substitute Algorithm on the extracted single-purpose loops** - e.g. `people.reduce((total,p) => total + p.salary, 0)` and `Math.min(...people.map(p => p.age))`.

#### Replace Loop with Pipeline

```js
// BEFORE
const names = [];
for (const i of input) { if (i.job === "programmer") names.push(i.name); }
// AFTER
const names = input.filter(i => i.job === "programmer").map(i => i.name);
```

- **Prefer a collection pipeline to a loop when the language provides one** - Collection Pipelines describe processing as a series of operations, each consuming and emitting a collection; logic is much easier to follow because you read top to bottom to see how objects flow.
- **The two most common pipeline operations are map and filter** - `map` uses a function to transform each element of the input collection; `filter` uses a function to select a subset of the input collection for later steps.

Mechanics:

1. Create a new variable for the loop's collection.
   - This may be a simple copy of an existing variable.
2. Starting at the top, take each bit of behavior in the loop and replace it with a collection pipeline operation in the derivation of the loop collection variable. Test after each change.
3. Once all behavior is removed from the loop, remove it.
   - If it assigns to an accumulator, assign the pipeline result to the accumulator.

Map loop behavior onto pipeline operations:

| Loop behavior | Pipeline operation |
|---|---|
| Skip the first line using a `firstLine` control flag | `.slice(1)` |
| `if (line.trim() === "") continue;` | `.filter(line => line.trim() !== "")` |
| `const record = line.split(",")` | `.map(line => line.split(","))` |
| `if (record[1].trim() === "India")` guard | `.filter(record => record[1].trim() === "India")` |
| `result.push({city: ..., phone: ...})` | `.map(record => ({city: ..., phone: ...}))` then assign pipeline to `result` |

- **Delete control variables that a pipeline operation makes redundant** - replacing a first-line skip with `.slice(1)` lets you delete the `firstLine` control flag.
- **Put the terminal semicolon on its own line** - when writing a pipeline, place its terminal semicolon on a line of its own.
- **Keep misleading original names during the move and rename later** - it is safer than renaming mid-refactoring.
- **Clean up afterwards** - inline the accumulator, rename lambda variables, and align the layout so the pipeline reads like a table. Keep an intermediate variable (e.g. `lines`) when its presence explains what is happening.

#### Remove Dead Code

```js
// BAD
if (false) { doSomethingThatUsedToMatter(); }
```

- **Once code is not used any more, delete it** - unused code is a significant burden when trying to understand how the software works; it carries no warning sign, so programmers still spend time working out what it does and why changing it does not alter the output as expected.
- **Do not keep dead code for possible future need** - the version control system can always dig it out again.
- **At most, leave a comment naming the removed code and the revision it was removed in** - and even that is rarely worth doing or regretted when skipped.
- **Do not comment out dead code** - that habit was useful only in the days before version control systems were widely used, or when they were inconvenient; now that even the smallest code base can be under version control, it is no longer needed.
- **Unused code is not a performance problem** - a few unused lines do not slow systems or take significant memory, and decent compilers remove them instinctively. Delete for understandability, not for speed.

Mechanics:

1. If the dead code can be referenced from outside, e.g. when it is a full function, do a search to check for callers.
2. Remove the dead code.
3. Test.

### Selecting a data-structure refactoring

- **A value used for different purposes is a breeding ground for confusion and bugs** - use Split Variable to separate the usages.
- **Getting a variable's name right is tricky and important** - use Rename Variable.
- **Sometimes the best thing to do with a variable is get rid of it completely** - use Replace Derived Variable with Query.
- **Confusion between references and values causes problems in a code base** - use Change Reference to Value and Change Value to Reference to change between these styles.

## Refactoring: Ch9 Organizing Data + Ch10 Simplifying Conditional Logic

### Chapter 9: Organizing Data

#### Split Variable

formerly: Remove Assignments to Parameters; formerly: Split Temp

```js
// BAD
let temp = 2 * (height + width);
console.log(temp);
temp = height * width;
// GOOD
const perimeter = 2 * (height + width);
const area = height * width;
```

- **Split any variable with more than one responsibility** - a variable set more than once is a sign it has more than one responsibility within the method; replace it with multiple variables, one per responsibility. Using one variable for two different things is very confusing for the reader.
- **Do not split loop variables or collecting variables** - these naturally get assigned many times. If the later assignments are of the form `i = i + something`, that is a collecting variable, so don't split it. Collecting variables are used for sums, string concatenation, writing to a stream, or adding to a collection.
- **Set an explaining variable only once** - variables that hold the result of a long-winded bit of code for later reference should be set only once.

Mechanics:

1. Change the name of the variable at its declaration and first assignment.
   - If the later assignments are of the form `i = i + something`, that is a collecting variable, so don't split it.
   - Choose the new name to represent only the first use of the variable.
2. If possible, declare the new variable as immutable (`const`), to ensure it is only assigned once. Then declare the original variable at its second assignment.
3. Change all references of the variable up to its second assignment.
4. Test.
5. Repeat in stages: at each stage rename the variable at the declaration and change references until the next assignment, until you reach the final assignment. The last stage removes the original variable name completely, replacing it with a variable named for its second use.

- **Split an input parameter that doubles as a result holder** - introduce a local initialized from the parameter, then apply Rename Variable twice so the parameter keeps the input name and the local becomes `result`. Where the language has call-by-value parameters (as JavaScript does), any modification of the parameter isn't seen by the caller anyway.

```js
// BAD
function discount (inputValue, quantity) {
  if (inputValue > 50) inputValue = inputValue - 2;
  return inputValue;
}
// GOOD
function discount (inputValue, quantity) {
  let result = inputValue;
  if (inputValue > 50) result = result - 2;
  return result;
}
```

- **Read conditions from the original input, not the accumulator** - in the split form, test `inputValue` in the guards: that line is about applying a modification to the result value based on the original input value, not the (coincidentally same) value of the result accumulator.
- **Locate every occurrence of a variable before splitting it** - when working out how a variable is used, find all occurrences of the symbol within the function or file; an editor that highlights all occurrences of a symbol makes this easy.

#### Rename Field

```js
// BAD                          // GOOD
class Organization {            class Organization {
  get name() {...}                get title() {...}
}                               }
```

- **Keep record-structure field names clear** - data structures are the key to understanding what is going on, and field names matter especially when the record structure is widely used across a program. Embed improved understanding of the data into the program as it grows.
- **Treat getters and setters as fields** - they form an effective field for users of the class, so renaming them is just as important as renaming bare record fields.

Mechanics:

1. If the record has limited scope, rename all accesses to the field and test; no need to do the rest of the mechanics.
2. If the record isn't already encapsulated, apply Encapsulate Record.
3. Rename the private field inside the object, adjust internal methods to fit.
4. Test.
5. If the constructor uses the name, apply Change Function Declaration to rename it.
6. Apply Rename Function to the accessors.

- **After encapsulating, there are four places to rename**: the getting function, the setting function, the constructor, and the internal data structure. Encapsulation is not extra work: it lets you change these independently instead of all at once, and smaller steps mean fewer things to go wrong per step.
- **Separate the internal field from the input data structure first** - define the new private field name and adjust the constructor and accessors to use it, before touching the public names.
- **Support both old and new constructor keys during migration** - `this._title = (data.title !== undefined) ? data.title : data.name;` (new name takes precedence). Migrate constructor callers one by one, then remove the support for the old name.
- **Full mechanics are a matter of judgment** - for a field used only locally, e.g. in a single function, just rename the properties in one go without encapsulating. As usual with refactoring, if the tests break, that is the sign you need the more gradual procedure.
- **For immutable data structures, copy instead of encapsulating** - copy the value to the new name, gradually change the users, then remove the old name. Duplicating data is a recipe for disaster with mutable data structures; removing such disasters is why immutable data is so popular.

#### Replace Derived Variable with Query

```js
// BAD
get discountedTotal() {return this._discountedTotal;}
set discount(aNumber) {
  const old = this._discount;
  this._discount = aNumber;
  this._discountedTotal += old - aNumber;
}
// GOOD
get discountedTotal() {return this._baseTotal - this._discount;}
set discount(aNumber) {this._discount = aNumber;}
```

- **Remove any variable you could just as easily calculate** - mutable data is one of the biggest sources of problems in software; data changes couple parts of code in awkward ways with knock-on effects that are hard to spot. A calculation often makes the meaning of the data clearer and is protected from corruption when you fail to update the variable as the source data changes.
- **Minimize the scope of mutable data as much as possible**, even though it is often not realistic to remove mutable data entirely.
- **Exception: keep derived data when the source data is immutable and the result can be forced immutable too** - transformation operations that create new data structures are reasonable to keep even if they could be replaced with calculations.
- **Choose between the object route and the transform route by source-data mutability** - there is a duality between objects that wrap a data structure with calculated properties and functions that transform one data structure into another. The object route is clearly better when the source data changes and you would otherwise have to manage the lifetime of the derived data structures. If the source data is immutable, or the derived data is very transient, both approaches are effective.

Mechanics:

1. Identify all points of update for the variable. If necessary, use Split Variable to separate each point of update.
2. Create a function that calculates the value of the variable.
3. Use Introduce Assertion to assert that the variable and the calculation give the same result whenever the variable is used.
   - If necessary, use Encapsulate Variable to provide a home for the assertion.
4. Test.
5. Replace any reader of the variable with a call to the new function.
6. Test.
7. Apply Remove Dead Code to the declaration and updates to the variable.

- **Treat duplication of data like duplication of code** - pushing an adjustment onto a list and also adding its amount into an accumulator is duplicated data; calculate instead of updating.
- **Use the assertion as a hypothesis test** - assert inside the getter that the stored field equals the calculated value (`assert(this._production === this.calculatedProduction);`); run the tests; only if the assertion does not fail, replace returning the field with returning the calculation, then Inline Function, then Remove Dead Code on the update.
- **When more than one element combines in the accumulator, apply Split Variable first** - the naive assertion fails for any case where the initial value is not zero. Split into an initial value plus an accumulator (`this._initialProduction + this._productionAccumulator`), then assert on the accumulator alone.
  - In that multi-source case, be inclined to leave the calculated-accumulator property as its own property, without inlining it.

#### Change Reference to Value

inverse of: Change Value to Reference

```js
// BAD
class Product { applyDiscount(arg) {this._price.amount -= arg;} }
// GOOD
class Product {
  applyDiscount(arg) {this._price = new Money(this._price.amount - arg, this._price.currency);}
}
```

- **Decide reference vs value by how you handle updates of the inner object's properties** - as a reference, update the inner object's property keeping the same inner object; as a value, replace the entire inner object with a new one that has the desired property.
- **Prefer value objects where the field is conceptually a value** - Value Objects are generally easier to reason about, particularly because they are immutable. An immutable data value can be passed out to other parts of the program without worrying it might change without the enclosing object being aware; values can be replicated around the program without maintaining memory links. Value objects are especially useful in distributed and concurrent systems.
- **Do not change a reference to a value when the object must be shared** - if you want to share an object between several objects so that any change to the shared object is visible to all its collaborators, then you need the shared object to be a reference.

Mechanics:

1. Check that the candidate class is immutable or can become immutable.
2. For each setter, apply Remove Setting Method.
3. Provide a value-based equality method that uses the fields of the value object.
   - Most language environments provide an overridable equality function for this purpose (`==` in Ruby, `Object.equals()` in Java). Usually you must override a hashcode generator method as well (e.g. `Object.hashCode()` in Java) to ensure collections that use hashing work properly with the new value.

- **Trigger for Change Reference to Value: an Extract Class where the old parent still holds update methods for the new object** - especially good to apply when there is only one reference to the new class.
- **Start Remove Setting Method with Change Function Declaration** - add the fields to the constructor and enhance the constructor to call the setters; then convert each caller of a setter into a reassignment that constructs a new value.
- **Value-based equality is the citizenship test for a value object.** JavaScript has nothing in the language or core libraries that replaces reference-based equality with value-based equality, so create your own `equals` method that first checks `instanceof` and then compares fields.
- **Test equality with two independently created objects** and assert they match as equal. Tests for non-equal values, comparisons to objects of other types, and null values are also worthwhile.
- **More than one client is not a problem** - the procedure is the same; applying Remove Setting Method just modifies several clients instead of one.

#### Change Value to Reference

inverse of: Change Reference to Value

```js
// BAD
let customer = new Customer(customerData);
// GOOD
let customer = customerRepository.get(customerData.id);
```

- **Convert copies into a single reference when the shared data needs updating** - with physical copies of the same logical data you must find and update every copy, and missing one gives a troubling inconsistency. Duplicate objects representing the same entity are confusing, and particularly awkward when the entity object is mutable, which can lead to inconsistencies between the copies: enriching one copy, for example from a customer service, would otherwise require updating every copy with the same data. With a reference, any change is visible to all the holders.
- **If the entity never needs to be updated, both approaches are reasonable** - multiple copies of the same data are a bit confusing but common enough to not be a problem. Memory issues from multiple copies exist but, like any performance issue, are relatively rare.
- **Changing value to reference means one object per entity, and usually a repository** - create the object for an entity once and retrieve it from the repository everywhere else.

Mechanics:

1. Create a repository for instances of the related object (if one isn't already present). Often the repository already exists, so just use it.
2. Ensure the constructor has a way of looking up the correct instance of the related object.
3. Change the constructors for the host object to use the repository to obtain the related object. Test after each change.

- **Repository shape**: a `register(id)` that creates only if absent and returns the found instance, plus a `find(id)`; this ensures only one object exists per ID.
- **Two population strategies** - create the entity lazily on first reference, or pre-populate the repository from a list of entities and link as records are read. With the pre-populated approach, an incoming ID not in the repository indicates an error.
- **Treat globals with care** - a constructor body coupled to a global repository is a concern; like a powerful drug, globals can be beneficial in small doses but a poison if used too much. If concerned, pass the repository as a parameter to the constructor.

### Chapter 10: Simplifying Conditional Logic - selection guide

- **Much of the complexity of programs lies in conditionals**; refactor conditional sections to make them easier to understand.

| Situation | Refactoring |
|---|---|
| Complicated conditional | Decompose Conditional |
| Logical combinations need to be clearer | Consolidate Conditional Expression |
| Pre-checks before the main processing | Replace Nested Conditional with Guard Clauses |
| Several conditions using the same switching logic | Replace Conditional with Polymorphism |
| Many conditionals handling special cases such as nulls, with mostly the same logic | Introduce Special Case (often called Introduce Null Object) - removes a lot of duplicate code |
| Want to communicate and check a program's state | Introduce Assertion |

#### Decompose Conditional

```js
// BAD
if (!aDate.isBefore(plan.summerStart) && !aDate.isAfter(plan.summerEnd))
  charge = quantity * plan.summerRate;
else
  charge = quantity * plan.regularRate + plan.regularServiceCharge;
// GOOD
charge = summer() ? summerCharge() : regularCharge();
```

- **Replace each chunk of a conditional with a function call named after the intention of that chunk** - condition checks and actions tell you what happens but easily obscure why it happens. Do this for the conditional part and for each of the alternatives, so that both what you branch on and the reason for the branching are highlighted.
- **Decompose Conditional is a particular case of Extract Function** that has often shown remarkably good value.
- **Length of a function is in itself a factor that makes it harder to read, and conditions increase the difficulty** - code doing various things depending on various conditions quickly ends up a long function.

Mechanics:

1. Apply Extract Function on the condition and each leg of the conditional.

- **Order of work in practice**: extract the condition, test/move on; extract the then leg; extract the else leg; then reformat the conditional using the ternary operator.

#### Consolidate Conditional Expression

```js
// BAD
if (anEmployee.seniority < 2) return 0;
if (anEmployee.monthsDisabled > 12) return 0;
if (anEmployee.isPartTime) return 0;
// GOOD
if (isNotEligableForDisability()) return 0;
```

- **Combine a series of different conditional checks that all produce the same resulting action** into a single conditional check with a single result, using and and or operators. It shows you are really making a single check that combines other checks, instead of looking like a sequence of separate checks that just happen to be close together.
- **Consolidating conditionals sets up Extract Function** - extracting a condition is one of the most useful things you can do to clarify code; it replaces a statement of what you are doing with why you are doing it.
- **Do not consolidate conditionals if the checks are truly independent** and should not be thought of as a single check.

Mechanics:

1. Ensure that none of the conditionals have any side effects.
   - If any do, use Separate Query from Modifier on them first.
2. Take two of the conditional statements and combine their conditions using a logical operator.
   - Sequences combine with `or`; nested `if` statements combine with `and`.
3. Test.
4. Repeat combining conditionals until they are all in a single condition.
5. Consider using Extract Function on the resulting condition.

- **Nested ifs combine with and**: `if (anEmployee.onVacation) if (anEmployee.seniority > 10) return 1;` becomes `if ((anEmployee.onVacation) && (anEmployee.seniority > 10)) return 1;`.
- **With a mix of ands and ors, things are likely to get messy** - use Extract Function liberally to make it all understandable.

#### Replace Nested Conditional with Guard Clauses

```js
// BAD
function getPayAmount() {
  let result;
  if (isDead) result = deadAmount();
  else { if (isSeparated) result = separatedAmount();
         else { if (isRetired) result = retiredAmount();
                else result = normalPayAmount(); } }
  return result;
}
// GOOD
function getPayAmount() {
  if (isDead) return deadAmount();
  if (isSeparated) return separatedAmount();
  if (isRetired) return retiredAmount();
  return normalPayAmount();
}
```

- **Distinguish the two styles of conditional and encode the distinction in the code** - if both legs are part of normal behavior, use a condition with an `if` and an `else` leg. If the condition is an unusual condition, check the condition and return if it's true; this kind of check is called a guard clause.
- **The key point is emphasis** - if-then-else gives equal weight to both legs, communicating that they are equally likely and important. A guard clause says "this isn't the core to this function, and if it happens, do something and get out."
- **One exit point is really not a useful rule** - one entry point is enforced by modern languages, but clarity is the key principle: if the method is clearer with one exit point, use one exit point; otherwise don't.

Mechanics:

1. Select the outermost condition that needs to be replaced, and change it into a guard clause.
2. Test.
3. Repeat as needed.
4. If all the guard clauses return the same result, use Consolidate Conditional Expression.

- **Remove the result variable once the guards are in** - after converting the nested conditions, a `result` variable that is only assigned once at the end is doing nothing useful; return the computation directly. Always take the extra strawberry for removing a mutable variable.
- **Reverse the conditional when installing the guard** - a guard often needs the negation of the original nesting condition (`if (anInstrument.capital > 0) {...}` becomes `if (anInstrument.capital <= 0) return result;`).
- **For a compound condition, do it in two steps** - first simply add a `not` around the whole condition, then simplify it (`!(a > 0 && b > 0)` becomes `a <= 0 || b <= 0`). Leaving nots in a conditional twists the mind around a painful angle.
- **Remove a result variable that is doing two things** - when its first setting indicates what to return if a guard triggers and its second value is the final computation, consolidate the guards that return the same result, then return the guard value directly from the guard and the computation directly at the end.

#### Replace Conditional with Polymorphism

```js
// BAD
switch (bird.type) {
  case 'EuropeanSwallow': return "average";
  case 'AfricanSwallow': return (bird.numberOfCoconuts > 2) ? "tired" : "average";
  default: return "unknown";
}
// GOOD
class EuropeanSwallow { get plumage() {return "average";} }
class AfricanSwallow { get plumage() {return (this.numberOfCoconuts > 2) ? "tired" : "average";} }
```

- **Use classes and polymorphism when logic separates into high-level cases** - complex conditional logic is one of the hardest things to reason about. Sometimes it is enough to represent the division within the structure of a conditional itself, but classes and polymorphism make the separation more explicit.
- **Case 1, a set of types**: when several functions have a switch statement on a type code, remove the duplication of the common switch logic by creating a class per case and using polymorphism to bring out the type-specific behavior.
- **Case 2, base case with variants**: put the most common or most straightforward logic into a superclass so you can reason about it without worrying about the variants, then put each variant case into a subclass expressed as its difference from the base case.
- **Do not replace all conditional logic with polymorphism** - polymorphism is prone to overuse. Most conditional logic should use basic conditional statements, if/else and switch/case; use polymorphism when you see complex conditional logic that can be improved by one of the two cases, a set of types each handling the logic differently or a base case with variants.

Mechanics:

1. If classes do not exist for polymorphic behavior, create them together with a factory function to return the correct instance.
2. Use the factory function in calling code.
3. Move the conditional function to the superclass.
   - If the conditional logic is not a self-contained function, use Extract Function to make it so.
4. Pick one of the subclasses. Create a subclass method that overrides the conditional statement method. Copy the body of that leg of the conditional statement into the subclass method and adjust it to fit.
5. Repeat for each leg of the conditional.
6. Leave a default case for the superclass method. Or, if the superclass should be abstract, declare that method as abstract or throw an error to show it should be the responsibility of a subclass.

- **Start from a set of functions by applying Combine Functions into Class** - you need a class structure before you can introduce polymorphism.
- **Put a `throw` into the leg you have just overridden** while migrating, out of paranoia, so a mistake surfaces; compile and test after each leg before doing the next.
- **In JavaScript you do not need a type hierarchy for polymorphism** - as long as objects implement the appropriately named methods, everything works. Keep an otherwise unnecessary superclass anyway when it helps explain how the classes are related in the domain.
- **Base-and-variation is particularly useful when you are about to introduce more special logic for the variant case** - the variant logic mixed into the base makes the base case harder to understand.

Base-and-variation mechanics, applied in order; steps 1 to 5 are formally the whole refactoring, steps 6 and 7 are follow-on cleanup:

1. Apply Combine Functions into Class to the family of functions that make up the calculation, to get the base class.
2. Create an empty subclass to house the variant behavior.
3. Create a factory function that returns the variant class when the variant condition holds, else the base class; modify all callers to use the factory instead of invoking the constructor directly.
4. For a simple variant adjustment, write the overriding method in terms of `super`: `get captainHistoryRisk() { const result = super.captainHistoryRisk - 2; return Math.max(result, 0); }` and delete the variant line from the superclass.
5. When the variant sits inside an if/else with an alternative path, you cannot simply remove it and call the superclass method, and you do not want to copy the whole superclass method down. First apply Extract Function to the entire conditional block, then push the variant leg into the subclass and leave the base leg in the superclass.
6. Then split the extracted method further: a function name with an "And" in it is a pretty bad smell and gives away that two separate modifications are going on. Apply Extract Function to each modification in both superclass and subclass, use Move Statements to Callers on the superclass case, apply Rename Function, and convert single-condition bodies to ternaries.
7. Move a constant offset out of a factor method into the overall result: `get voyageProfitFactor() {return super.voyageProfitFactor + 3;}` rather than adding 3 inside a length factor where it does not belong.

- **Introducing a method purely for overriding by a subclass is a common thing to do in base-and-variation inheritance** - but a crude catch-all method obscures what's going on instead of revealing it, so decompose it into separately named factors.
- **Payoff to aim for**: the superclass logic can ignore all complications of the variant case, and the variant class reads as a set of variations on the base.

#### Introduce Special Case

formerly: Introduce Null Object

```js
// BAD
if (aCustomer === "unknown") customerName = "occupant";
// GOOD
class UnknownCustomer { get name() {return "occupant";} }
```

- **Apply when many users of a data structure check a specific value and most of them then do the same thing** - this widespread testing for a special case plus a common response is the signal. Bring that reaction into a single place with the Special Case pattern: a special-case element that captures all the common behavior, so most special-case checks become simple calls.
- **Choose the special-case form by what clients do with it**:
  - reading data only: supply a literal object with all the values filled in;
  - more behavior than simple values needed: create a special object with methods for all the common behavior.
  - The special-case object can be returned by an encapsulating class, or inserted into a data structure with a transform.
- **Null Object is a special case of Special Case** - null is the most common value needing special-case processing, but the same approach applies to any special case.

Mechanics (precondition: a container data structure or class holds a subject property, and clients of the container compare that subject property to a special-case value; the goal is to replace the special-case value of the subject with a special-case class or data structure):

1. Add a special-case check property to the subject, returning false.
2. Create a special-case object with only the special-case check property, returning true.
3. Apply Extract Function to the special-case comparison code. Ensure that all clients use the new function instead of directly comparing.
4. Introduce the new special-case subject into the code, either by returning it from a function call or by applying a transform function.
5. Change the body of the special-case comparison function so that it uses the special-case check property.
6. Test.
7. Use Combine Functions into Class or Combine Functions into Transform to move all of the common special-case behavior into the new element.
   - Since the special-case class usually returns fixed values to simple requests, these may be handled by making the special case a literal record.
8. Use Inline Function on the special-case comparison function for the places where it's still needed.

- **Extracting the comparison function is the technique that breaks the all-at-once bind** - otherwise switching the container to return the special-case object forces every client testing the raw value to change in one step. Extract first so each client can be changed one at a time, testing after each change.
- **Put a trap for unexpected values in the extracted comparison function** while refactoring, to spot mistakes or odd behavior:

```js
function isUnknown(arg) {
  if (!((arg instanceof Customer) || (arg === "unknown")))
    throw new Error(`investigate bad value: <${arg}>`);
  return (arg === "unknown");
}
```

- **After all callers use the comparison function, change the container to return the special case**, then change the comparison function to consult the check property (`return arg.isUnknown;`), which also proves the raw sentinel string is no longer used. Test.
- **In JavaScript, do not make the special-case class a subclass of the real class** - JavaScript's subclassing rules and dynamic typing make it better not to. In other languages, particularly statically typed ones, do subclass.
- **Replace each client's conditional with the plain property access once the special case answers it** (`const customerName = aCustomer.name;`), then, after testing, apply Inline Variable to the now-pointless local.
- **For write behavior with no client action in the special case, let the setter be called and do nothing** (`set billingPlan(arg) { /* ignore */ }`).
- **Special-case objects are value objects, and thus should always be immutable, even if the objects they are substituting for are not.**
- **If a special case needs to return related objects, they are usually special cases themselves** - e.g. `get paymentHistory() {return new NullPaymentHistory();}` with `get weeksDelinquentInLastYear() {return 0;}`.
- **Expect exceptions among clients** - you may have 23 clients that use "occupant" for the name of an unknown customer, but there's always one that needs something different. For those, retain a special-case check, changed to use the method on the subject, essentially applying Inline Function to the comparison function: `aCustomer.isUnknown ? "unknown occupant" : aCustomer.name`.
- **When done with all the clients, apply Remove Dead Code to the global special-case comparison function**, as nobody should be calling it any more.

Variant: using an object literal

- **Use a literal instead of a class only when clients only read the data structure** - creating a class is a fair bit of work for what is really a simple value, but a class is required when the subject can be updated, and usually you should prefer a class anyway.
- **Add the standard responses to the literal one at a time**, each one replacing one client's conditional: `{isUnknown: true, name: "occupant", billingPlan: registry.billingPlans.basic, paymentHistory: {weeksDelinquentInLastYear: 0}}`.
- **If you use a literal, make it immutable, which you might do with freeze.**

Variant: using a transform

- **For a record rather than a class, introduce the special case with a transform step.**

Mechanics:

1. Run the input data structure through a transform that currently does nothing but a deep copy (`_.cloneDeep`).
2. Apply Extract Function to the test for the special-case value.
3. In the transform, build the special-case record and substitute it; set the check property to false on normal records: `if (isUnknown(result.customer)) result.customer = unknownCustomer; else result.customer.isUnknown = false;`
4. Modify the special-case condition test to also probe the new property, keeping the original test as well so the test works on both raw and enriched records: `if (aCustomer === "unknown") return true; else return aCustomer.isUnknown;`
5. Test, then apply Combine Functions into Transform one property at a time (name, then billing plan, then the nested null history), testing after each, deleting each client's conditional as its value moves into the enrichment function.

#### Introduce Assertion

```js
// GOOD
assert(this.discountRate >= 0);
if (this.discountRate)
  base = base - (this.discountRate * base);
```

- **Make an implicit assumption explicit by writing an assertion** rather than leaving it to be deduced by reading the algorithm, or stating it in a comment.
- **Definition** - an assertion is a conditional statement that is assumed to be always true. Failure of an assertion indicates a programmer error.
- **Assertion failures should never be checked by other parts of the system.**
- **Write assertions so that the program functions equally correctly if they are all removed** - some languages provide assertions that can be disabled by a compile-time switch. Since assertions should not affect the running of a system, adding one is always behavior-preserving.
- **Value assertions as communication, not only as error-finding** - they tell the reader something about the assumed state of the program at that point of execution. They are handy for debugging, and their communication value means you should be inclined to leave them in once the error is fixed. Self-testing code reduces their debugging value, since steadily narrowing unit tests often do that job better, but assertions remain worthwhile for communication.

Mechanics:

1. When you see that a condition is assumed to be true, add an assertion to state it.

- **Reformulate a ternary as an if-then statement first** if you cannot easily place an assertion into it.
- **Prefer asserting in the setting method over the using method** - if an assertion fails in the consumer, the first puzzle is how the bad value got into the field in the first place: `set discountRate(aNumber) { assert(null === aNumber || aNumber >= 0); this._discountRate = aNumber; }`. Such an assertion is particularly valuable when the error source is hard to spot, such as an errant minus sign in input data or an inversion elsewhere in the code.
- **There is a real danger of overusing assertions** - do not assert everything you think is true, only things that need to be true.
- **Remove all duplication in assertion conditions, usually by liberal use of Extract Function** - duplication is a particular problem because it's common to tweak these kinds of conditions.
- **Only use assertions for programmer errors** - if you are reading data from an external source, any value checking should be a first-class part of the program, not an assertion, unless you are really confident in the external source. Assertions are a last resort to help track bugs, though ironically you only use them when you think they should never fail.

### Refactoring APIs - selection guide

- **A good API clearly separates any functions that update data from those that only read data.**

| Situation | Refactoring |
|---|---|
| Update and read behavior combined in one function | Separate Query from Modifier |
| Functions that vary only due to a value | Parameterize Function |
| A parameter that really signals an entirely different behavior | Remove Flag Argument |
| Data structures unnecessarily unpacked when passed between functions | Preserve Whole Object (prefer keeping them together) |
| Deciding what should be passed as a parameter vs resolved by the called function | Replace Parameter with Query / Replace Query with Parameter (revisit both often) |
| A settable field on an object you want as immutable as possible | Remove Setting Method, whenever you can |
| A caller needs more flexibility than a simple constructor gives | Replace Constructor with Factory Function |
| A particularly complex function passing a lot of data around, hard to break down | Replace Function with Command, turning it into an object so Extract Function is easier on its body |
| A command object simplified to the point it is no longer needed | Replace Command with Function |

## Refactoring: Ch11 Refactoring APIs

### Separate Query from Modifier

```js
// BAD
function getTotalOutstandingAndSendBill() {
  const result = customer.invoices.reduce((total, each) => each.amount + total, 0);
  sendBill();
  return result;
}
// GOOD
function totalOutstanding() {
  return customer.invoices.reduce((total, each) => each.amount + total, 0);
}
function sendBill() { emailGateway.send(formatBill(customer)); }
```

- **Any function that returns a value should not have observable side effects** - this is the command-query separation rule. Some programmers treat it as an absolute rule; treat it as a rule to follow most of the time, not 100 percent purity.
- **Clearly signal the difference between functions with side effects and those without.**
- **If a method returns a value but also has side effects, always try to separate the query from the modifier.**
- **A side-effect-free value-returning function is a very valuable thing** - it can be called as often as you like, its call can be moved to other places in a calling function, and it is easier to test.
- **"Observable" is the operative word** - caching a query's value in a field so repeated calls go faster changes object state but is not an observable side effect, because any sequence of queries still returns the same result for each query. Such caching does not violate the rule.

#### Mechanics

1. Copy the function, name it as a query.
   - Look into the function to see what is returned. If the query is used to populate a variable, the variable's name should provide a good clue.
2. Remove any side effects from the new query function.
3. Run static checks.
4. Find each call of the original method. If that call uses the return value, replace the original call with a call to the query and insert a call to the original method below it. Test after each change.
5. Remove return values from original.
6. Test.

- **After the split, tidy the duplication** - there is often duplication between the query and the original method; use Substitute Algorithm so the modifier delegates to the query, e.g. `if (findMiscreant(people) !== "") setOffAlarms();`.

### Parameterize Function

formerly: Parameterize Method

```js
// BAD
function tenPercentRaise(aPerson)  { aPerson.salary = aPerson.salary.multiply(1.1); }
function fivePercentRaise(aPerson) { aPerson.salary = aPerson.salary.multiply(1.05); }
// GOOD
function raise(aPerson, factor) { aPerson.salary = aPerson.salary.multiply(1 + factor); }
```

- **When two functions carry out very similar logic with different literal values, remove the duplication with a single parameterized function** - this also increases the function's usefulness, since it can be applied elsewhere with different values.

#### Mechanics

1. Select one of the similar methods.
2. Use Change Function Declaration to add any literals that need to turn into parameters.
3. For each caller of the function, add the literal value.
4. Test.
5. Change the body of the function to use the new parameters. Test after each change.
6. For each similar function, replace the call with a call to the parameterized function. Test after each one.
   - If the original parameterized function doesn't work for a similar function, adjust it for the new function before moving on to the next.

- **Pick the middle case as the seed function** - when parameterizing related functions, take one function and add parameters to it with an eye to the other cases; with range-oriented things, usually start with the middle range (e.g. parameterize `middleBand` into `withinBand(usage, bottom, top)`, then retarget `bottomBand` as `withinBand(usage, 0, 100)` and `topBand` as `withinBand(usage, 200, Infinity)`).
- **Rename the seed function while adding its parameters** - give it a name that makes sense with the parameterization (`middleBand` -> `withinBand`), doing the rename as part of the Change Function Declaration step.
- **Use Infinity to fold an open-ended range into the parameterized form.**
- **Keep a guard clause that has become logically unnecessary** if it documents how that case is handled (e.g. `if (usage < 0) return usd(0);`).
- **Similarity that is less obvious can still qualify** - a set of functions that each compute one slice of the same numeric range (bottom, middle, top band) is similar enough to support a parameterized function, even though it is less obvious than the trivial case of two functions differing only in one literal value.

### Remove Flag Argument

formerly: Replace Parameter with Explicit Methods

```js
// BAD
function setDimension(name, value) {
  if (name === "height") { this._height = value; return; }
  if (name === "width")  { this._width  = value; return; }
}
// GOOD
function setHeight(value) {this._height = value;}
function setWidth (value) {this._width  = value;}
```

- **Definition** - a flag argument is a function argument that the caller uses to indicate which logic the called function should execute. Flag arguments can be booleans, enums (`bookConcert(aCustomer, CustomerType.PREMIUM)`), or strings/symbols (`bookConcert(aCustomer, "premium")`).
- **Remove flag arguments; provide an explicit function for the task instead** - flag arguments complicate understanding of what calls are available and how to call them; the list of available functions is the first route into an API and flags hide the differences between calls. After selecting a function you must then figure out what values the flag accepts.
- **Boolean flags are even worse than enums or strings** - they do not convey their meaning to the reader; at the call site you cannot tell what `true` means.
- **Two conditions must both hold for an argument to be a flag argument:**
  - the callers must be setting the value to a literal value, not data that's flowing through the program; and
  - the implementation function must be using the argument to influence its control flow, not as data that it passes to further functions.
- **If callers set the argument from data (`const isRush = determineIfRush(anOrder);`), the signature is fine** - do not remove it, though you would still want to apply Decompose Conditional inside.
- **Mixed callers: apply the refactoring but keep the original** - if some callers pass a literal and others pass data, still use Remove Flag Argument, but do not change the data callers and do not remove the original function at the end, so both interfaces are supported for their different uses.
- **Removing flag arguments also helps tooling** - code analysis tools can then more easily distinguish calls to the premium logic from calls to the regular logic.
- **More than one flag in a function can have a place** - otherwise you would need explicit functions for every combination of their values. But that is also a signal of a function doing too much; look for a way to create simpler functions that you can compose for this logic.

#### Mechanics

1. Create an explicit function for each value of the parameter.
   - If the main function has a clear dispatch conditional, use Decompose Conditional to create the explicit functions. Otherwise, create wrapping functions.
2. For each caller that uses a literal value for the parameter, replace it with a call to the explicit function.

- **Decompose Conditional only works when the dispatch on the parameter is the outer part of the function** (or you can easily refactor it to be so). When the parameter is used in a tangled way throughout the body, teasing out a top-level dispatch conditional is likely more work than it is worth.
- **For tangled cases, layer wrapping functions over the original** - these are essentially partial applications defined in program text rather than by composition of functions:

```js
function rushDeliveryDate   (anOrder) {return deliveryDate(anOrder, true);}
function regularDeliveryDate(anOrder) {return deliveryDate(anOrder, false);}
```

- **After wrapping, hide the flagged original** - if no callers use the parameter as data, restrict its visibility or rename it to a name conveying it should not be used directly (e.g. `deliveryDateHelperOnly`).
- **When all callers have been replaced, remove the original function** (in the non-mixed case).

### Preserve Whole Object

```js
// BAD
const low  = aRoom.daysTempRange.low;
const high = aRoom.daysTempRange.high;
if (aPlan.withinRange(low, high))
// GOOD
if (aPlan.withinRange(aRoom.daysTempRange))
```

- **When code derives a couple of values from a record and passes those values into a function, pass the whole record and let the function body derive what it needs.**
  - It handles change better: if the called function later needs more data from the whole, the parameter list need not change.
  - It reduces parameter list size, which usually makes the call easier to understand.
  - If many functions are called with the parts, they often duplicate the logic that manipulates those parts - logic that can often be moved to the whole.
- **Do NOT pass the whole record if you don't want the called function to have a dependency on the whole** - this is the main reason to refrain, and typically occurs when the caller and the called function are in different modules.
- **Pulling several values from an object to do logic on them alone is Feature Envy** - usually a signal that this logic should be moved into the whole itself.
- **Expect this refactoring right after Introduce Parameter Object** - hunt down occurrences of the original data clump and replace them with the new object.
- **If several bits of code only use the same subset of an object's features, consider Extract Class.**
- **Commonly missed case: an object calling another object with several of its own data values** - replace those values with a self-reference (`this` in JavaScript).

#### Mechanics

1. Create an empty function with the desired parameters.
   - Give the function an easily searchable name so it can be replaced at the end (e.g. same name with an `xxNEW` prefix).
2. Fill the body of the new function with a call to the old function, mapping from the new parameters to the old ones.
3. Run static checks.
4. Adjust each caller to use the new function, testing after each change.
   - This may mean some code that derives the parameter isn't needed, so can fall to Remove Dead Code.
5. Once all original callers have been changed, use Inline Function on the original function.
6. Change the name of the new function and all its callers.
   - The searchable prefix makes this a simple global replace even without robust rename support in the editor.

#### Variation: create the new function entirely by refactorings

- **Use this variation when you have a refactoring tool with robust extract and inline operations** - it composes the new function from refactorings instead of hand-writing it.

1. Start at a caller of the existing function; use Extract Variable to disentangle the call to the old function from the surrounding conditional (`const isWithinRange = aPlan.withinRange(low, high);`).
2. Use Extract Variable again to extract the input parameter (`const tempRange = aRoom.daysTempRange;`).
3. Use Extract Function on the now-adjacent code to create the new function.
4. If the original function lives in a different context (e.g. the `HeatingPlan` class), use Move Function to move the new function there.
5. Continue as in the main mechanics: replace other callers, inline the old function into the new one, and inline the variables you extracted to provide the clean separation for the extraction.

### Replace Parameter with Query

formerly: Replace Parameter with Method; inverse of: Replace Query with Parameter

```js
// BAD
availableVacation(anEmployee, anEmployee.grade);
function availableVacation(anEmployee, grade) { /* calculate vacation... */ }
// GOOD
availableVacation(anEmployee);
function availableVacation(anEmployee) { const grade = anEmployee.grade; /* ... */ }
```

- **A parameter list should summarize the points of variability of the function**, indicating the primary ways in which it may behave differently. Avoid duplication in it, and keep it short so it is easier to understand.
- **If a call passes a value the function can just as easily determine for itself, remove the parameter** - that is a form of duplication that unnecessarily complicates the caller.
- **The limit is the phrase "just as easily"** - removing the parameter shifts responsibility for determining its value from caller to function body. The usual habit is to simplify life for callers, which implies moving responsibility to the function body, but only if that responsibility is appropriate there.
- **Most common reason to avoid this refactoring: it adds an unwanted dependency to the function body** - forcing it to access a program element you'd rather it remained ignorant of. This may be a new dependency or an existing one you'd like to remove. Usually it shows up as needing to add a problematic function call to the body, or to access something in a receiver object you'd prefer to move out later.
- **Safest case: the parameter's value is determined merely by querying another parameter in the list** - there is rarely any point in passing two parameters if one can be determined from the other.
- **Do not replace a parameter with an access to a mutable global variable** - watch out for whether the function has referential transparency (it behaves the same way whenever it is called with the same parameter values); such functions are much easier to reason about and test, so do not alter them in a way that loses that property.

#### Mechanics

1. If necessary, use Extract Function on the calculation of the parameter.
2. Replace references to the parameter in the function body with references to the expression that yields the parameter. Test after each change.
3. Use Change Function Declaration to remove the parameter.

- **Typical trigger** - a parameter becomes unnecessary after other refactorings, e.g. after Replace Temp with Query turns `discountLevel` into a getter, `discountedPrice(basePrice, discountLevel)` can call `this.discountLevel` itself and drop the parameter.

### Replace Query with Parameter

inverse of: Replace Parameter with Query

```js
// BAD
targetTemperature(aPlan)
function targetTemperature(aPlan) { currentTemperature = thermostat.currentTemperature; /* ... */ }
// GOOD
targetTemperature(aPlan, thermostat.currentTemperature)
function targetTemperature(aPlan, currentTemperature) { /* ... */ }
```

- **When a function body references something in its scope that you're unhappy with - a global variable, or an element in the same module you intend to move away - replace the internal reference with a parameter**, shifting responsibility for resolving the reference to the caller.
- **The driver is dependency structure** - make the target function no longer dependent on the element being parameterized.
- **Hold the tension explicitly** - converting everything to parameters gives long repetitive parameter lists; sharing a lot of scope leads to a lot of coupling between functions. You cannot reliably get this decision right, so what matters is keeping the code reliably changeable as understanding grows.
- **Definition: referential transparency** - a function always gives the same result when called with the same parameter values. If a function accesses an element in its scope that isn't referentially transparent, the containing function also lacks referential transparency; fix that by moving that element to a parameter.
- **Use this refactoring to purify parts of a program** - a common pattern is modules consisting of pure functions wrapped by logic that handles I/O and other variable elements. Purified parts are easier to test and reason about.
- **Accept the cost** - moving a query to a parameter forces callers to figure out how to provide the value, complicating life for callers, against the usual bias to design interfaces that make life easier for their consumers. The calling code often looks more unwieldy than before; that is the trade-off for reduced coupling.
- **It boils down to allocation of responsibility around the program** - a decision that is neither easy nor immutable, which is why you must be very familiar with both this refactoring and its inverse.

#### Mechanics

1. Use Extract Variable on the query code to separate it from the rest of the function body.
2. Apply Extract Function to the body code that isn't the call to the query.
   - Give the new function an easily searchable name, for later renaming.
3. Use Inline Variable to get rid of the variable you just created.
4. Apply Inline Function to the original function.
5. Rename the new function to that of the original.

- **Secondary gain: immutability plus parameterization yields referential transparency** - with an immutable class (fields set in the constructor, no mutating methods), moving a global reference out of the body makes the method referentially transparent; if all methods of the class have referential transparency the class becomes much easier to test and reason about.
- **JavaScript caveat** - it is impossible to enforce an immutable class in JavaScript's class model (there is always a way to get at an object's data), but writing a class to signal and encourage immutability is often good enough.

### Remove Setting Method

```js
// BAD
class Person { get name() {...}  set name(aString) {...} }
// GOOD
class Person { get name() {...} }
```

- **If a field must not change once the object is created, provide no setting method and make the field immutable** - a setting method advertises that the field may be changed; without one the field is set only in the constructor, the intent is clear, and usually the very possibility of change is removed.
- **Case 1: accessors used even inside constructors** - when the only call to a setter is from the constructor, remove the setter to make clear that updates make no sense after construction.
- **Case 2: creation scripts** - clients create the object with a creation script: a constructor call followed by a sequence of setter calls. When the object is not expected to change some (or even all) of those fields once the script finishes, and the setters are only expected to be called during that initial creation, get rid of those setters to make intentions clearer.

#### Mechanics

1. If the value that's being set isn't provided to the constructor, use Change Function Declaration to add it. Add a call to the setting method within the constructor.
   - If you wish to remove several setting methods, add all their values to the constructor at once. This simplifies the later steps.
2. Remove each call of a setting method outside of the constructor, using the new constructor value instead. Test after each one.
   - If you can't replace the call to the setter by creating a new object (because you are updating a shared reference object), abandon the refactoring.
3. Use Inline Function on the setting method. Make the field immutable if possible.
4. Test.

### Replace Constructor with Factory Function

formerly: Replace Constructor with Factory Method

```js
// BAD
leadEngineer = new Employee(document.leadEngineer, 'E');
// GOOD
leadEngineer = createEngineer(document.leadEngineer);
```

- **Replace a constructor with a factory function to escape constructor limitations** - constructors carry awkward limitations that general functions do not:
  - a Java constructor must return an instance of the class it was called with, so it cannot be replaced with a subclass or proxy depending on environment or parameters;
  - constructor naming is fixed, so you cannot use a name clearer than the default;
  - constructors often require a special operator to invoke ("new" in many languages), making them hard to use in contexts that expect normal functions.
- **A factory function has none of those limitations** - it will likely call the constructor as part of its implementation, but you can freely substitute something else.

#### Mechanics

1. Create a factory function, its body being a call to the constructor.
2. Replace each call to the constructor with a call to the factory function. Test after each change.
3. Limit the constructor's visibility as much as possible.

- **It is generally a bad smell to pass a code as a literal string** - instead of `createEmployee(document.leadEngineer, 'E')`, create a factory function that embeds the kind into its name: `function createEngineer(name) { return new Employee(name, 'E'); }`.

### Replace Function with Command

formerly: Replace Method with Method Object; inverse of: Replace Command with Function

```js
// BEFORE
function score(candidate, medicalExam, scoringGuide) { let result = 0; /* long body */ }
// AFTER
class Scorer {
  constructor(candidate, medicalExam, scoringGuide) { /* fields */ }
  execute() { this._result = 0; /* long body */ }
}
```

- **Definition** - a command object (here, "command") is an object mostly built around a single method, whose request and execution is the purpose of the object, following the command pattern in Design Patterns.
- **Terminology discipline** - "command" is also used in the command-query separation principle to mean an object method that changes observable state; for that meaning prefer "modifier" or "mutator". When using the pattern sense, introduce it as "command object" to set context, then say "command".
- **Given the choice between a first-class function and a command, pick the function 95% of the time** - use a command only when you specifically need a facility that simpler approaches can't provide. The flexibility comes at a price paid in complexity.
- **Reasons that justify a command:**
  - complementary operations such as undo;
  - methods to build up parameters, supporting a richer lifecycle;
  - customizations built in using inheritance and hooks;
  - in a language with objects but without first-class functions, providing much of that capability;
  - using methods and fields to break down a complex function even in a language lacking nested functions, and calling those methods directly while testing and debugging.
- **Be ready to refactor functions into commands when needed**, but do not forget the complexity cost.

#### Mechanics

1. Create an empty class for the function. Name it based on the function.
2. Use Move Function to move the function to the empty class.
   - Keep the original function as a forwarding function until at least the end of the refactoring.
   - Follow any convention the language has for naming commands. If there is no convention, choose a generic name for the command's execute function, such as "execute" or "call".
3. Consider making a field for each argument, and move these arguments to the constructor.

- **Prefer constructor arguments with a no-parameter execute method** - most of the time pass arguments to the command on the constructor and have `execute` take no parameters. It matters less for a simple decomposition, but is very handy for a more complicated parameter-setting lifecycle or customizations: different command classes can have different parameters yet be mixed together when queued for execution.
- **Move parameters one at a time**, replacing body references with `this._field` as you go.
- **Follow-on decomposition steps (the point of the refactoring):**
  1. Change all the local variables into fields, one at a time (`let result` -> `this._result`, `let healthLevel` -> `this._healthLevel`, etc.).
  2. With all the function's state on the command object, apply Extract Function freely without getting tangled up in variables and their scopes (e.g. extract `scoreSmoking()`).
- **In JavaScript, nested functions are a reasonable alternative to a command for this decomposition** - a command is still preferable when you want to write tests and debugging calls against the subfunctions.

### Replace Command with Function

inverse of: Replace Function with Command

```js
// BEFORE
class ChargeCalculator {
  constructor (customer, usage){ this._customer = customer; this._usage = usage; }
  execute() { return this._customer.rate * this._usage; }
}
// AFTER
function charge(customer, usage) { return customer.rate * usage; }
```

- **Command objects are powerful for complex computations** - they break down easily into separate methods sharing common state through fields, can be invoked via different methods for different effects, and can have their data built up in stages.
- **If the function isn't too complex and you just want to invoke it and have it do its thing, a command object is more trouble than it's worth - turn it into a regular function.**

#### Mechanics

1. Apply Extract Function to the creation of the command and the call to the command's execution method.
   - This creates the new function that will replace the command in due course.
2. For each method called by the command's execution method, apply Inline Function.
   - If the supporting function returns a value, use Extract Variable on the call first and then Inline Function.
3. Use Change Function Declaration to put all the parameters of the constructor into the command's execution method instead.
4. For each field, alter the references in the command's execution method to use the parameter instead. Test after each change.
5. Inline the constructor call and command's execution method call into the caller (which is the replacement function).
   - This is a special kind of Inline Function, as it inlines both the constructor and the method call together.
6. Test.
7. Apply Remove Dead Code to the command class.

- **Delete the constructor's field assignments as you convert each field to a parameter** - you don't have to (the assignment would just be ignored), but removing it makes a test fail if you miss changing a use of the field to the parameter. If no test fails, consider adding a new test.

### Inheritance refactoring selection

- **Use inheritance carefully; it is both very useful and easy to misuse, and the misuse is often hard to see until it is in the rear-view mirror.**
- **To move features up or down the hierarchy** use Pull Up Method, Pull Up Field, Pull Up Constructor Body, Push Down Method, Push Down Field.
- **To add or remove classes from the hierarchy** use Extract Superclass, Remove Subclass, Collapse Hierarchy.
- **To replace a field used to trigger different behavior based on its value with a subclass** use Replace Type Code with Subclasses.
- **When inheritance is used in the wrong place, or the place it is used in becomes wrong, turn inheritance into delegation** with Replace Subclass with Delegate or Replace Superclass with Delegate.

## Refactoring: Ch12 Dealing with Inheritance

### Pulling members up the hierarchy

#### Pull Up Method

inverse of: Push Down Method

```js
// BEFORE
class Salesman extends Employee { get name() {...} }
class Engineer extends Employee { get name() {...} }
// AFTER
class Employee { get name() {...} }
class Salesman extends Employee {...}
class Engineer extends Employee {...}
```

- **Pull up duplicated subclass methods** - eliminating duplicate code is important; two duplicate methods may work fine as they are, but they are nothing but a breeding ground for bugs, because an alteration to one copy may not be made to the other, and duplicates are usually difficult to find.
- **Easiest case is identical bodies** - identical bodies imply copy and paste; that is the simplest application, but it is not always that obvious.
- **Do not rely on tests to find the difference** - you could just do the refactoring and see if the tests croak, but that puts a lot of reliance on your tests; it is usually valuable to look for the differences first, because they often show up behavior you forgot to test for.
- **Parameterize before pulling up** - when two methods in different classes can be parameterized so they end up as essentially the same method, the smallest step is to apply Parameterize Function separately first, then Pull Up Method.
- **Handle subclass-only references first** - the most awkward complication is a body that refers to features present on the subclass but not the superclass; use Pull Up Field and Pull Up Method on those elements first.
- **Similar flow, differing details** - if two methods have a similar overall flow but differ in details, consider Form Template Method instead.

Mechanics:
1. Inspect methods to ensure they are identical.
   - If they do the same thing but are not identical, refactor them until they have identical bodies.
2. Check that all method calls and field references inside the method body refer to features that can be called from the superclass.
3. If the methods have different signatures, use Change Function Declaration to get them to the one you want to use on the superclass.
4. Create a new method in the superclass. Copy the body of one of the methods over to it.
5. Run static checks.
6. Delete one subclass method.
7. Test.
8. Keep deleting subclass methods until they are all gone.

- **Static vs dynamic language obligation** - in a dynamic language a pulled-up method may call a member defined only on subclasses and still work; in a static language you must define an abstract method on the superclass. In a static language, compile to ensure all references are OK; when the compiler cannot help, remove the method from one subclass, test, then remove it from the next.
- **Signal subclass responsibility with a trap method** - when the pulled-up method calls a member the superclass does not define, add a trap so later subclasses know they must implement it. This is a subclass responsibility error, the name used in Smalltalk.

```js
// GOOD
class Party {
  get monthlyCost() { throw new SubclassResponsibilityError(); }
}
```

#### Pull Up Field

inverse of: Push Down Field

```java
// BEFORE
class Salesman extends Employee { private String name; }
class Engineer extends Employee { private String name; }
// AFTER
class Employee { protected String name; }
```

- **Look for duplicate fields in independently developed subclasses** - subclasses developed independently, or combined through refactoring, often duplicate features; such fields sometimes have similar names, but not always.
- **Decide by usage, not by name** - the only way to tell what is going on is by looking at the fields and examining how they are used; if they are used in a similar way, pull them up.
- **Two duplication wins** - pulling up removes the duplicate data declaration and then lets you move behavior that uses the field from the subclasses to the superclass.
- **Dynamic languages** - many dynamic languages do not define fields as part of the class definition; fields appear when first assigned to, so pulling up a field there is essentially a consequence of Pull Up Constructor Body.

Mechanics:
1. Inspect all users of the candidate field to ensure they are used in the same way.
2. If the fields have different names, use Rename Field to give them the same name.
3. Create a new field in the superclass.
   - The new field will need to be accessible to subclasses (protected in common languages).
4. Delete the subclass fields.
5. Test.

#### Pull Up Constructor Body

```js
// BEFORE
class Employee extends Party {
  constructor(name, id, monthlyCost) { super(); this._id = id; this._name = name; ... }
}
// AFTER
class Party { constructor(name) { this._name = name; } }
class Employee extends Party {
  constructor(name, id, monthlyCost) { super(name); this._id = id; ... }
}
```

- **Use a separate approach for constructors** - constructors are not quite normal methods, so you are more restricted in what you can do with them; for ordinary common subclass behavior the first thought is Extract Function followed by Pull Up Method, but constructors have special rules about what can be done in what order, so they need this refactoring.
- **Bail out to a factory when it gets messy** - if this refactoring starts getting messy, reach for Replace Constructor with Factory Function.

Mechanics:
1. Define a superclass constructor, if one doesn't already exist. Ensure it's called by subclass constructors.
2. Use Slide Statements to move any common statements to just after the super call.
3. Remove the common code from each subclass and put it in the superclass.
4. Add to the super call any constructor parameters referenced in the common code.
5. Test.
6. If there is any common code that cannot move to the start of the constructor, use Extract Function followed by Pull Up Method.

- **Test after the slide, before the move** - slide the common assignment next to the super call, test, then move it to the superclass.
- **Normal constructor shape** - most of the time constructor behavior works like this: do the common elements first (with a super call), then do the extra work the subclass needs.
- **Common behavior that must run late** - when common code depends on a field only the subclass can assign (for example a call to `isPrivileged` that needs `_grade`), it cannot move to the start of the constructor; Extract Function it into a `finishConstruction()` called at the end of the subclass constructor, then Pull Up Method it.

```js
// GOOD
class Manager extends Employee {
  constructor(name, grade) { super(name); this._grade = grade; this.finishConstruction(); }
}
class Employee {
  finishConstruction() { if (this.isPrivileged) this.assignCar(); }
}
```

### Pushing members down the hierarchy

#### Push Down Method

inverse of: Pull Up Method

```js
// BEFORE
class Employee { get quota {...} }
// AFTER
class Salesman extends Employee { get quota {...} }
```

- **Push down a method relevant to few subclasses** - if a method is only relevant to one subclass (or a small proportion of subclasses), removing it from the superclass and putting it only on the subclass(es) makes that clearer.
- **Precondition: the caller must know the concrete subclass** - you can only do this refactoring if the caller knows it's working with a particular subclass; otherwise use Replace Conditional with Polymorphism with some placebo behavior on the superclass.

Mechanics:
1. Copy the method into every subclass that needs it.
2. Remove the method from the superclass.
3. Test.
4. Remove the method from each superclass that doesn't need it.
5. Test.

- **Step 4 wording conflicts with the parallel refactoring** - the Push Down Method mechanics say "each superclass that doesn't need it", while the parallel Push Down Field step says "all subclasses that don't need it". Both statements stand as written; apply the field wording when working on fields and the method wording when working on methods.

#### Push Down Field

inverse of: Pull Up Field

```java
// BEFORE
class Employee { private String quota; }
// AFTER
class Salesman extends Employee { protected String quota; }
```

- **Push down a field used by few subclasses** - if a field is only used by one subclass (or a small proportion of subclasses), move it to those subclasses.

Mechanics:
1. Declare field in all subclasses that need it.
2. Remove the field from the superclass.
3. Test.
4. Remove the field from all subclasses that don't need it.
5. Test.

### Type codes and subclasses

#### Replace Type Code with Subclasses

subsumes: Replace Type Code with State/Strategy; subsumes: Extract Subclass; inverse of: Remove Subclass

```js
// BEFORE
function createEmployee(name, type) { return new Employee(name, type); }
// AFTER
function createEmployee(name, type) {
  switch (type) {
    case "engineer": return new Engineer(name);
    case "salesman": return new Salesman(name);
    case "manager":  return new Manager(name);
  }
}
```

- **A type code is the default tool** - to represent different kinds of a similar thing (employees by job type; orders by priority rush/regular), the first tool is a type code field: an enum, symbol, string, or number depending on the language. Often the type code comes from an external service supplying the data. Most of the time such a type code is all you need.
- **Reason 1 to go to subclasses: polymorphism** - subclasses let you use polymorphism to handle conditional logic; most helpful when several functions invoke different behavior depending on the value of the type code, so you can then apply Replace Conditional with Polymorphism to those functions.
- **Reason 2: members valid only for some type code values** - when fields or methods are only valid for particular type code values (a sales quota only applicable to the "salesman" code), create the subclass and apply Push Down Field. Validation logic could ensure a field is only used when the type code has the correct value, but using a subclass makes the relationship more explicit.
- **Choose direct or indirect inheritance deliberately** - decide whether to subclass the class you are looking at (make engineer a subtype of employee) or the type code itself (give employee an employee-type property with subtypes). Direct subclassing is simpler.
  - You cannot use direct subclassing for this type if you need the single inheritance axis for something else.
  - You cannot use direct subclasses if the type is mutable.
