- **Photograph whiteboards** - Reject the false choice between polished formal notation and no documentation; embedding digital photos of whiteboard drawings into ordinary documents yields about 80 percent of the benefit of saved design drawings for about 1 percent of the effort of a drawing tool.
- **Save flip charts** - Design drawings need not fit letter-size paper; archive large flip-chart sheets, or better, post them on the project area walls so they stay referenced and get updated.
- **Use CRC (Class, Responsibility, Collaborator) cards** - On each index card write the class name, its responsibilities, and its collaborators (the classes that cooperate with it); work the cards as a group until satisfied with the design, then save them. Cards are cheap, unintimidating, portable, and promote group interaction.
- **Use UML (Unified Modeling Language) at the right detail level** - UML, defined by the Object Management Group, supplies formalized representations for design entities and relationships. Explore and discuss approaches with informal UML: sketch minimally first, and add detail only once a final solution is settled. Because it is standardized it aids shared understanding and speeds group evaluation of alternatives.

### Comments on Popular Methodologies

- **Reject both extremes** - Two positions are always wrong: settling every design detail before coding, and doing no design at all. Reject the demand to finish every design decision up front, and equally reject the inference that because BDUF (Big Design Up Front) is bad, no design should precede coding.
- **Aim for LDUF or ENUF** - Replace BDUF with LDUF (Little Design Up Front) or ENUF (Enough Design Up Front). The right amount is a judgment call, never made perfectly and never knowable with confidence, so only the two extremes can be ruled out in advance.
- **Dogma reduces problem-solving power** - The more dogmatically a design method is applied, the fewer real problems get solved; dogmatic adherence to any single methodology damages both creativity and the resulting program.
- **Operating stance for design** - Treat design as a wicked, sloppy, heuristic process: never settle for the first design that occurs; collaborate; strive for simplicity; prototype when needed; iterate repeatedly.

### Design Practices Checklist

- **Iterate and select** - Confirm several design attempts were made and the best chosen, not the first.
- **Decompose multiple ways** - Confirm the system was decomposed more than one way to see which works best.
- **Both directions** - Confirm the problem was approached both top down and bottom up.
- **Prototype the risky parts** - Confirm risky or unfamiliar parts were prototyped with the absolute minimum throwaway code needed to answer specific questions.
- **Get it reviewed** - Confirm the design was reviewed by others, formally or informally.
- **Drive to obviousness** - Confirm the design was pushed until its implementation looks obvious.
- **Capture the design** - Confirm the design work was recorded by some appropriate means: Wiki, e-mail, flip charts, digital photography, UML, CRC cards, or code comments.

### Design Goals Checklist

- **Close the architectural leftovers** - Confirm the design handles the issues identified but deferred at the architecture level.
- **Stratify into layers** - Confirm the design is layered.
- **Sound decomposition into subsystems, packages, classes** - Confirm the program partitioning is satisfactory.
- **Sound decomposition of classes into routines** - Confirm the routine-level partitioning is satisfactory.
- **Minimal inter-class interaction** - Confirm classes are designed to interact with each other as little as possible.
- **Reusability** - Confirm classes and subsystems are designed so other systems can use them.
- **Maintainability** - Confirm the program will be easy to maintain.
- **Leanness** - Confirm every part of the design is strictly necessary.
- **Standard over exotic** - Confirm the design uses standard techniques and avoids exotic, hard-to-understand elements.
- **Complexity reduction overall** - Confirm the design minimizes both accidental and essential complexity.

### Class Foundations Carried Forward

- **Definition - class** - A collection of data and routines sharing a cohesive, well-defined responsibility; alternatively, a collection of routines providing a cohesive set of services even with no shared data.
- **Maximize what can be safely ignored** - Effective programming maximizes how much of the system a person can ignore safely while editing any single part of it; classes are the primary tool for achieving that.

## Code Complete: Ch6 Working Classes

### Class Foundations: Abstract Data Types (ADTs)

- **Definition of ADT** - An abstract data type is data bundled with the operations that act on it; those operations are both how surrounding code perceives the data and how it changes the data. "Data" is loose here: a graphics window, a file, an insurance-rates table, a reactor cooling system all qualify.
- **ADTs precede classes** - Design the ADT first, then express it as a class. Skipping this step yields "classes" in name only - containers for loosely related data and routines. Treat a class as an ADT plus inheritance and polymorphism, and evaluate every class interface from the ADT point of view.
- **Work in the problem domain** - Define operations over real-world entities (add a spreadsheet cell, add a train car) rather than over implementation structures (insert a linked-list node, index an array, flip a boolean).

#### Failure mode the ADT replaces

- **Ad hoc data manipulation is the smell** - When client code sets fields directly, the same manipulation gets duplicated at every call site and the type cannot evolve.
- **Direct field access blocks alternative representations** - A type cannot expose both `sizeInPixels` and `sizeInPoints` as data members, because the object has no way to know which one the client set. Routines remove the ambiguity.
- **Bit twiddling in client code is unverifiable** - Replace client-side flag arithmetic with a named operation.

```pseudocode
// BAD - client controls representation; unit ambiguous; flag math exposed
currentFont.size = 16
currentFont.attribute = currentFont.attribute or 0x02

// GOOD - operations own the representation
currentFont.SetSizeInPoints( sizeInPoints )
currentFont.SetSizeInPixels( sizeInPixels )
currentFont.SetBoldOn()
currentFont.SetBoldOff()
currentFont.SetTypeFace( faceName )
```

#### Benefits an ADT must deliver

- **Hide implementation details** - Changing the internal representation, moving the data to external storage, or rewriting the operations in another language then touches one place instead of every use site.
- **Localize change** - New capabilities (small caps, superscript, strikethrough) are added inside the ADT without rippling into the rest of the program.
- **Make the interface informative** - Collecting related operations lets the interface state its units and terms consistently, or distinguish them explicitly, instead of leaving a bare literal ambiguous.
- **Concentrate performance work** - Tuning means recoding a few defined routines, not scanning the whole program.
- **Make correctness obvious** - A call like `currentFont.SetBoldOn()` can only be wrong by being the wrong routine name; the inline equivalent can be wrong in the structure name, field name, operator, or constant value (`0x20` for `0x02`).
- **Self-documenting beats named constants** - Substituting `BOLD` for `0x02` helps, but a named operation call is still more readable.
- **Comprehension gain (hard data)** - Students answering questions about a program split into eight ADT routines scored over 30 percent higher than those working with the same program split into eight routines along functional lines.
- **Stop passing data around** - The ADT holds the data, and only ADT routines touch it directly; clients neither pass it to every routine nor promote it to global data.
- **Expect short routine bodies** - An ADT operation often contains the very code the ad hoc version had inline; the payoff is isolating those operations behind one abstraction layer and gaining a shield against representation change, not extra logic. Do not reject an ADT because its routines look trivial.
- **Callers stay ignorant of internal limits** - Clients driving an ADT must not need to know its data-structure implementation, that structure's limits, or when it changes.

#### Guidelines derived from ADT examples

- **Represent low-level types as ADTs, not as raw low-level types** - Stacks, lists, and queues should themselves be ADTs, and then ask what the structure represents: a stack of employees is an employees ADT, a list of billing records is a billing-records ADT, a queue of spreadsheet cells is a cell-collection ADT. Take the highest available level of abstraction.
- **Treat common built-in facilities as the ADTs they are** - Files are an ADT layered by the operating system (hiding head positioning, sector allocation, raw error codes) and again by the language. Layer your own ADTs the same way: a data-structure-level ADT is fine, with a problem-domain-level ADT built on top of it.
- **Even trivial items deserve ADTs** - A light with only `TurnLightOn()` and `TurnLightOff()` is worth wrapping: it self-documents, confines the effect of change to those two routines, and cuts the data passed around.
- **Name the ADT independently of its storage medium** - Do not name it after the medium (`RateFile.Read()`); that leaks storage detail and becomes wrong and misleading when the table moves from disk to memory. Use `rateTable.Read()` or `rates.Read()`.

| Entity | Operations that form its ADT |
|---|---|
| Cruise control | set speed, get current settings, resume former speed, deactivate |
| Blender | turn on, turn off, set speed, start "Insta-Pulverize", stop "Insta-Pulverize" |
| Fuel tank | fill tank, drain tank, get tank capacity, get tank status |
| List | initialize list, insert item, remove item, read next item |
| Stack | initialize stack, push item, pop item, read top of stack |
| Light | turn on, turn off |
| Set of help screens | add topic, remove topic, set current topic, display screen, remove display, display index, back up to previous screen |
| Menu | start new menu, delete menu, add item, remove item, activate item, deactivate item, display menu, hide menu, get menu choice |
| File | open, read, write, set current file location, close |
| Pointer | get pointer to new memory, dispose of memory from existing pointer, change amount allocated |
| Elevator | move up one floor, move down one floor, move to specific floor, report current floor, return to home floor |
| Cooling system | get temperature, set circulation rate, open valve, close valve |

#### Multiple instances of an ADT in non-object-oriented environments

- **Object-oriented languages handle instancing automatically** - Build instance machinery by hand only in non-object-oriented environments such as C.
- **Add create and delete services** - Supply instance lifecycle operations and design every other service to work against a specific instance, e.g. `CreateFont( fontId )`, `DeleteFont( fontId )`, plus an instance handle such as `fontId` to track created instances.
  - C: with no receiver object, fold the ADT name into each service name (`SetCurrentFontBoldOn()`, `SetCurrentFontTypeFace( faceName )`) so the grouping survives.
- **Pick exactly one of three interface styles**
  - Option 1 - identify the instance explicitly at every call: add the instance handle as a parameter to every ADT routine; there is no "current" instance; the ADT keeps the underlying data and the client keeps only the handle.
  - Option 2 - pass the ADT's data explicitly: declare the data type (e.g. `Font`) in the client and pass it into each service routine. Advantage: no handle lookup inside the ADT. Disadvantage: the data is exposed to the rest of the program, raising the chance client code exploits implementation details that should have stayed hidden. Even though the fields are reachable, access them only through the service routines - keeping the structure "closed".
  - Option 3 - implicit current instance, with great care: add a selector such as `SetCurrentFont( fontId )` and drop the handle from other services. Acceptable for simple applications; for complex ones this systemwide state dependence forces you to track the current instance across all client code, complexity tends to proliferate, and better alternatives exist for applications of any size.
- **Freedom is internal only** - Inside the ADT any instance-handling scheme is available; the three options above are the complete external choice set in a non-object-oriented language.

### Good Class Interfaces

#### Good abstraction

- **Interface first** - The first and most important step in a high-quality class is a good interface: a sound abstraction, with the details kept hidden behind it. Every class interface must present a consistent abstraction; many problems come from violating this single principle. Abstraction means viewing a complex operation in simplified form.
- **Routines must belong together** - Every routine in the public interface must work toward one consistent end. A class holding a command stack, report formatting, report printing, and global-data initialization has no connection among its routines, presents no consistent abstraction, and has poor cohesion.
  - Two repairs, used together: relocate routines to the class where they belong, and demote the rest to private routines called by the remaining public ones. The surviving public interface should read as a small set of paired lifecycle operations at one level (`InitializeUserInterface()` / `ShutDownUserInterface()`, `InitializeReports()` / `ShutDownReports()`).
- **One ADT per class** - Each class must implement one and only one ADT, so that the interface holds a single consistent level of abstraction. If a class implements more than one, or the ADT it implements cannot be named, reorganize it into one or more well-defined ADTs. Name the class well: the name must describe that one central purpose.
- **Hide the container or library you build on** - Mixed abstraction levels most often appear when a container or other library class is used for implementation and that fact is left visible. Ask whether "a container is used" belongs in this abstraction; usually it is an implementation detail that must stay hidden. Then hold the library as a private member instead of inheriting from it.

```cpp
// BAD - "employee"-level and "list"-level routines in one interface
class EmployeeCensus: public ListContainer {
public:
    void AddEmployee( Employee employee );
    void RemoveEmployee( Employee employee );
    Employee NextItemInList();
    Employee FirstItem();
    Employee LastItem();
};

// GOOD - one level of abstraction; the library is private
class EmployeeCensus {
public:
    void AddEmployee( Employee employee );
    void RemoveEmployee( Employee employee );
    Employee NextEmployee();
    Employee FirstEmployee();
    Employee LastEmployee();
private:
    ListContainer m_EmployeeList;
};
```

- **Inheritance is for "is a" only** - Convenience of polymorphism (letting an external search or sort accept the base type) does not justify inheritance: `EmployeeCensus` is not a `ListContainer`. If searchability or sortability is part of the abstraction, express it explicitly and consistently in the class's own interface.
- **Inconsistent public routines sink the class slowly** - They behave like leaky panels rather than an open hatch: each modification makes the program harder to understand until it degrades into unmaintainability.
- **Choose the right abstraction between similar candidates** - Similar classes force a deliberate choice about which abstraction the interface should capture. Wrapping a 150-routine spreadsheet control by re-exposing all 150 routines yields no encapsulation and commits the team to supporting 150 public routines if the implementation ever changes; the wrapper should expose only the 15 grid-control routines plus a 16th for cell coloring. Either abstraction can be the right one depending on circumstances, so decide which one is wanted, then expose only that.
- **Provide services in pairs with their opposites** - Nearly every operation has a corresponding, equal and opposite operation (on/off, add/delete, activate/deactivate). Check each public routine for whether its complement is needed, but do not manufacture an opposite gratuitously.
- **Move unrelated information out** - If half the routines use half the data and the other half uses the rest, that is two classes masquerading as one; break it up. For every class, consider subdividing it into component classes and subdivide it as far as you can.
- **Prefer programmatic interfaces over semantic ones** - Every interface has a programmatic part, the types and attributes a compiler can enforce, and a semantic part, the usage assumptions it cannot: required call ordering between two routines, or a routine that crashes unless a given member was initialized first. Document the semantic part in comments, but keep the interface minimally reliant on documentation, and convert semantic elements into programmatic ones with assertions or equivalent mechanisms. Treat anything the compiler cannot enforce as likely to be misused, and make correct usage obvious from the interface alone.
- **Resist erosion under maintenance** - Added functionality that does not fit but seems too hard to place elsewhere turns a clean abstraction into a hodgepodge: ZIP-code, phone-number, and job-classification validators have no logical connection to an employee, and SQL-query accessors sit far below the class's abstraction level and break it.
- **Gate every new public member** - Before adding a routine to an interface, ask whether it is consistent with the abstraction the existing interface presents. If not, find another way to make the change and preserve the abstraction.
- **Use abstraction and cohesion together** - A good interface abstraction usually implies strong cohesion; strong cohesion implies a good abstraction less reliably. Focusing on the interface abstraction yields more design insight than focusing on cohesion, so when cohesion is weak and the fix is unclear, ask instead whether the class presents a consistent abstraction.
- **Class-level abstraction does not confer routine-level abstraction** - Judge the class by its public routines, and still design each internal routine to present a good abstraction of its own.

#### Good encapsulation

- **Encapsulation is stronger than abstraction** - Abstraction manages complexity by supplying a model that lets details be ignored; encapsulation enforces that the details cannot be inspected at all. Without encapsulation, abstraction breaks down: either both hold or neither does, with no middle ground.
- **Hiding is the primary quality signal** - How thoroughly a module conceals its internal data and remaining implementation details from every other module is the one factor that most distinguishes good module design from bad. Every class interface must hide something: a system interface, a design decision, or an implementation detail.
- **Minimize accessibility of classes and members** - This is one of several rules whose purpose is to force encapsulation. Two guidelines apply together and can pull in different directions:
  - Favor the strictest workable privacy level when choosing among public, private, and protected.
  - Rank higher the question of which choice keeps the interface abstraction intact: a routine whose exposure fits the abstraction is probably fine to expose. When the answer is unclear, hide more rather than less.
- **Never expose member data publicly** - Public fields violate encapsulation and forfeit control of the abstraction: clients can alter values and the owning class may not even know they changed. Accessor routines preserve encapsulation because the client learns nothing about the underlying storage, conversion, or location of the values.

```cpp
// BAD - clients own the representation
float x;
float y;
float z;

// GOOD - representation is unknowable from the interface
float GetX();  void SetX( float x );
float GetY();  void SetY( float y );
float GetZ();  void SetZ( float z );
```

- **Keep private implementation details out of the interface file** - True encapsulation would hide details literally as well as figuratively, but widely used languages including C++ structurally force implementation details to be declared in the class interface. Private declarations in a class header invite other programmers to study the implementation and leak facts such as "addresses are actually stored as `String`" when clients are meant to use an `Address` type.
  - C++: separate interface from implementation by holding only a pointer to an implementation class in the class declaration, with no other implementation details, and putting all details in that implementation class, visible to the owning class alone.

```cpp
// GOOD - details live behind the pointer
class Employee {
public:
    Employee( ... );
    FullName GetName() const;
    String GetAddress() const;
private:
    EmployeeImplementation *m_implementation;
};
```

  - Legacy exception: converting a large existing codebase to this scheme may not be worth the effort; when reading code that does expose its details, still refuse the urge to mine the private section for implementation clues.
- **Make no assumptions about the class's users** - Design and implement to the contract the interface implies, and assume nothing about how that interface will or will not be used beyond what the interface itself documents. This includes making no assumptions about derived classes. A comment of this shape is proof the class knows more about its callers than it should:

```
-- initialize x, y, and z to 1.0 because DerivedClass blows
-- up if they're initialized to 0.0
```

- **Avoid friend classes** - They generally violate encapsulation, are tightly coupled to the class that grants them access, and enlarge the code you must reason about at once, increasing complexity. Exception: a few situations such as the State pattern use them in a disciplined, complexity-reducing way.
- **"Uses only public routines" is not a reason to publish a routine** - That fact is insignificant; the test is whether exposing the routine is consistent with the interface's abstraction.
- **Favor read-time convenience over write-time convenience** - Reading of code outnumbers writing of it many times over, initial development included, so any technique that buys writing speed by costing reading clarity is a false economy. This bites hardest on class interfaces: never add a routine that fits the abstraction poorly just because it is convenient for the one client under construction. Refuse the first step, not the tenth.
- **Guard against semantic violations of encapsulation** - Syntactic hiding (private data and routines) is easy; semantic hiding is much harder and its violations are harder to diagnose. Each of the following makes client code depend on private implementation rather than the public interface:
  - Skipping `InitializeOperations()` because `PerformFirstOperation()` is known to call it.
  - Skipping `database.Connect()` before `employee.Retrieve( database )` because `Retrieve()` is known to connect when no connection exists.
  - Skipping `Terminate()` because `PerformFinalOperation()` is known to have called it.
  - Using a pointer or reference to an object created by another object after that creator has gone out of scope, relying on knowledge that it is held in static storage and stays valid.
  - Using `ClassB.MAXIMUM_ELEMENTS` in place of `ClassA.MAXIMUM_ELEMENTS` because both currently hold the same value.
- **Reading the implementation to learn how to call it means encapsulation is already broken** - Consulting a class's implementation to figure out usage is programming through the interface to the implementation, not to the interface, and abstraction fails soon after. It is not abstract if the underlying implementation must be read to understand what is happening.
- **Procedure when a class's interface documentation is insufficient**
  1. Do not open the implementation.
  2. Tell the class's author the class cannot be understood from its interface.
  3. The author updates the class-interface documentation in the interface file itself and checks it back in, rather than explaining verbally.
  4. Re-read the updated interface. This keeps the answer available to future programmers, prevents subtle semantic dependencies from being baked into client code, and prevents a fix that benefits only one caller.
- **Watch for coupling that is too tight** - Coupling is the tightness of the connection between two classes; looser is generally better. Keep every class independent of other classes and as loosely coupled as the design allows.
- **Coupling tracks abstraction and encapsulation** - Tight coupling appears when an abstraction leaks or encapsulation is broken; if a class exposes an incomplete service set, callers start reading or writing its internals, turning a black box into a glass box and destroying encapsulation. Fix by completing the service set, not by opening the data.

### Containment ("has a" Relationships)

- **Definition** - Containment means a class holds a primitive data element or another object. It is the workhorse technique of object-oriented programming; inheritance gets more coverage only because it is trickier and more error-prone, not because it is better.
- **Implement "has a" with containment** - Model attributes (name, phone number, tax ID on `Employee`) as member data of the containing class.
- **Private inheritance for containment is a last resort** - Only when one object cannot be made a member of another, and only to reach protected members of the contained class. It creates an overly close relationship with the ancestor and violates encapsulation; treat the need as a signal of a design error to resolve some other way.
- **Be critical of classes holding more than about seven data members** - Above roughly seven data members, consider decomposing into smaller classes. Calibration: 7 plus or minus 2 is the count of discrete items a person can retain while doing other tasks. Allow the high end of 7 plus or minus 2 for primitive members (integers, strings); stay toward the low end for complex objects.

### Inheritance ("is a" Relationships)

- **Definition and purpose** - Inheritance says one class is a specialization of another. Use it to simplify code by centralizing elements common to two or more derived classes in a base class: routine interfaces, implementations, data members, or data types. Its mission is to avoid repeating code and data and to minimize complexity; if a use does not serve that mission, do not use it.
- **Decisions to make explicitly when inheriting** - For each member routine: visible to derived classes? default implementation provided? default overridable? For each data member (variables, named constants, enumerations, and so on): visible to derived classes?
- **Public inheritance means "is a"** - When public inheritance is used, the derived class must be a more specialized version of the base class. The base class sets expectations about and imposes constraints on derived-class behavior.
  - If the derived class will not honor the base class's interface contract completely, do not inherit; use containment or change the hierarchy further up.
- **Design and document for inheritance, or prohibit it** - Inheritance adds complexity and is therefore dangerous. If a class is designed for inheritance, state the inheritance strategy in the class's documentation. If a class is not designed for inheritance, seal it.
  - C++: make members non-virtual.
  - Java: make members `final`.
  - Visual Basic: make members non-overridable.
- **Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)** - Inherit from a base class only when the subclass genuinely is a narrower kind of it. Every subclass must work correctly when driven through the base-class interface by a caller that cannot tell subclasses apart: each base-class routine must carry identical meaning in every derived class.
  - Test: with base `Account` and derived `CheckingAccount`, `SavingsAccount`, `AutoLoanAccount`, any `Account` routine must be invocable on any subtype without the caller caring which subtype it holds.
  - Violation signature: the caller must reason about per-subclass semantics, for example `InterestRate()` returning interest paid by the bank for checking and savings but interest paid to the bank for an auto loan, forcing a sign change. Under LSP that subclass must not inherit from that base.
  - Payoff and inversion: honoring LSP lets a programmer work with generic attributes and reduces complexity; requiring constant thought about subclass semantic differences means inheritance is increasing complexity.
- **Inherit exactly what is intended** - Choose the inheritance flavor per member routine. Do not inherit implementation merely because the interface is wanted, and do not inherit an interface merely because the implementation is wanted. To reuse an implementation but not the interface, use containment.

| | Overridable | Not overridable |
|---|---|---|
| Default implementation provided | Overridable routine | Non-overridable routine |
| No default implementation provided | Abstract overridable routine | Not used (leaving a routine undefined while forbidding override makes no sense) |

  - Abstract overridable routine: derived class inherits the interface only, not the implementation.
  - Overridable routine: derived class inherits the interface plus a default implementation and may replace that default.
  - Non-overridable routine: derived class inherits the interface plus the default implementation and may not replace it.
- **Never "override" a non-overridable member function** - C++ and Java both let a derived class define a function with the same name as a private base-class function; it is not polymorphic, only identically named, and misleads readers. Equivalent rule: never give a derived-class routine the name of a non-overridable base-class routine.
- **Push common interfaces, data, and behavior as high as possible** - The higher they sit, the more easily derived classes use them. Let abstraction set the ceiling: stop promoting a routine at the point where the receiving class's abstraction would be broken.
- **Suspect classes with only one instance** - It may mean objects and classes are being confused. Consider creating an object instead of a new class, or representing the derived class's variation as data. Exception: the Singleton pattern.
- **Suspect base classes with only one derived class** - Usually speculative "designing ahead" for needs that are not understood. Prepare for future work by keeping current work clear, straightforward, and simple, and by creating no more inheritance structure than strictly necessary.
- **Suspect a derived class that overrides a routine to do nothing** - This signals a base-class design error.
  - It breaks the base class's interface contract by changing its semantics.
  - It scales badly: each new exception spawns another subclass, ending in names like `ScratchlessTaillessMicelessMilklessCat`.
  - It leaves ancestor interfaces and behavior implying nothing about descendants, making maintenance confusing.
  - Fix at the source: the wrong assumption was that all cats scratch, so extract a `Claws` class and contain it in `Cat` rather than patching at the derived class.
- **Avoid deep inheritance trees** - Deep hierarchies are significantly associated with increased fault rates and increase complexity, defeating the point of inheritance.
  - Published limit: at most six levels of hierarchy, based on 7 plus or minus 2. Practical limit: most people cannot hold more than two or three levels at once. Apply 7 plus or minus 2 instead as a cap on the total number of subclasses of a base class rather than on tree depth.
- **Prefer polymorphism to extensive type checking** - Frequently repeated case statements can indicate that inheritance is the better design, though not always. Where the switch dispatches on the object's own type, collapse it into a single polymorphic call.

```cpp
// BAD - switches on the object's own type
switch ( shape.type ) {
  case Shape_Circle: shape.DrawCircle(); break;
  case Shape_Square: shape.DrawSquare(); break;
}
// GOOD
shape.Draw();
```

  - Exception: keep the case statement when it separates genuinely different kinds of objects or behavior, such as dispatching UI commands (`Command_OpenFile`, `Command_Print`, `Command_Save`, `Command_Exit`). A polymorphic `DoCommand()` per command (the Command pattern) is possible, but in simple cases its meaning is diluted to nothing and the case statement is more understandable.
- **Make all data private, not protected** - Inheritance breaks encapsulation: inheriting grants privileged access to protected routines and data. Every data member in a base class must be private rather than protected, so derived classes are less tightly coupled to the base class. When a derived class genuinely needs base-class attributes, expose protected accessor functions instead of protected data.

### Multiple Inheritance

- **Default to not using it** - Multiple inheritance opens complexity problems that do not exist with single inheritance. Use it only after weighing the alternatives and the effect on system complexity and comprehensibility.
- **Restrict it to mixins** - Its primary defensible use is mixins: small classes whose job is to mix one property set into a derived class, such as `Displayable`, `Persistant`, `Serializable`, `Sortable`. Mixins are nearly always abstract and are not meant to be instantiated independently of other objects.
  - Mixins avoid the classic diamond-inheritance problem only as long as every mixin is truly independent of the others.
  - Mixins aid comprehension by chunking attributes: understanding that an object is `Displayable` and `Persistent` is easier than tracking the 11 more specific routines those two properties would otherwise need.
  - Java and Visual Basic: multiple inheritance of interfaces is allowed, class inheritance is single only.
  - C++: multiple inheritance of both interface and implementation is supported.
  - Contradicting positions to be aware of: some experts recommend broad use of multiple inheritance, while the rule here is a heavy restriction to mixins. Apply the restriction unless a specific design demonstrably needs more.

### Why Inheritance Carries So Many Rules: Inheritance vs Containment

- **Bias heavily against inheritance** - Inheritance works against the programmer's primary technical imperative, managing complexity; that is the reason for the volume of rules governing it. Maintain a heavy bias toward containment, and choose containment unless an "is a" relationship is genuinely being modeled.

| Situation | Choice |
|---|---|
| Multiple classes share data but not behavior | Create a common object those classes contain |
| Multiple classes share behavior but not data | Derive them from a common base class defining the common routines |
| Multiple classes share both data and behavior | Inherit from a common base class defining the common data and routines |
| The base class should control your interface | Inherit |
| You should control your own interface | Contain |

### Member Functions and Data

- **Keep the routine count per class as small as possible** - Higher numbers of routines per class correlate with higher fault rates in C++ programs, but other factors measured stronger: deep inheritance trees, large numbers of routines called from within a class, and strong inter-class coupling. Trade off routine-count minimization against those factors rather than optimizing routine count alone.
- **Disallow unwanted compiler-generated functions and operators** - To forbid assignment, construction, or another implicitly generated operation, declare that constructor, assignment operator, function, or operator private so clients cannot reach it. A private constructor is the standard way to define a singleton.
- **Minimize the number of distinct routines a class calls** - Fault count in a class is statistically correlated with the total number of routines called from inside it, and fault rate rises with the number of other classes a class uses. This is fan out.
- **Minimize indirect routine calls into other classes** - Direct connections are already hazardous; chained ones such as `account.ContactPerson().DaytimeContactInfo().PhoneNumber()` are worse.
  - **Law of Demeter** - Object A may call its own routines. If Object A instantiates Object B, A may call B's routines. A should avoid calling routines on objects that B hands back. So `account.ContactPerson()` is acceptable and `account.ContactPerson().DaytimeContactInfo()` is not. (Simplified statement of the law.)
- **Minimize collaboration breadth** - Collaborate with other classes only to the extent absolutely necessary, reducing all three counts: kinds of objects instantiated; distinct direct routine calls made on those objects; routine calls made on objects that those objects return.

### Constructors

- **Initialize all member data in every constructor** - Do it wherever possible; it is cheap defensive programming. Constructor guidelines are largely consistent across C++, Java, and Visual Basic; destructor behavior varies far more per language.
- **Enforce singleton via a private constructor** - Hide every constructor and expose a static accessor returning the single instance.

```java
public class MaxId {
   private MaxId() { ... }
   public static MaxId GetInstance() { return m_instance; }
   private static final MaxId m_instance = new MaxId();
}
```

  - The private constructor runs only when the static instance is initialized; clients then reference `MaxId.GetInstance()`.
- **Prefer deep copies to shallow copies until proven otherwise** - Deep copy: every member of the source object is copied. Shallow copy: the copy usually just points or refers to one shared instance. The precise sense of "deep" and "shallow" varies, so confirm which is meant in a given codebase.
  - Terminology: a deep-copy object is a value object; a shallow-copy object is a reference object.
  - Shallow copying is usually motivated by performance, yet copying large objects rarely produces measurable impact, and predictions about which code causes performance problems are usually wrong. Adding complexity for a dubious performance gain is a bad tradeoff.
  - Deep copies are simpler to write and maintain. Shallow copies add reference counting plus code for safe copies, comparisons, and deletes, all error-prone. Adopt shallow copies only for a compelling, measured reason.

### Reasons to Create a Class

- **Require a valid reason for every new class** - Create a class only when it serves at least one of the thirteen purposes named in this subsection.
- **Model real-world objects** - Create a class per real-world object type the program models; put the object's data in the class and add service routines modeling its behavior. Modeling real-world objects is a valid reason but not the only one.
- **Model abstract objects** - Create classes for abstractions over concrete objects, such as `Shape` over `Circle` and `Square`. Project abstractions are not ready-made; distilling them is non-deterministic and different designers will abstract differently, so deriving clean abstractions is a major design effort.
- **Reduce complexity** - The single most important reason to create a class. Hide information so it need not be thought about again after the class is written; then use the class with no knowledge of its internals. Smaller code, easier maintenance, and better correctness are valid additional motives, but only the abstractive power of classes makes a complex program manageable at all. Classes are the primary tool for managing complexity, so give class design as much attention as that objective requires.
- **Isolate complexity** - Localize complicated algorithms, large data sets, and intricate protocols in a class, because complexity in any form is error-prone. Benefits: errors are easier to find, fixes touch only that class, a better algorithm can replace the old one in place, and multiple designs can be tried during development.
- **Hide implementation details** - Valid whether the detail is a convoluted database access or merely whether a member is kept as a number versus a string.
- **Limit effects of changes** - Isolate change-prone areas so change impact stays inside one class or a few; design so that the most change-prone areas are the easiest to change. Change-prone areas include hardware dependencies, input/output, complex data types, and business rules.
- **Hide global data** - When global data is unavoidable, place it behind a class interface and use access routines. Benefits: data structure can change without changing the program, accesses can be monitored, and the discipline often reveals that the "global data" is really object data.
- **Streamline parameter passing** - Passing the same parameter among several routines suggests factoring those routines into a class sharing it as object data. Streamlined parameter passing is a signal, not a goal in itself.
- **Make central points of control** - Control each task in one place: knowledge of a table's entry count, control of files, database connections, printers, and so on. One class doing all database reads and writes localizes a later conversion to a flat file or in-memory data. Related to information hiding but keep it as its own distinct heuristic.
- **Facilitate reusable code** - Code in well-factored classes is easier to reuse elsewhere than the same code embedded in a larger class. Even code called from one place, and understandable inside a larger class, belongs in its own class if another program might use it.
  - Calibration: across ten projects pursuing reuse aggressively, functionally designed projects later took about 35 percent of their code from previous projects; object-oriented projects took more than 70 percent. Plan ahead to capture that share instead of rewriting it.
  - Precondition on those figures: the first projects in the set reused little, because no sufficient code base existed yet. Expect the payoff only once a base is established.
  - Do not "design for reuse" up front. Identify reuse candidates at the end of a project, then do the work to make those classes reusable as an end-of-project task or as the first step of the next project. This prevents gold-plating, that is, building unrequired functionality that adds complexity.
- **Plan for a family of programs** - When modification is expected, put the parts expected to change into their own classes so they can be modified or replaced wholesale. Reasoning about the whole family of programs rather than one program is a powerful heuristic for anticipating whole categories of change.
- **Package related operations** - When information hiding, data sharing, and flexibility planning do not apply, still group related operations (trig, statistics, string manipulation, bit manipulation, graphics). Classes are one grouping mechanism; packages, namespaces, or header files may serve depending on the language.
- **Accomplish a specific refactoring** - Refactorings that produce new classes are valid reasons: splitting one class into two, hiding a delegate, removing a middle man, introducing an extension class, each motivated by one of the other purposes in this subsection.

### Classes to Avoid

- **Avoid god classes** - Do not create omniscient, all-powerful classes. If a class spends its time pulling data out of other classes through `Get()` and `Set()` routines and directing them, move that functionality into those other classes.
- **Eliminate irrelevant classes** - A class with data but no behavior is probably not a class; demote its member data into attributes of other existing classes.
- **Avoid classes named after verbs** - A class with behavior but no data is generally not a class; turn `DatabaseInitialization()` or `StringBuilder()` into a routine on another class.

### Language-Specific Issues

- **Verify the override mechanism of the language in use** - Do not assume defaults carry across languages.
  - Java: all routines are overridable by default; declare a routine `final` to block overriding.
  - C++: routines are not overridable by default; declare a routine `virtual` in the base class to allow overriding.
  - Visual Basic: declare the base routine `overridable` and use the `overrides` keyword in the derived class.
- **Investigate these language-varying areas before relying on them** - Behavior of overridden constructors and destructors within an inheritance tree; behavior of constructors and destructors under exception handling; importance of default (no-argument) constructors; the moment a destructor or finalizer runs; whether overriding built-in operators including assignment and equality is wise; how memory is handled as objects are created, destroyed, declared, and go out of scope.

### Beyond Classes: Packages

- **Use packages for modularity above the class** - Classes are the best available modularity tool for programmers, but abstraction and encapsulation are better served by also aggregating groups of objects. Where the language supports packages, use them.
- **Emulate packages through standards when the language lacks them** - Enforce, via programming standards:
  - Naming conventions distinguishing public classes from classes private to the package.
  - Naming conventions, code-organization conventions (project structure), or both, identifying which package each class belongs to.
  - Rules stating which packages may use which other packages, including whether the usage may be inheritance, containment, or both.
- **Program into the language, not merely in it** - Supply missing constructs through convention rather than accepting the language's limits.

## Code Complete: Ch7 High-Quality Routines

### Definitions and Baseline Defects

- **Definition of routine** - Treat a routine as one method, function, or procedure invoked for a single purpose: a C++ function, a Java method, a Visual Basic function or sub procedure. C and C++ macros count as routines for most of these rules.
- **Routine as primary abstraction tool** - Use routines as the main mechanism for making code readable, for shrinking code size, and for making performance work tractable; a change made in one routine benefits every direct and indirect caller.
- **Never leave these defects in a routine** - Each item below is an independent defect; screen every routine for all of them:
  - No documentation of purpose or parameters.
  - Inconsistent layout - physical structure that does not mirror logical structure, or different formatting styles in different branches of the same routine.
  - Mutating an input variable. If a parameter is input-only, do not assign to it, and in C++ declare it `const`. If it is meant to be modified, rename it so the name does not claim it is input.
  - Reading or writing global variables instead of communicating through the interface.
  - No defense against bad data - for example dividing by a quarter counter that can be 0.
  - Magic numbers in place of named constants.
  - Wrongly declared parameters - for example a C++ reference parameter (`&`) that is never assigned inside the routine.

### 7.1 Valid Reasons to Create a Routine

- **Reduce complexity - the dominant reason** - Reducing complexity, and with it improving the program's intellectual manageability, is the single most important reason to create a routine. Extract a routine to hide information so callers never have to reason about it again; after it is written, its internals must be forgettable. Minimizing code size, maintainability, and correctness are secondary benefits; complexity reduction is the reason complex programs stay intellectually manageable. Improved readability, reliability, and modifiability are also strong reasons to extract a routine, saving space is a minor one, and many other good reasons exist.
  - **Deep nesting is an extraction signal** - When a loop or conditional is deeply nested, pull the nested part into its own routine.
- **Introduce an intermediate, understandable abstraction** - Replace a multi-statement sequence with a call to a well-named routine; the name documents the intent at a higher abstraction level, raises readability, and cuts complexity in the routine that held the code.
  - **A good name is most of the documentation a tiny routine needs** - Once an eight-line block becomes a short, accurately named routine, the name alone carries nearly all the documentation required.

```pseudocode
// BAD
if ( node <> NULL ) then
    while ( node.next <> NULL ) do
        node = node.next
    end while
    leafName = node.name
else
    leafName = ""
end if

// GOOD
leafName = GetLeafName( node )
```

- **Avoid duplicate code** - Similar code in two routines means the decomposition is wrong. Fix it one of two ways:
  1. Move a generic version of the shared code into a base class and push the two specialized variants into subclasses.
  2. Move the shared code into its own routine and have both callers call it.
  - Payoffs: less code, single-point modification, single-point verification, and no risk of making "identical" edits that silently differ.
- **Support subclassing** - Keep overrideable routines short and well factored; overriding a short routine takes less new code and produces fewer subclass implementation errors.
- **Hide sequences** - Hide the order in which events are processed so no routine depends on another having run first. Wrap paired ordered operations (for example reading the stack top and decrementing `stackTop`) into one routine such as `PopStack()` rather than baking the ordering assumption throughout the system.
- **Hide pointer operations** - Isolate pointer manipulation in routines: pointer code is hard to read and error prone, a single site is easier to verify, and a later switch to a better data type touches only that site.
- **Improve portability** - Wrap nonportable capabilities (nonstandard language features, hardware dependencies, operating-system dependencies) in routines so future porting work is explicitly identified and localized.
- **Simplify complicated boolean tests** - Move a complex boolean test into a function with a descriptive name: the details leave the main flow, the name summarizes the test's purpose, and both the flow and the test become clearer. This is a special case of reducing complexity.
  - Reading a complicated test in full detail is rarely needed to follow program flow, so hide it.
  - Giving a test its own function marks it as significant and creates the incentive to make its internals readable.
- **Improve performance** - Centralize code so optimization, profiling, algorithm replacement, or reimplementation in a faster language happens in one place.
- **Do not create routines merely to make all routines small** - Smallness is not a reason by itself; some jobs are done better in one larger routine.
- **Never refuse to extract a 2-3 line operation** - Reluctance to write a small routine for a simple purpose is a mental block, not a design principle. Small routines improve readability and absorb growth.
  - **Extract every part that would benefit** - Before accepting a routine, confirm that every part of it that would benefit from becoming its own routine has been put into a routine of its own; the operation that benefits most from becoming its own routine is sometimes a very simple one.
  - Extraction of a repeated one-line calculation into a named function makes each call site near self-documenting.
  - Small operations grow. A guard added inside one extracted function costs 3 lines; the same guard added to 12 duplicated call sites costs 36.

```pseudocode
// BAD - repeated in a dozen places
points = deviceUnits * ( POINTS_PER_INCH / DeviceUnitsPerInch() )

// GOOD - one place, and it absorbed a divide-by-zero guard later
Function DeviceUnitsToPoints( deviceUnits: Integer ): Integer
    if ( DeviceUnitsPerInch() <> 0 )
        DeviceUnitsToPoints = deviceUnits * ( POINTS_PER_INCH / DeviceUnitsPerInch() )
    else
        DeviceUnitsToPoints = 0
    end if
End Function
```

- **Accept only these nine reasons as routine-level justification** - Before creating a routine, confirm at least one of these applies: reducing complexity; introducing an intermediate, understandable abstraction; removing duplicate code; supporting subclassing; hiding sequences; hiding pointer operations; improving portability; simplifying complicated boolean tests; improving performance. The reasons overlap and are not an orthogonal set, so more than one may apply at once.
- **Also treat these class-level motives as valid for a routine** - Isolating complexity; hiding implementation details; limiting the reach of changes; hiding global data; creating central points of control; enabling reuse; carrying out a specific refactoring.

### 7.2 Design at the Routine Level - Cohesion

- **Cohesion is the working design heuristic for routines** - Abstraction and encapsulation give more insight at the class level and have largely displaced cohesion there, but cohesion remains the primary heuristic for individual routines. Cohesion (also called "strength") measures how closely the operations inside one routine are related.
- **Make each routine do one thing well and nothing else** - `Cosine()` is perfectly cohesive; `CosineAndTan()` is not. Reject any routine that serves more than one purpose, for example one that initializes data, writes to a database, and computes values in the same body.
- **Cohesion payoff is measured reliability** - Calibrating figures:
  - Of 450 routines studied, 50% of highly cohesive routines were fault free versus 18% of low-cohesion routines.
  - In a separate 450-routine study, routines with the highest coupling-to-cohesion ratios had 7 times as many errors and were 20 times as costly to fix as those with the lowest ratios.
- **Keep coupling to other routines loose** - Before accepting a routine, confirm its connections to other routines are small, intimate, visible, and flexible.
- **Target functional cohesion always** - Functional cohesion is one and only one operation per routine; it is the strongest and best kind. It is nearly always achievable, so aim there. Examples: `sin()`, `GetCustomerName()`, `EraseFile()`, `CalculateLoanPayment()`, `AgeFromBirthdate()`. Cohesion claims hold only if the routine actually does what its name says; extra behavior means both lower cohesion and a wrong name.
- **Learn the cohesion concepts, not the vocabulary** - The terms are aids to thinking about improving routines, not sacred categories.

| Cohesion kind | Definition | Acceptability | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| Functional | Performs one and only one operation | Best - target this | None needed |
| Sequential | Ordered operations sharing data step to step that do not together form a complete function | Less than ideal | Split into complete-function routines; let one call the other |
| Communicational | Operations related only by using the same data | Less than ideal | Split; move each operation next to the code that owns its data |
| Temporal | Operations grouped because they happen at the same time | Less than ideal, usable as an orchestrator | Have it call other routines rather than doing the work itself |
| Procedural | Operations grouped only because they occur in a specified order | Unacceptable | Extract each operation; make the caller a single complete job |
| Logical | Several unrelated operations selected by a passed-in control flag | Unacceptable, except pure dispatchers | Replace with one routine per operation; share code via a lower-level routine in a class |
| Coincidental | Operations with no discernible relationship ("no cohesion", "chaotic cohesion") | Unacceptable | Deeper redesign and reimplementation |

- **Sequential cohesion - split into complete functions** - A routine that computes an employee's age from a birth date and then feeds that age into a time-to-retirement computation has sequential cohesion. Make it functional by creating one routine for age-from-birth-date and one for time-to-retirement-from-birth-date, letting the second call the first; callers may then use either or both. If the second computation merely reuses the same birth date without using the age result, the routine has only communicational cohesion.
- **Communicational cohesion - do not reinitialize data inside a consumer** - A routine that prints a summary report and then reinitializes the summary data passed to it is communicationally cohesive. Split it: one routine prints, one reinitializes next to the code that creates or modifies the data, and the original caller calls both.
- **Temporal cohesion - make it an orchestrator, never a dumping ground** - `Startup()`, `CompleteNewEmployee()`, and `Shutdown()` are temporally cohesive. Some practitioners reject temporal cohesion outright because of its usual failure mode: a hodgepodge of unrelated inline code inside `Startup()`. Treat a temporal routine as an organizer of events and have it call routines for each specific activity (read config file, initialize scratch file, set up memory manager, show initial screen) so its purpose is visibly orchestration rather than doing the work.
  - **Name at the right abstraction level** - `Startup()` reads as a single purpose and functional cohesion; `ReadConfigFileInitScratchFileEtc()` advertises coincidental cohesion.
- **Procedural cohesion - order of user prompts is not a reason to group** - A routine that gets an employee name, then address, then phone number only because that is the input-screen order has procedural cohesion. Extract each operation and give the caller a single complete job: `GetEmployee()`, not `GetFirstPartOfEmployeeData()`. Expect to modify two or more original routines before any of them reaches functional cohesion.
- **Logical cohesion - never pass a flag to select another routine's processing** - `InputAll()`, `ComputeAll()`, `EditAll()`, `PrintAll()`, and `SaveAll()` that switch on a flag are logically cohesive. Write one routine per distinct operation; if they share code or data, move the shared part into a lower-level routine and package the routines in a class.
  - The only tie between the operations is the routine's own control flow - one shared `if` or `case` chain - not any real relationship, so "illogical cohesion" describes it more accurately.
  - **Exception - event handlers** - A logically cohesive routine is usually acceptable when its body is only `if`/`case` statements plus calls to other routines and it performs no processing itself. That dispatch-only form is the "event handler" and is a good design in interactive GUI environments.
  - Separately consider whether a `case` statement should be replaced with polymorphism at the design level.
- **Prefer rewriting over diagnosing bad cohesion** - When a routine has procedural, logical, or coincidental cohesion, invest in a rewrite for better cohesion rather than a pinpoint diagnosis; such code is poorly organized, hard to debug, and hard to modify.

### 7.3 Good Routine Names

- **Name must describe everything the routine does** - Include all outputs and all side effects in the name. A routine that computes report totals and opens an output file is not adequately named `ComputeReportTotals()`; `ComputeReportTotalsAndOpenOutputFile()` is accurate but absurdly long.
  - **Fix the code, not the name** - Long silly names are a symptom of side effects. Eliminate the side effects so effects happen directly; do not respond by choosing a less descriptive name.
- **Treat the name as a quality signal** - Judge every routine by its name: a bad name that accurately reports what the routine does means the routine is probably poorly designed, and a bad name that is inaccurate means the name does not report what the code does. Either way the program must be changed.
- **Ban elastic verbs** - Reject names built on verbs that stretch to cover anything, and reject any name that reveals nothing about behavior: `HandleStuff()`, `HandleCalculation()`, `PerformServices()`, `OutputUser()`, `ProcessInput()`, `DealWithOutput()`.
  - **Exception** - "handle" is acceptable in its precise technical sense of handling an event.
  - **Wishy-washy name over sound code** - If only the name is weak, rename it precisely: `HandleOutput()` becomes `FormatAndPrintOutput()`.
  - **Wishy-washy name over weak purpose** - If the verb is vague because the operations themselves are vague, restructure that routine and its related routines until each has a strong purpose and a name that accurately describes it.
- **Never differentiate routine names by number** - `OutputUser`, `OutputUser1`, `OutputUser2` and `Part1`, `Part2` style names carry no information about the abstractions they represent and are by definition poorly named.
- **Length: as long as needed to be clear** - Research puts the best average variable name at 9 to 15 characters; routines are more complicated than variables, so their good names run longer. An attached object name supplies part of the meaning for free. Size the name for maximum clarity - as long or as short as understanding requires - not to a character budget.
- **Name a function for its return value** - A function returns a value, so name it after that value: `cos()`, `customerId.Next()`, `printer.IsReady()`, `pen.CurrentColor()`.
- **Name a procedure with a strong verb plus an object** - A functionally cohesive procedure operates on an object, so use verb-plus-object: `PrintDocument()`, `CalcMonthlyRevenues()`, `CheckOrderInfo()`, `RepaginateDocument()`.
  - **Object-oriented languages: omit the object** - The call already supplies it: write `document.Print()`, `orderInfo.Check()`, `monthlyRevenues.Calc()`. `document.PrintDocument()` is redundant and becomes inaccurate in derived classes: if `Check` derives from `Document`, `check.Print()` reads correctly while `check.PrintDocument()` does not read as printing a check.
- **Use opposites precisely and symmetrically** - Follow a naming convention for opposite pairs; asymmetric pairs such as `FileOpen()` paired with `_lclose()` are confusing. Common opposites:

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| add/remove | increment/decrement | open/close |
| begin/end | insert/delete | show/hide |
| create/destroy | lock/unlock | source/target |
| first/last | min/max | start/stop |
| get/put | next/previous | up/down |
| get/set | old/new | |

- **Establish conventions for common operations** - Where a system must distinguish kinds of operations, a naming convention is the cheapest and most reliable way to signal the distinction. Failure mode: four classes each exposing an object id differently (`employee.id.Get()`, `dependent.GetId()`, `supervisor()`, `candidate.id()`) becomes unrememberable and too entrenched to unify mid-project, taxing everyone who touches it.

### 7.4 How Long Can a Routine Be?

- **Do not impose a length limit; let complexity decide** - Never cap routines by line count and never let an artificial coding standard decide length. Let length follow the routine's own function and logic: its cohesion, its nesting depth, how many variables and decision points it carries, how much commentary it needs to be explainable, and any other complexity signal. Historical hard caps do exist (IBM once limited routines to 50 lines, TRW to two pages) and the classic theoretical ceiling is one screen or one to two printed pages of code, about 50 to 150 lines; both statements stand, each in its own scope.
- **Allow a complex algorithm to grow to 100-200 lines** - In object-oriented code, most routines are very short accessors; when a complex algorithm demands it, let a routine grow organically to 100-200 noncomment, nonblank lines. Decades of evidence show routines of that length are no more error prone than shorter ones.
- **Be careful past about 200 lines** - No study reporting lower cost or lower error rates for larger routines distinguished sizes above 200 lines, and understandability hits an upper limit beyond 200 lines.
- **Routines above 500 lines are the worst risk** - An IBM study found routines larger than 500 lines were the most error prone, with error rate proportional to size beyond 500 lines.
- **Size-versus-defect evidence conflicts; keep both readings** - Do not reconcile these into a single rule; apply each only within its own scope:
  - Routine size inversely correlated with errors: errors per line of code decreased as routine size grew, up to 200 lines.
  - Routine size not correlated with errors at all, while structural complexity and amount of data were correlated.
  - Small routines (32 lines or fewer) were not correlated with lower cost or fault rate; larger routines (65 lines or more) were cheaper to develop per line of code (1986 study).
  - Small routines (fewer than 143 source statements including comments) had 23% more errors per line of code than larger routines, but were 2.4 times cheaper to fix (450-routine study).
  - Code needed the fewest changes when routines averaged 100 to 150 lines.
- **Extreme lengths still occur in shipped code** - Modern codebases hold large numbers of very short routines plus a few long ones, and long routines are not extinct: routines of roughly 4,000 lines and of more than 12,000 lines have been found in production, with their maintainers struggling to work in them.

### 7.5 How to Use Routine Parameters

- **Treat interfaces as the top defect zone** - Routine-to-routine interfaces are among the most error-prone parts of a program: 39 percent of all errors in one measured study were internal interface errors, i.e. faults in communication between routines. Apply the parameter rules below with that weight.
- **Order parameters input, then input-output, then output** - List input-only parameters first, modify (input-and-output) parameters second, output-only parameters last, so the list mirrors the routine's flow of inputting, changing, and returning data. Do not order parameters randomly or alphabetically.
  - Contradiction to hold, not resolve: the C library convention puts the modified parameter first, which conflicts with input-modify-output. Input-modify-output is the recommended default, but either convention serves readers as long as it is applied consistently; pick one and apply it codebase-wide.
  - Ada: use the `in`, `out`, and `in out` keywords to declare parameter direction explicitly.

```ada
procedure ChangeSentenceCase(
  desiredCase: in StringCase;
  sentence: in out Sentence
);
```

- **Optionally define IN/OUT documentation macros, with eyes open** - In languages without direction keywords, preprocessor macros can document direction, but weigh two real drawbacks first: the extension is unfamiliar to most readers, and the compiler cannot enforce it, so a parameter labeled `IN` can still be modified inside the routine and mislead a reader into trusting incorrect code. If adopted, apply it consistently, preferably projectwide.
  - C++: prefer `const` as the means of marking input-only parameters; it is normally the better choice than macro-keywords.
  - A parameter still must be passed by pointer or reference for the callee to change its value; the macro alone changes nothing.

```cpp
#define IN
#define OUT
void InvertMatrix( IN Matrix originalMatrix, OUT Matrix *resultMatrix );
void ChangeSentenceCase( IN StringCase desiredCase, IN OUT Sentence *sentenceToEdit );
```

- **Keep similar parameters in the same order across similar routines** - Parameter order is a memory aid; inconsistent order across related routines makes signatures hard to recall. C's `fprintf()` adds the file as the first argument while `fputs()` adds it as the last: a pointless difference that costs recall. `strncpy()` and `memcpy()` both take target string, source string, maximum number of bytes, in that order: the shared order aids recall of both.
- **Use every parameter, or delete it** - Confirm that every input parameter and every output parameter is used, and remove any parameter the routine does not use. Unused parameters correlate with higher error rates: 46 percent of routines with no unused variables were error-free, versus only 17 to 29 percent of routines carrying more than one unreferenced variable.
  - Exception: with conditional compilation, a parameter's only use may be compiled out. Be wary of this, but leaving the parameter is acceptable when there is a genuine reason. Absent a good reason, clean up the code.
- **Put status and error parameters last** - Status variables and error indicators are incidental to the routine's purpose and are output-only, so they belong at the end of the list.
- **Never use a parameter as a working variable** - Copy the incoming value into an explicit local working variable and compute on that. Reassigning a parameter makes its name a lie: later code that reads it expecting the original input silently gets a partially computed value. Renaming the parameter does not fix this; only a separate local does.
  - Copying the input into a local also signals where the value originates and removes any chance of altering a parameter-list variable by accident.
  - Renaming attempts all fail: `workingVal` hides that the value came from outside, `inputValThatBecomesWorkingVal` is absurd, and `x` or `val` gives up. Do not adopt `inputVal` or `workingVal` as real names; they are illustration-only and poor variable names.
  - C++: enforce this with `const` on the parameter, which forbids modification inside the routine.

```java
// BAD - inputVal no longer holds the input value
int Sample( int inputVal ) {
    inputVal = inputVal * CurrentMultiplier( inputVal );
    inputVal = inputVal + CurrentAdder( inputVal );
    return inputVal;
}
// GOOD - original input stays available
int Sample( int inputVal ) {
    int workingVal = inputVal;
    workingVal = workingVal * CurrentMultiplier( workingVal );
    workingVal = workingVal + CurrentAdder( workingVal );
    return workingVal;
}
```

- **Document parameter interface assumptions as they are made** - Write the assumption at the moment it is made, both in the routine and at its call sites; assumptions recalled after the routine is finished are incomplete. Prefer encoding assumptions as assertions in code over comments alone. Document at minimum:
  - Direction of each parameter: input-only, modified, or output-only.
  - Units carried by numeric parameters, e.g. inches, feet, meters.
  - Meanings of status codes and error values, when enumerated types are not used.
  - Expected value ranges.
  - Values that must never appear.
- **Cap parameters at about seven** - People generally cannot track more than about seven chunks of information at once, so hold routines to roughly seven parameters or fewer; about 7 is the upper limit for an understandable parameter list.
  - A structured composite type counts as one chunk even with 13 fields, so languages with structured data allow more data behind fewer parameters; primitive languages may force all 13 fields to be passed individually.
  - Consistently passing more than a few arguments means coupling between routines is too tight: redesign the routine or the group. If the same data goes to many routines, group those routines into a class and make the data class data.
- **Add an input/modify/output naming convention only when direction matters** - When distinguishing direction is important, adopt a prefix convention such as `i_`, `m_`, `o_`, or the verbose `Input_`, `Modify_`, `Output_`.
- **Choose whole object vs. specific members by the interface's abstraction** - The parameter list, taken as a whole, must present a consistent interface abstraction. Neither "always pass only the needed elements" nor "always pass the whole object" is correct; decide by what abstraction the routine's interface presents.
  - Pass the individual elements when the abstraction is that the routine needs those specific data items and their shared origin in one object is incidental.
  - Pass the whole object when the abstraction is that the caller always holds that object and the routine acts on it; exposing the specific elements then breaks the abstraction.
  - Arguments each school makes, both of which are too simplistic on their own, for the case of an object that exposes data through 10 access routines where the callee needs 3 of those data elements: passing only the 3 needed elements minimizes inter-routine connections, reduces coupling, and eases understanding and reuse, and it avoids exposing all 10 access routines to the callee; passing the whole object keeps the interface stable because the callee can later use more members without a signature change, and it avoids advertising which specific data elements the callee consumes.
  - Smell - creating an object, filling it with the few needed elements, then extracting them after the call means pass the elements instead. Generally, code that "sets up" before a call or "takes down" after it signals a badly designed routine.
  - Smell - repeatedly changing the parameter list with the new parameters always coming from the same object means pass the whole object.
- **Use named (explicitly associated) parameters where supported** - Binding actual parameters to formal parameters by name makes calls self-documenting and prevents mismatch errors. Highest value with long lists of identically typed arguments, where a mismatch can escape the compiler. May be overkill in ordinary environments; worth the cost in safety-critical or other high-reliability code.

```vb
Distance = Distance3d( xDistance := latitude, yDistance := longitude, _
    zDistance := elevation )
```

- **Check that actual parameters match formal parameters** - Formal parameters (also called dummy parameters) are those declared in the routine definition; actual parameters are the variables, constants, or expressions at the call site. Habitually verify argument types in parameter lists and act on compiler warnings about mismatched types.
  - Passing the wrong type, such as an integer where floating point is needed, is a hazard in weakly typed languages like C without full compiler warnings; strongly typed languages such as C++ and Java do not have this problem.
  - Input-only arguments are usually converted from actual to formal type by the compiler, and mismatches usually raise a warning; arguments used for both input and output are where a wrong type actually bites.

### 7.6 Special Considerations in the Use of Functions

- **Definitions** - Function: a routine yielding a return value. Procedure: a routine yielding none. C++ calls all routines functions, but a `void`-returning one is semantically a procedure. Classify by semantics, not syntax.
- **Use a function only when returning the value its name names** - If the routine's primary purpose is to produce the value described by its name (`sin()`, `CustomerID()`, `ScreenHeight()`), make it a function; otherwise make it a procedure.
  - Strict position: a function takes input parameters only and returns exactly one value through itself, named for that value; a procedure may take any number of input, modify, and output parameters.
  - A function that behaves as a procedure and returns a status value is acceptable when the return value is unrelated to the routine's main purpose and name and the technique is applied consistently.
  - Prefer separating the call from the status test rather than combining them; combining raises statement density and complexity.

```pseudocode
// AVOID - call and test fused, higher density
if ( report.FormatOutput( formattedReport ) = Success ) then ...
// OK - explicit status parameter
report.FormatOutput( formattedReport, outputStatus )
if ( outputStatus = Success ) then ...
// OK - function result captured, then tested
outputStatus = report.FormatOutput( formattedReport )
if ( outputStatus = Success ) then ...
```

#### Setting the Function's Return Value

- **Guarantee a return value on every path** - Functions risk returning an incorrect value when one of several paths fails to set it. Mentally execute every path to confirm a valid value is returned under all possible circumstances, and initialize the return value to a default at the start of the function as a safety net.
- **Never return a reference or pointer to local data** - Once the routine ends and locals go out of scope, the reference or pointer is invalid. If an object must expose information about its internals, store it as class member data and provide accessor functions returning the member values.

### 7.7 Macro Routines and Inline Routines

- **Use a macro instead of a routine only as a last resort** - Substituting macros for function calls is risky and hard to understand, and is bad practice; use it only when the specific circumstances demand it, and handle any macro routine you do write with care. The rules here are stated for the C++ preprocessor; adapt them to another language or preprocessor.
- **Fully parenthesize macro expressions** - Parenthesize each argument and the entire expansion, because macros and arguments expand into code and adopt surrounding operator precedence.
  - `#define Cube( a ) a*a*a` breaks on nonatomic arguments: `Cube( x+1 )` expands to `x+1 * x + 1 * x + 1`.
  - `#define Cube( a ) (a)*(a)*(a)` still breaks when used inside an expression containing operators of higher precedence than multiplication, which tears the expansion apart.
  - Correct form: `#define Cube( a ) ((a)*(a)*(a))`.
- **Wrap multi-statement macros in curly braces** - A macro holding several statements silently misbehaves when written as if it were one statement: under a controlling `for` or `if`, only the expansion's first statement is governed by it, and the remaining statements sit outside.

```cpp
// BAD - only the first line runs in the for loop
#define LookupEntry( key, index ) \
    index = (key - 10) / 5; \
    index = min( index, MAX_INDEX ); \
    index = max( index, MIN_INDEX );
// GOOD
#define LookupEntry( key, index ) { \
    index = (key - 10) / 5; \
    index = min( index, MAX_INDEX ); \
    index = max( index, MIN_INDEX ); \
}
```

- **Name code-expanding macros like routines when they could be replaced by routines** - The C++ convention is all capitals for macros, but a macro that a routine could replace should follow the routine naming convention, so macro and routine are interchangeable without touching call sites.
  - Risk of doing this: a macro that looks like a routine burns callers who pass `++` or `--` as side effects inside other statements. One more reason to avoid side effects entirely.

#### Limitations on the Use of Macro Routines

- **Prefer the language feature over the macro** - Modern C++ alternatives to macros:

| Need | Use instead of a macro |
|---|---|
| Constant values | `const` |
| Functions compiled as inline code | `inline` |
| Type-safe standard operations such as min, max | `template` |
| Enumerated types | `enum` |
| Simple type substitutions | `typedef` |

  - Bjarne Stroustrup's position: nearly every macro exposes a flaw in the language, the program, or the programmer, and macro use degrades service from debuggers, cross-reference tools, and profilers.
  - Legitimate remaining macro use: supporting conditional compilation.

#### Inline Routines
