- **Definition** - C++ `inline` lets code be written as a routine while the compiler generally expands each invocation into inline code at compile time, in theory removing routine-call overhead.
- **Use inline routines sparingly** - `inline` breaks encapsulation because C++ requires the implementation in the header file, exposing it to every user of that header. It also regenerates the routine's full code at every invocation, which increases code size for an inline routine of any size and creates problems of its own.
- **Justify inlining by measurement, like any performance technique** - Profile the code and measure the improvement. If the expected gain does not warrant profiling to verify it, it does not warrant the loss of code quality either.

### Defensive Programming - Premise

- **Definition and stance** - Defensive programming means a routine handed bad data is not harmed by it, even when the bad data is another routine's fault, and more broadly that code is written in anticipation of problems and modifications. It does not mean defending your own code against criticism. Protect against invalid data, events that supposedly can never happen, and other programmers' mistakes.

## Code Complete: Ch8 Defensive Programming

### 8.1 Protecting Your Program from Invalid Inputs

- **Reject "garbage in, garbage out"** - never emit garbage regardless of input; production code must implement "garbage in, nothing out", "garbage in, error message out", or "no garbage allowed in". Tolerating garbage through to output marks the program as sloppy and nonsecure.
- **Handling garbage in has three required parts** - check all data from external sources, check all routine input parameters, and decide how bad inputs are handled. Do all three; none substitutes for another.
- **Validate all data from external sources** - for data from files, users, the network, or any other external interface, confirm it is inside the allowed range: numeric values within tolerance, strings short enough to process.
  - If a string is meant to encode a restricted value set (financial transaction ID and similar), verify validity for that intended purpose and reject it otherwise.
  - In secure applications, treat input as potentially hostile: check for attempted buffer overflows, injected SQL, injected HTML or XML, integer overflows, data forwarded to system calls, and any other malicious input.
- **Validate all routine input parameters** - every routine must protect itself from bad input data: check parameters arriving from other routines by the same standard as external data; the only difference is the source. Use the barricade approach - declaring specific interfaces the boundary of a trusted zone and validating everything that crosses inward - to decide which routines must check.
- **Decide the response to bad input explicitly** - detection is only half; once an invalid parameter is detected, pick one of roughly a dozen defined error-handling techniques based on the situation rather than leaving the outcome implicit.
- **Prefer defect prevention over defensive coding** - the best defensive coding is not inserting the defect at all; defensive programming is an adjunct to other quality-improvement techniques, not a substitute. Iterative design, pseudocode before code, test cases before code, and low-level design inspections prevent defect insertion and therefore rank higher in priority; combine them with defensive programming rather than replacing them.
- **Guard the small stuff** - protection against seemingly minor problems yields disproportionate benefit; do not skip a cheap check because the failure looks trivial. Defensive-programming techniques make errors easier to find, easier to fix, and less damaging to production code.

### 8.2 Assertions

- **Assertion definition** - an assertion is development-time code (routine or macro) that lets a program check itself while running. True means the state matches expectations; false means an unexpected error in the code has been detected. Example: a system assuming a customer-information file never exceeds 50,000 records asserts record count <= 50,000, staying silent below the limit and firing loudly above it.
- **Apply assertions where they pay off most** - assertions detect errors early, and the payoff is largest in large, complicated programs, high-reliability programs, and fast-changing code bases; they surface mismatched interface assumptions and errors introduced by later modification faster.
- **Give an assertion two arguments** - a boolean expression stating the assumption and a message to display when it is false.

```java
assert denominator != 0 : "denominator is unexpectedly equal to 0.";
```

- **Assert documented assumptions** - use assertions both to document assumptions and to flush out unexpected conditions. Standard targets:
  - Input parameter value inside its expected range; likewise output parameter values.
  - A file or stream is open (or closed) at routine entry (or exit).
  - A file or stream is positioned at beginning (or end) at routine entry (or exit).
  - A file or stream is open read-only, write-only, or read-write as required.
  - An input-only variable is not modified by the routine.
  - A pointer is non-null.
  - A passed-in array or container can hold at least X elements.
  - A table has been initialized with real values.
  - A container is empty (or full) at routine entry (or exit).
  - Results of a highly optimized, complicated routine match those of a slower but clearly written equivalent.
  - Extend with the assumptions specific to each routine.
- **Normally keep assertion messages out of production builds** - assertions serve development and maintenance; compile them in during development and compile them out for production so they do not degrade system performance. During development they surface contradictory assumptions, unexpected conditions, and bad values passed to routines.

#### Building Your Own Assertion Mechanism

- **Use built-in support when present, otherwise write one** - C++, Java, and Microsoft Visual Basic support assertions directly; an assertion routine is easy to write where the language lacks one.
  - **C++**: the standard `assert` macro carries no text message; wrap it to add one.

```cpp
#define ASSERT( condition, message ) { \
   if ( !(condition) ) { \
      LogError( "Assertion failed: ", \
         #condition, message ); \
      exit( EXIT_FAILURE ); \
   } \
}
```

#### Guidelines for Using Assertions

- **Split the two mechanisms by expectation** - write error-handling code for conditions expected to occur; write assertions for conditions that should never occur. Error handling covers anticipated off-nominal cases that production code must handle gracefully, typically bad input data; assertions target bugs in the code.
  - A fired assertion's remedy is not graceful degradation: it is changing the source, recompiling, and shipping a new version.
- **Treat assertions as executable documentation** - they cannot be relied on to make code work, but they state assumptions more actively than comments.
- **Avoid putting executable code inside an assertion** - the compiler may remove that code when assertions are turned off, silently dropping work the program depended on. Put executable statements on their own lines, assign results to a status variable, and assert on the variable.

```vb
' BAD - the action disappears when assertions are compiled out
Debug.Assert( PerformAction() ) ' Couldn't perform action

' GOOD
actionPerformed = PerformAction()
Debug.Assert( actionPerformed ) ' Couldn't perform action
```

- **Use assertions to document and verify preconditions and postconditions** - these are the elements of "design by contract", in which each routine or class forms a contract with the rest of the program.
  - Precondition: a property the client code promises is true before calling the routine or instantiating the object; it is the caller's obligation.
  - Postcondition: a property the routine or class promises is true when it finishes; it is the callee's obligation to its users.
  - Prefer assertions over comments for these, because assertions check the conditions dynamically.

```vb
Private Function Velocity ( _
   ByVal latitude As Single, ByVal longitude As Single, ByVal elevation As Single _
   ) As Single
   ' Preconditions
   Debug.Assert ( -90 <= latitude And latitude <= 90 )
   Debug.Assert ( 0 <= longitude And longitude < 360 )
   Debug.Assert ( -500 <= elevation And elevation <= 75000 )
   ...
   ' Postconditions
   Debug.Assert ( 0 <= returnVelocity And returnVelocity <= 600 )
   Velocity = returnVelocity
End Function
```

  - Exception on source of data: if such values arrive from an external source, validate and handle them with error-handling code, not assertions. Assertions are appropriate only when the values come from a trusted internal source and the routine's design assumes they are in range.
- **Assert and then handle the error anyway when the code must be highly robust** - for a given error condition a routine will generally use an assertion or error-handling code, not both, and some experts hold that only one kind is needed. Real-world programs and projects are too messy to rely on assertions alone, so both may cover the same error when the system is large, complex, and long-lived.
  - Conditions that justify doubling up: parts designed by different designers over 5-10 years or more across many versions and technologies, geographically separated teams, acquired external components, coding standards that shifted over the system's lifetime, uneven conscientiousness and review rigor, uneven unit testing, and test coverage varying by release under business pressure so comprehensive system-level regression testing cannot be assumed.
  - Precedent: Microsoft Word asserts conditions that should always be true and also handles those errors in production code in case the assertion fails; with millions of lines and many generations of modification, assuming every conceivable error is found before shipping is unrealistic.
  - Implementation shape: keep the precondition assertions, then sanitize at run time by clamping out-of-range inputs to the closest legal value.

```vb
   ' Preconditions
   Debug.Assert ( -90 <= latitude And latitude <= 90 )
   ...
   ' Sanitize input data: clamp to the closest legal value if out of range
   If ( latitude < -90 ) Then
      latitude = -90
   ElseIf ( latitude > 90 ) Then
      latitude = 90
   End If
```

### 8.3 Error-Handling Techniques

- **Choose a technique per expected error** - assertions cover errors that should never occur; expected errors get one of the following responses, or a combination, chosen by circumstance: return a neutral value, substitute the next valid data, return the previous answer, substitute the closest legal value, log a warning, return an error code, call an error-processing routine or object, display an error message, or shut down.
- **Return a neutral value** - continue running and return a value known to be harmless: 0 for a numeric computation, an empty string for a string operation, an empty pointer for a pointer operation, the default background or foreground color for a game drawing routine given a bad color.
  - Do not do this when a wrong-but-plausible value is dangerous: a routine displaying x-ray data for cancer patients is better off shutting the program down than displaying incorrect patient data.
- **Substitute the next piece of valid data** - when processing a data stream, skip forward: on a corrupted database record, keep reading until a valid record appears; on a missed reading from a thermometer sampled 100 times per second, wait 1/100th of a second and take the next one.
- **Return the same answer as the previous time** - acceptable where the quantity cannot plausibly change between samples (temperature within 1/100th of a second) or where a stale value is harmless (repainting a screen region with the previously used color after an invalid color request).
  - Never do this where the retained value belongs to a different subject: reusing the last answer when authorizing cash-machine transactions would reuse the previous user's bank account number.
- **Substitute the closest legal value** - reasonable for readings from a calibrated instrument: with a thermometer calibrated 0-100 degrees Celsius, clamp readings below 0 to 0 and above 100 to 100; clamp a reported string length below 0 to 0.
- **Log a warning message to a file** - on detecting bad data, log and continue; combine with clamping to the closest legal value or skipping to the next valid datum. Decide whether the log can be published safely or must be encrypted or otherwise protected.
- **Return an error code** - designate which parts of the system handle errors and which only report them upward for a caller higher in the calling hierarchy to handle. Reporting mechanisms:
  - Set a status variable.
  - Return status as the function's return value.
  - Throw an exception using the language's built-in mechanism.
  - The choice of mechanism matters less than the decision about which parts handle errors directly. Where security is at stake, calling routines must always check return codes.
- **Call an error-processing routine or object** - centralizing handling in a global error handler eases debugging by concentrating responsibility. Tradeoff: the whole program knows about and is coupled to that facility, so reusing any code elsewhere drags the error-handling machinery along.
  - Security constraint: after a buffer overrun has occurred at run time, an attacker may have compromised the handler's address, so this approach is no longer safe in that process.
- **Display an error message at the point of detection** - minimizes error-handling overhead, but risks spreading user-interface messages across the whole application, which obstructs a consistent UI, clean UI/logic separation, and localization. Also withhold detail from potential attackers, who mine error messages for attack information.
- **Handle the error however works best locally** - use this only where the design calls for handling all errors locally and leaves the choice of specific method to the developer implementing the part that encounters the error; it gives maximum flexibility to the individual developer, at significant risk that overall system correctness or robustness misses requirements, and it also tends to scatter user interface code through the system, inheriting every problem of displaying error messages locally.
- **Shut down** - appropriate for safety-critical applications: radiation-treatment control software receiving bad dosage input should shut down rather than reuse the last value, clamp, or substitute a neutral value; rebooting beats risking a wrong dosage.
  - Microsoft Windows by default keeps operating when its security log fills; configuring it to halt the server when the security log fills is appropriate in a security-critical environment.

#### Robustness vs. Correctness

- **Definitions, at opposite ends of one scale** - correctness means never returning an inaccurate result, preferring no result to an inaccurate one; robustness means always attempting to keep the software operating, accepting occasionally inaccurate results.
- **Pick the end that matches the software type** - the architecture or high-level design must state whether error handling favors robustness or correctness. Safety-critical applications favor correctness over robustness, since no result beats a wrong result (radiation machine). Consumer applications favor robustness over correctness, since almost any result beats shutting down (a word processor drawing a partial line of text should keep running, because the next page-up or page-down refreshes the display).

#### High-Level Design Implications of Error Processing

- **Fix the approach architecturally** - deciding the general response to bad parameters and bad inputs is a key error-handling decision and a key architectural or high-level design decision, because it determines whether the software meets correctness, robustness, and other nonfunctional requirements; the architecture or high-level design must specify the set of error-handling techniques to be used. Handle invalid parameters consistently program-wide.
- **Follow the chosen approach consistently** - if high-level code is designated to handle errors and low-level code only to report them, the high-level code must actually handle them.
- **Never ignore returned error information** - test every function return value even where the language permits discarding it (C++ does not require using a return value). Check it even when no error is expected, since defensive programming exists precisely to guard against unexpected errors.
- **Check system calls too** - unless an architectural guideline explicitly waives it, check for error codes after every system call, and on detecting an error include the error number and its description.

### 8.4 Exceptions

- **Exception definition and mechanics** - an exception passes an error or exceptional event from a routine to its caller when the routine cannot handle the condition itself, returning control to code that has more context to interpret and act on it; exception handling operates in a dimension separate from the normal flow of the code. A routine uses `throw` to throw an exception object; code higher in the calling hierarchy catches it in a `try-catch` block. Exceptions can also straighten out tangled logic within one stretch of code by rewriting that logic with try-finally.
- **Like inheritance, exceptions cut both ways** - judicious use reduces complexity; imprudent use makes code almost impossible to follow, and code using exceptions as part of normal processing acquires the readability and maintainability problems of spaghetti code.

| Exception attribute | C++ | Java | Visual Basic |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Try-catch support | yes | yes | yes |
| Try-catch-finally support | no | yes | yes |
| What can be thrown | Exception object or object derived from Exception class; object pointer; object reference; a data type such as string or int | Exception object or object derived from Exception class | Exception object or object derived from Exception class |
| Effect of uncaught exception | Invokes `std::unexpected()`, which by default invokes `std::terminate()`, which by default invokes `abort()` | Terminates the thread of execution if the exception is a "checked exception"; no effect if it is a "runtime exception" | Terminates the program |
| Exceptions thrown must be declared in the class interface | No | Yes | No |
| Exceptions caught must be declared in the class interface | No | Yes | No |

- **Use exceptions for errors that must not be ignored** - their overriding benefit is signaling an error condition in a way that cannot be ignored; other error-reporting approaches allow an error to propagate through a code base undetected, and exceptions remove that possibility.
- **Throw only for truly exceptional conditions** - reserve exceptions for conditions unaddressable by other coding practices, in the same circumstances that justify assertions: events that should never occur, not merely infrequent ones.
  - Tradeoff to weigh: exceptions weaken encapsulation, because callers must know which exceptions the called code may throw, raising complexity and working against Software's Primary Technical Imperative: Managing Complexity.
- **Never use an exception to pass the buck** - if an error condition can be handled locally, handle it locally; do not throw an uncaught exception from code that could deal with the error itself.
- **Avoid throwing from a constructor or destructor unless the throw is caught in the same place** - the rules governing how such exceptions are processed become very complicated very quickly.
  - **C++**: a destructor is not called unless the object is fully constructed, so an exception thrown inside a constructor skips the destructor and can leak resources; comparably complicated rules govern exceptions inside destructors. Avoid writing such code rather than relying on remembering the rules.
- **Throw exceptions at the right level of abstraction** - thrown exceptions are part of a routine's and a class's interface just like its data types, so an exception passed to the caller must match the abstraction level of that interface. Leaking a lower-level exception couples the client to the code beneath the class instead of to the class, breaking encapsulation and reducing intellectual manageability.

```java
// BAD - low-level exception leaks through the Employee abstraction
class Employee {
   public TaxId GetTaxId() throws EOFException { ... }
}

// GOOD - exception matches the class interface's abstraction
class Employee {
   public TaxId GetTaxId() throws EmployeeDataNotAvailable { ... }
}
```

  - Mapping the lower-level condition (for example `io_disk_not_ready`) onto the interface-level exception inside the routine is sufficient and acceptable, since it preserves the interface abstraction.
- **Put everything that led to the exception into its message** - every exception occurs in specific circumstances that are detected at throw time; include all of that information plus every value needed to diagnose the fault without a debugger, so the message alone explains why the exception was thrown. For an array index violation, report the offending illegal index value plus both the lower and upper legal array bounds.
- **Avoid empty catch blocks** - an empty catch admits one of two defects: the `try` body raises an exception without cause, or the handler drops a valid exception. Identify which is the root cause and fix that block; do not silence the symptom.
  - Exception: rarely, a low-level exception is genuinely not exceptional at the caller's abstraction level. Only then may the catch body be non-handling, and it must be documented - by comment or, better, by logging.

```java
// BAD
try { /* lots of code */ }
catch ( AnException exception ) {
}

// GOOD
try { /* lots of code */ }
catch ( AnException exception ) {
  LogError( "Unexpected exception" );
}
```

- **Know every exception your libraries throw** - in languages that do not force a routine or class to declare its exceptions, enumerate what third-party and library code can throw. An uncaught library exception crashes the program exactly as fast as an uncaught exception of your own.
  - If the library documents nothing, write throwaway prototype code that exercises it to surface the exception set empirically.
- **Consider a centralized exception reporter** - one component that owns knowledge of which exceptions exist, how each is handled, and how messages are formatted, giving uniform handling across the codebase. Scale its logic from trivial to elaborate as the application requires.
  - Before adopting it, weigh the general drawbacks of centralized error handling: the whole program becomes coupled to that facility, so reusing any code elsewhere drags the error-handling machinery along, and after a run-time buffer overrun an attacker may have compromised the handler's address.

```vb
' Centralized reporter: callers pass class name plus the exception object
Sub ReportException( ByVal className, ByVal thisException As Exception )
  Dim message As String
  message = "Exception: " & thisException.Message & "." & ControlChars.CrLf & _
            "Class: " & className & ControlChars.CrLf & _
            "Routine: " & thisException.TargetSite.Name
  MessageBox.Show( message, "Exception", MessageBoxButtons.OK, MessageBoxIcon.Exclamation )
End Sub

Try
  ...
Catch exceptionObject As Exception
  ReportException( CLASS_NAME, exceptionObject )
End Try
```

- **Standardize project-wide exception usage** - decide these points once, at project level, so exception handling stays intellectually manageable:
  - **C++ and similar** - where objects, raw data, and pointers may all be thrown, fix what is throwable; for cross-language compatibility, restrict throws to objects derived from the `Exception` base class.
  - Create a project-specific exception base class for all exceptions the project throws, so logging and reporting can be centralized and standardized.
  - Define exactly when code may use local throw-catch to process an error in place.
  - Define exactly when code may throw an exception that is not handled locally.
  - Decide whether a centralized exception reporter is used.
  - Decide whether exceptions are permitted in constructors and destructors.
- **Weigh exceptions against every other error-handling option** - choosing exceptions merely because the language offers them is programming in a language rather than into it. Evaluate handling locally, returning an error code, logging debug data to a file, shutting the system down, and other approaches before defaulting to a throw.
  - Exception support has existed in several languages for 5-10 years or longer, yet little conventional wisdom about using it safely has emerged.
- **Consider handling no exceptions at all** - for some serious run-time errors the correct response is to release acquired resources and abort, leaving the user to rerun with valid input.

### 8.5 Barricade Your Program to Contain the Damage Caused by Errors

- **Barricade definition** - a damage-containment strategy: partition the software so a failure in one region cannot spread, like sealed hull compartments in a ship or firewalls between parts of a building. (Barricades were formerly called firewalls; that term now means blocking hostile network traffic.)
- **Designate interfaces as boundaries of safe areas** - put barricades in place to contain the damaging effect of errors: declare specific interfaces the border of a trusted zone, validate all data crossing inward, and respond sensibly to invalid data. Code inside the zone is then relieved of bad-data checking, which reduces the amount of code that has to be concerned with error processing.
- **Apply the same split at class level** - public methods treat incoming data as unsafe and own validating and sanitizing it; once data passes them, private methods may assume it is safe.
- **Operating-room model** - data is sterilized before admission; anything already inside is assumed safe. The key design decision is which routines sit inside the safety zone, which sit outside, and which do the sanitizing (the doors).
  - Sanitizing on arrival is usually the easiest placement, but one pass is not always enough; where cleaning is needed at several levels, use multiple sterilization layers.
- **Convert input to its target type immediately** - input arrives as strings or numbers; map it to the real type (boolean, enumerated types such as `Color_Red`, `Color_Green`, `Color_Blue`) as soon as it is read. Carrying loosely typed values around raises complexity and lets input like a color of "Yes" crash the program.
- **Structure the barricade in layers** - untrusted sources (GUI, command line, real-time data feeds, external files, other external objects) feed validation classes that constitute the barricade; internal classes behind them operate only on clean, trusted data.

#### Relationship Between Barricades and Assertions

- **Outside the barricade, use error handling** - no assumption about data is safe there, so handle errors rather than assert.
- **Inside the barricade, use assertions** - data was sanitized on the way in, so bad data detected inside indicates a program defect, not a data defect.
- **Decide barricade placement at architecture level** - which code is inside versus outside the barricade is an architectural decision, not a per-routine one.

### 8.6 Debugging Aids

- **Never assume production constraints bind the development build** - the production version must be fast, resource-frugal, and free of dangerous user-exposed operations; the development version may be slow, resource-extravagant, and expose unguarded operations. Trade development-time speed and resource usage for tooling that speeds development, and add code to the development version specifically to flush out errors quickly.
  - Add integrity-checking operations for error-prone data structures, for example a menu command that validates a complex linked list's integrity.
  - In a debug build, verify the integrity of a central data object from the idle loop every few seconds; corruption is then caught fast and diagnosis is far easier.
- **Introduce debugging aids early** - the code must actually contain debugging aids, and they pay off in proportion to how long they exist. Write the aid after the first occurrence of a problem, or reuse one from a prior project, rather than waiting until the problem has bitten several times.
- **Use offensive programming** - use offensive-programming techniques to make errors and exceptional cases impossible to miss during development while remaining recoverable in production. A dead program does less damage than a crippled one.
  - Development-time example: a `case` statement expected to cover five events must make its default branch shout that an unhandled case exists; in production the same default writes to an error log instead.
  - Make assertions abort the program, so a known problem cannot be dismissed by pressing Enter; keep the pain high enough that it gets fixed.
  - Fill all allocated memory completely to expose allocation errors.
  - Fill all allocated files or streams completely to expose file-format errors.
  - Make every `default` or `else` branch fail hard (abort) or otherwise be impossible to overlook.
  - Overwrite an object with junk immediately before deleting it.
  - Where appropriate for the product, have the program e-mail error logs to the developer so real released-software failures are visible.
  - Rule of thumb: fail hard during development so production can fail softly.

#### Plan to Remove Debugging Aids

- **Decide removal strategy up front** - for personal code, leaving all debug code in may be acceptable; for commercial code the size and speed cost can be prohibitive. Plan the build so debug code never has to be shuffled in and out by hand: debugging aids must be installable and removable, or activatable and deactivatable, without significant effort.
- **Use version control and build tools** - build different versions from identical sources with tools such as `ant` or `make`: development builds include all debug code, production builds exclude what must not ship.
- **Use a built-in preprocessor** - where the environment provides one, as C++ does, gate debug code by a compiler switch, either directly or through a macro.

```cpp
// Define DEBUG to include the debug code; leave it undefined to exclude it.
#define DEBUG
#if defined( DEBUG )
  // debugging code
#endif
```

  - Assign `DEBUG` a value and test the value instead of mere definition to get debug levels: `#if DEBUG > 0` for code wanted always, `#if DEBUG == POINTER_ERROR` for single-purpose code, `#if DEBUG > LEVEL_A` for graduated levels.
  - To avoid scattering `#if defined()` through the code, wrap the pattern in a macro:

```cpp
#define DEBUG
#if defined( DEBUG )
#define DebugCode( code_fragment ) { code_fragment }
#else
#define DebugCode( code_fragment )
#endif

DebugCode(
  statement 1;
  statement 2;
);
```

- **Write your own preprocessor when the language lacks one** - define a convention marking debug code and a precompiler that honors it (in Java, for example, `//#BEGIN DEBUG` and `//#END DEBUG`), then script preprocess-then-compile so the unpreprocessed source can never be built by mistake.
- **Use debugging stubs** - route checks through a routine that does full work in development and is swapped for a stub that returns immediately (or does a couple of cheap operations) in production. Cost is a small performance penalty, and it is faster to adopt than writing a preprocessor. Retain both versions so builds can switch back and forth later.

```cpp
void DoSomething( SOME_TYPE *pointer, ... ) {
  CheckPointer( pointer );   // full validation in development, stub in production
  ...
}
// development: check for NULL, verify the dogtag, verify the pointed-to data is intact, ...
// production:  void CheckPointer( void *pointer ) { }
```

### 8.7 Determining How Much Defensive Programming to Leave in Production Code

- **Accept the core tension** - development wants errors loud, even obnoxious, so none is overlooked; production wants errors unobtrusive, with graceful recovery or graceful failure. Resolve it separately for each class of error.
- **Keep checks for consequential errors** - classify program areas by whether an undetected error there is affordable. A spreadsheet can tolerate undetected screen-update errors, whose worst outcome is a messy display; it cannot tolerate undetected calculation-engine errors, which yield subtly wrong results in user data.
- **Strip checks for truly trivial errors** - remove detection whose failure has negligible consequence, for example the spreadsheet's screen-update check.
  - "Remove" means exclude from the build via version control, precompiler switches, or equivalent - not delete the source.
  - When space is not constrained, an alternative is to keep the check and have it log quietly to an error file.
- **Strip anything that hard-crashes in production** - printing a diagnostic and crashing is the right development response even to minor errors, but production users must get the chance to save work; they will tolerate some anomalies in exchange for the program staying alive long enough. Remove any debug code that can cost users their data, however much it aids debugging.
- **Keep code that makes a crash graceful** - retain debug code that detects potentially fatal errors and brings the program down cleanly. Mars Pathfinder shipped with debug aids left in deliberately; after an in-flight error following landing, those aids let engineers diagnose it, upload corrected code, and complete the mission.
- **Convert, do not delete, aids that support technical support** - leave debugging aids in production with production-appropriate behavior; assertions that halt the program during development should log to a file in production rather than being eliminated.
- **Make every surviving message user-friendly** - internal error text that reaches users must be non-insulting and comprehensible. Preferred pattern: report an "internal error" and give an e-mail address or phone number for reporting it.

### 8.8 Being Defensive About Defensive Programming

- **Bound the amount of defensive code** - checking every parameter in every conceivable way at every conceivable place makes the program fat and slow, and worse, adds complexity.
- **Treat defensive code as defect-prone code** - it is no more immune to defects than any other code, and more defect-prone if written casually.
- **Prioritize deliberately** - decide where defensiveness is needed and set priorities accordingly, rather than applying it uniformly; the amount of defensive-programming code must be appropriate, neither too much nor too little.

### Checklist: Defensive Programming - Security Issues

- **Catch every exception** - no exception may escape unhandled.
- **Non-revealing error messages** - error messages must not disclose information that would help an attacker break into the system.

### Named Process Carried Forward

- **Pseudocode Programming Process (PPP)** - the process for constructing an individual class and its routines; it cuts the effort spent on design and documentation while improving the quality of both. Its main alternatives are test-first development and design by contract.

## Code Complete: Ch9 The Pseudocode Programming Process

### Summary of Steps in Building Classes and Routines

- **Treat class construction as iterative, not linear** - Expect to loop between general class design, enumerating its routines, building those routines, and checking the whole; the process is as messy as design itself. Do not force a single forward pass.
- **Class construction step 1 - create a general design for the class** - Before writing routines, settle all of:
  - The problem the class solves.
  - The class's specific responsibilities.
  - The "secrets" the class hides.
  - The exact abstraction its interface captures.
  - Whether the class derives from another class, and whether other classes may derive from it.
  - Its key public methods.
  - Its nontrivial data members, identified and designed.
  - Iterate over these points as many times as needed until the design is straightforward.
- **Class construction step 2 - construct each routine in the class** - Build each routine identified in the design step. Expect construction to surface additional routines, minor and major, and expect the issues they raise to ripple back into the class design; feed those changes back rather than suppressing them.
- **Class construction step 3 - review and test the class as a whole** - Test each routine as it is created, then, once the class is operational, review and test the class as a unit specifically for defects that cannot be exposed at the individual-routine level.
- **Reserve systematic routine construction for nontrivial routines** - Accessors, pass-throughs to other objects' routines, and similarly simple routines need no ceremony; apply a systematic approach to the complicated ones.
- **Routine construction activity order** - Perform these in order, repeating the cycle if necessary:
  1. Design the routine.
  2. Check the design.
  3. Code the routine.
  4. Review and test the code.

### Pseudocode for Pros

- **Definition - pseudocode** - An informal, English-like notation describing how an algorithm, routine, class, or program will work.
- **Definition - Pseudocode Programming Process (PPP)** - A specific discipline for using pseudocode to streamline creating the code inside routines.
- **Do not assume any English-like description works equally well** - Styles of pseudocode differ in usefulness; follow the pseudocode guidelines in this section rather than writing free-form prose.
- **Describe specific operations precisely** - Use English-like statements that state exactly what happens, not vague summaries.
- **Exclude target-language syntax** - Keep pseudocode above the code's level. Language constructs drop you to a lower level, destroy the benefit of designing higher up, and impose needless syntactic restrictions.
  - Do not use language-specific pointer notation or language-specific library calls (for example C's `*hRsrcPtr` or `malloc()`) in pseudocode.
  - Do not encode return-value coding details (for example returning `1` versus `0`); say what the outcome means instead.
- **Write at the level of intent** - State the meaning of the approach, not how it will be expressed in the target language.
- **Write low enough that code generation is nearly automatic** - Pseudocode pitched too high hides problematic details. Refine it in increasing detail until writing the actual code would be easier than refining further.
- **Language-neutrality is a test of quality** - Pseudocode that could only be implemented in one language is too low-level; good pseudocode leaves the language choice open while remaining precise and detailed enough to serve as the direct basis for code.
- **Build the code around the pseudocode and keep the pseudocode as comments** - The pseudocode statements become programming-language comments, which removes most commenting effort; if the pseudocode follows the guidelines the resulting comments are complete and meaningful.

```pseudocode
// BAD - target-language details, focus on mechanism, return codes
increment resource number by 1
allocate a dlg struct using malloc
if malloc() returns NULL then return 1
*hRsrcPtr = resource number
return 0

// GOOD - pure English, level of intent, still precise, no language committed to
Track how many resources are currently in use
If a further resource is available
  Try to allocate a dialog box structure
  If that allocation succeeded
    Record one more resource in use
    Initialize the resource
    Write the resource number to the caller-supplied location
  Endif
Endif
Report whether a new resource was created
```

- **Benefit - easier reviews** - Detailed design can be reviewed without reading source code, which lowers the cost of low-level design review and reduces the need to review the code itself.
- **Benefit - supports iterative refinement** - Move high-level design to pseudocode, then pseudocode to source. Successive refinement in small steps lets each defect be caught at the same level of detail at which it was introduced, before it becomes a problem or contaminates more detailed work.
- **Benefit - changes are cheap** - A few lines of pseudocode change far more easily than a page of code. Catch errors at the "least-value stage" - the stage with the least effort invested. Far less is invested at the pseudocode stage than after coding, testing, and debugging.
- **Benefit - minimal commenting effort** - Under the PPP the pseudocode is already the comments, so removing them costs more work than keeping them.
- **Benefit - design documentation stays maintained** - Design kept separately from code drifts out of agreement with it; pseudocode-as-comments stays accurate as long as the inline comments are maintained.
- **Default to pseudocode for detailed design, but not as the only tool** - For detailed design work, pseudocode is hard to beat; reach for it first. Survey evidence: programmers preferred pseudocode for easing construction in a programming language, for exposing designs that lack sufficient detail, and for ease of documentation and ease of modification. Pseudocode is still not the only detailed-design tool: keep pseudocode and the PPP available as tools rather than applying them as a universal mandate.

### Constructing Routines by Using the PPP

- **PPP activity list** - Perform these activities, repeating as needed:
  1. Design the routine.
  2. Code the routine.
  3. Check the code.
  4. Clean up loose ends.

#### Design the Routine

- **Design every complicated routine before coding it** - Once a class's routines are identified, the first construction step for each of the more complicated ones is to design it, using the design steps in this section.
- **Check the prerequisites first** - Before any work on the routine itself, confirm its job is well defined, that it fits cleanly into the overall design, and that it is called for by the project's requirements at least indirectly. Do not build a routine no requirement reaches.
- **Define the problem the routine solves** - State it in enough detail to build from. If the high-level design is detailed enough, this is already done. The high-level design must at minimum supply:
  - The information the routine hides.
  - The routine's inputs.
  - The routine's outputs.
  - The preconditions guaranteed true before the call - for example input values within stated ranges, initialized streams, files in a known open or closed state, buffers filled or flushed.
  - The postconditions the routine guarantees true before it hands control back - for example output values within stated ranges, plus the same classes of stream, file, and buffer state.
  - State explicitly when a routine has no guaranteed preconditions, rather than leaving that entry blank.
- **Name the routine, and treat a bad name as a design signal** - Give every routine a clear, unambiguous name. Difficulty naming it usually means its purpose is not clear. If the name can be made clearer, do it. If the vague name comes from a vague design, stop, back up, and improve the design instead of accepting the name.
  - The high-level design must be clear enough to give the class and each of its routines a good name; if it is not, that is one of the vague designs to back up and improve.
- **Decide how to test the routine while writing it** - Plan how the class and each of its routines will be tested, during design, for your own unit testing and for an independent tester. For simple inputs, plan to cover all valid input values plus a variety of invalid ones.
- **Research standard-library functionality before writing anything** - Reuse of good code is the largest single lever on both code quality and productivity. When a routine's design feels overly complicated, check whether part or all of the functionality already exists as a routine or component in the standard libraries of the language, platform, or tools, or in libraries maintained in-house. Prefer algorithms already invented, tested, published, reviewed, and improved over writing an equivalent from scratch.
- **Plan error handling explicitly** - Enumerate everything that could go wrong inside the routine, including bad input values and invalid values returned from other routines. Choose the error-handling approach consciously.
  - If the program's architecture defines an error-handling strategy, follow that strategy.
  - Otherwise, decide the approach that works best for this specific routine.
- **Decide which of the two efficiency framings applies** - Before designing, determine and be able to state whether efficiency for this routine is addressed mainly through stable, well-abstracted interfaces and readable implementations or mainly through meeting resource and speed budgets.
- **Handle efficiency by case - non-critical systems** - In the vast majority of systems efficiency is not critical. There, make the interface well abstracted and the code readable so it can be improved later. Good encapsulation lets a slow, resource-hogging, high-level implementation be swapped for a better algorithm or a fast, lean, low-level one without affecting any other routine.
- **Handle efficiency by case - performance-critical systems** - In the minority of systems where performance is critical, the constraint is typically a scarce resource: database connections, memory, available handles, or ambitious timing constraints. The architecture should state how many resources each routine or class may use and how fast it must operate. Design the routine to meet those resource and speed goals, trading resources for speed or speed for resources according to which is more critical. Tuning the routine during initial construction is acceptable, but only to the extent needed to hit its resource and speed budgets.
- **Do not micro-optimize individual routines speculatively** - Outside those two situations (efficiency not critical, and performance critical with stated resource and speed budgets), working on efficiency at the individual-routine level is usually wasted effort. Big optimizations come from refining the high-level design. Use micro-optimizations only after the high-level design has proven unable to meet performance goals, which is not knowable until the whole program is done. Do not chase incremental gains before they are known to be needed.
- **Research algorithms and data types when libraries fall short** - If the functionality is not in the available libraries, check an algorithms reference before writing complicated code from scratch. When adopting a predefined algorithm, adapt it correctly to the target language.
- **Expect little written output from the preceding design steps** - Their main purpose is to establish the mental orientation needed to write the routine, not to produce documents.
- **Write the pseudocode in the real editor** - Draft the pseudocode directly in the programming editor or IDE, because it will shortly become the basis for the programming-language code.
- **Work from general to specific, starting with a header comment** - A routine's most general element is its header comment, which states the routine's job; write that concise purpose statement first, since writing it clarifies understanding.
  - State in the header comment the routine's purpose, any state or data the routine retrieves or derives on its own rather than receiving as a parameter, and what it returns.
  - Trouble writing the general comment is a warning that the routine's role in the program is not understood well enough. If summarizing the role is hard, assume something is wrong and fix the design.
- **Fill in high-level pseudocode after the header comment** - Keep it high-level and in precise English, never in a programming language, expressing exactly what the routine must do.
- **Think about the data at whatever point it matters** - The routine's data can be designed at several points in the process. When data manipulation is prominent in the routine, settle the major pieces of data before the logic; have definitions of key data types in hand while the logic is designed. When the data is simple and manipulation is not prominent, this can wait.
- **Check the pseudocode before coding** - After writing the pseudocode and designing the data, step back and review it as if explaining it to someone else.
  - Have another person read it or listen to the explanation, even for a block as small as 11 lines. Pseudocode exposes assumptions and high-level mistakes more readily than programming-language code does, and reviewers accept a few pseudocode lines more readily than 35 lines of C++ or Java.
  - Require an easy, comfortable understanding of what the routine does and how; understanding at the pseudocode level is a precondition for understanding at the programming-language level, for you and for everyone else.
- **Iterate in pseudocode and keep the best version** - Try as many ideas as possible in pseudocode before coding, because once coding starts, emotional investment makes discarding a bad design and restarting harder. Never settle for the first design you think of: pick the best of the iterations before writing any code, rather than stopping after the first.
  - Iterate until each pseudocode statement is simple enough that code can be filled in beneath it while the original pseudocode remains as documentation.
  - Decompose any first-attempt statements that are still too high-level; do not skip that decomposition.
  - If you are unsure how to code something, keep working the pseudocode until you are sure.
  - Stop refining and decomposing only when writing more pseudocode instead of the actual code would be a waste of time.

#### Code the Routine

- **Follow a near-standard order, but vary it as needed** - The coding steps below are performed in a nearly standard order; deviate when the routine calls for it. All of the steps get performed, not necessarily in a fixed order.
  1. Start with the pseudocode.
  2. Write the routine declaration.
  3. Add the opening and closing statements, then convert each pseudocode line into a high-level comment.
  4. Fill in the code below each comment.
  5. Repeat as needed.
  6. Check the code.
  7. Clean up leftovers.
- **Write the routine declaration** - Write the routine's interface statement in whatever form the language requires, then convert the original header comment into a programming-language comment and leave it positioned above the pseudocode already written.
  - C++: a function declaration.
  - Java: a method declaration.
  - Microsoft Visual Basic: a function or sub procedure declaration.
- **Record every assumption at the moment it is made** - Document each assumption as you make it. Writing the declaration is the point to note any assumptions about the interface. An interface variable that is straightforward and typed for its specific purpose needs no documentation.

```cpp
/* Outputs a message for a caller-supplied error code. Output channel
   depends on the processing state, which this routine reads itself.
   Returns success or failure.
*/
Status ReportErrorMessage(
   ErrorCode errorToReport
   )
default the status to failure
find the message for the error code
if the code is valid
   interactive mode: show the message to the user, declare success
   command line mode: log the message to the command line, declare success
if the code is invalid, report an internal error to the user
return the status
```

- **Add the enclosing statements, convert each pseudocode line to a comment, then fill code beneath it** - Write the routine's opening and closing statements (`{` and `}` in C++), turn each pseudocode line into a comment in the implementation language in place, and once the design feels solid write the code for that line directly below its comment, translating the pseudocode into code accurately.
- **Stop designing only when translation is mechanical** - The design is finished only when the routine's character and behavior are graspable from the pseudocode alone, with no code written, and converting it to code feels mechanical, natural and easy; otherwise keep designing in pseudocode until it feels solid.
- **One comment equals one code paragraph** - Each pseudocode comment must expand into a complete block expressing one thought; block length varies with the thought, and block quality tracks how focused and vivid that thought was.
- **Expect 2 to 10 lines of code per comment** - Use that as the normal expansion band; a comment yielding far more code is a factoring signal, and one-or-two-line expansions are below what real work produces.
- **Do not delete pseudocode comments because they look redundant with line counts** - Two comment lines over two code lines would be overkill for after-the-fact commenting, but here the comments carry intent and are already written, so keep them; the one exception is a comment that ends up merely restating the code it precedes, which is deleted during the cleanup step.
- **Declare and define each variable next to first use** - When filling in code, introduce every new variable at the point the block that uses it needs it.
- **Flesh out every branch, including empty ones** - Filling in code exposes branches the pseudocode implied; give each one an explicit block with a comment stating why nothing can be done there when it is intentionally empty.
- **Expect real design work below the spec** - A detailed five-sentence spec expanding to roughly 15 lines of pseudocode and then to a page of code is normal; low-level design at code level is substantive, not clerical.
- **Default a status result to the failure value** - Initialize the routine's status variable to failure in its first statement, so any path that does not explicitly succeed still returns failure.
- **Guard on validity before dispatching** - Wrap the processing branches in the validity check for the input, so only valid input reaches them.
- **Set the success status only on the path that actually succeeded** - Assign the success value inside the branch that completed the work, never before the work or outside the branch.
- **Name the faulting routine in internal-error text** - When a routine reports an internal error such as an invalid input code, include the name of the routine that detected it in the message text.
- **Return the accumulated status once, at the end** - Let the branches assign the status variable and end the routine with a single return of that variable.

### Factoring during translation

- **Treat a code explosion under one pseudocode line as a defect in decomposition** - When one pseudocode line yields much more code than expected, take one of the two actions below; never just write dozens of lines under it.
  - **Factor into a new routine** - move the block into its own routine and replace it with the call; a well-written pseudocode line hands you the routine name directly. Finish the current routine first, then apply the PPP to the new one.
  - **Apply the PPP recursively** - decompose the offending pseudocode line into several finer pseudocode lines, then fill code under each of those.

### Checking the code

- **Check your work at every step and have others check it too** - check the result of each construction activity as you finish it, and encourage other people to check it; this catches mistakes at the least expensive level, when the least effort has been invested.
- **Check correctness as the third construction step** - after designing and implementing the routine, verify it is correct and find every error you can at this point; anything missed here stays hidden until later testing, where finding and correcting it costs more.
- **Review even when pseudocode looked right** - review is mandatory because full coding can reveal a pseudocode logic error, a design that is elegant in pseudocode but clumsy in the target language, a flaw in the architecture, high-level design or requirements, or an ordinary coding mistake.
- **Check the routine mentally first** - the first formal check is mental: execute every path in your head, including nominal paths, endpoints and all exception conditions. The cleanup and informal checking steps are themselves mental checks.
  - Keep routines small enough to execute mentally; the difficulty of mental execution is a direct argument for small routines.
  - Do it alone (desk checking) and with peers; peer forms are peer review, walk-through and inspection, differing by how they are run.
- **Suspect your own code before the toolchain** - only about 5 percent of errors were hardware, compiler or operating-system errors, and that 5 percent share is probably even lower now, so treat roughly 95 percent of errors as your own and check your work first. Habitually suspecting the compiler or the hardware is superstition: substituting feelings about the code for understanding it.
- **Never accept "it seems to work"** - know the role of and need for every line, understand the finished code thoroughly, and confirm it is easy to understand. Code you cannot explain probably is broken in a way not yet observed; if a routine works but you do not know why, study it, discuss it, and try alternative designs until you do.
- **Compile late, after you believe the routine is correct** - earlier compiling would let the machine catch undeclared variables and naming conflicts, but the first compile starts a self-imposed clock and produces the "Just One More Compile" syndrome: hasty, error-prone edits that cost more overall.
  - Once free of the hack-compile-fix cycle, compile whenever it seems appropriate; the constraint is on the hacking pull, not on the compiler.
  - Compiling before you are convinced the code is right is a symptom of the hacker mindset.
- **Set compiler warnings to the pickiest level available** - let the compiler find subtle errors instead of finding them by hand.
- **Use validators beyond the compiler** - supplement compiler checks with tools such as lint for C; run validation tools on non-compiled artifacts too, including HTML and JavaScript.
- **Eliminate the cause of every warning and error message, not the message** - read what each warning says about the code; many warnings usually signal low-quality code. Repeatedly tolerated warnings either camouflage more important ones or become noise, so rewriting the code to remove the underlying problem is usually safer and cheaper than living with them.
- **Step through every line in the debugger** - once it compiles, single-step the routine and confirm each line executes as expected; this alone catches many errors.
- **Run the test cases planned during development** - execute the cases created while designing and implementing the routine.
  - Build scaffolding when needed: throwaway code not shipped in the product, either a test harness that calls the routine with test data or stubs that the routine calls.
- **Remove every error you detect** - a detected error must be removed, not deferred.
- **Rewrite an unusually buggy routine instead of patching it** - a routine that is buggy at this point will likely stay buggy, so start over with an entirely new design rather than hacking around it; hacks signal incomplete understanding and guarantee errors now and later.

### Cleaning up leftovers

- **Run the cleanup checks after problem-checking** - once the routine has been checked for problems, run every check in this section against it before considering the routine done.
- **Check the interface** - all input and output data accounted for, and every parameter actually used.
- **Check general design quality** - the routine does one thing and does it well, is loosely coupled to other routines, and is defensively designed.
- **Check the variables** - hunt inaccurate names, unused objects, undeclared variables and improperly initialized objects.
- **Check statements and logic** - hunt off-by-one errors, infinite loops, improper nesting and resource leaks.
- **Check the layout** - white space must clarify the logical structure of the routine, its expressions and its parameter lists.
- **Check the documentation** - confirm the comments derived from pseudocode are still accurate; confirm algorithm descriptions, documented interface assumptions, documented nonobvious dependencies and justifications for unclear coding practices are present.
- **Remove comments that became redundant** - a pseudocode comment can end up restating the code it precedes, most often after recursive PPP application where the comment merely precedes a call to a well-named routine; delete those.

### Repeating steps as needed

- **Return to pseudocode when routine quality is poor** - high-quality programming is iterative; loop back through the construction activities rather than accepting a weak result.
- **Heed the warnings that send you back to design** - treat signals such as use of global data, or operations that seem better suited to another class or another routine, as a requirement to go back to design rather than to continue coding.

### Alternatives and supplements to the PPP

- **Prefer the PPP for creating classes and routines** - the three named approaches in this section may be used as alternatives to the PPP or as supplements to it, but the PPP is the default.
- **Alternative or supplement - test-first development** - write the test cases before writing any code.
- **Alternative or supplement - refactoring** - improve existing code through a series of semantics-preserving transformations, using bad-code patterns ("smells") to locate what needs improvement.
- **Alternative or supplement - design by contract** - treat every routine as having preconditions and postconditions, documented and verified with assertions.
- **Hacking is not an alternative** - these symptoms mean switch to the PPP: coding yourself into a corner and having to restart, losing your train of thought mid-routine, forgetting to write part of a class or routine (which the PPP nearly eliminates), or staring at the screen unsure where to start.

### Scope of construction-level design

- **Fill small requirements and architecture gaps during construction** - this is normal and desirable; specifying every microscopic detail up front in blueprints is inefficient.
- **Re-examine habitual practices for hazards** - hazardous practices get adopted before their alternatives are known and then persist out of habit even after safer ones are learned; experience is not evidence that a practice is safe.

## Code Complete: Ch10 General Issues in Using Variables

### Terminology

- **"variable" covers objects too** - Treat "variable" as covering both objects and built-in types (integers, arrays); "data type" means a built-in type; "data" means either an object or a built-in type. Apply every rule in this chapter to objects, not only to primitives.
- **Declaration vs definition** - A declaration fixes a variable's type; a definition gives it a specific value.

### 10.1 Data Literacy

- **Choose the data type before writing the code** - The first act of creating effective data is picking the right kind of data; treat a broad repertoire of data types as a prerequisite, not an optimization.
- **Required vocabulary** - Be able to select correctly among: abstract data type, array, bitmap, boolean variable, B-tree, character variable, container class, double precision, enumerated type, floating point, heap, index, integer, linked list, named constant, literal, local variable, lookup table, member data, pointer, private, referential integrity, stack, string, structured variable, tree, typedef, union, variant. A gap in this list is a gap to close before choosing a representation.
- **Reject non-types** - "elongated stream", "retroactive synapse" and "value chain" are not data types; do not treat such phrases as representation choices.

### 10.2 Making Variable Declarations Easy

- **Invest in declaration habits** - Declaring variables is individually small but done constantly; adopt the declaration habits in this chapter permanently rather than deciding them case by case.

#### Implicit Declarations

- **Treat implicit declaration as the most hazardous language feature available** - Where a language auto-declares an undeclared variable (Visual Basic, depending on compiler settings), a single typo silently creates a second variable, e.g. a routine that assigns `acctNum = 0` and later reads `acctNo` ends up with two variables, and the one being read never received the value.
- **Value explicit declaration as a correctness barrier** - With mandatory declarations, the same bug needs two independent mistakes (using both names in the routine body and declaring both), which effectively eliminates the synonymous-variable class of defect. Requiring explicit declaration is a primary advantage of such languages, because it forces more careful use of data.
- **When stuck with implicit declarations, apply all four countermeasures**
  - **Turn implicit declarations off** - If the compiler permits it, disable them. Visual Basic: use `Option Explicit` to force declaration before use.
  - **Declare every variable anyway** - Declare each new variable as it is typed even when the compiler does not demand it; this catches some, not all, of the errors.
  - **Standardize confusable suffixes** - Fix a naming convention for suffixes such as `Num` and `No` so one concept never gets two variables.
  - **Audit the name list** - Use the compiler's or a utility's cross-reference listing of a routine's variables to spot near-duplicate pairs like `acctNum`/`acctNo`, and to spot variables declared but never used.

### 10.3 Guidelines for Initializing Variables

- **Treat initialization as a top defect source** - Faulty data initialization ranks among the richest defect sources in programming; invest in prevention techniques rather than in debugging time later.
- **Know the three failure shapes** - The root cause is always a variable holding an unexpected initial value:
  - Never assigned at all, so its value is whatever bits occupied that memory at program start.
  - Assigned once but now stale, holding a value that is no longer valid.
  - Partly assigned, partly not - including an object with only some members initialized.
- **Uninitialized pointers corrupt arbitrary memory** - Forgetting to allocate and then "initializing" through the uninitialized pointer writes a random region of memory, which may hold data, code, or the operating system. Expect symptoms that differ on every run; that non-repeatability is what makes pointer defects harder to debug than others.
- **Initialize each variable at its declaration** - Cheap defensive programming, and it guarantees re-initialization on every call to the enclosing routine.
  - C++: `float studentGrades[ MAX_STUDENTS ] = { 0.0 };`
- **Initialize as close as possible to first use** - Where the language cannot initialize at declaration (Visual Basic), never batch all declarations then all initializations far from first use.
  - Batching is harmful for four reasons: the value can be modified between the initialization and the use (now, or after a later edit); grouped initialization falsely implies every variable is used throughout the whole routine when one may be used only at the end; later edits that wrap a loop around the use site will need re-initialization that the distant code does not provide; and the distant form is more prone to initialization errors under modification.

```vb
' BAD - all declarations, then all initializations, far from use
Dim accountIndex As Integer
Dim total As Double
Dim done As Boolean
accountIndex = 0
total = 0.0
done = False
```

```vb
' GOOD - declare and initialize immediately before use
Dim accountIndex As Integer
accountIndex = 0
' code using accountIndex
Dim done As Boolean
done = False
While Not done
```

- **Principle of Proximity** - Keep related actions together. Apply it beyond initialization: comments beside the code they explain, loop setup beside the loop, statement grouping in straight-line code, and other areas where actions belong together.
- **Ideally declare and define together at first use** - In languages that support it (C++, Java), declare and define each variable close to first use, and prefer defining it in the same statement that declares it. C++ and Java support initialization at declaration; use it.
  - Java: `int accountIndex = 0;` then `double total = 0.0;` immediately before the code that uses `total`, then `boolean done = false;` immediately before `while ( ! done ) {`.
  - C++:
    ```cpp
    int receiptIndex = 0;
    float dailyReceipts = TodaysReceipts();
    double totalReceipts = TotalReceipts( dailyReceipts );
    ```
- **Use `final` / `const` wherever the value must not change** - Java `final`, C++ `const` block assignment after initialization; apply them to class constants, input-only parameters, and any local whose value is meant to stay fixed after initialization.
- **Scrutinize counters and accumulators** - `i`, `j`, `k`, `sum`, `total` are the usual offenders; forgetting to reset one before its next use is a common error. Initialize every counter and accumulator correctly, and re-initialize it each time it is used where the code needs that.
- **Initialize member data in the constructor** - A class's data is initialized in its constructor, mirroring a routine initializing its own variables. Memory allocated in the constructor must be freed in the destructor.
- **Explicitly check whether re-initialization is required** - Ask whether a loop in the routine uses the variable repeatedly, or whether the variable keeps its value between calls and must be reset per call. If so, place the initialization statement inside the repeated code.
- **Split named-constant emulation from true variables** - A variable that emulates a named constant may legitimately be set once at program start inside a `Startup()` routine. Every genuine variable instead gets its value from executable code sitting near the point of use.
  - Failure mode: a routine originally called once is later called many times; anything initialized in a program-level `Startup()` is not re-initialized on the second pass.
- **Auto-initialize via compiler setting, but document it** - Enable a compiler option that initializes all variables if one exists. Depending on specific compiler settings can break the code once it is moved to a different machine and compiler, so document the dependency; assumptions of this kind are otherwise hard to uncover.
- **Act on uninitialized-variable warnings** - Many compilers report use of an uninitialized variable; treat those warnings as defects. Turn on all available compiler warnings and require the code to compile with no warnings at all.
- **Validate input parameters before assigning them anywhere** - Every routine checks its input parameters for validity. Parameter validity checking is itself a form of initialization; confirm values are reasonable before they propagate.
- **Use a memory-access checker for pointer operations** - Some operating systems check invalid pointer references and some do not; where the OS does not, use a purchased memory-access checker rather than going unchecked.
- **Initialize working memory at program start to a known value** - A known starting value helps expose initialization defects. Options:
  - Fill memory with a predictable value using a preprogram memory filler. `0` is useful because uninitialized pointers then point to low memory and are relatively easy to detect on use. On Intel processors `0xCC` is useful: it is the machine code for a breakpoint interrupt, so executing data instead of code under a debugger floods with breakpoints; it is also easy to recognize in memory dumps and rarely legitimate. `0xDEADBEEF` is an alternative filler that is easy to recognize in a debugger.
  - Change the filler value occasionally; varying the environmental background uncovers problems that a constant background hides.
  - Have the program initialize its own working memory at startup. Note the opposing purposes: a preprogram memory filler exists to expose defects, while filling working memory with the same value every run exists to hide them, by guaranteeing the program is unaffected by random startup-memory variation.

### 10.4 Scope

- **Definition of scope** - Scope, also called visibility, measures how much of a program knows about a variable and can reference it. Small scope: only a small area sees it, e.g. an index confined to one short loop. Large scope: many places see it, e.g. an employee-information table used program-wide.
- **Know the scope levels the language offers** - Some primitive languages make every variable global, which leaves no scope control at all and causes many problems. C++ and similar languages offer these visibility levels: block (code inside curly brackets), routine, class (optionally its derived classes too), and program-wide. Java and C# add one more level: package or namespace, meaning a collection of classes.

#### Localize References to Variables

- **Close the window of vulnerability** - The code between two references to a variable is a window in which new code can inadvertently alter it, or a reader can lose track of what it should hold. Always keep references to a variable close together.
- **Measure span** - Span is the number of lines between successive references to a variable; average the individual spans to get its average span. Lower is better.

```java
// span of a is 2, span of b is 1, span of c is 0
a = 0;
b = 0;
c = 0;
a = b + c;
```

```java
// b: first-to-second span 1, second-to-third span 0, average span (1+0)/2 = 0.5
a = 0;
b = 0;
c = 0;
b = a + 1;
b = b / c;
```

- **The payoff of small span is readability** - Close references let a reader concentrate on one section at a time; far-apart references force jumping around the program. Improved readability is the main advantage of minimizing span.

#### Keep Variables "Live" for as Short a Time as Possible

- **Definition of live time** - Live time counts every statement over which a variable stays live: its life opens at the first statement that references it and closes at the last one. Measure it by counting lines from the first to the last reference inclusive.
- **Live time is independent of usage density** - Unlike span, live time ignores how often the variable is used in between. First reference on line 1 and last on line 25 gives live time 25 whether the variable is used on only those two lines (average span 23) or on every line in between (average span 0).
  - Span and live time are separate axes: a long live time can carry either short spans or long spans, while a short live time carries short spans. Minimize both, not one.
- **Minimize live time** - Keep the count low for five reasons:
  - It shrinks the window of vulnerability, reducing the chance of altering the variable between the points where alteration is intended.
  - It makes the code tell the truth: a value assigned on line 10 and next used on line 45 implies use across lines 10-45, whereas assignment on line 44 and use on line 45 implies nothing more and confines reasoning to a small section.
  - It reduces initialization errors: as a program is modified, straight-line code becomes loops, and initializations made far from the loop get forgotten; keeping initialization next to the loop prevents that.
  - It improves readability: fewer lines must be held in mind at once, and all references to the variable fit on one screen while editing and debugging.
  - It makes splitting a large routine easier, because closely grouped references refactor into their own routine cleanly.
- **Shorten a long live time by moving the initialization down** - Measured rewrite: initializations of `recordIndex`, `total` and `done` at lines 2-4, with last references at lines 28, 69 and 70, moved down to lines 25, 62 and 63 just above the loops that use them, which cut average live time from about 54 to about 7.

| Variable | Live time before | Live time after |
|---|---|---|
| `recordIndex` | 28 - 2 + 1 = 27 | 28 - 25 + 1 = 4 |
| `total` | 69 - 3 + 1 = 67 | 69 - 62 + 1 = 8 |
| `done` | 70 - 4 + 1 = 67 | 70 - 63 + 1 = 8 |
| Average | (27+67+67)/3 ~= 54 | (4+8+8)/3 ~= 7 |

- **No published threshold exists** - Researchers have not yet produced quantitative data separating a good live time or span from a bad one, so no number defines the boundary; minimize both span and live time anyway.
- **Avoid global variables** - Applying span and live time to a global variable yields enormous values for both, which counts as one among many sound reasons to keep variables out of global scope.

#### Minimizing Scope

- **Initialize loop variables adjacent to the loop** - place initialization of any variable used by a loop immediately before that loop, not at the top of the enclosing routine.
  - Rationale to enforce: a later edit to the loop then keeps its initialization in view.
  - Failure mode this prevents: wrapping an outer loop around the existing loop leaves the initialization outside it, so it runs only on the first outer pass instead of every pass.
- **Delay assignment until the point of use** - do not give a variable a value earlier than just before that value is consumed; the place a variable receives its value must be obvious.
- **Group statements that touch the same variables** - order code so all references to one variable set are contiguous, rather than interleaving two sets of variables.
  - Interleaving two parallel data sets forces the reader to track all variables of both sets at once (6 live variables in the interleaved form versus 3 per block when split).
  - Split form is shorter per block, holds fewer variables per block, and makes later extraction into well-defined routines straightforward.
  ```cpp
  // BAD - interleaved: 6 variables live at once
  GetOldData( oldData, &numOldData );
  GetNewData( newData, &numNewData );
  totalOldData = Sum( oldData, numOldData );
  totalNewData = Sum( newData, numNewData );
  PrintOldDataSummary( oldData, totalOldData, numOldData );
  PrintNewDataSummary( newData, totalNewData, numNewData );
  SaveOldDataSummary( totalOldData, numOldData );
  SaveNewDataSummary( totalNewData, numNewData );
  ```
  ```cpp
  // GOOD - grouped: 3 variables live per block
  GetOldData( oldData, &numOldData );
  totalOldData = Sum( oldData, numOldData );
  PrintOldDataSummary( oldData, totalOldData, numOldData );
  SaveOldDataSummary( totalOldData, numOldData );

  GetNewData( newData, &numNewData );
  totalNewData = Sum( newData, numNewData );
  PrintNewDataSummary( newData, totalNewData, numNewData );
  SaveNewDataSummary( totalNewData, numNewData );
  ```
- **Extract related statement groups into separate routines** - other factors equal, a variable in a shorter routine has smaller span and shorter live time; breaking groups out mechanically reduces achievable scope.
- **Start at the most restricted visibility and widen only on demand** - scope is cheap to widen and expensive to narrow, so default to the tightest.
  - Widening is easy (class variable to global, private to protected); narrowing is hard (global to class variable, protected member to private).
