  - When in doubt, pick the smallest scope from this ordered ladder: loop-local, routine-local, class-private, protected, package (only where the language provides it), global as the final fallback.
- **Reject the "convenience" justification for wide scope** - making variables global to skip parameter lists and class-scoping rules trades write-time ease for read, debug, and modify cost; optimize for intellectual manageability instead.
  - A program where any routine may touch any variable at any time cannot be understood one routine at a time: every routine sharing the global data must also be understood.
  - Minimizing scope is an application of information hiding - the less that is visible, the less must be held in mind, and the fewer forgotten details can produce a defect.
- **Declare each variable visible to the smallest code segment that needs it** - apply this fallback chain:
  1. Confine to a single loop or single routine.
  2. If that is impossible, restrict visibility to the routines of one class.
  3. If it cannot be confined to the class most responsible for it, expose it to other classes through access routines.
  4. Naked global data is rarely, if ever, necessary.

### Persistence

- **Definition of persistence** - persistence is the life span of a piece of data. Forms:
  - Life of a block or routine - for example a variable declared inside a C++ or Java `for` loop.
  - As long as permitted - Java objects created with `new` live until garbage collected; C++ objects created with `new` live until `delete`.
  - Life of the program - globals in most languages, plus `static` variables in C++ and Java.
  - Forever - values stored outside the program, such as user preferences written to a database or file and reloaded on each run.
- **Never assume longer persistence than the language guarantees** - the core persistence defect is using a value after its real life span ended.
  - Failure mode: sometimes the stale read yields an obviously bad value and surfaces as an error; sometimes the old value is still sitting in memory, the code appears correct, and the defect stays hidden.
- **Check critical variables for reasonable values with debug code or assertions** - on an unreasonable value, emit a warning that points at improper initialization.
- **Assign an unreasonable value to every variable once finished with it** - for example, set a pointer to null after deleting it.
- **Write code that assumes data is not persistent** - do not assume a variable holds, on the next entry to a routine, the value it had on exit.
  - Exception: this does not apply when using a language feature that guarantees retention, such as `static` in C++ and Java.
- **Declare and initialize all data immediately before use, as a habit** - treat data used with no nearby initialization as suspect.

### Binding Time

- **Definition of binding time** - binding time is the moment a variable and its value are joined: code-writing, compile, load, run, or later. Treat the choice as an initialization decision with wide consequences for maintainability and modifiability, and bind every variable at a deliberately chosen time.
- **Prefer the latest binding time that requirements actually demand** - later binding buys flexibility, but each step later costs complexity and error-proneness; build in exactly as much flexibility as the software's requirements need and no more, because minimizing complexity is what makes the program succeed.
  - Advantage of late binding: the later the bind, the more flexibility the code carries.
  - General law: earlier binding means lower flexibility and lower complexity; later binding means higher flexibility, higher complexity, and more error-prone code.
- **Binding-time ladder, earliest to latest**

  | Binding time | Mechanism | Effect |
  |---|---|---|
  | Coding time | magic number hard-coded in source | least flexible, least complex |
  | Compile time | named constant | readable, single point of change, no run-time cost |
  | Load time | value read at startup from outside the program (Windows registry file, Java properties file) | changeable without rebuilding |
  | Object instantiation time | re-read the value each time the object (for example a window) is created | per-instance flexibility |
  | Just in time | re-read the value each time it is needed (for example each time the window is drawn) | most flexible, most complex |

- **Treat hard-coded literals as nearly always wrong** - a literal bound at code-writing time drifts out of sync with copies of the same value elsewhere that must stay equal to it.
  ```java
  // BAD - bound at code-writing time
  titleBar.color = 0xFF; // 0xFF is hex value for color blue
  ```
  ```java
  // GOOD - bound at compile time
  private static final int COLOR_BLUE = 0xFF;
  private static final int TITLE_BAR_COLOR = COLOR_BLUE;
  ...
  titleBar.color = TITLE_BAR_COLOR;
  ```
- **Use a named constant over a magic number whenever the language supports it** - it is nearly always better than hard-coding: the name states what the value represents, one edit covers every occurrence, and there is no run-time performance penalty.
- **Use run-time binding for values a user may customize** - read the value through a routine so the program need not change when the value changes; only the read source changes.
  ```java
  titleBar.color = ReadTitleBarColor();
  ```
- **Treat call frequency as a separate binding decision** - a value-reading routine invoked once at load, once per object creation, or once per use represents successively later binding; choose the frequency deliberately.
- **Take the free flexibility first** - named constants deliver the compile-time step of the ladder through ordinary good practice; anything beyond that must be justified by a requirement.

### Relationship Between Data Types and Control Structures

- **Match control structure to data shape** - the shape of the data dictates the shape of the code (Michael Jackson's data/control correspondence); make code patterns mirror data patterns.

  | Data type | Definition | Required control structure |
  |---|---|---|
  | Sequential | a cluster of distinct values used together in a fixed order (name, id, address, phone, age read from a file) | sequential statements |
  | Selective | a collection in which exactly one of several values applies at a time (hourly versus salaried employee) | `if-then-else` or `case` statements |
  | Iterative | the same kind of data repeated (elements in a container, records in a file, elements in an array) | `for`, `repeat`, `while` loops |

- **Compose the three shapes for real data** - real data is usually a combination of sequential, selective, and iterative; build the description and the code from these building blocks.

### Using Each Variable for Exactly One Purpose

- **Give each variable one and only one purpose** - never reuse a single variable for two unrelated activities, even a temporary.
  - Smell: the variable is named correctly for only one of its uses, or it is a "temporary" carrying an unhelpful name like `x` or `temp`.
  - Reusing one name for unrelated jobs implies a relationship that does not exist; distinct names per purpose are the fix.
  ```cpp
  // BAD - one temp, two unrelated jobs
  temp = Sqrt( b*b - 4*a*c );
  root[0] = ( -b + temp ) / ( 2 * a );
  root[1] = ( -b - temp ) / ( 2 * a );
  // swap the roots
  temp = root[0];
  root[0] = root[1];
  root[1] = temp;
  ```
  ```cpp
  // GOOD - one variable per purpose
  discriminant = Sqrt( b*b - 4*a*c );
  root[0] = ( -b + discriminant ) / ( 2 * a );
  root[1] = ( -b - discriminant ) / ( 2 * a );
  // swap the roots
  oldRoot = root[0];
  root[0] = root[1];
  root[1] = oldRoot;
  ```
- **Apply the one-purpose rule to routine parameters too** - a parameter carries exactly one purpose.
- **Never give a variable hidden meanings (hybrid coupling)** - keep every variable's meaning explicit, with no value carrying a second, concealed meaning. Overloading particular values of a variable to signal something outside its normal meaning is hybrid coupling; it forces the variable to be the wrong type for at least one of its jobs.
  - Banned patterns of this kind:
    - `pageCount` holds a page count except when it is -1, which flags an error - the integer is doubling as a boolean.
    - `customerId` holds a customer number except when it exceeds 500,000, where subtracting 500,000 yields a delinquent account number.
    - `bytesWritten` holds the byte count except when negative, where it identifies the output disk drive.
  - Do not exempt a double use because it is clear to the author; it will not be clear to anyone else. Spend the second variable and the extra storage.
- **Ensure every declared variable is used** - measured result: code containing unreferenced variables shows higher fault rates. Check declarations for use as a habit, and enable the compiler or tool warnings (for example `lint`) that flag unused variables.

### Choosing Good Names

- **A variable's quality is essentially its name** - a variable and its name are effectively the same entity, so choose names deliberately rather than for sound or appearance.
- **Naming guidance generalizes** - variable-naming rules apply primarily to objects and primitive data, but also govern names of classes, packages, files, and other program entities.

## Code Complete: Ch11 The Power of Variable Names

### 11.1 Considerations in Choosing Good Names

- **Name must fully describe the entity** - A variable name must state completely and accurately what the variable holds. This is the single most important naming consideration. Judge every name against three targets: readable, memorable, appropriate.
  - Derivation technique: state in words what the variable represents, then use that statement (condensed) as the name. Such a name needs no decoding, cannot be confused with another entity, and is easy to recall because it mirrors the concept.
  - Prefer the obvious ordinary words for the concept (`currentDate`, `todaysDate` for a current date). The easiest correct name is frequently the plain one, and it is frequently skipped.
- **Never use `x`, `x1`, `x2`** - These are always bad names; `x` conventionally denotes an unknown, so it advertises that the value is unknown. Replace with a described entity (`rate` or `interestRate`, not `r` or `x`).
- **Reject names that are too general to be specific** - Names usable for more than one purpose (`x`, `temp`, `i`) carry less information than they could and are usually bad. Make each name as specific as the entity allows.
- **Reject near-miss names that omit a qualifier** - A name that names only part of the entity is still a bad name: `date` fails for a current date because it does not say *current*; `current` fails because it does not say what is current.

#### Good vs bad descriptors

| Purpose of variable | Good names | Bad names |
|---|---|---|
| Running total of checks written to date | `runningTotal`, `checkTotal` | `written`, `ct`, `checks`, `CHKTTL`, `x`, `x1`, `x2` |
| Velocity of a bullet train | `velocity`, `trainVelocity`, `velocityInMph` | `velt`, `v`, `tv`, `x`, `x1`, `x2`, `train` |
| Current date | `currentDate`, `todaysDate` | `cd`, `current`, `c`, `x`, `x1`, `x2`, `date` |
| Lines per page | `linesPerPage` | `lpp`, `lines`, `l`, `x`, `x1`, `x2` |

```java
// BAD
x = x - xx;
xxx = fido + SalesTax( fido );
x = x + LateFee( x1, x ) + xxx;

// GOOD
balance = balance - lastPayment;
monthlyTotal = newPurchases + SalesTax( newPurchases );
balance = balance + LateFee( customerID, balance ) + monthlyTotal;
```

#### Problem Orientation

- **Name the problem, not the solution** - A mnemonic name expresses *what* the entity is in the problem domain, not *how* the machine handles it. If a name refers to a computing concept rather than the problem, replace it.
  - `employeeData` over `inputRec` (input and record are computing terms).
  - `printerReady` over `bitFlag` for a printer-status bit field.
  - `sum` over `calcVal` in an accounting program.

#### Optimum Name Length

- **Target 10 to 16 characters average** - Debugging effort measured lowest at an average name length of 10 to 16 characters; an average of 8 to 20 characters debugged almost as easily.
  - Do not force individual names into that band. Use it as an audit signal: if many names in the code are shorter than that, verify each is still as clear as it needs to be.
- **Too short loses meaning, too long loses structure** - Make every name long enough that a reader never has to puzzle it out. Very short names do not carry enough meaning, and pairs like `x1`/`x2` hide the relationship between the two values even if `x` is deciphered. Very long names are laborious to type and obscure the program's visual structure.
- **Aim between the extremes** - Choose the middle name, not the extreme in either direction.

| Too long | Too short | Just right |
|---|---|---|
| `numberOfPeopleOnTheUsOlympicTeam` | `n`, `np`, `ntm` | `numTeamMembers`, `teamMemberCount` |
| `numberOfSeatsInTheStadium` | `n`, `ns`, `nsisd` | `numSeatsInStadium`, `seatCount` |
| `maximumNumberOfPointsInModernOlympics` | `m`, `mp`, `max`, `points` | `teamPointsMax`, `pointsRecord` |

#### The Effect of Scope on Variable Names

- **Let length signal scope** - Short names are not always bad: a name like `i` itself communicates that the value is a scratch value with a tiny scope, a plain loop counter or array index with no meaning beyond those few lines. A reader is entitled to assume the value is not used outside a few lines.
- **Scale name length with rarity and reach** - Use longer names for rarely used variables and global variables; shorter names for local and loop variables.
- **Competing stricter policy** - Short names carry many risks, and some careful programmers refuse them entirely as a defensive-programming policy. Both positions are in force: short names are legitimate for genuinely tiny local scopes, but a project may adopt a blanket ban on them as defensive policy.
- **Qualify names in the global namespace** - For anything globally visible (named constants, class names, and similar), decide whether a convention is needed to partition the global namespace and prevent naming collisions.
  - C++ and C#: partition with the `namespace` keyword, then disambiguate as `UserInterfaceSubsystem::Employee` vs `DatabaseSubsystem::Employee`.
  - Java: use packages for the same effect.
  - Languages with no namespaces or packages: prefix globally visible classes with a subsystem mnemonic (`uiEmployee`, `dbEmployee`) to minimize global-namespace collision risk.

```cpp
namespace UserInterfaceSubsystem {
   // declarations
}
namespace DatabaseSubsystem {
   // declarations
}
```

#### Computed-Value Qualifiers in Variable Names

- **Put computed-value qualifiers last** - Place modifiers such as `Total`, `Sum`, `Average`, `Max`, `Min`, `Record`, `String`, `Pointer` at the end of the name (`revenueTotal`, not `totalRevenue`).
  - Rationale carried by the rule: the meaning-bearing part is read first; the convention blocks using `totalRevenue` and `revenueTotal` as if they were different variables; a family like `revenueTotal`, `expenseTotal`, `revenueAverage`, `expenseAverage` stays symmetric; consistency aids reading and maintenance.
- **Exception - `Num` by position** - The customary `Num` qualifier breaks the suffix rule: leading `Num` means a total (`numCustomers` = total customers), trailing `Num` means an index (`customerNum` = the current customer's number).
  - A trailing plural on the total form (`numCustomers`) is a second signal separating it from the index form.
  - Because `Num` so often confuses, sidestep it: use `Count` or `Total` for totals (`customerCount`) and `Index` for a specific item (`customerIndex`).

#### Common Opposites in Variable Names

- **Use opposites precisely** - Pair names using standard, common-language opposites; pairs that deviate from ordinary opposites are hard to remember and confusing. Consistency here directly buys readability.
  - Standard pairs: `begin`/`end`, `first`/`last`, `locked`/`unlocked`, `min`/`max`, `next`/`previous`, `old`/`new`, `opened`/`closed`, `visible`/`invisible`, `source`/`target`, `source`/`destination`, `up`/`down`.

### 11.2 Naming Specific Types of Data

#### Naming Loop Indexes

- **`i`, `j`, `k` only for simple loop indexes** - The customary short loop names are acceptable, but if they are used at all they must not be used for anything except indexes of simple loops; the convention is too entrenched to violate without confusing readers.
- **Name any loop variable used outside the loop descriptively** - If the value is read after the loop ends, give it a meaningful name (`recordCount` for a count of records read), not `i`, `j`, or `k`.
- **Name the index descriptively once the loop exceeds a few lines** - Loop index names must be meaningful, never `i`, `j`, or `k`, whenever the loop is more than one or two lines long or is nested; in a longer loop the meaning of `i` is easily lost. Because code is so often modified, extended, and copied elsewhere, many experienced programmers avoid `i` entirely.
- **Use longer index names in nested loops** - Nesting is a common cause of loop growth; give each nested loop variable a longer name to keep the code readable and to prevent index cross-talk (writing `i` where `j` was meant). Array access reads better as `score[ teamIndex ][ eventIndex ]` than `score[ i ][ j ]`.
- **Simplest resolution** - Devising a descriptive name instead of `i`, `j`, `k` removes every loop-index problem at once: meaning lost in a long loop, and index cross-talk between nested loops.

```java
// GOOD - nested loops with descriptive indexes
for ( teamIndex = 0; teamIndex < teamCount; teamIndex++ ) {
   for ( eventIndex = 0; eventIndex < eventCount[ teamIndex ]; eventIndex++ ) {
      score[ teamIndex ][ eventIndex ] = 0;
   }
}
```

#### Naming Status Variables

- **Definition** - A status variable describes the state of the program.
- **Never put `flag` in a name** - `flag` conveys nothing about what the variable controls. Think of status variables rather than flags, and name the state.
- **Assign and test status values through named symbols** - Set and compare status variables using enumerated types, named constants, or globals acting as named constants, never bare magic numbers. `statusFlag = 0x80` is unreadable without external documentation; `characterType = CONTROL_CHARACTER` is self-explanatory, and `if ( reportType == ReportType_Annual )` beats `if ( printFlag == 16 )`.

```cpp
// BAD
if ( statusFlag & 0x0F ) ...
if ( printFlag == 16 ) ...
printFlag = 16;

// GOOD
if ( characterType & PRINTABLE_CHAR ) ...
if ( reportType == ReportType_Annual ) ...
characterType = CONTROL_CHARACTER;
```

```cpp
// Supporting declarations: named constants for bit values, enum for report type
const int LETTER = 0x01;
const int DIGIT = 0x02;
const int PUNCTUATION = 0x04;
const int LINE_DRAW = 0x08;
const int PRINTABLE_CHAR = ( LETTER | DIGIT | PUNCTUATION | LINE_DRAW );
const int CONTROL_CHARACTER = 0x80;

enum ReportType {
   ReportType_Daily, ReportType_Monthly, ReportType_Quarterly,
   ReportType_Annual, ReportType_All
};
```

- **Rename rather than decode** - Any time a section of code has to be figured out before it can be understood, treat that as the signal to rename its variables. Code must be readable, not solvable.

#### Naming Temporary Variables

- **Definition** - Temporary variables hold intermediate results of calculations, act as placeholders, or carry housekeeping values, and are typically named `temp`, `x`, or something equally vague.
- **Treat "temporary" as a warning sign** - A temporary variable generally signals that the problem is not yet fully understood. Their official "temporary" status also invites casual treatment, which raises the error rate.
- **Distrust the label itself** - Preserving a value temporarily is often necessary, but in some sense most variables in a program are temporary; singling a few out as "temporary" may indicate their real purpose is not yet clear.
- **Name the intermediate result for what it is** - Rename every variable labeled temporary, including every `temp`, to something meaningful. Keep the variable if the expression is reused, but name the concept.

```cpp
// BAD
temp = sqrt( b^2 - 4*a*c );
solution[0] = ( -b + temp ) / ( 2 * a );

// GOOD - assumes (b^2 - 4*a*c) is positive
discriminant = sqrt( b^2 - 4*a*c );
solution[0] = ( -b + discriminant ) / ( 2 * a );
```

#### Naming Boolean Variables

- **Use the established boolean names** - Keep this vocabulary in mind and follow its polarity exactly:
  - `done` - whether something (a loop or another operation) is finished; false before, true on completion.
  - `error` - whether an error occurred; false when none has, true when one has.
  - `found` - whether a value was located; false until found, true once found. Applies to any search: array lookup, employee ID in a file, a given amount among paychecks, and so on.
  - `success` or `ok` - whether an operation succeeded; false on failure, true on success. Replace it with a more specific name whenever possible (`processingComplete` when success means processing finished, `found` when success means a value was located).
- **Name booleans so the name implies true or false and its meaning when true is clear** - `done` and `success` are good because the entity is inherently binary. `status` and `sourceFile` are poor because neither is obviously true or false and neither reading of `true` is determinable. Replace `status` with `error` or `statusOK`; replace `sourceFile` with `sourceFileAvailable` or `sourceFileFound`, or whatever it actually represents.
- **`Is` prefix - tradeoff, not a mandate** - Prefixing with `Is` turns the name into a question answered by its value (`isFound`, `isProcessingComplete`).
  - Benefit: it fails audibly on vague names, since `isStatus?` is meaningless, exposing the bad name.
  - Drawback: it degrades simple conditionals; `if ( isFound )` reads slightly worse than `if ( found )`.
- **Use positive boolean names** - Never name a boolean with a built-in negation (`notFound`, `notdone`, `notSuccessful`); negating them produces unreadable code such as `if not notFound`. Name the positive state (`found`, `done`, `processingComplete`) and apply the negation operator where needed.

#### Naming Enumerated Types

- **Mark members with the group name** - Make membership in one group explicit by giving every member a prefix or suffix naming the category (`Color_`, `Planet_`, `Month_`), as in `Color_Red`, `Color_Green`, `Color_Blue`, `Planet_Earth`, `Month_January`.
- **Drop the redundant prefix where the language already scopes members** - In languages that treat enums like classes and always require the enum name as a qualifier (`Color.Color_Red`), repeating the prefix adds nothing; use the enum type name as the prefix and shorten members to `Color.Red`, `Planet.Earth`.
- **Choose one format for the enum type name and hold to it** - The type itself (`Color`, `Planet`, `Month`) may be all caps or prefixed (`e_Color`, `e_Planet`, `e_Month`). Two defensible arguments conflict: an enum is a user-defined type, so format it like a class; an enum is also a set of constants, so format it like constants. Default to mixed case for enumerated type names.

```vb
Public Enum Color
   Color_Red
   Color_Green
   Color_Blue
End Enum
```

#### Naming Constants

- **Name the abstract entity, never the literal value** - A constant's name must denote what the value means, not the number it currently holds. `FIVE` is bad even if the value is 5.0, because `FIVE = 6.0` is absurd; `CYCLES_NEEDED` is good because it survives a change from 5.0 to 6.0. `BAKERS_DOZEN` is poor; `DONUTS_MAX` is good.

### 11.3 The Power of Naming Conventions

#### Why Have Conventions?

- **Adopt a convention because one exists, not because it is optimal** - Any convention at all usually beats none. The power comes from having a convention that adds structure and removes decisions, not from the specific choice, which may be arbitrary. Rigid, ineffective standards do exist and do damage creativity and program quality; effective ones are among the strongest available tools.
- **Benefits a convention must be expected to deliver** - Use these as the test of whether a convention is earning its keep:
  - Fewer local decisions: one global decision replaces many local ones, freeing attention for more important properties of the code.
  - Knowledge transfer across projects: similar names make unfamiliar variables' purposes easier and safer to infer.
  - Faster onboarding: one consistent style instead of per-author styles.
  - Less name proliferation: without a convention the same concept gets two names (`pointTotal` and `totalPoints`), which is far more confusing to a later reader than to the author.
  - Compensation for language weaknesses: emulate named constants and enumerated types, distinguish local from class from global data, and encode type information the compiler does not support.
  - Visible relationships among related items: with object data the compiler handles this; without object support, a shared prefix does it, so `employeeAddress`, `employeePhone`, `employeeName` show a relationship that `address`, `phone`, `name` hide.

#### When You Should Have a Naming Convention

- **Always run some convention; scale its extent to the situation** - Adopt a variable naming convention regardless of the kind of project, and set how extensive it is from the size of the program and the number of people working on it. There are no hard-and-fast triggers, but a convention is worthwhile when:
  - Several programmers work on the project.
  - The program will be handed to another programmer for modification and maintenance, which is nearly always the case.
  - Other programmers in the organization review the code.
  - The program is too large to hold in one head and must be reasoned about piecewise.
  - The program will live long enough that work on it may pause for weeks or months.
  - The project has many unusual terms needing standard terms or abbreviations in code.

#### Degrees of Formality

- **Match formality to people, size, and lifespan** - Set the degree of formality from three inputs: headcount on the program, program size, and expected life span.
  - Informal end: a convention as thin as "use meaningful names" is a valid convention.
  - Tiny, throwaway programs: a strict convention may be pure overhead; do not impose one.
  - Larger programs with several people involved, whether at the start or over the lifetime: formal conventions are indispensable for readability.

### 11.4 Informal Naming Conventions

#### Guidelines for a Language-Independent Convention

- **Differentiate variable names from routine names** - Use a fixed casing split; the convention here is lower-case-initial for variables and objects, upper-case-initial for routines: `variableName` vs `RoutineName()`.
- **Differentiate classes from objects (types from variables of those types)** - Pick one of these options and apply it consistently; every option trades something away.

| Option | Form | Weakness / condition |
|---|---|---|
| 1 - initial capitalization | `Widget widget;` | Common in case-sensitive C++ and Java, but some programmers reject splitting names by capitalization alone, which arguably leaves too little "psychological distance" and too small a visual gap; unusable in mixed-language environments containing a case-insensitive language (Visual Basic treats `widget` and `Widget` as one token, so `Dim widget as Widget` is a syntax error) |
| 2 - all caps for the type | `WIDGET widget;` | Clearer type/variable distinction, but all caps already means "constant" in C++ and Java, and it has the same mixed-language problem as Option 1 |
| 3 - `t_` prefix on types | `t_Widget Widget;` | Works adequately in every language; some programmers reject prefixes on aesthetic grounds |
| 4 - `a` prefix on variables | `Widget aWidget;` | Alternative to Option 3, but it alters every instance name instead of the single class name |
| 5 - more specific variable names | `Widget employeeWidget;` | Requires per-variable thought; usually yields more readable code, but when an object really is a generic widget it forces weak names like `genericWidget`. Preferred default, because it is understandable to readers who do not know the convention |

- **Identify global variables with a prefix** - Misuse of globals is a common defect source; a prefix such as `g_` (`g_RunningTotal`) tells a reader the variable is global so it is handled as such.
- **Identify member variables with a prefix** - Mark a class's member data, for example with `m_`, so it is distinguishable from both local and global data.
- **Identify type definitions** - A type-naming convention must both mark the name as a type and prevent clashes with variable names; a prefix or suffix satisfies both.
  - C++: the customary form is all uppercase for a type name (`COLOR`, `MENU`), applying to typedefs and structs, not class names. Because that collides visually with named preprocessor constants, a `t_` prefix (`t_Color`, `t_Menu`) removes the ambiguity.
- **Identify named constants** - Mark constants so it is clear whether a variable is being assigned from another variable, whose value can change, or from a constant.
  - Visual Basic: also from a function, since VB does not require parentheses on function names, whereas C++ requires them even with no parameters, making the distinction visible there.
  - Options: a `c_` prefix (`c_RecsMax`, `c_LinesPerPageMax`), or the C++ and Java convention of all uppercase with optional underscores (`RECSMAX` or `RECS_MAX`, `LINESPERPAGEMAX` or `LINES_PER_PAGE_MAX`).
- **Identify elements of enumerated types** - Mark enum members for the same reason as constants, so they are distinguishable from variables, named constants, and functions: all caps or an `e_` / `E_` prefix for the type name itself, plus a type-specific member prefix such as `Color_` or `Planet_`.
- **Identify input-only parameters in languages that do not enforce them** - Input parameters get modified by accident; guard against it by convention where the language cannot.
  - C++ and Visual Basic: the intent to return a modified value must be stated explicitly, via `*`, `&`, and `const` in C++ or `ByRef` and `ByVal` in Visual Basic.
  - Other languages return the modification whether or not it was wanted, especially for objects. Java passes all objects "by value", so passing an object to a routine still lets the called routine change the object's contents.
  - Remedy: prefix input-only parameters with `const` (or `final`, `nonmodifiable`, or an equivalent). Anything with that prefix appearing on the left of an assignment is then a visible defect, and `constMax.SetNewMax( ... )` is recognizable as a mistake.
  - This is programming *into* a language rather than merely *in* it: augmenting the language with a convention to cover its limitations.
- **Format names to enhance readability** - Separate words using capitalization or an underscore separator: `GYMNASTICSPOINTTOTAL` is less readable than `gymnasticsPointTotal` or `gymnastics_point_total`. C++, Java, Visual Basic, and others support both mixed case and the `_` separator.
  - Do not mix the two techniques; mixing makes code hard to read.
  - Any of these techniques applied honestly and consistently improves the code.
  - Whether the first character is capitalized (`TotalPoints` vs `totalPoints`) barely matters as long as the team is consistent. Initial lowercase is used here, following Java practice and for cross-language similarity.

#### Guidelines for Language-Specific Conventions

- **Follow the host language's conventions** - Adopt the established naming style of the language in use rather than inventing one, keep the project convention as compatible as possible with the language's standard conventions, and treat the convention as environment-dependent: the same language has different conventions on different platforms.
- **C conventions (generic UNIX/Linux style)**
  - `c` and `ch` hold characters; `i` and `j` are integer indexes; `n` is a count of something; `p` is a pointer; `s` is a string.
  - Preprocessor macros in `ALL_CAPS`; extend the same rule to typedefs.
  - Variable and routine names in `all_lowercase`.
  - Separate words with `_`: `letters_in_lowercase` beats `lettersinlowercase`.
  - Exception by environment: Microsoft Windows C code tends toward a Hungarian-style convention with mixed case; Macintosh C code tends toward mixed-case routine names because the toolbox and OS routines were designed for a Pascal interface.
- **C++ conventions**
  - `i` and `j` are integer indexes; `p` is a pointer.
  - Constants, typedefs and preprocessor macros in `ALL_CAPS`.
  - Class and other type names in `MixedUpperAndLowerCase`.
  - Variable and function names: first word lowercase, later words capitalized - `variableOrRoutineName`.
  - Do not use `_` as an intra-name separator, except in all-caps names and certain prefixes such as global-variable markers.
  - This convention is not standard; environments have standardized on differing details.
- **Java conventions** - Well established since the language's start.
  - `i` and `j` are integer indexes.
  - Constants in `ALL_CAPS` with underscores between words.
  - Class and interface names capitalize every word including the first - `ClassOrInterfaceName`.
  - Variable and method names: first word lowercase, later words capitalized - `variableOrRoutineName`.
  - Do not use `_` as an intra-name separator except in all-caps names.
  - Use `get` and `set` prefixes for accessor methods.
- **Visual Basic conventions** - No firm language-wide conventions exist; adopt an explicit project convention instead of assuming one.
- **Mixed-language projects** - Optimize naming, formatting and documentation conventions for consistency and readability across the whole codebase, accepting deviation from one member language's convention when overall consistency is better served.

#### Sample Naming Conventions

- **Encode three facts in a variable name** - A convention should express (1) the variable's contents, i.e. what it represents, (2) the kind of data - named constant, primitive variable, user-defined type, or class - and (3) the scope - private, class, package, or global.
  - The convention must distinguish local, class and global data.
  - The convention must distinguish type names, named constants, enumerated types and variables.
- **Do not stop at the standard language conventions** - The standard C, C++, Java and Visual Basic naming styles ignore scope distinctions (private/class/global) and distinctions among class, object, routine and variable names; extend them.
- **Keep the convention adaptable** - A convention need not be complex; tailor it to the project's needs. The sample conventions in this subsection are illustrative examples of what an informal convention contains, not mandated schemes.

**Sample convention - C++ and Java**

| Entity | Rule |
|---|---|
| `ClassName` | Mixed case, initial capital. |
| `TypeName` | Type definitions, including enumerated types and typedefs: mixed case, initial capital. |
| `EnumeratedTypes` | As type names, and always stated in the plural. |
| `localVariable` | Mixed case, initial lowercase; name independent of the underlying data type and referring to what the variable represents. |
| `routineParameter` | Formatted as local variables. |
| `RoutineName()` | Mixed case. |
| `m_ClassVariable` | Member variables reachable by several routines inside one class only: prefix `m_`. |
| `g_GlobalVariable` | Global variables: prefix `g_`. |
| `CONSTANT` | Named constants in `ALL_CAPS`. |
| `MACRO` | Macros in `ALL_CAPS`. |
| `Base_EnumeratedType` | Prefix each enumerated value with a singular mnemonic of its base type - `Color_Red`, `Color_Blue`. |

**Sample convention - C**

| Entity | Rule |
|---|---|
| `TypeName` | Mixed case, initial capital. |
| `GlobalRoutineName()` | Public routines in mixed case. |
| `f_FileRoutineName()` | Routines private to one module (file): prefix `f_`. |
| `LocalVariable` | Mixed case; name independent of the underlying data type and referring to what the variable represents. |
| `RoutineParameter` | Formatted as local variables. |
| `f_FileStaticVariable` | Module (file) variables: prefix `f_`. |
| `G_GLOBAL_GlobalVariable` | Global variables: prefix `G_` plus an all-caps mnemonic of the defining module - `SCREEN_Dimensions`. |
| `LOCAL_CONSTANT` | Named constants private to one routine or module: all uppercase - `ROWS_MAX`. |
| `G_GLOBALCONSTANT` | Global named constants: all uppercase, prefixed `G_` plus an all-caps module mnemonic - `G_SCREEN_ROWS_MAX`. |
| `LOCALMACRO()` | Macros private to one routine or module: all uppercase. |
| `G_GLOBAL_MACRO()` | Global macros: all uppercase, prefixed `G_` plus an all-caps module mnemonic - `G_SCREEN_LOCATION()`. |

**Sample convention - Visual Basic**

- **Case-insensitivity forces extra markers** - Because Visual Basic is not case-sensitive, add explicit prefixes to separate type names from variable names.

| Entity | Rule |
|---|---|
| `C_ClassName` | Mixed case, initial capital, prefix `C_`. |
| `T_TypeName` | Type definitions, including enumerated types and typedefs: mixed case, initial capital, prefix `T_`. |
| `T_EnumeratedTypes` | As type definitions, and always stated in the plural. |
| `localVariable` | Mixed case, initial lowercase; independent of underlying data type, naming what it represents. |
| `routineParameter` | Formatted as local variables. |
| `RoutineName()` | Mixed case. |
| `m_ClassVariable` | Member variables used across routines within a single class: prefix `m_`. |
| `g_GlobalVariable` | Global variables: prefix `g_`. |
| `CONSTANT` | Named constants in `ALL_CAPS`. |
| `Base_EnumeratedType` | Prefix enumerated values with a singular base-type mnemonic - `Color_Red`, `Color_Blue`. |

### 11.5 Standardized Prefixes

- **Standardize prefixes for recurring meanings** - a fixed set of terse abbreviations gives naming that is short yet consistent and readable. The best-known scheme is the **Hungarian naming convention**, a detailed guideline set for naming variables and routines, once widespread in Microsoft Windows programming; it is no longer in broad use, but standardizing on terse, precise abbreviations remains valuable.
- **Compose a standardized prefix from two parts** - the user-defined type (UDT) abbreviation plus the semantic prefix.
- **UDT abbreviation** - identifies the data type of the named object or variable.
  - Use it for program-domain entities such as windows, screen regions and fonts; generally do not use it for the language's predefined data types.
  - Invent short mnemonic codes per program and then standardize on them for that program - `wn` for windows, `scr` for screen regions.
  - Also declare programming-language data types whose names reuse the same abbreviations, so declarations pair type and prefix:

```cpp
CH chCursorPosition;
SCR scrUserWorkspace;
DOC docActive;
PA firstPaActiveDocument;
PA lastPaActiveDocument;
WN wnMain;
```

  - Derive your own UDT set from the entities most common in the target environment. Sample set for a word processor:

| UDT abbreviation | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ch` | Character - the data type a word processor uses for a character in a document, not the C++ sense. |
| `doc` | Document. |
| `pa` | Paragraph. |
| `scr` | Screen region. |
| `sel` | Selection. |
| `wn` | Window. |

- **Semantic prefixes** - describe how the variable or object is used, one level beyond the UDT; unlike UDTs, which change per project, semantic prefixes are fairly stable across projects.

| Semantic prefix | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `c` | Count - of records, characters, and so on. |
| `first` | First element to be processed in an array; like `min`, but scoped to the current operation instead of to the array itself. |
| `g` | Global variable. |
| `i` | Index into an array. |
| `last` | Last element to be processed; counterpart of `first`, and a final legal element. |
| `lim` | Noninclusive upper bound of the elements to be processed; not a valid index; counterpart of `first`; generally `lim` equals `last + 1`. |
| `m` | Class-level variable. |
| `max` | Absolute last element of the array or list itself, not of an operation on it. |
| `min` | Absolute first element of the array or list. |
| `p` | Pointer. |

- **Combine prefixes** - format semantic prefixes in lowercase or mixed case and stack them with UDTs and with each other: `firstPa` (first paragraph), `iPa` (index into paragraphs), `cPa` (count of paragraphs), `firstPaActiveDocument` and `lastPaActiveDocument` (first and last paragraphs of the active document).
- **Benefits to expect** - all the general benefits of any naming convention (fewer local decisions, knowledge transfer across projects, faster onboarding, less name proliferation, compensation for language weaknesses, visible relationships among related items), plus fewer distinct names to remember per program or class; precision in areas normally left vague, notably the distinctions among `min`, `first`, `last` and `max`; and shorter names - `cpa` instead of `totalParagraphs`, `ipa` instead of `indexParagraphs` or `paragraphsIndex`.
- **Use prefixes as a manual type check** - with abstract data types the compiler cannot verify, mismatched prefixes flag bugs: `paReformat = docReformat` is probably wrong because `pa` and `doc` are different UDTs.
- **Main pitfall - prefix without meaning** - never let the prefix be the whole name. Even when `ipa` is unambiguous, finish the name descriptively, e.g. `ipaActiveDocument`.

### 11.6 Creating Short Names That Are Readable

- **Prefer long names; shorten only under a real constraint** - short names are a holdover from assembler, generic Basic and Fortran, which capped names at 2-8 characters, and from mathematics' `i`, `j`, `k`. Modern languages such as C++, Java and Visual Basic allow names of nearly any length, so there is almost never a reason to shorten a meaningful name.
- **When shortening is required, choose a good method** - build short names by dropping needless words, substituting short synonyms, or applying an abbreviation strategy. Learn several abbreviation techniques because no single one works in every case.

#### General abbreviation guidelines

- **These guidelines conflict with each other by design** - do not apply them all at once; pick the one that fits the name.
  - Use standard abbreviations - ones in common use and listed in a dictionary.
  - Remove all nonleading vowels: `computer` to `cmptr`, `screen` to `scrn`, `apple` to `appl`, `integer` to `intgr`.
  - Remove articles and conjunctions: `and`, `or`, `the`, and the like.
  - Use the first letter or first few letters of each word.
  - Truncate consistently after the first, second or third letter of each word, whichever suits.
  - Keep the first and last letters of each word.
  - Use every significant word in the name, up to a maximum of three words.
  - Remove useless suffixes - `ing`, `ed`, and so on.
  - Keep the most noticeable sound of each syllable.
  - Never change the variable's meaning while abbreviating.
  - Iterate over these techniques until each name is between 8 and 20 characters, or down to the language's name-length limit.
- **Avoid phonetic abbreviations** - spelling-by-sound forms are not recommended: `sk8ing` for skating, `hilite` for highlight, `b4` for before, `xqt` for execute. They force the reader to decode a name like a personalized license plate.

#### Abbreviation pitfalls to avoid

- **Never abbreviate by deleting a single character** - one keystroke saved does not pay for the lost readability, and nobody can recall afterwards whether a character was dropped (as with "Jun" for June). Drop at least two characters or keep the whole word.
- **Abbreviate consistently** - pick one form and use it everywhere: `Num` throughout or `No` throughout, never both. Likewise, never abbreviate a word in some names and spell it out in others (`Number` here, `Num` there).
- **Make names pronounceable** - `xPos` over `xPstn`, `needsComp` over `ndsCmptg`. Apply the **telephone test**: any name that cannot be dictated over a phone call is too indistinct and must be renamed.
- **Avoid letter combinations that invite misreading or mispronunciation** - for a name meaning the end of a value named `B`, prefer `ENDB` to `BEND`. This guideline becomes unnecessary under a good word-separation technique, because `B-END`, `BEnd` and `b_end` cannot be mispronounced.
- **Resolve abbreviation collisions with a thesaurus** - when two concepts abbreviate to the same token, substitute a synonym. Under a three-character limit, `fired` and `full revenue disbursal` both collapse to `frd`; renaming to `dismissed` and `complete revenue disbursal` yields `dsm` and `crd`.
- **Document extremely short names with an in-code translation table** - in languages that permit only very short names, place a comment table mapping each name to its mnemonic content at the start of the code block. This still applies to real systems: as of mid-2003, hundreds of thousands of lines of RPG code carried a 6-character variable-name limit.

```pseudocode
C  Variable   Meaning
C  --------   -------
C  XPOS       x-Coordinate Position (in meters)
C  NDSCMP     Needs Computing (=0 if no computation needed; =1 if needed)
C  PTVLMX     Point Value Maximum
```

- **Maintain a project-level "Standard Abbreviations" document** - it counters the two risks abbreviations create: a reader not understanding an abbreviation, and different programmers coining several abbreviations for the same word.
  - Capture every coding abbreviation used on the project; a document, spreadsheet, or on a very large project a database.
  - Keep it in version control; check it out whenever a new abbreviation is created in code.
  - Sort entries by the full word, not by the abbreviation.
  - Treat the checkout-edit-checkin friction as a feature: it stops abbreviations from being coined unless they are common enough to be worth documenting, and it makes an author notice an existing abbreviation instead of inventing a redundant one.
  - Alternative to the project abbreviations document: adopt the standardized-prefixes approach instead.
- **Optimize for read time, not write time** - programmers spend far more time over a system's life reading code than writing it; accept write-time inconvenience that buys read-time clarity. Names matter more to the reader than to the writer; re-read code at least six months old, find the names that require effort, and change the practices that produced them.

### 11.7 Kinds of Names to Avoid

- **Avoid misleading names and abbreviations** - a name must be unambiguous. `FALSE` is understood as the opposite of `TRUE`, so it is a bad abbreviation for "Fig and Almond Season".
- **Avoid names with similar meanings** - if two variables' names can be swapped without harming the program, rename both. Pairs like `input`/`inputValue`, `recordNum`/`numRecords`, `fileNumber`/`fileIndex` are semantically close enough that co-locating them invites subtle, hard-to-find errors.
- **Avoid similar names with different meanings** - rename one or change the abbreviation. `clientRecs` and `clientReps` differ by one easily missed letter; require at least a two-letter difference, or place the difference at the start or the end - `clientRecords` and `clientReports`.
- **Avoid names that sound alike** - homonyms such as `wrap` and `rap` break spoken discussion of the code; the telephone test applies to similar-sounding names as much as to odd abbreviations.
- **Avoid numerals in names** - if the numeral is genuinely meaningful, use an array; if an array does not fit, a numeral fits even less. Reject `file1`/`file2`, `total1`/`total2`; a better distinguishing name almost always exists.
  - Exception: some real-world entities carry embedded numerals (Route 66, Interstate 405), so numerals are not banned outright - exhaust the alternatives first.
- **Avoid deliberately misspelled words** - readers cannot remember which misspelling was chosen (`highlite`? `hilite`? `hilight`? `hilit`?); saving three characters on `highlight` is not worth it.
- **Avoid words commonly misspelled in English** - e.g. absence, accumulate, ascend, calendar, conceive, deferred, definite, independence, occasionally, preferred, receipt, supersede. Consult an English handbook's list of commonly misspelled words and keep those words out of names.
- **Never differentiate names by capitalization alone** - in a case-sensitive language such as C++, do not use `frd`, `FRD` and `Frd` for three distinct meanings; the mapping is arbitrary and no rule helps anyone recall which is which.
- **Use one natural language across the project** - on multinational projects enforce a single natural language for all code including class and variable names. Also standardize on one variant of English when several English-speaking countries contribute, so "color" versus "colour" and "check" versus "cheque" never have to be guessed.
- **Avoid the language's standard type, variable and routine names** - reread the language guide's list of reserved and predefined names periodically and stay off it. Legality is not justification: `if if = then then / then = else; else else = if;` compiles in PL/I and is still unacceptable.
- **Never use names unrelated to what the variable represents** - arbitrary names like `margaret` or `pookie` make code unintelligible to everyone else. If the program really is about a person or a product, still prefer generic names such as `boyfriend`, `wife`, `favoriteBeer`, because the specific referent can change.
- **Avoid hard-to-read characters in names** - do not let two names differ only by a visually confusable character. Confusable pairs: (`1` and `l`), (`1` and `I`), (`.` and `,`), (`0` and `O`), (`2` and `Z`), (`;` and `:`), (`S` and `5`), (`G` and `6`). Character-level detail carries real cost: a comma used where a period belonged in a Fortran FORMAT statement in the 1970s produced a miscalculated spacecraft trajectory and a lost space probe worth $1.6 billion.

## Code Complete: Ch12 Fundamental Data Types

### 12.1 Numbers in General

- **Avoid magic numbers** - a literal number appearing mid-program without explanation (100, 47524) must become a named constant. If the language has no named constants, fall back to a global variable when feasible.
  - Reliability: with a named constant you cannot miss one occurrence of `100`, nor accidentally change a `100` that meant something else.
  - Modifiability: changing a limit from 100 to 200 with literals forces you to also hunt down every `101` and `99` produced by `100+1` / `100-1`; with a constant you edit one definition.
  - Readability: `for i = 0 to MAX_ENTRIES-1` states the intent that `for i = 0 to 99` only hints at. Use the named constant even when the value provably will never change - the readability gain alone justifies it.
- **Allow only 0 and 1 as bare literals** - hard-coded `0` and `1` are acceptable for incrementing, decrementing, and starting a loop at the first array element (`for i = 0 to CONSTANT`, `total = total + 1`). Rule of thumb: 0 and 1 are the only literals permitted in the body of a program; replace every other literal with something descriptive.
- **Guard every division** - at each use of `/`, decide whether the denominator can be 0; if it can, write code that prevents the divide-by-zero before it happens.
- **Make type conversions explicit and visible** - write the conversion so a reader sees it, e.g. `y = x + (float) i` in C++ or `y = x + CSng( i )` in Visual Basic. Explicit conversion also pins down which conversion occurs, since compilers differ; leaving it implicit is gambling.
- **Avoid mixed-type comparisons** - `if ( i = x )` with integer `i` and floating-point `x` is almost guaranteed to misbehave after the compiler picks a type, converts, and rounds. Convert manually so both operands have the same type and the comparison is the one you intended.
- **Heed every compiler warning** - modern compilers report mixed numeric types in one expression; fix the code until no warnings remain. Letting the compiler do this work is easier than checking by hand, and an ignored warning is often exactly the bug later being hunted.
  - Whenever variables of two different types appear in the same expression, confirm the expression evaluates the way you intended it to.

### 12.2 Integers

- **Reorder expressions so integer division happens last** - integer `7/10` is not 0.7; it yields 0, or minus infinity, or the nearest integer, depending on the language. This applies to intermediate results too: `10 * (7/10)` is 0 while `(10*7) / 10` is 7. Push divisions to the end of the expression.
- **Bound every multiplication and addition against the maximum integer** - largest unsigned integer is often 2^32-1, sometimes 2^16-1 (65,535). Overflow raises no error, it wraps: with a 65,535 maximum, `250 * 300` probably yields 9464 instead of the correct 75,000 (75,000 - 65,536 = 9464).
  - Prevention: for each term, estimate its largest attainable value, then compute the largest attainable value of the whole expression.
    - `m = j * k` with max `j` = 200 and max `k` = 25 gives max `m` = 5,000 - safe on a 32-bit machine whose maximum integer is 2,147,483,647.
    - Same expression with max `j` = 200,000 and max `k` = 100,000 gives 20,000,000,000 - exceeds 2,147,483,647, so switch to 64-bit integers or floating point.
  - Also size for expected future growth, not just today's maximum; a value that fits now but grows steadily over years must be typed for the later value.
- **Check intermediate results for overflow, not just the final value** - the final assignment fitting the type proves nothing.

```java
// BAD - intermediate product needs 1,000,000,000,000
int termA = 1000000;
int termB = 1000000;
int product = termA * termB / 1000000;   // prints -727, not 1000000
```

  - With a 2,147,483,647 ceiling, the intermediate 1,000,000,000,000 becomes -727,379,968, so the division yields -727. Fix it the same way as ordinary integer overflow: move to a long-integer or floating-point type.

| Integer Type | Range |
|---|---|
| Signed 8-bit | -128 through 127 |
| Unsigned 8-bit | 0 through 255 |
| Signed 16-bit | -32,768 through 32,767 |
| Unsigned 16-bit | 0 through 65,535 |
| Signed 32-bit | -2,147,483,648 through 2,147,483,647 |
| Unsigned 32-bit | 0 through 4,294,967,295 |
| Signed 64-bit | -9,223,372,036,854,775,808 through 9,223,372,036,854,775,807 |
| Unsigned 64-bit | 0 through 18,446,744,073,709,551,615 |

### 12.3 Floating-Point Numbers

- **Assume fractional decimals are inexact** - many fractional decimal values cannot be represented exactly in binary. Nonterminating values such as 1/3 or 1/7 typically carry only 7 or 15 digits of accuracy; a 32-bit representation of 1/3 is 0.33333330, accurate to 7 digits - enough for most uses, and inexact enough to produce surprises.
- **Avoid additions and subtractions across greatly different magnitudes** - in 32-bit floating point, `1,000,000.00 + 0.1` likely stays 1,000,000.00 and `5,000,000.02 - 5,000,000.01` likely yields 0.0, because the significant digits cannot span both magnitudes.
  - When summing a sequence with huge magnitude spread, sort first and accumulate from the smallest values upward.
  - When summing an infinite series, start from the smallest term - sum backwards. This minimizes round-off; it does not eliminate it.
- **Avoid equality comparisons on floating-point values** - values that should be equal are not always equal, because two computation paths to the same number do not reliably arrive at the same number; 0.1 added 10 times rarely equals 1.0. Find an alternative to `==`.

```java
// BAD
double nominal = 1.0;
double sum = 0.0;
for ( int i = 0; i < 10; i++ ) { sum += 0.1; }
if ( nominal == sum ) { ... }   // false: sum is 0.9999999999999999
```

  - The running values of `sum` drift visibly (0.30000000000000004, 0.7999999999999999, 0.8999999999999999, 0.9999999999999999).
  - Fix the range of accuracy that is acceptable, then use a boolean predicate that returns true when the values fall inside it and false otherwise.

```java
// GOOD
final double ACCEPTABLE_DELTA = 0.00001;
boolean Equals( double Term1, double Term2 ) {
  return Math.abs( Term1 - Term2 ) < ACCEPTABLE_DELTA;
}
...
if ( Equals( Nominal, Sum ) ) ...
```

  - Exception: a hard-coded delta is inappropriate for some applications; compute `ACCEPTABLE_DELTA` from the magnitude of the two operands being compared when the application demands it.
- **Anticipate rounding errors** - rounding is the same phenomenon as unequal magnitudes and responds to the same techniques, plus these specific remedies:
  - Raise precision: single-precision to double-precision floating point, and onward.
  - Switch to binary coded decimal (BCD): slower and larger in storage, but prevents many rounding errors; use it especially for dollars-and-cents or any quantity that must balance exactly.
  - Switch from floating point to integers - a hand-rolled BCD. Expect to need 64-bit integers for the required precision, and accept that you now track the fractional part yourself: store cents as integers and dollars as multiples of 100 cents, keeping cents in the 0-to-99 range. Effective for both speed and accuracy. Hide the integer representation behind a class such as `DollarsAndCents` that exposes the needed numeric operations.
- **Check language and library support for rounding-sensitive data types** - some languages, Visual Basic among them, ship types such as `Currency` built for data sensitive to rounding errors; when a built-in type provides that functionality, use it instead of rolling your own.

### 12.4 Characters and Strings

- **Avoid magic characters and magic strings** - literal characters (`'A'`) and literal strings (`"Gigamatic Accounting Program"`) appearing throughout code must become named constants; where the language lacks them, use global variables. Applies in every language. Reasons:
  - Frequently occurring strings - program name, command names, report titles - change over releases ("Gigamatic Accounting Program" becomes "New and Improved! Gigamatic Accounting Program").
  - Translation for international markets is far cheaper when strings sit grouped in a string resource file than scattered in place.
  - String literals consume large amounts of space in menus, messages, help screens, and entry forms; unchecked they cause memory problems. Irrelevant in many environments, but decisive in embedded systems and other storage-constrained applications, where fixes are only tractable if strings are kept independent of the source code.
  - Literals are cryptic; a named constant or comment states the intent.

```cpp
// BAD
if ( input_char == 0x1B ) ...
// GOOD
if ( input_char == ESCAPE ) ...
```

- **Watch for off-by-one errors on substring indexes** - substrings are indexed like arrays, so guard against reads and writes past the end of the string.
- **Know your language's Unicode support before writing string code** - in Java all strings are Unicode; in C and C++ Unicode handling needs its own function set, and conversion between Unicode and other character sets is routinely required to talk to standard and third-party libraries. Where some strings will not be Unicode (C, C++), decide early whether to use Unicode at all, and if so exactly where and when.
- **Fix the internationalization/localization strategy early in the program's life** - decide whether all strings live in an external resource, and whether each language gets a separate build or the language is resolved at run time.
- **Choose the character-set standard by language scope**
  - Single alphabetic language only (English, for instance), with no requirement for several languages and none for an ideographic script such as written Chinese: ISO 8859, an extended-ASCII-style standard, is a sound alternative to Unicode.
  - Several languages required: use Unicode - its coverage of international character sets is more comprehensive than ISO 8859 or any other standard.
- **Adopt one consistent conversion strategy across string types** - when several string types coexist, hold every string in a single format inside the program and convert to other formats as near to the input and output boundaries as possible.

#### Strings in C

- **Prefer the C++ standard template library string class** - it removes most traditional C string problems; the remaining rules apply to code working directly with C strings.
- **Keep string pointers and character arrays distinct**
  - Treat any string expression containing an equal sign as suspect: C string work is nearly always done with `strcmp()`, `strcpy()`, `strlen()` and relatives, so an equal sign often signals a pointer error. `StringPtr = "Some Text String";` only points `StringPtr` at a literal; it copies no contents.
  - Encode the distinction in a naming convention - `ps` prefix for a pointer to a string, `ach` prefix for an array of characters. Expressions mixing `ps` and `ach` prefixes are not always wrong but must be regarded with suspicion.
- **Declare C-style strings as CONSTANT+1 and use CONSTANT everywhere else** - a string of length n needs n + 1 bytes for the null terminator (the 0 byte ending the string), which makes off-by-one errors common in C and C++. Declare with the named constant plus one, then refer to the length as the bare constant in all operations, the same way every time.

```c
char name[ NAME_LENGTH + 1 ] = { 0 };          /* declared as constant+1 */
for ( i = 0; i < NAME_LENGTH; i++ )            /* operate with constant */
  name[ i ] = 'A';
strncpy( name, some_other_name, NAME_LENGTH ); /* operate with constant */
```

  - Without such a convention you will sometimes declare `NAME_LENGTH` and operate on `NAME_LENGTH-1`, other times declare `NAME_LENGTH+1` and operate on `NAME_LENGTH`, and be forced to remember each string's individual treatment. Uniformity removes that mental load and the errors it causes.
- **Initialize strings to null to avoid endless strings** - C locates a string's end only at a 0 byte, regardless of the intended length, so a missing terminator makes string operations misbehave. Two defenses:
  - Initialize character arrays to 0 at declaration: `char EventName[ MAX_NAME_LENGTH + 1 ] = { 0 };`
  - For dynamic allocation use `calloc()` rather than `malloc()`: `calloc()` allocates and zeroes; `malloc()` allocates without initializing, leaving the contents to chance.
- **Declare string variables as arrays of characters rather than pointers in C** - do this whenever memory is not a constraint, which it often is not; it avoids pointer problems and lets the compiler warn you more.
- **Use the length-bounded string routines** - in C, call `strncpy()`, `strncat()`, and `strncmp()` instead of `strcpy()`, `strcat()`, and `strcmp()`. The unbounded routines run until they hit a null terminator; the bounded ones take a maximum length, so the call terminates even if the strings do not.

### 12.5 Boolean Variables

- **Use boolean variables as documentation** - instead of testing a raw boolean expression, assign it to a named variable that states what the test means; an inline compound condition leaves it unclear whether the check is for completion, for an error, or for something else.

```java
// BAD
if ( ( elementIndex < 0 ) || ( MAX_ELEMENTS < elementIndex ) ||
     ( elementIndex == lastElementIndex ) ) { ... }
// GOOD
finished = ( ( elementIndex < 0 ) || ( MAX_ELEMENTS < elementIndex ) );
repeatedEntry = ( elementIndex == lastElementIndex );
if ( finished || repeatedEntry ) { ... }
```

- **Split complicated tests into named boolean variables** - a complicated condition takes several attempts to get right and resists later modification because its original intent is lost. Name each underlying condition (a condition that combines index-bounds checks with a repeated-entry check tests two things: whether the routine is finished and whether the entry is repeated); the resulting test reads clearly, is less error prone, and is simpler to change later.
  - Failure signal: a dense inline condition imposes enough mental load that readers postpone understanding it and come back only if forced. Treat that reaction as the trigger to decompose the test, since every other reader of the code does the same.

```vb
' BAD
If ( ( document.AtEndOfStream() ) And ( Not inputError ) ) And _
   ( ( MIN_LINES <= lineCount ) And ( lineCount <= MAX_LINES ) ) And _
   ( Not ErrorProcessing() ) Then
' GOOD
allDataRead = ( document.AtEndOfStream() ) And ( Not inputError )
legalLineCount = ( MIN_LINES <= lineCount ) And ( lineCount <= MAX_LINES )
If ( allDataRead ) And ( legalLineCount ) And ( Not ErrorProcessing() ) Then
```

- **Define a boolean type where the language lacks one** - C++, Java, and Visual Basic have a predefined boolean type; C does not. Declaring variables `BOOLEAN` instead of `int` makes their intended use obvious and the program more self-documenting.

```c
typedef int BOOLEAN;
/* or, which also defines the two values: */
enum Boolean { True=1, False=(!True) };
```

### 12.6 Enumerated Types

- **Definition** - an enumerated type describes each member of a class of objects in English; available in C++ and Visual Basic. Use one when all possible values of a variable are known and are best expressed as words (e.g. `Color` with `Color_Red`, `Color_Green`, `Color_Blue`; `Output` with `Output_Screen`, `Output_Printer`, `Output_File`).
- **Prefer enumerated types over numeric encodings for readability** - replace "1 stands for red, 2 stands for green" schemes: write `if chosenColor = Color_Red`, not `if chosenColor = 1`. On seeing any numeric literal, ask whether an enumerated type belongs there instead.
  - Apply this to routine parameters especially: `RetrievePayrollData( data, true, false, false, true )` is unreadable; `RetrievePayrollData( data, EmploymentStatus_CurrentEmployee, PayrollType_Salaried, SavingsPlan_NoDeduction, MedicalCoverage_IncludeDependents )` is not.
- **Use enumerated types for reliability** - in a few languages (Ada in particular) an enumerated type gives the compiler stronger type checking than integers and named constants allow. With named constants the compiler cannot know that only `Color_Red`, `Color_Green`, `Color_Blue` are legal and will accept `color = Country_England` or `country = Output_Printer`; declaring the variable as `Color` restricts assignment to that type's values.
- **Use enumerated types for modifiability** - a flawed numeric encoding forces you to find and change every 1, 2, and 3 in the code; an enumerated type is extended by adding members to the type definition and recompiling.
- **Use an enumerated type instead of a boolean whenever the variable's use cannot be completely captured by true and false** - that is, whenever the domain is richer than two values. A routine returning true for success and false otherwise breaks down as soon as two kinds of failure appear: one confined to the routine, one fatal and needing propagation to the rest of the program. Model it as `Status_Success`, `Status_Warning`, `Status_FatalError`, which extends cleanly to further distinctions among kinds of success or failure.
- **Check for invalid values when testing an enumerated type** - in every `if` or `case` over an enumerated type, handle values outside the legal set. Every branch construct over an enumerated type must carry a default/else arm that reports an internal error rather than silently continuing; use the `case` statement's `else` clause to trap invalid values.
  - Visual Basic: put the check in `Case Else`.

  ```vb
  Select Case screenColor
      Case Color_Red
      ...
      Case Else
          DisplayInternalError( False, "Internal Error 752: Invalid color." )
  End Select
  ```

- **Define explicit First and Last members for loop limits** - Give each enumeration `<Type>_First` and `<Type>_Last` members with explicit values so loops and array dimensions can be driven off the enumeration itself instead of literals.

  ```vb
  Public Enum Country
      Country_First = 0
      Country_China = 0
      ...
      Country_Usa = 6
      Country_Last = 6
  End Enum

  Dim usaCurrencyConversionRate( Country_Last ) As Single
  For iCountry = Country_First To Country_Last
      usaCurrencyConversionRate( iCountry ) = ConversionRate( Country_Usa, iCountry )
  Next
  ```

- **Reserve the first entry as invalid** - Declare an `<Type>_InvalidFirst = 0` member and start valid values at 1, because many compilers map the first enumeration element to 0 and uninitialized variables are far more likely to hold 0 than any other invalid value; this converts missed initialization into a detectable invalid value.

  ```vb
  Public Enum Country
      Country_InvalidFirst = 0
      Country_First = 1
      Country_China = 1
      ...
      Country_Usa = 7
      Country_Last = 7
  End Enum
  ```

- **Standardize InvalidFirst/First/Last usage project-wide** - The InvalidFirst/First/Last convention improves array declarations and loops but creates ambiguity over whether valid entries start at 0 or 1 and whether the boundary members are themselves valid; if the technique is used at all, the project coding standard must mandate the exact meaning and require it consistently in every enumeration.

- **Treat explicitly assigned enumeration values as a hazard** - Where the language permits per-member values, account for the gaps they create: bit-flag values 1, 2, 4, 8 make an index of that type iterating First to Last also pass through 3, 5, 6, and 7, which map to no member. Do not drive a loop off an enumeration whose values are non-contiguous.

  ```cpp
  // BAD: looping First..Last also hits 3, 5, 6, 7
  enum Color {
      Color_InvalidFirst = 0,
      Color_First = 1, Color_Red = 1, Color_Green = 2,
      Color_Blue = 4, Color_Black = 8, Color_Last = 8
  };
  ```

#### If the language lacks enumerated types

- **Simulate enumerations with a class of static final instances** - Give the class a private constructor and one `public static final` instance per member; references then read as `Country.England` or `Output.Screen` rather than named constants.
  - This form is typesafe: since each enumeration is its own class, the compiler rejects cross-type assignment such as `Output output = Country.England`.

  ```java
  class Country {
      private Country() {}
      public static final Country China = new Country();
      public static final Country England = new Country();
  }
  ```

- **Without classes, fall back to disciplined global variables** - In languages with no class support, declare one global variable per enumeration element and rely on convention to get the same effect.

### 12.7 Named Constants

- **Definition** - A named constant behaves like a variable whose value cannot be reassigned after definition; it names a fixed quantity (`MAXIMUM_EMPLOYEES` in place of `1000`).

- **Treat named constants as single-point control** - Named constants parameterize the program: an aspect that may change lives in one definition instead of being replicated at every use site, so a size change is one edit. Named constants have been shown to substantially aid maintenance; more generally, centralizing control over anything liable to change lowers maintenance cost.

- **Use named constants in data declarations and in code that depends on data size** - Declare lengths and capacities as constants and use the same constant in the type declaration and in every loop or validation that walks that data.

  ```vb
  Const AREA_CODE_LENGTH = 3
  Const LOCAL_NUMBER_LENGTH = 7
  Type PHONE_NUMBER
      areaCode( AREA_CODE_LENGTH ) As String
      localNumber( LOCAL_NUMBER_LENGTH ) As String
  End Type
  For iDigit = 1 To LOCAL_NUMBER_LENGTH
  ```

- **Eliminate literals even when a literal looks safe** - Replace a literal with a named constant whenever the code leaves any doubt about the number's meaning, even if the underlying quantity will never change (months in a year will not change, but `12` still hides intent). Hunt literals out aggressively: search the source for 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 to find accidental uses.
  - Escalate clarity in this order: literal -> named constant -> named constant plus a meaningful loop index -> enumerated type as the loop range.

  ```vb
  ' BAD
  For i = 1 To 12
      profit( i ) = revenue( i ) - expense( i )
  Next

  ' GOOD
  For month = Month_January To Month_December
      profit( month ) = revenue( month ) - expense( month )
  Next
  ```

- **Simulate named constants when unsupported** - Where the language has no named constants, build them from appropriately scoped variables or classes: a class with a private constructor and one `public static final` instance per value, or one variable per value where classes are unavailable. Prefer local scope, then class scope, then global scope in that order.

- **Never mix a named constant and a literal for the same entity** - Using the constant in one place and the hard-coded value in another guarantees that a value change updates only some sites, producing defects that are hard to trace.

### 12.8 Arrays

- **Definition** - An array holds a group of same-typed items reached directly by index; it is the simplest and most common structured type, and in some languages the only one.

- **Keep every index within bounds** - All array problems trace back to random-access reachability of elements; the dominant failure is an out-of-bounds access, which raises an error in some languages and produces arbitrary, unpredictable behavior in others.

- **Prefer sequentially accessed containers over raw arrays** - Consider sets, stacks, and queues before defaulting to an array; random array access is analogous to random gotos - undisciplined, error prone, and hard to prove correct. Designs built on sequential access were found to use fewer variables and fewer variable references, ran with acceptable efficiency, and yielded highly reliable software.
  - If an array is used, reason about it as a sequential structure.

- **Check array end points** - Verify explicitly that the code hits the true first element rather than the one before or after it, that the last element is reached without an off-by-one error, and that middle elements are addressed correctly.

- **Verify subscript order in multidimensional arrays** - `Array[i][j]` is easily written where `Array[j][i]` is meant; double-check order, and rename indexes to something meaningful when their roles are not self-evident.

- **Guard against index cross-talk** - In nested loops, writing `Array[j]` where `Array[i]` was intended (index cross-talk) must be checked for; the preventive fix is index names more descriptive than `i` and `j`.

- **C: derive array length with an ARRAY_LENGTH() macro** - Use the macro instead of a named constant for the upper bound, so adding or removing entries needs no separate edit; it is especially useful for dimensionless arrays and removes the need for an extra size constant, while still working for dimensioned arrays.

  ```c
  #define ARRAY_LENGTH( x ) (sizeof(x)/sizeof(x[0]))
  for ( ratioIdx = 0; ratioIdx < ARRAY_LENGTH( ConsistencyRatios ); ratioIdx++ );
  ```

### 12.9 Creating Your Own Types (Type Aliasing)

- **Use programmer-defined types where the language allows them** - In C, C++, or any language with user-defined types, alias types for domain quantities; this clarifies the program, insulates it from unforeseen change, and improves readability without the cost of designing, building, and testing a new class. Declare a different type for each kind of data that might change.

- **Alias once, change once** - Define the domain type in a single `typedef` (or equivalent) so a representation change is one edit.

  ```cpp
  typedef float Coordinate;   // later: typedef double Coordinate;
  Coordinate latitude;        // declarations never mention float or double
  ```

- **Back string and array types with a named constant for their size** - When the aliased type wraps a string or array, it is usually right to declare a length constant and use it in the type definition rather than hard-coding the bound; the same constant will be needed at many later sites.

  ```pascal
  Const NAME_LENGTH = 30;
  Type employeeName = array[ 1..NAME_LENGTH ] of char;
  ```

- **Understand how far the language hides the underlying type** - Consistently using the alias instead of the built-in type hides the representation only by convention in C++ (figurative information hiding), because the definition ships in header files and readers must choose not to look it up. Languages such as Ada give literal information hiding: declaring `type Coordinate is private` inside a package confines the definition to that package's private part, and distributing only the package specification makes the underlying type genuinely unavailable.

- **Reasons to create your own type** - Apply the technique for these purposes:
  - Make modification easy: a new type costs almost nothing and buys large flexibility.
  - Prevent excessive information distribution: hard typing scatters type decisions through the program instead of centralizing them, violating centralization as an information-hiding practice.
  - Increase reliability: range-constrained types (Ada `type Age is range 0..99`) make the compiler emit run-time checks that every variable of that type stays inside the range.
  - Compensate for language gaps: define a missing predefined type yourself, for example C lacking a boolean type - `typedef int Boolean;`.

- **Recognize the semantic loss in languages without range types** - A declaration carrying a range (`currentTemperature: INTEGER range 0..212;`) encodes semantics that `int temperature;` does not, and a named range type lets the compiler restrict assignment to variables of the same type at near-zero coding cost. A hand-written class can enforce the same semantics, but the effort gap between a one-line type definition and a class is large enough that the class often does not get written; account for that when choosing.

#### Guidelines for Creating Your Own Types

- **Name types after the problem domain, never after machine representation** - Name types for real-world entities (coordinate, name, currency, payment code, age), and make each name descriptive enough to document the declarations that use it. Type names referencing predefined types (`BigInteger`, `LongString`) describe computer data, puncture the insulation layer between program and language, and deliver little benefit over the predefined type; problem-oriented names give easy modifiability and self-documenting declarations.

- **Avoid predefined types outside type definitions** - If a type might ever change, mention the predefined type only inside the `typedef`/type definition and declare everything else with the domain type; changing hardwired types across a program is hard, and `Coordinate x` documents more than `float x`.

- **Do not redefine a predefined type** - Never reuse a standard type's own name for a type of your own; if the language defines `Integer`, do not declare an `Integer`, because readers will forget the redefinition and assume the standard meaning.

- **Define parallel substitute types for portability** - Standing alongside the rule against redefining a predefined type, and not in conflict with it: when a variable must represent exactly the same entity on every hardware platform, declare separately named substitutes such as `INT32` for `int` or `LONG64` for `long` and use those.
