At first they differ from the language types only in capitalization; on a new platform, redefine the substitutes so they still match the original hardware's data types.
  - Condition that separates the two rules: never shadow or alter the meaning of an existing standard type name; do add distinctly named substitutes beside it.
  - Keep substitute names impossible to mistake for language types: use `INT32`, not `INT`.

- **Consider a class instead of a typedef** - Whenever you create a simple type with `typedef` or its equivalent, evaluate whether a new class is the better construct before settling on the redefined type. Simple typedefs hide much about a variable's underlying type, but choose a class when the extra flexibility and control are needed; in many cases a class is the better choice than a simple data type.

### Key Points

- **Apply the per-type rules explicitly rather than from memory** - Working with specific data types means remembering many individual rules for each type; check the numeric, integer, floating-point, character and string, boolean, enumerated-type, named-constant, array, and user-defined-type rules in this chapter against the code so the common problems are all considered.

## Code Complete: Ch13 Unusual Data Types

### Structures

- **Definition** - A structure is data assembled from other types - `struct` in C and C++, `Structure` in Visual Basic; arrays are a special case handled separately. A Java or C++ class also functions as a structure when every member is public data and it exposes no routines.
- **Default to classes over structures** - Prefer a class so the code gains privacy and behavior on top of the public data a structure offers; use a structure only where directly manipulating a block of data is genuinely useful.
- **Use structures to expose data relationships** - Group items that belong to the same real-world entity into a structure so the grouping is visible in code; flat parallel variables hide the fact that two distinct entities are being assigned.
  - Unstructured assignments imply every statement belongs to one thing, when in fact some fields belong to one entity and some to another.

```vb
' BAD - no signal that two entities exist
name = inputName
address = inputAddress
title = inputTitle
department = inputDepartment

' GOOD - membership is explicit
employee.name = inputName
employee.address = inputAddress
supervisor.title = inputTitle
supervisor.department = inputDepartment
```

- **Use structures to operate on data blocks as a unit** - Operate on the whole structure instead of repeating the same operation per element; it is shorter, more reliable, and immune to field additions.
  - Copying a group field-by-field forces you to hunt down every assignment block whenever a new field is added.
  - A three-way swap of two entities collapses from one statement per field per step (18 statements for 6 fields) to three statements total, independent of field count.

```vb
' GOOD - swap two whole records regardless of field count
previousOldEmployee = oldEmployee
oldEmployee = newEmployee
newEmployee = previousOldEmployee
```

  - Adding a field means editing only the structure declaration; the block operations need no change.
  - C++ and other languages offer equivalent capability - the rule is not Visual Basic specific.
- **Use structures to shorten parameter lists** - Pass one structure rather than each related element, so adding a field does not force edits at every call site.

```vb
' BAD - every new field breaks every caller
HardWayRoutine( name, address, phone, ssn, gender, salary )

' GOOD - adding a field to Employee leaves callers untouched
EasyWayRoutine( employee )
```

- **Avoid bundling beyond logical necessity** - The technique can be pushed to an extreme (one giant variable holding every program variable, passed everywhere); bundle only what is logically related.
- **Pass fields, not the structure, when only one or two fields are needed** - Passing a whole structure to reach a couple of fields over-shares data; pass those specific fields instead.
  - Treat this as information hiding at the parameter list: hide some data inside a routine, hide other data from the routine, and hand out data strictly on a need-to-know basis.
- **Use structures to reduce complexity and maintenance cost** - Structures make a program less complicated, easier to understand, and easier to maintain; grouping related data means a structure change touches fewer places in the program, and fewer changes mean fewer errors.
  - Deleting a field (for example `title` from `Employee`) requires no edits to parameter lists or whole-structure assignments.
  - Code that genuinely deals with the deleted field must still change, but that code is conceptually tied to the change and therefore hard to miss.
  - The real win is in code with no logical relation to the field - code that touched the field only because it was part of the collection. Such sites are easy to overlook, and with structures overlooking them is safe.
- **Weigh a class against every structure** - Whenever a structure looks like the right choice, consider whether a class would work better before settling on the structure.

### Pointers - Conceptual Model

- **Treat pointer usage as one of the most error-prone areas of programming** - Modern languages (Java, C#, Visual Basic) omit a pointer data type for this reason. Protect yourself wherever pointers are used by working through access routines or classes and by applying defensive-programming practices.
  - Correct pointer use requires an excellent understanding of the compiler's memory-management scheme.
  - Many common security defects, buffer overruns above all, trace back to bad pointer use.
  - Even in a language without pointers, understand them to understand how the language works, and apply defensive programming liberally.
- **Model every pointer as two parts** - A location in memory plus knowledge of how to interpret the contents of that location.
  - The location is an address, commonly written in hexadecimal; on a 32-bit processor it is a 32-bit value such as `0x0001EA40`. The pointer holds only this address.
  - Interpretation comes from the pointer's base type. An integer pointer, a string pointer, and a floating-point pointer can all address the same location, and only one of them interprets it correctly.
  - Memory carries no inherent interpretation; bits become meaningful data only through the type of pointer used to reach them.
- **Expect the same bytes to mean different things under different base types** - The number of bytes consumed and the value produced both follow from the base type (and from the processor).

Same raw memory (hex `0A 61 62 63 64 65 66 67 68 69 6A`), pointer at the `0A`:

| Viewed as | Interpreted as |
|---|---|
| no pointer variable | no interpretation possible |
| `char` | linefeed character (ASCII hex 0A, decimal 10) |
| 2-byte integer | 24842 |
| 4-byte integer | 1667391754 |
| 4-byte floating point | 4.17595656202980E+0021 |
| `String[10]` (Visual Basic layout, length byte first) | abcdefghij |

### Pointers - General Tips

- **Assume locating the cause is the hard part of a pointer defect** - Unlike most defects, the fix is easy and the diagnosis is not, because pointer-error symptoms tend to be unrelated to their causes.
  - A pointer error usually means the pointer addresses somewhere it should not; assigning through such a pointer writes into memory that must not be written, which is "memory corruption".
  - Memory corruption may crash the system, silently alter a calculation in an unrelated part of the program, cause routines to be skipped unpredictably, or produce no effect at all.
  - Treat the no-effect case as latent, not fixed: it surfaces at an arbitrary later time.
- **Attack pointers on two fronts** - Prevent the error from being written, and detect any error as soon after coding as possible.
  - Extra preventive measures are justified because pointer errors are so hard to find.
  - Extra measures to make symptoms predictable are justified because the symptoms are otherwise erratic.
- **Isolate pointer operations in routines or classes** - Never traverse a linked structure by hand at each use site; provide access routines such as `NextLink()`, `PreviousLink()`, `InsertLink()`, `DeleteLink()`.
  - Fewer access points means fewer careless mistakes that propagate program-wide.
  - Code becomes relatively independent of the data implementation, improving reuse.
  - Also write routines for pointer allocation to centralize control over the data.
- **Declare and initialize a pointer in the same statement** - Move the declaration down to where the initial value is available; a declaration far above its `new` invites use of an uninitialized pointer as the code is modified.

```cpp
// BAD
Employee *employeePtr;
// lots of code
employeePtr = new Employee;

// GOOD
Employee *employeePtr = new Employee;
```

- **Deallocate at the same scoping level as allocation** - Keep allocation and deallocation symmetric.
  - Allocated with `new` in one scope, deleted with `delete` in that same scope.
  - Allocated inside a routine, deallocated inside a sister routine.
  - Allocated in a constructor, deallocated in the destructor.
  - Never allocate memory and expect client code to free it manually; that asymmetry is ripe for error.
- **Check the pointer before using it** - Before use in a critical section, verify the address is plausible - for example within the environment's valid data range `StartData` to `EndData`; treat anything before `StartData` or after `EndData` as suspect.
  - Determine the actual bounds for your environment.
  - Confirm the pointer is not dangling: never dereference a pointer that may address memory already deallocated.
  - This check can run automatically when pointers are only reached through access routines.
- **Check the referenced value before using it** - Apply reasonableness checks on the pointed-to data: an integer expected in 0..1000 is suspect above 1000; a C++-style string is suspect at length greater than 100.
  - Also automatable via access routines.
- **Use dog-tag fields to detect corrupted memory** - A "tag field" or "dog tag" is a field added to a structure purely for error checking: store a value at allocation that must stay unchanged, and verify it on use, especially on deletion. A mismatch means the data was corrupted.
  1. Allocate 4 bytes more than requested (104 bytes for a 100-byte request).
  2. Write the dog-tag value into the first 4 bytes and return a pointer to the memory that begins after the tag.
  3. On deletion, check the tag.
  4. If the tag is intact, overwrite it with 0 or any other value the program treats as an invalid tag, so a freed block cannot pass a later tag check; for the same reason overwrite the payload with a fixed non-random pattern such as 0 or `0xCC`.
  5. Delete the pointer, freeing the whole 104 bytes.
  - A tag at the start of the block detects redundant deallocation attempts without maintaining a list of every allocated block.
  - A tag at the end of the block detects writes past the intended region.
  - Use tags at both ends to get both properties.
  - Combine with the range check: instead of testing a probable memory range, test that the pointer appears in the list of allocated pointers.
  - Checking the tag only immediately before deletion tells you corruption happened sometime in the variable's life; checking more often localizes the cause more precisely.
- **Add explicit redundancies as an alternative to a tag field** - Store selected fields twice and compare; a mismatch means memory was corrupted.
  - This costs a lot of overhead when pointers are manipulated directly; when pointer operations are isolated in routines, the duplicate code exists in only a few places.
- **Spend pointer variables freely for clarity** - A variable must serve one purpose only, and this holds especially for pointers: declare and use every intermediate pointer variable that readability calls for. Do not reuse a single `genericLink` repeatedly, and do not force readers to decode `pointer->next->last->next`.
  - Name every object a linked-list operation actually involves. Node insertion involves three: the start node, the node currently following it, and the node being inserted.

```cpp
// BAD - the third object is implicit and the flagged line is needlessly hard
void InsertLink( Node *currentNode, Node *insertNode ) {
   insertNode->next = currentNode->next;
   insertNode->previous = currentNode;
   if ( currentNode->next != NULL ) {
      currentNode->next->previous = insertNode;   // hard to read
   }
   currentNode->next = insertNode;
}

// GOOD - one extra line, all three objects named
void InsertLink( Node *startNode, Node *newMiddleNode ) {
   Node *followingNode = startNode->next;
   newMiddleNode->next = followingNode;
   newMiddleNode->previous = startNode;
   if ( followingNode != NULL ) {
      followingNode->previous = newMiddleNode;
   }
   startNode->next = newMiddleNode;
}
```

- **Simplify complicated pointer expressions** - Assign an expression like `p->q->r->s.data` to a well-named variable that states the intent; deep chains must be figured out rather than read.

```cpp
// BAD
for ( rateIndex = 0; rateIndex < numRates; rateIndex++ ) {
   netRate[ rateIndex ] = baseRate[ rateIndex ] * rates->discounts->factors->net;
}

// GOOD
quantityDiscount = rates->discounts->factors->net;
for ( rateIndex = 0; rateIndex < numRates; rateIndex++ ) {
   netRate[ rateIndex ] = baseRate[ rateIndex ] * quantityDiscount;
}
```

  - Hoisting the expression out of the loop may also improve performance, but measure before relying on that.
- **Draw a picture for pointer work** - Diagram initial linkage and desired linkage before relinking; code-only descriptions of pointer rearrangement are confusing.
- **Delete linked-list pointers in the correct order** - Obtain the pointer to the next element before freeing the current one; freeing the head first strands the rest of the list.
- **Allocate a reserve memory parachute** - A program using dynamic memory must not simply run out and lose the user's work: size the memory needed to save work, clean up, and exit gracefully, allocate that block at program start, leave it untouched, and on exhaustion free it, clean up, and shut down.
- **Shred garbage before deallocating** - The moment at which pointed-to memory becomes invalid is not deterministic: contents may still look valid long after the free, or may change immediately. In C, overwrite a block with junk data immediately before deallocating it so use-after-free fails consistently.
  - Do this automatically inside access routines.
  - C: `pointer->SetContentsToGarbage(); delete pointer;`
  - C++ limitation: the technique does not work where the pointer points to an object, and it requires a set-contents-to-garbage routine implemented for every object.
- **Set pointers to null after deleting or freeing them** - Blocks the "dangling pointer" defect, meaning use of a pointer already `delete`'d or `free`'d; such errors are hard to detect precisely because they sometimes produce no symptom.
  - Nulling does not prevent a read through a dangling pointer from returning data, but it forces a write through one to fail loudly and immediately rather than staying hidden until a customer hits it.

```cpp
pointer->SetContentsToGarbage();
delete pointer;
pointer = NULL;
```

- **Check for a bad pointer before deleting a variable** - Deleting or freeing an already-deleted or already-freed pointer is one of the surest ways to wreck a program, and few languages detect it.
  - Nulling freed pointers is what makes the null check possible before use or before a second delete; without nulling that option does not exist.

```cpp
ASSERT( pointer != NULL, "Attempting to delete null pointer." );
pointer->SetContentsToGarbage();
delete pointer;
pointer = NULL;
```

- **Keep track of pointer allocations** - Maintain a list of allocated pointers and verify membership before disposal.

```cpp
ASSERT( pointer != NULL, "Attempting to delete null pointer." );
if ( IsPointerInList( pointer ) ) {
   pointer->SetContentsToGarbage();
   RemovePointerFromList( pointer );
   delete pointer;
   pointer = NULL;
}
else {
   ASSERT( FALSE, "Attempting to delete unallocated pointer." );
}
```

- **Write cover routines to centralize the pointer strategy** - The safety code per `new`/`delete` is large; wrap common pointer operations once instead of repeating it.
  - Some of these techniques are mutually exclusive or redundant; never run multiple conflicting strategies in one code base. Example: dog tags are unnecessary if you maintain your own list of valid pointers.
  - `SAFE_NEW` - calls `new`, adds the pointer to the allocated-pointer list, returns it, and is the single place that checks for an exception or null return from `new` (an out-of-memory error), which simplifies error handling everywhere else.
  - `SAFE_DELETE` - verifies the pointer is in the allocated list; if so, garbages the pointed-to variable, removes it from the list, calls `delete`, and nulls the pointer; if not, prints a diagnostic and halts the program.

```cpp
#define SAFE_DELETE( pointer ) { \
   ASSERT( pointer != NULL, "Attempting to delete null pointer."); \
   if ( IsPointerInList( pointer ) ) { \
      pointer->SetContentsToGarbage(); \
      RemovePointerFromList( pointer ); \
      delete pointer; \
      pointer = NULL; \
   } \
   else { \
      ASSERT( FALSE, "Attempting to delete unallocated pointer." ); \
   } \
}
```

  - C++: this handles individual pointers only; implement a parallel `SAFE_DELETE_ARRAY` for arrays.
  - Centralizing memory handling lets the cover routines differ between debug and production - for example halting on an attempted null free during development while merely logging and continuing in production.
  - Adapt the same scheme to `calloc` and `free` in C and to other pointer-bearing languages.
- **Prefer a nonpointer technique when one works reasonably** - Pointers cost more comprehension effort than most constructs, invite defects, and usually drag in machine-dependent, non-portable code; take any workable alternative instead and use a pointer only as a last resort, when no other method is available.

### C++ Pointers

- **Know the difference between pointers and references** - Use `object->field` for pointers and `object.field` for references, and never treat the two as interchangeable: in C++ both `*` (pointer) and `&` (reference) reach an object indirectly, and the gap between them only looks like a cosmetic difference in field-access syntax to someone unfamiliar with the language.
  - A reference must always denote some object and may not be null, whereas a pointer can point to null.
  - What a reference refers to cannot be changed after the reference is initialized.
- **Pointer for pass-by-reference, const reference for pass-by-value** - C++ passes by value by default, copying the object on the way in and again on the way back, which burns time and resources for large objects; so pass large objects by reference and encode the intent in the declaration.
  - Declare a parameter that must not be modified as a `const` reference (pass-by-value semantics, pass-by-reference implementation); declare a parameter that will be modified as a pointer.
  - Side benefit: inside the routine, modifiable objects read as `object->member` and nonmodifiable ones as `object.member`, so mutability is visible at every use site.

```cpp
void SomeRoutine(
    const LARGE_OBJECT &nonmodifiableObject,
    LARGE_OBJECT *modifiableObject
);
```

  - **Exception - const does not propagate through code you do not own** - In your own code base, apply `const` wherever possible and declare pass-by-value parameters as `const` references. With library or third-party code that is not const-correct, fall back to non-const references for read-only parameters: you lose compiler enforcement against modification but keep the `object->member` vs. `object.member` visual distinction.
- **Use auto_ptr** - Make `auto_ptr` a habit; it deletes memory when it leaves scope and thereby removes many leaks that raw pointers cause.
- **Use smart pointers** - Prefer smart pointers over "dumb" raw pointers; they behave like pointers while giving control over resource management, copying, assignment, construction, and destruction. C++-specific concern only.

### C Pointers

- **Declare explicit pointer types, never the default** - C permits `char` or `void` pointers to stand in for any type, which silences the compiler; use the specific pointer type so mismatched pointer types and bad dereferences are reported.
  - Corollary: when a conversion is unavoidable, cast explicitly so the allocated type is stated in the code.

```c
NodePtr = (NODE_PTR) calloc( 1, sizeof( NODE ) );
```

- **Avoid type casting** - Forcing a variable of one type into another type's space disables the compiler's type checking and punches a hole in defensive programming; heavy cast usage signals architectural gaps, so redesign when possible and otherwise minimize casts.
- **Asterisk rule for passing values back** - In C, a value returns to the caller only if the assignment statement dereferences the parameter with `*`, no matter how many asterisks appear in the declaration.

```c
// BAD - value is not passed back
void TryToPassBackAValue( int *parameter ) {
    parameter = SOME_VALUE;
}
// GOOD - value is passed back
void TryToPassBackAValue( int *parameter ) {
    *parameter = SOME_VALUE;
}
```

- **Size allocations with sizeof()** - Use `sizeof()` instead of hardcoded sizes from a manual: it also covers your own structures, is computed at compile time so it costs no runtime performance, is portable across recompilation environments, and auto-adjusts allocations when a type definition changes.

### Global Data - Definition

- **Global means program-wide accessibility** - A global variable is reachable anywhere in the program; a variable reachable anywhere within one class is class data, not global data, even though the term is often used loosely for any scope broader than local.
- **Global data is riskier than local data, yet shared access across routines is genuinely useful** - Global variables do not always produce errors, but they are almost never the best available design. Avoid global variables for two reasons: they are dangerous, and something better can take their place.
- **Wanting unrestricted globals is a symptom** - Treating restrictions on global data as an obstacle indicates information hiding and modularity have not been absorbed; write routines and classes with minimal coupling to globals and to the outside world.

### Common Problems with Global Data

- **Inadvertent changes (side effects)** - Never assume a global keeps its value across a call that could reach it; a global changed in one place while assumed unchanged elsewhere corrupts dependent computations.

```vb
' BAD - GetOtherAnswer() also changes the global theAnswer, so the average is wrong
theAnswer = GetTheAnswer()
otherAnswer = GetOtherAnswer()
averageAnswer = (theAnswer + otherAnswer) / 2
```

- **Aliasing** - Never pass a global variable into a routine that also uses that same global directly; the routine then reaches one variable under two names and the code's apparent logic is false.

```vb
' BAD - called as WriteGlobal( globalVar ): inputVar and globalVar are the same variable
Sub WriteGlobal( ByRef inputVar As Integer )
    inputVar = 0
    globalVar = inputVar + 5
    MsgBox( "Input Variable: " & Str( inputVar ) )   ' prints 5, not 0
    MsgBox( "Global Variable: " & Str( globalVar ) ) ' prints 5
End Sub
```

  - Failure signature: two messages intended to show different values print identical values.

- **Re-entrancy** - Code reachable from several threads of control at once is increasingly common; with multithreading, global data is shared across routines and across concurrent copies of the program, so a global must keep its meaning while several copies run at once. Treat this as a significant problem and prevent it by routing all access through access routines and by requiring a global to be checked out and locked before use.
- **Blocked reuse** - A class that reads or writes global data cannot be lifted into another program as-is. Take the high road and remove the class's dependence on global data so future reuse is plug-in; taking the low road by recreating the global data in the new program spreads the global like a virus into every program that reuses the old code.
- **Undefined initialization order across translation units** - Some languages, notably C++, do not define the initialization order of data across separate files; a global initialized from a global in another file has an unpredictable value unless the sequence is explicitly forced, so take explicit steps to force that sequence whenever such a dependency exists. Workarounds exist but their trickiness is itself evidence of the complexity globals add.
- **Damaged modularity and intellectual manageability** - Beyond a few hundred lines, managing complexity by decomposing into independently understandable pieces is the core task, and modularization is the strongest tool for it. Global data prevents reasoning about one routine in isolation, since every other routine touching the same global must be held in mind; it weakens rather than destroys modularity, and that alone justifies seeking a better solution.

### Legitimate Reasons to Use Global Data

- **"Never use globals" is too absolute** - Most programs use global data under a broad reading: database contents, configuration data such as the Windows registry, and named constants are all global data; named constants are global data without being global variables. Disciplined use is what matters.
- **Preserving program-wide values** - Use a global for data that genuinely applies to the whole program: program-state flags such as interactive vs. command-line mode or normal vs. error-recovery mode, or a data table every routine consumes.
- **Emulating named constants** - When the language lacks named constants (Python, Perl, Awk, UNIX shell script; C++, Java, Visual Basic and most modern languages have them), substitute global variables: replace literal `1` and `0` with `TRUE` and `FALSE`, replace a literal `66` lines per page with `LINES_PER_PAGE = 66`. Improves later changeability and readability - an instance of programming *into* a language rather than *in* it.
- **Emulating enumerated types** - Use global variables to stand in for enumerated types in languages such as Python that lack them.
- **Streamlining extremely common data** - When a variable would otherwise appear in every routine's parameter list, a global is defensible; but verify first, because a variable that appears to be accessed everywhere is usually accessed by a limited set of routines that should be packaged into a class together with that data.
- **Eliminating tramp data** - Data passed to a routine or class only so it can be forwarded onward - for example an error-processing object threaded through a call chain whose middle routines never use it - is tramp data; a global variable can remove it.

### Use Global Data Only as a Last Resort

1. Make every variable local to its routine first.
2. If it is needed more widely, promote it to a private or protected class variable.
3. Only when program-wide access is proven necessary, make it global.

- **Direction of promotion is one-way in practice** - Starting global means it will never be narrowed later; starting local often removes the need to go global at all.
- **Distinguish global variables from class variables** - Access a class variable freely inside the set of routines that use it heavily; expose it to outside routines only through an access routine. Never read or write class data directly from outside the class as if it were global, even when the language permits it.

### Using Access Routines Instead of Global Data

- **Anything global data can do, access routines do better** - When global data cannot be avoided, work with it only through access routines: they give you everything a global variable gives you and more, and creating them is the workhorse technique for avoiding the problems of global data. Access routines are the core mechanism behind both information hiding and the implementation of abstract data types; even short of a full abstract data type, use them to centralize control of the data and to insulate callers from change.
- **Centralized control** - With all access funneled through routines, replacing the underlying implementation changes only the access routines instead of rippling through every reference.
- **Guaranteed barricading** - Direct manipulation such as `stack.array[ stack.top ] = newElement` lets a caller forget the overflow check; putting the check inside `PushStack( newElement )` makes it run on every call automatically.
- **Automatic information hiding** - Access routines hide implementation whether or not they were designed for that purpose: the interior can change while the exterior stays recognizable to callers.
- **Easy upgrade path to an abstract data type** - Access routines create a level of abstraction that direct global access cannot: `if PageFull()` documents intent in the code where `if lineCount > MAX_LINES` only states mechanics.

#### How to implement access routines

1. Hide the data inside a class.
2. Declare it with `static` or the language equivalent so exactly one instance exists.
3. Write routines to read and to change it.
4. Require all code outside the class to use those routines rather than the data.

- **Worked pattern** - Replace a global `g_globalStatus` with data hidden in a class exposing `globalStatus.Get()` and `globalStatus.Set()`; callers get every benefit of the former global through those two routines.
- **No class support in the language** - Still write access routines, and enforce the restriction on direct global use through coding standards since the compiler will not.
  - **Naming enforcement** - Prefix all global data with `g_` and forbid any code except that variable's own access routines from touching a `g_` name; all other code goes through the access routines.
- **Do not lump all globals together** - A single undifferentiated pile of globals behind access routines removes the global-data problems but forfeits the information-hiding and abstract-data-type benefits; decide which class each global belongs to and package it with that class's data and routines.
- **Lock global access** - Borrow multiuser-database concurrency control: require a global to be checked out before its value is read or updated and checked back in when finished; if another part of the program attempts a check-out while it is held, have the lock/unlock routine display an error or fire an assertion.
  - This scheme ignores real concurrency subtleties, so restrict it to development unless it is very carefully designed; it is not reliable enough for production as-is.
  - For production, replace the error display with something safer and more graceful, for example logging an error to a file when two parts of the program try to lock the same global.
  - This safeguard is cheap to add behind access routines and awkward to add when global data is used directly.
- **Build abstraction into access routines** - Write them at the problem-domain level, not the implementation level, buying readability plus insulation from implementation change; direct structure use does two things at once, exposing both the mechanism and the domain action.

| Direct use of global data | Same access through access routines |
|---|---|
| `node = node.next` | `account = NextAccount( account )` |
| `node = node.next` | `employee = NextEmployee( employee )` |
| `node = node.next` | `rateLevel = NextRateLevel( rateLevel )` |
| `event = eventQueue[ queueFront ]` | `event = HighestPriorityEvent()` |
| `event = eventQueue[ queueBack ]` | `event = LowestPriorityEvent()` |

- **Keep every access to one structure at the same abstraction level** - If one operation on a structure goes through an access routine, all of them must; read and write through routines alike. `InitStack()` plus `PushStack()` is consistent, while popping via `value = array[ stack.top ]` creates an inconsistent view that makes the code harder to understand - write `PopStack()` instead.
  - Failure mode to watch for: only the complicated operations (queue insert, queue remove) get wrapped in routines while the simple ones stay as direct data manipulation, producing nonparallel use of the structure.

| Nonparallel use of complex data | Parallel use of complex data |
|---|---|
| `event = EventQueue[ queueFront ]` | `event = HighestPriorityEvent()` |
| `event = EventQueue[ queueBack ]` | `event = LowestPriorityEvent()` |
| `AddEvent( event )` | `AddEvent( event )` |
| `eventCount = eventCount - 1` | `RemoveEvent( event )` |

- **Applies at every program size** - Access routines are a productive way to avoid global-data problems in small programs as well as large ones, and they add readability and flexibility.
- **Needing access routines for a queue signals a missing class** - Wrapping something like an event queue in access routines is an indication to create a class for it.

### How to Reduce the Risks of Using Global Data

- **Classify the case before applying any risk-reduction guideline** - Most data called global belongs to a class that was never properly designed or implemented; in a few cases the data must be global but every access can still be wrapped in access routines; only in a very small remainder is raw global data actually required. The risk-reduction guidelines that follow are unpleasant but they raise the survival odds for that remainder.
- **Make globals obvious by naming convention** - Some mistakes disappear simply because the code shows that the data is global, so the naming convention must tell local, class, and global data apart on sight; when globals serve more than one purpose (real variables vs. named-constant substitutes), the naming convention must distinguish those uses too.
- **Maintain an annotated list of all globals** - Once naming marks a variable as global, document what it does; the list of global variables is among the most useful artifacts for anyone working on the program.
- **Never hold intermediate results in a global** - Compute the value locally and assign the global once, at the end of the computation.
- **Never disguise global data inside one monster object passed everywhere** - A single huge object satisfies the letter of the rule against global variables while delivering none of the benefits of encapsulation and adding pure overhead; if global data is used, use it openly rather than hiding it in obese objects.

## Code Complete: Ch14 Organizing Straight-Line Code + Ch15 Using Conditionals

### Statements That Must Be in a Specific Order

- **Straight-line code still affects quality** - Sequential ordering is simple, but its subtleties influence correctness, readability, and maintainability.
- **Order statements by dependency** - Dependency is the governing concept: when a statement consumes what an earlier statement produces, the sequence is fixed, and the code must be written in that order (read data, then compute results from it, then print those results).

```java
data = ReadData();
results = CalculateResultsFromData( data );
PrintResults( results );
```

- **When statements must run in a fixed order, take deliberate steps to make that order clear** - treat the order as unclear unless a reader of the calling code alone, with no domain knowledge and no access to the routine bodies, can see that order matters and why. Ranked strategy, applied in this order:
  1. Restructure so no order dependency exists.
  2. If a dependency must exist, restructure so it is obvious from names and data flow.
  3. Only if the code still cannot be made explicit, document the dependency with a comment.
  4. For critical code, additionally enforce the dependency with assertions or error-handling state.
- **Rank a dependency by how a reader could discover it** - obvious from the routine names is acceptable; reachable only through domain knowledge or common sense is not obvious enough; carried through shared member data with no parameters is hidden and must be restructured.
  - Domain-knowledge dependency: `revenue.ComputeMonthly(); revenue.ComputeQuarterly(); revenue.ComputeAnnual();` - quarterly consumes monthly results and annual consumes quarterly, but only accounting sense reveals it. The dependency is real and invisible in the code.
  - Hidden dependency: parameterless calls that communicate through class member variables, e.g. a `ComputeMarketingExpense` that secretly initializes the member data every sibling routine writes into, so it must run first. Absence of parameters at most hints that the routines touch class data; it never proves which one must run first.
- **Avoid burying shared initialization inside a peer routine** - when routines are named as parallel operations differing only in the data they handle, letting one of them also initialize the shared member data is arbitrary: nothing explains why that routine rather than a sibling does the setup. Unless there is a specific good reason to leave it there, extract a separate routine such as `InitializeExpenseData()` whose name announces that it must run before the others.
- **Name a routine for everything it does, not for its main job** - if you refuse to extract the setup step, rename the routine so the extra work is in the name (`ComputeMarketingExpenseAndInitializeMemberData`). A long name that describes all the routine's functions is not the problem; a routine that needs such a name is the problem. Length is never a reason to keep a name that hides a function.
- **Pass the shared data as a parameter so the dependency shows in the call sequence** - routines that communicate invisibly through member data give a reader no signal; routing the same object through every call signals that they operate on one piece of state and that order may matter.
  - Prefer converting the routines into functions that take the data as input and return the updated data as output; the assignment chain makes the order dependency unmistakable rather than merely suggested.

```vb
' BAD - no data passed, so no evidence of shared state or required order
ComputeMarketingExpense
ComputeSalesExpense
DisplayExpenseSummary

' BETTER - the repeated argument hints at shared state and an order dependency
InitializeExpenseData( expenseData )
ComputeMarketingExpense( expenseData )
ComputeSalesExpense( expenseData )
DisplayExpenseSummary( expenseData )

' BEST - functions taking and returning the data make the dependency explicit
expenseData = InitializeExpenseData( expenseData )
expenseData = ComputeMarketingExpense( expenseData )
expenseData = ComputeSalesExpense( expenseData )
DisplayExpenseSummary( expenseData )
```

- **Use parameters to advertise the absence of a dependency too** - giving each routine its own distinct data (`ComputeMarketingExpense( marketingData )`, `ComputeSalesExpense( salesData )`, ...) tells a reader the call order among them is free, while a final routine that consumes all four data items (`DisplayExpenseSummary( marketingData, salesData, travelData, personnelData )`) tells the reader it must run after them. Design the signatures so both facts are readable.
- **Comment an order dependency only as a fallback** - a comment stating which routines share the member data and which routine must be called last is worth writing when the code itself cannot be improved, e.g. tightly controlled code or an external constraint on restructuring. Comments compensate for code weaknesses; they never substitute for restructuring, naming, and parameter passing.
  - An unclear dependency is a coding assumption; recording assumptions is critical to keeping code maintainable and modifiable.
- **Enforce a critical sequential dependency with state flags plus assertions or error handling** - for code critical enough to justify the cost, initialize a flag such as `isExpenseDataInitialized` to false in the constructor, set it to true in `InitializeExpenseData()`, and have every routine that depends on the data verify the flag before touching that data. Extensive dependencies need one flag per step (`isMarketingExpenseComputed`, `isSalesExpenseComputed`, and so on).
  - Tradeoff, mandatory to weigh before using this: the technique adds variables, initialization code, and error-checking code, each of which is a new opportunity for defects. Adopt it only when the protection outweighs the added complexity and the increased chance of secondary errors.

### Statements Whose Order Doesn't Matter

- **Principle of Proximity** - Keep related actions together. Applies whenever no statement depends on or logically follows another, because ordering still governs readability, performance, and maintainability even then; where there is no order dependency, place related statements as close together as possible.
- **Order by secondary criteria** - Ordering by dependency is the strongest organizing principle for straight-line code and every other criterion is secondary. With no execution-order dependency to obey, settle the order of statements or blocks using secondary criteria: proximity of related actions, readability, and performance.
- **Read top to bottom** - Arrange code so it can be read straight down; do not force a reader to jump around the routine or file to reconstruct how a value is produced. Top-to-bottom order is the largest single contributor to readability.
  - Run-time control flowing top to bottom is not sufficient; if finding needed information requires searching the whole program, reorganize.
  - Interleaving operations on several objects forces the reader to hold every intervening line in mind to answer how one object is computed; group each object's operations instead.

```cpp
// BAD - references to each object are scattered; every line must be read to trace one object
travelData.ComputeQuarterly();
salesData.ComputeQuarterly();
marketingData.ComputeQuarterly();
salesData.ComputeAnnual();
marketingData.ComputeAnnual();
travelData.ComputeAnnual();

// GOOD - each object's references localized, short live range, decomposition now visible
MarketingData marketingData;
marketingData.ComputeQuarterly();
marketingData.ComputeAnnual();
marketingData.Print();
```

- **Minimize live lines** - Keep the span of lines over which a variable or object is live as small as possible by clustering all references to it.
- **Grouping exposes routines** - Localized grouping makes extractable routines visible; scattered code hides that a decomposition is even possible.
- **Group related statements** - Put statements together when they operate on the same data, perform similar tasks, or depend on each other's ordering.
- **Box test for grouping** - Verify grouping by drawing boxes around related statement sections: well-ordered code yields boxes that never overlap (nesting is allowed); overlapping boxes mean the ordering is wrong and the code must be reorganized.
- **Extract strongly related clusters** - When a group is strongly self-related and has no meaningful relationship to the statements before or after it, refactor that group into its own routine.
- **Pseudocode Programming Process side effect** - Following the Pseudocode Programming Process produces statement grouping automatically.

### Conditionals - Definition and Scope

- **Definition of conditional** - A conditional is a statement that controls whether other statements execute: `if`, `else`, `case`, `switch`. Loop controls (`while`, `for`) are conditionals logically but are treated as a separate topic by convention.
- **Complexity ladder** - Plain `if` / `if-then` is the simplest form, `if-then-else` is somewhat more complex, and chains of `if-then-else-if` are the most complex. Which forms are available depends on the language.

### Plain if-then Statements

- **Nominal path first** - Write the normal path through the code first, then the unusual cases, so rare cases never obscure the normal flow; this serves both readability and performance.
- **Branch correctly on equality** - Deliberately reason about the equals case: using `>` where `>=` is required (or `<` where `<=` is required) is the conditional-statement equivalent of an off-by-one error in array indexing or a loop index. Think through endpoints in loops and the equality case in conditionals.
- **Normal case after the if, not the else** - Put the case you normally expect into the `if` clause; keep code resulting from a decision as close as possible to that decision. Pay particular attention to the order of the `if` and `else` clauses in a simple `if-else` statement that processes a lot of errors, and make sure the nominal case is unmistakable.
  - Error-processing code that sometimes tests success and sometimes tests failure makes it impossible to see which `if` the nominal path belongs to; test the success condition consistently.
  - A stack of error cases collecting at the bottom of a nest is the signature of well-written error handling.

```vb
' BAD - error and nominal cases interleaved, tests alternate polarity
OpenFile( inputFile, status )
If ( status = Status_Error ) Then
  errorType = FileOpenError
Else
  ReadFile( inputFile, fileData, status )
  If ( status = Status_Success ) Then ...

' GOOD - nominal case always in the if clause, errors stacked at the bottom
OpenFile( inputFile, status )
If ( status = Status_Success ) Then
  ReadFile( inputFile, fileData, status )
  If ( status = Status_Success ) Then ...
  Else errorType = ErrorType_FileReadError
  End If
Else
  errorType = ErrorType_FileOpenError
End If
```

- **Consistent-success nesting is one option, not the only one** - Nesting that always tests the success condition and stacks errors at the bottom is one valid treatment of interleaved nominal and error cases; other valid treatments include guard clauses, converting to polymorphic dispatch, and extracting the inner part of the test into a separate routine.
- **Never leave a null if clause** - An `if` must be followed by a meaningful statement. Replace `if (test) ; else { ... }` by negating the predicate, moving the `else` body into the `if`, and deleting the `else`.

```java
// BAD
if ( someTest )
    ;
else {
    // do something
}

// GOOD
if ( !someTest ) {
    // do something
}
```

- **Consider the else clause** - Before settling on a plain `if`, check whether an `if-then-else` is actually required. Empirical calibration: between 50 and 80 percent of plain `if` statements should have had an `else` clause.
- **Account for the else case** - At minimum, take the `else` case into account explicitly. Coding a null `else` purely to prove the case was considered may be overkill, but where an `if` has no `else` and the reason is not obvious, add a comment explaining why no `else` is needed.

```java
// GOOD - documented absence of else
if ( COLOR_MIN <= color && color <= COLOR_MAX ) {
    // do something
}
else {
    // else color is invalid
    // screen not written to - safely ignore command
}
```

- **Test the else clause** - Do not assume only the `if` branch needs testing; whenever the `else` clause is testable, test it for correctness.
- **Check for reversed clauses** - Actively inspect for the common defect of swapping the `if` and `else` bodies or inverting the test logic.

### Chains of if-then-else Statements

- **Chains are the fallback for missing case support** - Write `if-then-else-if` chains where the language has no `case` statement or supports it only partially; that is the situation the following chain guidelines govern. Before keeping a chain, confirm it is genuinely a better implementation than a `case` statement.
- **Encapsulate complicated tests in boolean functions** - Replace long compound conditions with calls to well-named boolean functions (`IsControl`, `IsPunctuation`, `IsDigit`, `IsLetter`); the chain then reads as a list of categories.
- **Most common cases first** - Order chain branches most-frequent first: readers reach the usual cases without wading through exception handling, and the number of tests executed for common inputs drops.
- **Cover all cases with a trapping final else** - End every chain with an `else` that raises an error message or assertion for unplanned cases; word that message for the developer, not the end user.

```cpp
else {
    DisplayInternalError( "Unexpected type of character detected." );
}
```

- **Chains replace deep nesting** - An `if-then-else-if` chain is a legitimate technique for flattening deeply nested code.
- **Prefer a richer construct when the language has one** - Where the language offers `case` over strings, enums, ranges, or logical functions (Visual Basic, Ada), use it instead of an `if-then-else` chain; it is easier to write and to read.
  - Visual Basic: `Select Case` supports range and value-list labels (`Case "a" To "z"`, `Case " ", ",", "."`) plus `Case Else` for the internal-error trap.

### case Statements - Language Support

- **Know the language's case limits before choosing it** - `case`/`switch` capability varies sharply by language; verify support before designing around it.
  - C++ and Java: `case` supports ordinal types only, one value per label.
  - Visual Basic: `case` supports ordinal types plus shorthand for ranges and combinations of values.
  - Many scripting languages: no `case` statement at all.

### Choosing the Most Effective Ordering of Cases

- **Order matters only at scale** - Ordering barely matters in a tiny `case` statement (roughly three labels, one line of code each); it becomes significant in a long one, for example a statement dispatching dozens of events in an event-driven program. Where ordering matters, in a `case` statement or an `if-then-else` chain, choose the order that maximizes readability.
- **Alphabetic or numeric order when cases are peers** - If all cases are equally important, use A-B-C (or numeric) order so an individual case can be located quickly.
- **Normal case first when exceptions exist** - Where exactly one case is normal and the rest are exceptions, put the normal one at the top and use comments to mark it as normal and the rest as unusual.
- **Frequency order so readers find common cases fast** - Otherwise sort labels by execution frequency, most frequent at the top and least frequent at the bottom; a reader scanning for a label is usually after a common case, so the search ends sooner.

### Tips for Using case Statements

- **Keep each case's action simple** - Keep the code under each label short so the statement's structure stays visible; when a case's work is complicated, move it into a routine and call that routine from the case.
- **Never fabricate a variable to enable a case statement** - Use `case` only for simple, easily categorized data. If the data is not simple, use an `if-then-else` chain; manufactured control variables are confusing and the real data may not map onto the labels as intended.
  - Failure mode: switching on `userCommand[0]` dispatches `Copy()` for any input starting with "c" (`copy`, `clambake`, `cellulite`), and the error-detecting default only catches bad first letters rather than bad commands. Compare whole strings in an `if-then-else-if` chain instead.
  - Countervailing condition (do not conflate): assigning a complicated expression to a well-named boolean variable or function to simplify a test is good practice; the prohibition is specifically against inventing a control variable so that a `case` statement can be used on data that is not simple.

```java
// BAD - phony case variable peeled off a user string
action = userCommand[ 0 ];
switch ( action ) {
    case 'c': Copy(); break;
    case 'd': DeleteCharacter(); break;
    default: HandleUserInputError( ErrorType.InvalidUserCommand );
}

// GOOD - test the real value
if ( UserCommand.equals( COMMAND_STRING_COPY ) ) { Copy(); }
else if ( UserCommand.equals( COMMAND_STRING_DELETE ) ) { DeleteCharacter(); }
else { HandleUserInputError( ErrorType_InvalidCommandInput ); }
```

- **Default clause must be a legitimate default** - Never demote the last remaining real case into `default`. Doing so discards the self-documentation of the case label and the error-detection capability of the default, and it breaks under modification: with a legitimate default, adding a case is trivial; with a phony default, a new case must be added, possibly promoted to default, and the old pseudo-default converted back into a real label.
- **Use default to detect and report errors** - If the default is not needed for real processing and should never be reached, emit a diagnostic message from it.
  - Such messages are valuable in production as well as debugging; users prefer an internal-error-with-support-contact message over a crash or over subtly wrong results that look correct until reviewed.
  - Also code a label with an explicit "no action required, but case was considered" comment where a valid case legitimately does nothing.

```java
switch ( commandShortcutLetter ) {
    case 'a': PrintAnnualReport(); break;
    case 'p': // no action required, but case was considered
        break;
    case 'q': PrintQuarterlyReport(); break;
    default:
        DisplayInternalError( "Internal Error 905: Call customer support." );
}
```

- **If default does real work, prove every selector is legal** - Using the default for non-error processing asserts that every possible selector value is valid; re-verify each value that could reach the statement, and if any illegitimate value exists, restructure so the default checks for errors.
- **C, C++, Java: avoid dropping through the end of a case** - These languages do not break out of a case automatically; leave the end of a case uncoded and control drops into the next case's body. Code the end of every case explicitly, and expect a `break` on each one during review.
  - Never interleave a `case` label inside another control construct (for example a `case 'B':` placed inside an `if` block belonging to `case 'A':`). Overlapping control constructs are effectively unmaintainable and must be untangled before any modification will work. Good formatting can disguise this defect - judge the structure, not the indentation.
- **C++: mark intentional fall-through unmistakably** - If a drop-through is deliberate, comment the exact place and the reason (`// FALLTHROUGH -- ...` on each falling label). This is rarely justified; fall-through invites defects during later modification and should generally be avoided.

```cpp
switch ( errorDocumentationLevel ) {
    case DocumentationLevel_Full:
        DisplayErrorDetails( errorNumber );
        // FALLTHROUGH -- Full documentation also prints summary comments
    case DocumentationLevel_Summary:
        DisplayErrorSummary( errorNumber );
        // FALLTHROUGH -- Summary documentation also prints error number
    case DocumentationLevel_NumberOnly:
        DisplayErrorNumber( errorNumber );
        break;
    default:
        DisplayInternalError( "Internal Error 905: Call customer support." );
}
```

### Choosing the Control Construct

- **Control constructs are not interchangeable** - Choose the control construct that best fits each specific section of code; do not default to one form everywhere.

## Code Complete: Ch16 Controlling Loops

### Selecting the Kind of Loop

- **Definition of loop** - Any iterative control structure that repeatedly executes a block: `for`, `while`, `do-while` in C++ and Java; `For-Next`, `While-Wend`, `Do-Loop-While` in Visual Basic. Choosing how and when to use each kind is decisive for software quality.
- **Match the loop kind to the iteration model** - Classify the iteration before writing the loop:
  - Counted loop - runs a specific number of times, perhaps once per item.
  - Continuously evaluated loop - iteration count unknown in advance; tests for completion on each iteration (while resources remain, until the user quits, until an error occurs).
  - Endless loop - runs forever once started; typical of embedded systems such as pacemakers, microwave ovens, cruise controls.
  - Iterator loop - performs its action once per element of a container class.
- **Classify a loop on two axes before choosing a construct** - decide (a) flexibility: fixed iteration count versus a completion test re-evaluated each pass, and (b) where the completion test sits.
- **Test location determines the minimum execution count** - derive this before writing the body.
  - Test at the beginning: the body may execute zero times.
  - Test at the end: the body executes at least once.
  - Test in the middle: the part before the test executes at least once; the part after the test may execute zero times.
- **Pick the construct from the flexibility/test-location pair** - use this mapping.

| Language | Kind of loop | Flexibility | Test location |
|---|---|---|---|
| Visual Basic | For-Next | rigid | beginning |
| Visual Basic | While-Wend | flexible | beginning |
| Visual Basic | Do-Loop-While | flexible | beginning or end |
| Visual Basic | For-Each | rigid | beginning |
| C, C++, C#, Java | for | flexible | beginning |
| C, C++, C#, Java | while | flexible | beginning |
| C, C++, C#, Java | do-while | flexible | end |
| C# only (planned for others, including Java) | foreach | rigid | beginning |

- **Use a `while` loop when the iteration count is not known in advance** - the only remaining decision is whether to test at the beginning or the end.
  - Never assume the exit condition is monitored continuously; it is evaluated exactly once per pass, so the loop does not stop the instant the condition turns false mid-body. Novices commonly hold the wrong model here.
  - Test at the beginning: `while` in C++, C#, Java, Visual Basic and most languages; emulate it elsewhere.
  - Test at the end when the loop must be flexible but must run at least once: `do-while` in C++, C#, Java; `Do-Loop-While` in Visual Basic; emulate end-tested loops elsewhere.

### Loop-With-Exit Loops

- **Definition** - a loop-with-exit loop places the exit condition in the middle of the body rather than at the top or bottom.
  - Available explicitly in Visual Basic (`Do` ... `Exit Do` ... `Loop`); emulate with `while` plus `break` in C++, C and Java, or with `goto` where neither exists.
- **Use a loop-with-exit loop to eliminate a loop-and-a-half** - when testing at the top or the bottom forces duplicating setup statements before the loop and again at the loop's end, replace the duplication with an infinite loop containing a mid-body exit.
  - The duplicated form breaks under maintenance: the two copies must be edited in parallel, a later editor will not know that, and incomplete modification produces defects.

```cpp
// BAD - loop-and-a-half: first two lines duplicated at the loop end
score = 0;
GetNextRating( &ratingIncrement );
rating = rating + ratingIncrement;
while ( ( score < targetScore ) && ( ratingIncrement != 0 ) ) {
   GetNextScore( &scoreIncrement );
   score = score + scoreIncrement;
   GetNextRating( &ratingIncrement );
   rating = rating + ratingIncrement;
}
```

```cpp
// GOOD - infinite loop plus break emulates loop-with-exit; no duplication
score = 0;
while ( true ) {
   GetNextRating( &ratingIncrement );
   rating = rating + ratingIncrement;
   if ( !( ( score < targetScore ) && ( ratingIncrement != 0 ) ) ) {
      break;
   }
   GetNextScore( &scoreIncrement );
   score = score + scoreIncrement;
}
```

```vb
' GOOD - native Visual Basic form
score = 0
Do
   GetNextRating( ratingIncrement )
   rating = rating + ratingIncrement
   If ( not ( score < targetScore and ratingIncrement <> 0 ) ) Then Exit Do
   GetNextScore( ScoreIncrement )
   score = score + scoreIncrement
Loop
```

- **Collect every exit condition in one place** - scattering exit conditions through the body all but guarantees one is missed during debugging, modification or testing.
- **Comment the emulation** - when the language lacks a native loop-with-exit, state in comments what the infinite-loop-plus-break construct is doing.
- **Simplify a negated compound exit test** - a condition such as `!( a && b )` can be reduced using DeMorgan's Theorems.
- **Status of the loop-with-exit technique** - a one-entry, one-exit structured construct, rated the preferred form of loop control, and demonstrably easier to comprehend than loops that exit at the top or the bottom.
  - Student programmers scored 25 percent higher on a comprehension test with loop-with-exit loops than with top-exit or bottom-exit loops; the structure was judged a closer match to how people reason about iteration.
  - It is not yet in wide production use and its suitability for production code is unsettled; treat it as an available technique to use carefully, not as a mandate.
- **Never enter the middle of a loop with a `goto`** - this abnormal variant also avoids a loop-and-a-half, and it turns up in simulations where the loop's first block must be skipped on the first pass while the second block must run. It is genuinely one-in/one-out (the `goto` is the only entry, the `while` test the only exit) and still bad practice, for two reasons: it uses `goto`, and it is rare enough to confuse readers.

```cpp
// BAD - goto jumps into the middle of the loop
goto Start;
while ( expression ) {
   // do something
   Start:
   // do something else
}
```

```cpp
// GOOD - swap the blocks around a break; no goto
while ( true ) {
   // do something else
   if ( !( expression ) ) {
      break;
   }
   // do something
}
```

  - If the language has no `break`, emulate `break` with a `goto` rather than entering the loop mid-body.

### When to Use a for Loop

- **Choose `for` when the iteration count is specified** - a good fit for a fixed number of passes; available in C++, C, Java, Visual Basic and most languages.
- **Restrict `for` to simple activities needing no internal loop control** - simple increments or decrements, such as walking a container's elements; set it up in the header and then ignore control inside the body.
- **Switch to `while` whenever execution must jump out of the loop** - a condition that forces an early exit disqualifies `for`.
- **Keep `for` for simple uses; send complicated looping to `while`** - route any task with non-trivial loop control into a `while` loop.

### When to Use a foreach Loop

- **Use `foreach` to apply an operation to every member of an array or container** - `foreach` in C#, `For-Each` in Visual Basic, `for-in` in Python.
- **Prefer it because it removes loop-housekeeping arithmetic** - with no housekeeping arithmetic there is no chance of an error in it.

```csharp
// GOOD - no index arithmetic to get wrong
foreach ( int fibonacciNumber in fibonacciSequence ) {
   if ( ( fibonacciNumber % 2 ) == 0 ) {
      evenFibonacciNumbers++;
   }
   else {
      oddFibonacciNumbers++;
   }
}
```

### Controlling the Loop - Failure Modes and Two Governing Practices

- **Guard against the standard loop defects** - check each of these before accepting a loop.
  - Loop initialization wrong or absent.
  - Accumulators and other loop-related variables left uninitialized.
  - Nesting done wrong.
  - Termination done wrong.
  - Loop variable never advanced, or advanced by the wrong amount.
  - Array element derived from the loop index with the wrong subscript.
- **Practice 1: minimize the number of factors affecting the loop** - loops are inherently complicated, so simplify aggressively for the benefit of whoever reads the code: avoid exotic kinds of loops, minimize nesting, make entries and exits clear, and keep housekeeping code in one place.
- **Practice 2: treat the loop body as a routine and keep control outside it** - state explicitly the conditions under which the body runs; a reader must not have to open the body to understand the control.
  - Treat the loop as a black box: control conditions are visible to the enclosing code, body contents are not. `while ( !inputFile.EndOfFile() && moreDataAvailable )` tells a reader everything needed about termination - it stops once `inputFile.EndOfFile()` turns true or `moreDataAvailable` turns false - without opening the body.
  - Tradeoff to accept knowingly: the `while ( true )`-plus-`break` technique puts the exit condition inside the black box, so even with a single exit condition the black-box benefit is lost.

### Entering the Loop

- **Enter from exactly one location** - the available loop constructs allow testing at the beginning, middle or end, which is expressive enough to always enter from the top; multiple entry points are never needed.
- **Place initialization code immediately before the loop (Principle of Proximity)** - keep related statements together; statements scattered across a routine get overlooked and modified incorrectly.
  - Detached initialization breaks when the loop is generalized into a larger loop and the initialization is not updated, and when the loop is moved or copied into another routine without it.
  - Avoid parking loop initialization in the data-declaration section or in a housekeeping block at the top of the enclosing routine; that invites initialization defects.
- **Write infinite loops as `while ( true )`** - the standard idiom in C++, Java, Visual Basic and comparable languages; `for( ;; )` is an accepted alternative.
  - Applies to loops that genuinely never terminate (firmware such as a pacemaker or microwave oven) and to event loops that exit only on an event.
  - Never fake an infinite loop with a large bound such as `for i = 1 to 99999` or `for i = 1 to 9999` - the bound obscures the intent, 99999 could be a legitimate value, and the fake breaks down under maintenance.
- **Prefer a `for` loop when one is appropriate** - it packages all control code in one place at the top, so modifications stay correct; a common maintenance defect is changing the initialization above a `while` loop and forgetting the matching code at its bottom.
- **Do not use `for` when `while` fits better** - never cram a `while` loop's contents into a `for` header. C++'s `for` header accepts more kinds of initialization and termination information than other languages', and that flexibility invites statements unrelated to loop control.
- **Reserve the `for` header for loop-control statements only** - statements that initialize the loop, terminate it, or advance it toward termination. Housekeeping statements such as a record counter do not control progress; hoisting them into the header while leaving the real advancing call in the body falsely implies the counter drives the loop. Apply this to C++, C and Java `for` headers in particular.

```cpp
// BAD - recordCount housekeeping in the header, real advance (GetRecord) in the body
for ( inputFile.MoveToStart(), recordCount = 0; !inputFile.EndOfFile();
      recordCount++ ) {
   inputFile.GetRecord();
}
```

```cpp
// GOOD - header holds only init, test and advance
recordCount = 0;
for ( inputFile.MoveToStart(); !inputFile.EndOfFile(); inputFile.GetRecord() ) {
   recordCount++;
}
```

```cpp
// BEST for this job - a while loop
inputFile.MoveToStart();
recordCount = 0;
while ( !inputFile.EndOfFile() ) {
   inputFile.GetRecord();
   recordCount++;
}
```

### Processing the Middle of the Loop

- **Enclose every loop body in `{` and `}` or the language equivalent** - use brackets every time; they cost nothing in run-time speed or space, aid readability, prevent defects introduced by later edits (a later edit cannot fall outside the body), and are sound defensive programming.
- **Avoid empty loops** - never leave the body empty; in C++ and Java the loop's work can be coded inside the test expression, leaving an empty body; recode so the work is visible.

```cpp
// BAD - work (the assignment) hidden in the test; body is just a semicolon
while ( ( inputChar = dataFile.GetChar() ) != CharType_Eof ) {
   ;
}
```

```cpp
// GOOD - work in the body, test does only testing
do {
   inputChar = dataFile.GetChar();
} while ( inputChar != CharType_Eof );
```

  - Occupying three lines instead of one line plus a semicolon is appropriate, because the code does the work of three lines.
- **Keep loop-housekeeping expressions at the very beginning or the very end of the body** - housekeeping means expressions like `i = i + 1` or `j++` whose purpose is controlling the loop rather than doing its work.
  - Expect the variables initialized before the loop to be the same ones manipulated in the housekeeping section.
- **Make each loop perform exactly one function** - that a single loop is capable of doing two things is not a reason to merge them; a loop, like a routine, should do one thing well.
  - When merging two loops looks more efficient, still write two loops, add a comment that they could be combined for efficiency, and merge only after benchmarks show that section is a real performance problem.

### Exiting the Loop

- **Prove to yourself that the loop terminates** - mentally simulate execution until termination is certain in all circumstances, covering nominal cases, endpoints, and every exceptional case.
- **Make the termination condition obvious by keeping control in one place** - a `for` loop qualifies if the index is untouched and no `goto` or `break` leaves the loop; a `while` or `repeat-until` loop qualifies if all control lives in the `while` or `repeat-until` clause.
- **Never manipulate a `for` loop index inside the body** - do not modify the index in the body, and never jam it to force early termination; once a `for` loop is set up, its counter is off limits; use a `while` loop when more control over exit conditions is needed.

```java
// BAD - jamming the index to 100 to escape a 0..99 loop
for ( int i = 0; i < 100; i++ ) {
   if ( ... ) {
      i = 100;
   }
}
```

- **Avoid code that reads a loop index after the loop** - using the index's final value is bad form: that value varies across languages and implementations, and differs between normal and abnormal termination; even when it is known, the next reader must stop and work it out.
  - Assign the value that is actually needed to a separate variable at the right point inside the loop; that form is better and self-documenting.
  - Failure mode: a post-loop test against the loop bound reads as a search result, but nobody can recall whether the index advanced past the range end, so off-by-one errors slip in.

```cpp
// BAD - reuses recordCount after the loop; off-by-one waiting to happen
for ( recordCount = 0; recordCount < MAX_RECORDS; recordCount++ ) {
   if ( entry[ recordCount ] == testValue ) {
      break;
   }
}
if ( recordCount < MAX_RECORDS ) { return( true ); }
else { return( false ); }
```

```cpp
// GOOD - extra boolean keeps recordCount local and the intent explicit
found = false;
for ( recordCount = 0; recordCount < MAX_RECORDS; recordCount++ ) {
   if ( entry[ recordCount ] == testValue ) {
      found = true;
      break;
   }
}
return( found );
```

  - The extra boolean variable localizes references to the index and, as usually happens when a boolean is introduced, yields clearer code.
- **Consider safety counters** - a safety counter is a variable incremented on each pass through the loop, checked to detect that the loop has run too many times. Use safety counters to guarantee that all loops end in programs where an error would be catastrophic, and add one to any loop whose termination depends on unverified data: increment the counter each iteration and assert-fail when it reaches a `SAFETY_LIMIT` constant, so a corrupt structure produces a diagnosable failure instead of an infinite loop.

```cpp
// BAD - runs forever if the list is malformed
do {
   node = node->Next;
   ...
} while ( node->Next != NULL );

// GOOD
safetyCounter = 0;
do {
   node = node->Next;
   ...
   safetyCounter++;
   if ( safetyCounter >= SAFETY_LIMIT ) {
      Assert( false, "Internal Error: Safety-Counter Violation." );
   }
   ...
} while ( node->Next != NULL );
```

- **Never treat safety counters as a general cure** - each one added in isolation raises complexity and can introduce its own defects.
- **Institute safety counters as a project-wide standard for critical loops rather than ad hoc** - because they are absent from most loops, ad hoc use leads maintainers to forget the counter code when editing a loop that has one; under a uniform standard the counter code is expected and no more defect-prone than any other code. Once such a standard is in force, use a safety counter in every loop it covers.

### Exiting Loops Early

- **Definitions** - `break` (and Visual Basic `Exit-Do` / `Exit-For`, or a `goto`-simulated equivalent) terminates the loop through its normal exit and resumes at the first statement after the loop. `continue` skips the rest of the body and starts the next iteration; it is shorthand for an `if-then` that would suppress the remaining body.
- **Prefer a break over boolean exit flags in a while loop** - flags added only to emulate an early exit make the loop hard to read; a break can remove several indentation levels and a chain of `if` tests.
- **Place each break condition in its own statement next to the code that triggers it** - reduces nesting and makes the exit readable.
- **Treat many scattered breaks as a design smell** - a proliferation of breaks signals unclear thinking about the loop's structure or its role in surrounding code, and raises the possibility that a series of loops would express it more clearly than one loop with many exits. Multiple breaks are a warning sign, not proof of a defect.
- **Never let a break's target be ambiguous** - a `break` inside `if` nested in `switch` inside `do` binds to the `switch`, not the `if`. An extra `break` of exactly this shape took down the New York City phone system for 9 hours on January 15, 1990.

```cpp
// BAD - break was meant for the if, but exits the switch
do {
   ...
   switch
      ...
      if () {
         ...
         break;
         ...
      }
      ...
} while ( ... );
```

- **Use a labeled break where the language supports it** - Java labeled breaks can exit a `for`, an `if`, or any brace-enclosed block with an unambiguous target; use them for the nested `do-switch-if` case.

```java
do {
   ...
   switch
      ...
      CALL_CENTER_DOWN:
      if () {
         ...
         break CALL_CENTER_DOWN;
         ...
      }
      ...
} while ( ... );
```

- **Use continue only for a guard test at the top of the loop** - e.g. read a record, `continue` when its type is not the target type, then process; this avoids indenting the whole body inside an `if`.

```pseudocode
while ( not eof( file ) ) do
   read( record, file )
   if ( record.Type <> targetType ) then
      continue
   -- process record of targetType
   ...
end while
```

  - If the skip decision falls in the middle or at the end of the body, use an `if` instead of `continue`.
- **Use break and continue only with caution** - a break destroys the loop's black-box property and forces a reader to inspect the body to understand loop control; restricting exit control to a single condition is a strong simplification.
- **Justify every break and continue before writing it** - consider the alternatives first; whether they are legitimate structured programming is unsettled, so use them with the assumption you may be wrong. If a break or continue cannot be defended, remove it.

### Checking Endpoints

- **Mentally execute three cases for every loop you write** - the first iteration, an arbitrary middle iteration, and the last iteration, to catch off-by-one errors.
  - Also trace any special case that differs from the first or last case.
  - Hand-compute complex in-loop calculations with a calculator rather than trusting inspection.
- **Never debug a loop by perturbing operators or indexes at random** - flipping `<` to `<=` or adding/subtracting 1 until the loop appears to work either hides a subtler defect or yields correct code nobody understands. Simulation and hand calculation yield fewer defects during coding, faster defect detection during debugging, and real understanding of the code.

### Using Loop Variables

- **Use ordinal or enumerated types for array and loop limits; never floating point** - loop counters must be integers, since floating-point increments can silently fail to advance (adding 1.0 to 26,742,897.0 can yield 26,742,897.0) and produce an infinite loop.
- **Name loop indexes meaningfully whenever the array has two or more dimensions** - `i`, `j`, `k` are tolerable only for a single-dimension index; meaningful names state both the loop's purpose and which slice of the array is touched.

```java
// BAD
for ( int i = 0; i < numPayCodes; i++ ) {
   for ( int j = 0; j < 12; j++ ) {
      for ( int k = 0; k < numDivisions; k++ ) {
         sum = sum + transaction[ j ][ i ][ k ];
      }
   }
}

// GOOD
for ( int payCodeIdx = 0; payCodeIdx < numPayCodes; payCodeIdx++ ) {
   for ( int month = 0; month < 12; month++ ) {
      for ( int divisionIdx = 0; divisionIdx < numDivisions; divisionIdx++ ) {
         sum = sum + transaction[ month ][ payCodeIdx ][ divisionIdx ];
      }
   }
}
```

  - Write for human readers: both versions cost the machine the same, so pick the one people parse faster.
- **Avoid index cross-talk** - use each index for exactly one purpose; index cross-talk is reusing one index name for two different purposes, and reflexive use of `i` can bind it to two nested loops in the same nest, so the inner loop conflicts with the outer.

```cpp
// BAD - i controls two loops in one nest
for ( i = 0; i < numPayCodes; i++ ) {
   ...
   for ( j = 0; j < 12; j++ ) {
      ...
      for ( i = 0; i < numDivisions; i++ ) {
         sum = sum + transaction[ j ][ i ][ k ];
      }
   }
}
```

  - Ban `i`, `j`, `k` when the loop body exceeds a couple of lines, is likely to grow, or sits inside a group of nested loops.
- **Declare loop indexes inside the loop to confine their scope** - Ada makes `for` indexes invalid outside their loop and rejects outside use at compile time; C++ and Java permit but do not require in-loop declaration.

```cpp
for ( int recordCount = 0; recordCount < MAX_RECORDS; recordCount++ ) {
   // looping code that uses recordCount
}
```

  - **C++ caveat** - declaring the index in the header documents its purpose and in principle lets two loops reuse the name with no risk of confusing the two variables, but never rely on the compiler to enforce that scope. The language definition makes the index loop-scoped; three real compilers gave three behaviors on redeclaring `recordCount` in a second `for` loop in the same scope: one rejected it as a duplicate declaration, one accepted it yet allowed the first index to be used after its loop, and one accepted both and confined each to its own loop. Expect implementations to differ on esoteric language features.

### Loop Length and Nesting

- **Measure loop size two ways** - lines of code and depth of nesting; both are bounded.
- **Keep a loop short enough to see in one view** - the display height bounds it (a 50-line display implies a 50-line restriction); one page is the suggested outer limit, and simple code rarely exceeds 15 to 20 lines.
- **Limit nesting to three levels** - comprehension degrades significantly past three levels; beyond that, extract part of the body into a routine or simplify the control structure to shorten the loop conceptually.
- **Move the innards of a long loop into routines** - a well-designed loop body extracts cleanly into one or more routines called from inside the loop.
