Measurement tells you whether the plan is a success or failure and lets you vary your process in a controlled way to see how it can be improved. Measure the quality attributes themselves too: correctness, usability, efficiency, and so on, so you can tell whether quality is improving or degrading.
- **Prototype key functions** - prototyping is the development of realistic models of a system's key functions: prototype parts of a user interface to determine usability, critical calculations to determine execution time, or typical data sets to determine memory requirements. A survey of 16 published and 8 unpublished case studies comparing prototyping to traditional specification-development methods found prototyping can lead to better designs, better matches with user needs, and improved maintainability.

### Setting objectives

- **State quality objectives explicitly** - identify the specific quality characteristics, external and internal, that are important to your project and set an explicit objective for each. This is a simple, obvious step that is easy to overlook. Without explicit goals, programmers might work to maximize characteristics different from the ones you expect. Programmers will work to achieve the objectives if they know what the objectives are and that the objectives are reasonable; they cannot respond to objectives that change daily or that are impossible to meet.
- **Expect people to do what you ask them to do** - programmers have high achievement motivation: they work to the objectives specified, but they must be told what the objectives are.
- **Expect objectives to conflict** - not all quality-assurance goals are simultaneously achievable and it is generally not possible to do well on all of them; none of the five teams that were each told to optimize a different quality objective did consistently well in all objectives. Explicitly decide which goals you want to achieve, and communicate those goals to other people on your team.
- **Empirical result: teams hit the objective they are told to optimize** - five teams built five versions of the same program; each was given the same five quality objectives but told to optimize a different one. Four of the five teams finished first in the objective they were told to optimize; the fifth finished second in its objective.

| Objective (measured) | Told: minimum memory use | Told: most readable output | Told: most readable code | Told: least code | Told: minimum programming time |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Minimum memory | 1 | 4 | 4 | 2 | 5 |
| Output readability | 5 | 1 | 1 | 5 | 3 |
| Program readability | 3 | 2 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
| Least code | 2 | 5 | 3 | 1 | 3 |
| Minimum programming time | 4 | 3 | 5 | 4 | 1 |

### Relative effectiveness: percentage of defects detected

- **Do not assume quality-assurance practices are equally effective** - different methods find different kinds of defects, and effectiveness at detecting and removing defects is known and measured.

| Removal step | Lowest rate | Modal rate | Highest rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Informal design reviews | 25% | 35% | 40% |
| Formal design inspections | 45% | 55% | 65% |
| Informal code reviews | 20% | 25% | 35% |
| Formal code inspections | 45% | 60% | 70% |
| Modeling or prototyping | 35% | 65% | 80% |
| Personal desk-checking of code | 20% | 40% | 60% |
| Unit test | 15% | 30% | 50% |
| New function (component) test | 20% | 30% | 35% |
| Integration test | 25% | 35% | 40% |
| Regression test | 15% | 25% | 30% |
| System test | 25% | 40% | 55% |
| Low-volume beta test (<10 sites) | 25% | 35% | 40% |
| High-volume beta test (>1,000 sites) | 60% | 75% | 85% |

- **Never expect any single technique to be sufficient** - no single defect-detection technique is completely effective by itself, and testing by itself is not optimally effective at removing errors. Modal rates do not rise above 75 percent for any single technique, and the techniques average about 40 percent. For the most common kinds of defect detection, unit testing and integration testing, the modal rates are only 30-35 percent.
- **Do not settle for a test-heavy defect-removal approach** - the typical organization uses a test-heavy approach and achieves only about 85 percent defect-removal efficiency; leading organizations use a wider variety of techniques and achieve defect-removal efficiencies of 95 percent or higher.
- **Combine techniques to raise the detection rate** - cumulative defect-detection efficiency is significantly higher than that of any individual technique. Use several different error-detection techniques suited to finding several different kinds of errors.
- **Empirical result: any two methods nearly double the defects found** - programmers with a minimum of 7 and an average of 11 years of professional experience hunted 15 known errors in a program using one of: execution testing against the specification; execution testing against the specification with the source code; walk-through/inspection using the specification and the source code. Defects found ranged from 1.0 to 9.0, averaging 5.1 (about a third of those known). Used individually, no method had a statistically significant advantage over any other, but any combination of two methods, including two independent groups using the same method, increased the total number of defects found by a factor of almost 2.
- **Expect different people to find different defects** - only about 20 percent of the errors found by inspections were found by more than one inspector (NASA Software Engineering Laboratory, Boeing, and others).
- **Pair human review with computer-based testing** - human processes such as inspections and walk-throughs tend to be better at finding certain kinds of errors, and computer-based testing is better for other kinds. Code reading detected more interface defects; functional testing detected more control defects.
- **Use a coverage analyzer** - informal test approaches typically achieve only 50-60 percent test coverage unless you use one.
- **Never rely on testing alone for production software** - a combination of unit testing, functional testing, and system testing often results in cumulative defect detection of less than 60 percent, which is usually inadequate for production software.
- **Attribute Extreme Programming's defect-removal results to its specific practices, not to synergy** - the expected cumulative efficiency is about 90 percent in the average case and 97 percent in the best case, far better than the 85 percent industry average. Other combinations of practices can work equally well or better; determining which specific defect-removal practices to use to achieve a desired quality level is part of effective project planning.

| Removal step (Extreme Programming) | Lowest rate | Modal rate | Highest rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Informal design reviews (pair programming) | 25% | 35% | 40% |
| Informal code reviews (pair programming) | 20% | 25% | 35% |
| Personal desk-checking of code | 20% | 40% | 60% |
| Unit test | 15% | 30% | 50% |
| Integration test | 25% | 35% | 40% |
| Regression test | 15% | 25% | 30% |
| Expected cumulative defect-removal efficiency | ~74% | ~90% | ~97% |

### Cost of finding defects

- **Prefer the practices with the least cost per defect found, all other things being equal** - per-defect cost is also influenced by the total number of defects found, the stage at which each defect is found, and other factors besides the economics of a specific defect-detection technique, so the "all other things equal" qualification matters.
- **Prefer inspections over testing on cost grounds** - most studies have found inspections are cheaper than testing.
  - Code reading detected about 80 percent more faults per hour than testing (Software Engineering Laboratory).
  - It cost six times as much to detect design defects by using testing as by using inspections.
  - Only 3.5 staff hours were needed to find each error using code inspections, versus 15-25 hours per error through testing (IBM).

### Cost of fixing defects

- **Find defects earlier to lower fix cost** - the longer a defect remains in the system, the more expensive it becomes to remove, so a detection technique that finds the error earlier results in a lower cost of fixing it.
- **Prefer one-step techniques over two-step techniques** - inspections detect the symptoms and causes of defects in one step; testing finds symptoms but requires additional work to diagnose and fix the root cause. One-step techniques are substantially cheaper overall.
  - Code inspection (one-step): three hours to find and fix a defect. Testing (two-step): 12 hours to find and fix a defect (Microsoft applications division).
  - On a 700,000-line program built by over 400 developers, code reviews were several times as cost-effective as testing: 1.38 return on investment versus 0.17.
- **Combine techniques across all development stages** - an effective software-quality program must include a combination of techniques that apply to all stages of development. Recommended combination for achieving higher-than-average quality:
  - Formal inspections of all requirements, all architecture, and designs for critical parts of a system.
  - Modeling or prototyping.
  - Code reading or inspections.
  - Execution testing.

### When to do quality assurance

- **Catch requirements and architecture errors before they affect later activities** - the earlier an error is inserted into software, the more entangled it becomes in other parts of the software and the more expensive it becomes to remove. A fault in requirements can produce one or more corresponding faults in design, which can produce many corresponding faults in code. A requirements error can produce extra architecture or bad architectural decisions; extra architecture produces extra code, test cases, and documentation. Or a requirements error can result in architecture, code, and test cases that are thrown away.
- **Treat upstream errors as broader in scope** - a single architectural error can affect several classes and dozens of routines, whereas a single construction error is unlikely to affect more than one routine or class. This is a second reason it is cost-effective to catch errors as early as you can.
- **Emphasize quality-assurance work in the early stages and throughout the rest of the project** - defects creep into software at all stages. Apply effective techniques during construction and the many equally powerful techniques available before construction; the earlier you find a defect, the less intertwined it becomes with the rest of your code and the less damage it causes. QA should be planned into the project as work begins, be part of the technical fiber of the project as work continues, and punctuate the end of the project, verifying the quality of the product as work ends; plan steps to assure software quality during each stage of development.

### The General Principle of Software Quality

- **The General Principle of Software Quality** - improving quality reduces development costs. Quality is free, in the end, but it requires a reallocation of resources so that defects are prevented cheaply instead of fixed expensively; ensure management understands that quality assurance incurs additional costs up front in order to save costs later.
- **Reduce time spent reworking code as the best way to improve productivity and quality** - whether the rework arises from changes in requirements, changes in design, or debugging.
- **Industry-average productivity** - about 10 to 50 lines of delivered code per person per day, including all noncoding overhead. Part of the reason these figures look low is that industry-average numbers factor in nonprogrammer time (tester, project manager, administrative support) and noncoding activities such as requirements development and architecture work; but none of that is what consumes most of the time.
- **Debugging and correcting code that does not work properly is the single biggest activity on most projects** - debugging plus associated refactoring and other rework consume about 50 percent of the time on a traditional, naive software-development cycle. Reducing debugging by preventing errors improves productivity, so the most obvious method of shortening a development schedule is to improve the quality of the product and decrease time spent debugging and reworking.
- **Field data confirming the principle**
  - A review of 50 development projects involving over 400 work-years of effort and almost 3 million lines of code found that increased quality assurance was associated with decreased error rate but did not increase overall development cost (NASA Software Engineering Laboratory).
  - IBM: software projects with the lowest levels of defects had the shortest development schedules and the highest development productivity; software defect removal is actually the most expensive and time-consuming form of work for software.
  - 1985 study: 166 professional programmers wrote programs from the same specification, averaging 220 lines of code and a little under five hours to write. Programmers who took the median time produced programs with the greatest number of errors; programmers who took more or less than the median time produced programs with significantly fewer errors. The two slowest groups took about five times as long to achieve roughly the same defect rate as the fastest group.
- **Do not assume defect-free work takes longer** - it is not necessarily the case that writing software without defects takes more time than writing software with defects; it can take less. Neither the fastest nor the slowest development approach produces the software with the most defects.
- **Exception: on certain kinds of projects, quality assurance does cost money** - for space shuttle code or a medical life-support system, the degree of reliability required makes the project more expensive.
- **Redistribute resources upstream** - compared to the traditional code-test-debug cycle, an enlightened software-quality program saves money by moving resources away from debugging and refactoring into upstream quality-assurance activities. Upstream activities have more leverage on product quality than downstream activities, so time invested upstream saves more time downstream. Net effect: fewer defects, shorter development time, lower costs.

### Collaborative construction premise

- **Treat every collaborative construction technique as a way to formalize showing your work to someone else for the purpose of flushing out errors** - that is what they all are, in one way or another.
  - Explaining the problem aloud to another programmer can flush out the error before the helper has said a word.

## Code Complete: Ch21 Collaborative Construction

### 21.1 Overview of Collaborative Development Practices

- **Definition of collaborative construction** - Treat "collaborative construction" as covering pair programming, formal inspections, informal technical reviews, and document reading, plus any other technique in which developers share responsibility for creating code and other work products.
- **Assume you are blind to your own defects** - Every collaborative technique rests on the premise that developers are blind to some trouble spots in their own work and that others do not share those blind spots, so always get someone else to look at your work.
  - Developers insert an average of 1 to 3 defects per hour into designs and 5 to 8 defects per hour into code.
- **Never rely on testing alone** - Collaborative practices tend to find a higher percentage of defects than testing does and to find them more efficiently. Average defect-detection rates: unit testing about 30 percent, integration testing about 35 percent, low-volume beta testing about 35 percent; design inspections average 55 percent and code inspections average 60 percent effective.
- **Use reviews and testing together** - Collaborative practices find different kinds of errors than testing does; a human reviewer can spot unclear error messages, inadequate comments, hard-coded variable values, and repeated code patterns that should be consolidated, and testing will not. Even when testing is done effectively, reviews or other kinds of collaboration are still needed as part of a comprehensive quality program, so use both reviews and testing to ensure the quality of your software.
- **Expect a review-awareness effect** - When people know their work will be reviewed, they scrutinize it more carefully; this is a secondary benefit, not a substitute for the review.
- **Expect shorter schedules as a secondary benefit** - Collaborative construction's primary purpose is to improve software quality; it also decreases development time, which lowers development costs (the General Principle of Software Quality: reducing defects also improves development time).
- **Industry data supporting reviews and inspections** - Use these figures when calibrating the value of review work:
  - IBM: each hour of inspection prevented about 100 hours of related work (testing and defect correction).
  - Raytheon: reduced cost of defect correction (rework) from about 40 percent of total project cost to about 20 percent through an inspection-focused initiative.
  - Hewlett-Packard: inspection program saved an estimated $21.5 million per year.
  - Imperial Chemical Industries: maintaining a portfolio of about 400 inspected programs cost only about 10 percent as much as maintaining a similar set of uninspected programs.
  - Large-program study: each hour spent on inspections avoided an average of 33 hours of maintenance work; inspections were up to 20 times more efficient than testing.
  - Software-maintenance organization: 55 percent of one-line maintenance changes were in error before code reviews; only 2 percent after. Across all changes, 95 percent were correct the first time after reviews were introduced, versus under 20 percent before.
  - 11 programs by the same group: the first 5, developed without reviews, averaged 4.5 errors per 100 lines of code; the other 6, inspected, averaged 0.82 errors per 100 lines of code - reviews cut errors by over 80 percent.
  - Every studied project achieving 99 percent defect-removal or better used formal inspections; no project that achieved less than 75 percent defect-removal efficiency used formal inspections.
- **Pair programming cost/benefit data** - Early reports suggest pair programming achieves a code-quality level similar to formal inspections; full-up pair programming probably costs 10-25 percent more than solo development, but reduction in development time appears to be on the order of 45 percent, which in some cases may be a decisive advantage over solo development, though not over inspections, which have produced similar results. Pair programming typically costs about the same as inspections and is especially valuable when schedule reduction is desired.

#### Mentoring through collaboration

- **Do not expect written standards to be followed on their own** - Standards can be written down and distributed, but if no one talks about them or encourages their use, they will not be followed; use reviews as the mechanism for giving programmers feedback about their code, the standards, and the reasons for meeting them.
- **Review the subjective aspects too** - Give feedback on formatting, comments, variable names, local and global variable use, design approaches, and the-way-we-do-things-around-here, not only on objective standards compliance.
- **Use reviews as a mentoring venue** - Inexperienced programmers need guidance from more knowledgeable ones, and busy knowledgeable programmers need to be encouraged to share what they know; one team using formal inspections reported that inspections quickly brought all developers up to the level of the best developers.
  - Treat reviews as an opportunity for cultivating quality improvements in the future as much as in the present, not only as a defect filter for the work in hand.

#### Collective ownership

- **Adopt collective ownership** - Let all code be owned by the group rather than by individuals, accessible and modifiable by group members, because it yields:
  - Better code quality from multiple sets of eyes and multiple programmers working the code.
  - Reduced impact when someone leaves, since multiple people know each section.
  - Shorter overall defect-correction cycles, since any of several programmers can be assigned to fix bugs on an as-available basis.
  - Collective ownership increases the need for work coordination, especially configuration management.
- **Formal pairing is not required for coverage** - Some methodologies (Extreme Programming) recommend formally pairing programmers and rotating assignments over time, but cross-coverage can also be achieved through a combination of formal and informal technical reviews, pair programming when needed, and rotation of defect-correction assignments.
- **Apply collaboration before construction as well** - The same collaborative practices apply to estimates, plans, requirements, architecture, testing, and maintenance work, not just detailed design and code; formal inspections in particular can be used on work products such as requirements, designs, and test cases as well as on code.

### 21.2 Pair Programming

- **Definition** - One programmer types in code at the keyboard while the other watches for mistakes and thinks strategically about whether the code is being written correctly and whether the right code is being written.
- **Support pair programming with coding standards** - Have a coding standard in place before pairing, so the pair stays focused on programming rather than on philosophical coding-style discussions. Pair programming will not be effective if the pair spends its time arguing about coding style; standardize the "accidental attributes" of programming so the pair can focus on the "essential" task at hand.
- **Do not let pair programming turn into watching** - The person without the keyboard must be an active participant: analyzing the code, thinking ahead to what will be coded next, evaluating the design, and planning how to test the code. Verify that both partners are participating actively.
- **Do not force pair programming of the easy stuff** - Avoid pair programming everything; select the assignments that will really benefit from it. One group that used pair programming for the most complicated code found it more expedient to do detailed design at the whiteboard for 15 minutes and then program solo; most organizations that try pair programming settle into using pairs for part of their work but not all of it.
- **Rotate pairs and work assignments regularly** - Benefit arises from different programmers learning different parts of the system; some experts recommend changing pairs as often as daily.
- **Encourage pairs to match each other's pace** - One partner going too fast limits the benefit of the other partner; the faster partner needs to slow down, or the pair should be broken up and reconfigured with different partners.
- **Make sure both partners can see the monitor** - Mundane issues such as monitor visibility and fonts that are too small cause real problems.
- **Do not force people who do not like each other to pair** - Personality conflicts prevent effective pairing; be sensitive to personality matches.
- **Avoid pairing all newbies** - Pair programming works best when at least one partner has paired before.
- **Assign a team leader** - Even at 100 percent pairing, assign one person to coordinate work assignments, be accountable for results, and act as the focal point for management and other people outside the project.
- **Benefits to expect** - Expect these benefits from pair programming:
  - Holds up better under stress than solo development; pairs encourage each other to keep quality high even under pressure to write quick and dirty code.
  - Improves code quality; readability and understandability tend to rise to the level of the best programmer on the team.
  - Shortens schedules; pairs tend to write code faster and with fewer errors, so less time is spent correcting defects at the end.
  - Produces the general benefits of collaborative construction: disseminating corporate culture, mentoring junior programmers, fostering collective ownership.

### 21.3 Formal Inspections

- **Definition and distinguishing properties** - An inspection is a specific kind of review shown to be extremely effective at detecting defects and relatively economical compared with testing. An inspection differs from a run-of-the-mill review in that:
  - Checklists focus reviewers' attention on areas that have been problems in the past.
  - The inspection focuses on defect detection, not correction.
  - Reviewers prepare beforehand and arrive with a list of the problems they discovered.
  - Distinct roles are assigned to all participants - moderator, reviewer, scribe, and so on.
  - The moderator is not the author of the work product under inspection.
  - All participants have received specific training in conducting inspections, and the moderator has received special training in moderation skills.
  - Reviewers are given enough time to prepare before the meeting, and the inspection meeting is held only if all participants have adequately prepared.
  - Data is collected at each inspection, including error types, and fed into future inspections to improve them.
  - General management does not attend the inspection meeting unless a project plan or other management material is being inspected; technical leaders might attend.
- **Results to expect** - Expect these results from inspections:
  - Individual inspections typically catch about 60 percent of defects, higher than other techniques except prototyping and high-volume beta testing.
  - Combined design and code inspections usually remove 70-85 percent or more of the defects in a product.
  - Inspections identify error-prone classes early and result in 20-30 percent fewer defects per 1000 lines of code than less formal review practices.
  - Designers and coders learn to improve their work through participating in inspections, and inspections increase productivity by about 20 percent.
  - On a project using inspections for design and code, inspections take about 10-15 percent of project budget and typically reduce overall project cost.
- **Use inspections to assess technical progress** - Inspections answer two questions as byproducts: is the technical work being done, and is it being done well.

#### Roles during an inspection

- **Moderator** - Keeps the inspection moving fast enough to be productive but slow enough to find the most errors possible; must be technically competent, not necessarily an expert in the particular design or code but capable of understanding relevant details; distributes the design or code and the inspection checklist, sets up the meeting room, reports inspection results, and follows up on assigned action items.
- **Author** - Plays a relatively minor role; the design or code must speak for itself. If it turns out to be unclear, the author is assigned the job of making it clearer. Otherwise the author's duties are to explain unclear parts and occasionally to explain why things that seem like errors are actually acceptable; if the project is unfamiliar to reviewers the author might present a project overview in preparation.
- **Reviewer** - Anyone with a direct interest in the design or code who is not the author (for a design, the programmer who will implement it; a tester or higher-level architect may be involved). The reviewers' role is to find defects; they usually find defects during preparation, and the group should find considerably more during the meeting discussion.
- **Scribe** - Records detected errors and the assignment of action items during the meeting; neither the author nor the moderator should be the scribe.
- **Management** - Do not include management in inspections, and make sure management understands that it should not attend inspection meetings; management's presence makes people feel they, instead of the review materials, are under evaluation, changing the focus from technical to political. Management has a right to know the results, so an inspection report is prepared to keep them informed.
- **Never use inspection results for performance appraisals** - Code examined in an inspection is still under development; evaluate performance on final products, not on unfinished work.
- **Participant count** - No fewer than three participants, because separate moderator, author, and reviewer roles cannot exist with fewer, and those roles should not be combined. Traditional advice is to limit an inspection to about six people, since more becomes too large to manage.
  - Researchers have generally found that more than two to three reviewers does not appear to increase the number of defects found.
  - However, these findings are not unanimous and results appear to vary depending on the kind of material being inspected; pay attention to your own experience and adjust accordingly.

#### General procedure for an inspection (in order)

1. **Planning** - The author gives the design or code to the moderator; the moderator decides who will review it and when and where the meeting occurs, then distributes the design or code plus a checklist that focuses inspectors' attention. Print materials with line numbers to speed up error identification during the meeting.
2. **Overview** - Only when reviewers are unfamiliar with the project, the author may spend up to an hour or so describing the technical environment. Treat overviews as dangerous: they can lead to glossing over unclear points. The design or code should speak for itself; the overview should not speak for it.
3. **Preparation** - Each reviewer works alone scrutinizing the design or code for errors, using the checklist to stimulate and direct examination.
   - Preparation rates: about 500 lines of code per hour for application code written in a high-level language; only about 125 lines of code per hour for system code written in a high-level language.
   - The most effective rate varies a great deal, so keep records of preparation rates in your organization to determine the most effective rate for your environment.
   - Consider assigning each reviewer a specific perspective (maintenance programmer, customer, designer); research on perspective-based reviews is not comprehensive but suggests they might uncover more errors than general reviews.
   - Consider assigning each reviewer one or more scenarios: specific questions to answer ("Are there any requirements that are not satisfied by this design?") or a specific task to perform (listing the specific requirements a particular design element satisfies). You can also assign reviewers to read the material front to back, back to front, or inside out.
4. **Inspection Meeting** - The moderator chooses someone other than the author to paraphrase the design or read the code. All logic is explained, including each branch of each logical structure. The scribe records errors as they are detected, but discussion of an error stops as soon as it is recognized as an error; the scribe notes the type and severity of the error and the inspection moves on. If discussions will not stay focused, the moderator might ring a bell to get the group's attention and put the discussion back on track.
   - Keep the rate neither too slow (attention lags, meeting is unproductive) nor too fast (the group overlooks errors it would otherwise catch). Keep records to determine the optimal rate for your environment.
   - Reference rates: 90 lines of code per hour is optimal for system code in some organizations; for applications code the inspection rate can be as rapid as 500 lines of code per hour; an average of about 150-200 nonblank, noncomment source statements per hour is a good place to start.
   - Never discuss solutions during the meeting; stay focused on identifying defects. Some inspection groups do not even allow discussion about whether a defect is really a defect, assuming that if someone is confused enough to think it is a defect, the design, code, or documentation needs clarification.
   - The meeting generally should not last more than two hours, because reviewers cannot concentrate much longer than about two hours at a time; for the same reason, do not schedule more than one inspection on the same day.
5. **Inspection Report** - Within a day of the meeting the moderator produces a report (e-mail or equivalent) listing each defect with its type and severity. The report ensures all defects will be corrected and is used to develop a checklist emphasizing problems specific to the organization.
   - Collect data on time spent and number of errors found over time so you can answer challenges to inspection efficacy with hard data, and so you can tell if inspections are not working in your environment and modify or abandon them as appropriate. Any new methodology needs to justify its existence.
6. **Rework** - The moderator assigns defects to someone, usually the author, for repair; the assignee resolves each defect on the list.
7. **Follow-Up** - The moderator is responsible for seeing that all assigned rework is carried out, and must have a follow-up plan that assures the fixes are made correctly. Follow up the action items assigned at each inspection either personally by the moderator or with a reinspection: depending on the number and severity of errors found, have reviewers reinspect the entire work product, have them reinspect only the fixes, or allow the author to complete the fixes without any follow-up.
8. **Third-Hour Meeting** - Hold an optional informal third-hour meeting after the official inspection so interested parties can discuss solutions, since solution discussion is banned during the inspection itself.

#### Fine-tuning the inspection

- **Never change the inspection process without measuring** - "Instrument" the process so you know whether your changes are beneficial; if you have measured and know your changed process works better, go ahead.
- **Do not remove or combine stages** - Companies have often found that removing or combining any of the stages costs more than is saved.
- **Evolve the checklist from your own error data** - Add the kinds of errors that occur frequently and are not yet on the checklist; remove errors from the checklist that cease to occur. Error data also reveals trouble areas where programmers need more training or support.
- **Limit the checklist to one page or less** - Longer checklists are hard to use at the level of detail needed in an inspection.

#### Egos in inspections

- **Keep the inspection about defects, not people** - The point is to discover defects in the design or code, not to explore alternatives, debate who is right, or criticize the author. Comments like "Anyone who knows Java knows that it's more efficient to loop from 0 to num-1, not 1 to num" are totally inappropriate, and the moderator must make their inappropriateness unmistakably clear.
  - The experience must be a positive one for the author, in which it is obvious that group participation improves the program and is a learning experience for all involved; it must not convince the author that some people in the group are jerks or that it is time to look for a new job.
- **Author behavior: acknowledge and move on** - The author should expect to hear criticisms of several defects that are not really defects and several more that seem debatable, and should still acknowledge each alleged defect and move on. Acknowledging a criticism does not imply agreement. The author must not defend the work under review; after the review the author can think about each point in private and decide whether it is valid.
- **Reviewer behavior: respect author authority** - The author has ultimate responsibility for deciding what to do about a defect; each reviewer must respect the author's ultimate right to decide how to resolve an error. It is fine to enjoy finding defects, and to enjoy proposing solutions only outside the review.
- **Formal inspection finds what informal review misses** - Text that had passed a self-review, review by about a dozen peers, another self-review, copy editor / technical editor / proofreader review, and 10 years of reader-reported corrections (about 200) still yielded several hundred previously undetected errors under formal inspection by teams of three to four prepared reviewers.

#### Inspection summary

- **Why inspection works** - Formal inspection maximizes error-detection efficiency through checklists, preparation, well-defined roles, and continual process improvement: checklists encourage focused concentration; standard checklists and standard roles make the process systematic; a formal feedback loop that improves the checklists and monitors preparation and inspection rates makes it self-optimizing. With that control and continuing optimization, inspection quickly becomes a powerful technique almost no matter how it begins.
- **Inspection models the highest maturity level** - The Capability Maturity Model (CMM) defined by the Software Engineering Institute (SEI) measures the effectiveness of an organization's software-development process; the inspection process demonstrates what the highest level is like - systematic, repeatable, and using measured feedback to improve itself. Apply the same ideas to other techniques to move an organization to the highest possible level of quality and productivity.

### 21.4 Other Kinds of Collaborative Development Practices

- **Weigh the weaker evidence base** - Walk-throughs, code reading, and dog-and-pony shows have not accumulated the body of empirical support that inspections or pair programming have.

#### Walk-Throughs

- **Definition is loose** - A walk-through is any review involving two or more people discussing a design or code, ranging from an impromptu session around a whiteboard to a scheduled meeting with a formal presentation and a formal summary sent to management.
- **Properties all walk-throughs share** - Expect every walk-through to have these properties:
  - Usually hosted and moderated by the author of the design or code under review.
  - Focuses on technical issues; it is a working meeting.
  - All participants prepare by reading the design or code and looking for errors.
  - Serves as a chance for senior programmers to pass on experience and corporate culture to junior programmers, and for junior programmers to present new methodologies and challenge timeworn, possibly obsolete, assumptions.
  - Usually lasts 30 to 60 minutes.
  - Emphasizes error detection, not correction.
  - Management does not attend.
  - The concept is flexible and can be adapted to the organization's specific needs.
- **Results to expect** - Used intelligently and with discipline, a walk-through can produce results similar to those of an inspection, typically finding between 20 and 40 percent of the errors in a program. In general, however, walk-throughs have been found to be significantly less effective than inspections. (Both statements stand: the similar-to-inspection outcome applies only to disciplined, intelligent use; the general finding covers walk-throughs as actually practiced.)
- **Used unintelligently, walk-throughs cost more than they are worth** - The low end of their effectiveness, 20 percent, is not worth much; at least one organization (Boeing Computer Services) found peer reviews of code "extremely expensive," found it difficult to motivate project personnel to apply walk-through techniques consistently, and found walk-throughs became nearly impossible as project pressures increased.
- **Bad review experiences come from informal practices** - When people have bad experiences with technical reviews, it is nearly always with informal practices such as walk-throughs rather than with formal inspections.
- **If the meeting overhead is justified, make it an inspection** - A review is a meeting, and meetings are expensive; if you are going to incur the overhead of a meeting, structure it as a formal inspection. If the work product does not justify the overhead of a formal inspection, it does not justify the overhead of a meeting at all - use document reading or another less interactive approach instead.
- **When to choose a walk-through anyway** - Choose a walk-through over an inspection in these two cases:
  - With a large review group, because it brings many diverse viewpoints to bear; if everyone in the walk-through can be convinced the solution is all right, it probably has no major flaws.
  - When reviewers from other organizations are involved, because inspection roles are more formalized and require practice; reviewers who have never participated in inspections are at a disadvantage, so a walk-through may be the best way to solicit their contributions.
- **Default to inspections** - Inspections are more focused than walk-throughs and generally pay off better; when choosing a review standard for your organization, choose inspections first unless you have good reason not to.

#### Code Reading

- **Definition** - In code reading you read source code and look for errors, and you also comment on qualitative aspects such as design, style, readability, maintainability, and efficiency.
- **Results to expect** - A NASA Software Engineering Laboratory study found code reading detected about 3.3 defects per hour of effort versus about 1.8 errors per hour for testing, and code reading found 20 to 60 percent more errors over the life of the project than the various kinds of testing did.
- **Procedure** - Run a code reading like this:
  - In preparation, the author hands out source listings to the code readers; listings run from 1000 to 10,000 lines of code, with 4000 lines typical.
  - Two or more people read the code. Use at least two to encourage competition between reviewers. If you use more than two, measure everyone's contribution so you know how much the extra people contribute.
  - Reviewers read the code independently; estimate a rate of about 1000 lines a day.
  - When reading is finished, the author hosts a code-reading meeting lasting one or two hours, focused on problems discovered by the readers. No one attempts to walk through the code line by line. The meeting is not even strictly necessary.
  - The author fixes the problems identified by the reviewers.
- **Why code reading can beat meeting-centric reviews** - Treat walk-throughs and code reading as the alternatives to inspections, with code reading offering more flexibility in using each person's time effectively: it focuses on individual review rather than the meeting, so each reviewer's time goes to finding problems instead of sitting in a meeting where each person contributes only part of the time and substantial effort goes into moderating group dynamics, and less time is lost delaying meetings until everyone can meet for two hours.
- **Prefer code reading when reviewers are geographically dispersed** - Code readings are especially valuable in that situation.
- **The meeting is overrated** - A study of 13 reviews at AT&T found 90 percent of the defects were found in preparation for the review meeting and only about 10 percent during the review itself.

#### Dog-and-Pony Shows

- **Definition** - Reviews in which a software product is demonstrated to a customer; common in software developed for government contracts, which often stipulate reviews for requirements, design, and code. The purpose is to demonstrate to the customer that the project is OK, so it is a management review rather than a technical review.
- **Never rely on dog-and-pony shows for technical quality** - Preparing for them might have an indirect effect on technical quality, but usually more time goes into making good-looking presentation slides than into improving software quality; rely on inspections, walk-throughs, or code reading for technical quality improvements.

#### Comparison of Collaborative Construction Techniques

| Property | Pair Programming | Formal Inspection | Informal Review (Walk-Throughs) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Defined participant roles | Yes | Yes | No |
| Formal training in how to perform the roles | Maybe, through coaching | Yes | No |
| Who "drives" the collaboration | Person with the keyboard | Moderator | Author, usually |
| Focus of collaboration | Design, coding, testing, and defect correction | Defect detection only | Varies |
| Focused review effort - looks for the most frequently found kinds of errors | Informal, if at all | Yes | No |
| Follow-up to reduce bad fixes | Yes | Yes | No |
| Fewer future errors because of detailed error feedback to individual programmers | Incidental | Yes | Incidental |
| Improved process efficiency from analysis of results | No | Yes | No |
| Useful for nonconstruction activities | Possibly | Yes | Yes |
| Typical percentage of defects found | 40-60% | 45-70% | 20-40% |

- **Pair programming versus inspection evidence** - Pair programming lacks the decades of data supporting formal inspection, but initial data suggests it is on roughly equal footing with inspections, with positive anecdotal reports.
- **Choose between pair programming and inspection on work-style preference** - Because they produce similar results for quality, cost, and schedule, the choice is a matter of personal style rather than technical substance; some developers prefer working in pairs to working solo, so let a team's developers' work-style preferences drive it, allow subgroups within the team to choose how they do most of their work, and use different techniques within a project as appropriate.

## Code Complete: Ch22 Developer Testing

### Scope and definitions

- **Developer testing defined** - Treat "developer testing" as unit tests, component tests, and integration tests, sometimes extended with regression tests and system tests; it excludes beta, customer-acceptance, performance, configuration, platform, stress, and usability testing, which belong to specialized test staff.
- **System testing** - Execute the software in its final configuration, integrated with the other software and hardware it ships with; use it for security, performance, resource loss, and timing defects that lower integration levels cannot expose.
- **Black-box vs white-box** - Black-box testing hides the internals from the tester and therefore cannot apply to code the tester wrote; white-box (glass-box) testing uses knowledge of the internals and is the developer's mode. Both have distinct strengths; neither replaces the other.
- **Test the class as a glass box, design it as a black box** - Design each class so callers need nothing beyond its interface, but when testing it, read its source alongside its inputs and outputs to test more thoroughly.
  - Accept the tradeoff: white-box testing inherits the same blind spots that produced the code, which is why black-box testing still adds value.

### Role of Developer Testing in Software Quality

- **Do not rely on testing as the only quality practice** - Testing is only one part of a software-quality program; high-quality development methods, especially minimizing defects in requirements and design, are at least as important. Collaborative development practices find a higher percentage of errors than testing, cost less than half as much per error found, and find different kinds of errors than testing finds; combine both rather than substituting testing for review.
- **Assume each testing step misses most defects** - A single testing step (unit, component, or integration) typically finds under 50 percent of the errors present; the combination of testing steps often finds under 60 percent. Plan additional detection practices accordingly.
- **Defects are inserted, not caught** - Bugs enter code only because a programmer put them there; treat every defect as an authored artifact with a traceable cause.
- **Adopt the error-finding goal explicitly** - A successful test breaks the software. This inverts the goal of every other construction activity, so state it deliberately when switching into test mode.
- **Never read an empty test result as proof of correctness** - Testing cannot demonstrate the absence of errors; zero failures is equally consistent with weak or incomplete test cases.
- **Testing alone does not raise quality** - Test results only measure quality. To improve quality, change the development techniques that determine how many defects exist; adding test volume to a bad process does not fix it.
- **Expect to find errors, or you will not see them** - Executing a program while assuming it is clean makes visible errors easy to skip. In a study of experienced programmers testing a program with 15 known defects, the average tester found 5 and the best found 9; the dominant cause of misses was insufficiently careful examination of erroneous output.
  - Actively want the defects surfaced, and want to be the one who surfaces them rather than someone downstream.
- **Budget 8 to 25 percent of total project time for developer testing** - Set the share from project size and complexity; scale toward the low end as size grows, because developer testing consumes a smaller share of total development time on larger projects.
  - Reject the commonly cited "50 percent of project time for testing" figure as a planning target: it lumps testing with debugging, records what projects typically do rather than what they should do, and includes independent testing.
- **Use test results three ways** - Assess current product reliability, direct the specific corrections, and accumulate a defect record over time; use that record to pick training, target future reviews, and design future test cases.
- **Test each unit before integrating it** - Write, mentally check, then review or test each routine or class in isolation before combining it with others, regardless of the integration or system-testing strategy.
  - The gain is debugging, not testing: adding one already-tested routine at a time localizes any new failure to that routine or its interactions. Throwing several untested routines together leaves every one of them suspect.

### Recommended Approach to Developer Testing

- **Cover all four bases systematically** - A systematic approach maximizes defect detection per unit of effort; omit none of the following.
  1. Give every requirement that applies to the class or routine its own test case, confirming the requirement was implemented. Plan these cases at requirements time, preferably before writing the unit under test.
  2. Give every design element that applies to the class or routine its own test case, confirming the design was implemented. Plan these cases at design time, before detailed coding of the routine or class.
  3. Add structured basis testing cases, then data-flow cases, then whatever further cases are needed to exercise the code thoroughly. At an absolute minimum, execute every line of code.
  4. Apply a checklist of the error kinds already made on this project or on previous projects, writing a test case for each error kind that has occurred frequently before, including the recurring construction errors every programmer accumulates: off-by-one errors, failing to reinitialize a loop variable, and the like.
- **Test requirements that are commonly omitted** - Explicitly test security level, storage, the installation procedure, and system reliability; these are legitimate test targets and are routinely left out of requirements.
- **Design test cases alongside the product** - Doing so surfaces requirements and design errors, which cost more to fix than coding errors, and plans detection as early as possible because early fixes are cheaper.

### Test first or test last

- **Write test cases before the code** - Write the test cases for a unit before writing that unit. Test-first minimizes the interval between inserting a defect and detecting it, shortening defect-detection-debug-correction cycles, and is a good general approach.
  - Writing cases first costs no more effort than writing them later; it only reorders the activity.
  - Defects found earlier are corrected more easily.
  - Writing cases first forces some thinking about requirements and design before coding, which tends to yield better code.
  - Writing cases first exposes requirements problems before code exists, because a poor requirement resists being turned into a test case.
  - Save the test cases; testing first does not preclude also testing last with the same suite.
- **Do not treat test-first as a panacea** - It remains bound by every general limitation of developer testing.

### Limitations of developer testing

- **Write dirty tests, not just clean tests** - Developers gravitate to tests that confirm the code works (clean) instead of tests that break it (dirty). Immature test organizations run about five clean tests per dirty test; mature ones run five dirty tests per clean test.
  - Reach that ratio by creating roughly 25 times as many dirty tests, never by deleting clean tests.
- **Distrust your own coverage estimate** - Hundreds of tests can still leave large parts of the code unexecuted, so never treat a sense of good coverage as evidence of adequate coverage. Average programmers believe they achieve 95 percent coverage; actual coverage is about 80 percent at best, 30 percent at worst, and 50 to 60 percent typically.
- **Set the coverage standard at 100 percent branch coverage** - 100 percent statement coverage is a starting point and is not sufficient. Require every predicate term to be tested with at least one true and one false value.
- **Supplement developer testing** - Developer testing is a key part of a full testing strategy, but even done well it cannot supply adequate quality assurance alone; always pair it with independent testing and collaborative construction.

### Bag of testing tricks - incomplete testing

- **Never attempt exhaustive testing** - Proving correctness by test requires every conceivable input value and every combination of them, which is prohibitive even for trivial programs. A program storing a 20-character name, a 20-character address (26 possible characters each), and a 10-digit phone number has 26^20 * 26^20 * 10^10, roughly 10^66, possible inputs; at a trillion cases per second the run would still be far under 1 percent complete after the whole of human history.
- **Select test cases for distinct information** - The art of testing is picking the cases most likely to expose errors. Prefer a few cases that each tell you something different over many cases that repeat the same signal.
- **Eliminate redundant cases** - Drop any planned case whose data is similar to data that already passed and therefore is unlikely to produce a new error.

### Structured basis testing

- **Execute every statement at least once** - Structured basis testing requires each statement to run; for logical statements such as `if` and `while`, vary the cases with the complexity of the controlling expression so the statement is fully exercised.
- **Compute the minimum case count, then build exactly those cases** - Determine the number of paths and develop the minimum set of cases that exercises every path.
  1. Start at 1 for the straight-line path through the routine.
  2. Add 1 for each `if`, `while`, `repeat`, `for`, `and`, and `or`, or their equivalents.
  3. Add 1 for each case in a `case` statement, plus 1 more if the `case` statement has no default.
- **Prefer basis testing over unqualified code/logic coverage** - "Code coverage" and "logic coverage" testing also exercise all paths but omit the minimal-set constraint, so they tend to produce many more test cases than are needed for the same logic.
- **The count is a floor, not a recipe** - Six required cases does not mean any six cases suffice. Construct each case against the same keywords used for the count, ensuring at least one case drives each keyword's condition true and at least one drives it false.
  - For a compound condition, count the operator too and give each part its own falsifying case: one case where the first operand of an `&&` is false, and a separate case where the second operand is false.
  - Falsify a loop's controlling condition on entry so the body runs zero times, for example a record count below 1 for a `for` loop over records.
  - Include one nominal case in which every boolean condition is true, then derive the remaining cases from the individual keyword falsifications.
- **Keep routines short and boolean expressions simple** - Shorter routines have fewer paths and expressions with fewer `and`/`or` operators have fewer variations, so both directly reduce required test cases.
- **Basis testing is not sufficient** - Satisfying it proves only that all code executed; it accounts for no variation in data. Follow it with data-flow, boundary, and bad/good-data cases.

### Data-flow testing

- **Test data usage as rigorously as control flow** - Treat how data is used as no less defect-prone than control flow, and weight it accordingly: declarations plus initializations account for 50 percent or more of code volume.
- **Classify each variable state** - Reason about every variable in terms of three states plus two control-flow markers:
  - **Defined** - initialized but not yet used.
  - **Used** - consumed in a computation, passed as an argument, or otherwise read.
  - **Killed** - previously defined, then undefined: a freed pointer, a `for`-loop index after loop exit in a language that leaves it undefined, a record pointer whose file has been closed.
  - **Entered** - control enters the routine immediately before the variable is acted on, as with a working variable initialized at the top of a routine.
  - **Exited** - control leaves the routine immediately after the variable is acted on, as with a status variable assigned a return value at the end of a routine.
- **Expect only the normal sequence** - Normal usage is define, use one or more times, and possibly kill. Treat any other sequence as suspect.
- **Inspect for anomalous state sequences before testing starts** - Flag each of these patterns:

| Pattern | Why it is suspect | Exception |
|---|---|---|
| Defined-Defined | Defining twice before the value sticks is wasteful and error-prone even when not wrong | none |
| Defined-Exited | Defining then exiting without use is meaningless for a local variable | acceptable for a routine parameter or global variable |
| Defined-Killed | Signals either an extraneous variable or missing code that was meant to use it | none |
| Entered-Killed | A local variable needs no kill if never defined or used | acceptable for a routine parameter or global variable defined elsewhere before the kill |
| Entered-Used | A local variable must be defined before use | acceptable for a routine parameter or global variable defined elsewhere before the use |
| Killed-Killed | Variables do not revive; a double kill is sloppy, and double-freeing a pointer can hang the machine | none |
| Killed-Used | Using a killed variable is a logical error; if it appears to work, as with a pointer into freed memory, that is accidental and will fail at the worst moment | none |
| Used-Defined | May or may not be a defect; always check whether a definition preceded the use | fine when the variable was also defined before that use |

- **Exercise all defined-used paths** - After the anomaly inspection, the core of data-flow testing is covering every path from a definition to a use, at one of two strengths:
  - **All definitions** - test every place any variable receives a value. This is weak: exercising every line of code satisfies it by default.
  - **All defined-used combinations** - test every pairing of a definition site with a use site. This is strictly stronger, because executing every line does not guarantee every defined-used pair is exercised.
- **Derive data-flow cases by extending basis cases** - Start from the structured basis set, which yields some but not necessarily all defined-used flows, then add only the missing pairs.
  - Worked pattern: with `x` defined in both arms of one `if` and used in both arms of a following `if`, the two basis cases (both conditions true; both false) cover every line and give the weak all-definitions form for free, but two more cases with the conditions crossed (true/false and false/true) are required for all defined-used combinations.
  - When stuck, enumerate every defined-used combination exhaustively; it is tedious but guaranteed to reveal the pairs basis testing did not cover for free.
  - Expect several data-flow cases per routine that no basis case covers, typically a variable defined at one site (for example a default initialization) and first used at a distant site inside or after the conditional blocks; each distinct definition site paired with each distinct first-use site is its own case.

### Equivalence partitioning

- **Collapse inputs into equivalence classes** - A good case covers a large region of the possible input data; when two cases would surface exactly the same errors, keep one. Equivalence partitioning formalizes this to cut the case count.
- **Derive classes from each condition** - A comparison such as `withheld < MAX` yields exactly two classes for that condition: values below the limit and values at or above it. Test one representative per class for that part of the program.
  - Other parts of the program may impose additional related classes on the same variable, requiring more than two values overall; scope the class count to the condition being tested.
- **Apply it where basis and data-flow testing are blind** - Equivalence partitioning adds little once basis and data-flow coverage exist, but it is especially valuable when testing from a specification rather than source, or when the data is complicated in ways the program's logic does not reflect.

### Error guessing

- **Use error guessing as a deliberate heuristic** - Generate cases deterministically first, from structured basis testing, data-flow analysis, boundary analysis, classes of bad data, and classes of good data; then add cases from informed guesses about where the program is likely to be wrong, driven by intuition and past experience rather than randomness.
- **Maintain a defect history to guide the guesses** - Keep records of the error kinds you have made before and check new code against that list; recorded history raises the hit rate of guessed cases.

### Boundary analysis

- **Attack boundary conditions first** - Off-by-one errors are among the most productive targets: writing `num - 1` for `num`, or `>=` for `>`.
- **Use three cases per boundary** - For a range bounded by `max`, test just below `max`, exactly `max`, and just above `max`; all three are needed to rule out the common mistakes.
  - For a condition `value < MAX`, the first true-side case sets `value` to `MAX - 1`, the false-side case sets it to `MAX + 1`, and a third case sets it exactly to `MAX`. The first two usually already exist from basis testing; the on-the-boundary case must be added deliberately.
- **Apply boundary analysis to minimum and maximum allowable values** - Include the minimum and maximum legal value of each relevant quantity, but exclude values whose computation lies outside the routine under test.

### Compound boundaries

- **Test boundaries formed by combinations of variables** - A boundary can arise from interacting values, not a single limit; test the combinations of input data that could drive a computed variable too small or too large. For multiplied operands, test both large positive, both large negative, and zero. Test the case where every string passed in is unusually long.
- **Test accumulators against many large inputs at once** - Drive running totals with a large group of maximal records, for example 1000 employees each at a $250,000 salary with no prior withholding and all opting into retirement withholding, and check every accumulated total. What counts as "large" is defined by the system under development, not by this figure.
- **Test the mirror-image case with minimal values** - Also run a small group of records whose values are all zero, for example 10 employees each with a $0.00 salary.

### Classes of bad data

- **Test each class of bad data** - Beyond boundaries, guess errors by feeding:
  - Starved input - no data at all, or less than the routine needs.
  - Excess input - for example an array of 100,000,000 records, with the threshold for excess defined per system.
  - Invalid input, meaning data of the wrong kind - for example a negative salary, or a negative record count.
  - Data of the wrong size.
  - Data that was never initialized.
- **Skip classes already covered, and accept that some yield nothing** - Cases such as "too little data" are often already covered by earlier basis and compound-boundary cases, and some classes (for example wrong size of data) may produce no case for a given routine; do not manufacture filler cases.

### Classes of good data

- **Test the nominal case as a defect candidate** - The expected, middle-of-the-road path can itself be wrong; never assume it is correct because it is normal. Basis-testing nominal cases supply one kind of good data.
- **Test the minimum normal configuration** - Build the set of minimum values from what is normally expected, not from the absolute legal limits, and exercise a group of items together: saving an empty spreadsheet, saving an empty document, processing a group of one record.
- **Test the maximum normal configuration** - Build the set of maximum expected values: saving or printing a spreadsheet at the maximum size advertised on the packaging, saving a document at the largest recommended size, processing the maximum normal record count (for example 500 employees).
- **Test compatibility with old data** - When a routine or program replaces an older one, require identical results on old data, except where the old behavior was defective. Test old hardware, old operating-system versions, and interfaces with old versions of other software as well. This continuity requirement is the basis of regression testing: confirm that corrections and enhancements do not backslide below previous quality levels.
  - This criterion adds no cases when there is no predecessor.

### Use test cases that make hand-checks convenient

- **Choose round, easily hand-computed test values** - Verifying that a case found an error requires knowing the correct answer, which usually means computing it by hand. Values like $90,783.82 make the hand calculation as error-prone as the code; values like $20,000 make it trivial.
- **Do not assume ugly values find more errors** - An awkward number is no more likely to reveal a defect than any other member of its equivalence class.

### Case accumulation for one routine - technique to cases added

| Technique | What it contributes |
|---|---|
| Structured basis testing | Cases 1-6: nominal all-true case, plus one case falsifying each counted keyword, including a separate case for each operand of a compound `&&` |
| Data-flow testing (all defined-used) | Cases 7-9: each definition site paired with a distinct first-use site not guaranteed by the basis cases |
| Boundary analysis | Case 10: value exactly on the boundary; the just-below and just-above cases already exist |
| Compound boundaries | Cases 11-12: large group with large values; small group with zero values |
| Classes of bad data | Cases 13-15: too much data; wrong kind of data (negative value, negative count) |
| Classes of good data | Cases 16-17: minimum normal configuration; maximum normal configuration |

### Where Errors Concentrate

- **Never assume defects spread evenly** - do not estimate defect count by multiplying a project-wide density (for example 10 defects per 1000 lines) by a class's size; defects cluster instead.
- **80/20 defect clustering** - expect 80% of errors in 20% of classes or routines, and 50% of errors in 5% of classes; target testing, review, and rework at that minority.
- **Cost clustering** - 20% of routines consume 80% of development cost; the expensive 20% is not provably the same set as the defect-heavy 20%, so treat the overlap as strongly suggestive, not certain.
- **Error-prone routines are the most expensive code that exists** - an error-prone routine can carry as many as 50 defects per 1000 lines, and fixing such routines has often run to 10 times what building the whole system cost (counting field maintenance and customer support).
- **Also suspect overly complex routines** - routines with high complexity are a second reliable error-heavy class; simplify them.
- **Maintenance policy: rewrite, do not patch** - focus maintenance on locating the clustered error-prone classes and routines, then redesigning and rewriting them from scratch rather than repairing them incrementally.
  - Repairing or redeveloping 31 of 425 error-prone classes in IBM's IMS cut customer-reported defects 10 to 1 in under a year, cut total maintenance cost by roughly 45%, raised satisfaction from "unacceptable" to "good", and raised release productivity about 15%.
- **General Principle of Software Quality** - improving quality shortens the schedule and lowers cost; removing ~80% of the cost carried by troublesome routines removes a matching chunk of schedule.

### Error Classification and What Follows From It

- **Treat error-taxonomy percentages as suggestive only** - error-type research is inconclusive: studies report wildly different error kinds, and studies covering similar kinds diverge by about 50%, not by hundredths of a percent. Two-decimal precision is spurious, and merging several studies into one combined taxonomy probably yields no meaningful data. Use the split for direction only, never as a planning input.

| Error category (combined multi-study taxonomy) | Share |
|---|---|
| Structural | 25.18% |
| Data | 22.44% |
| Functionality as implemented | 16.19% |
| Construction | 9.88% |
| Integration | 8.98% |
| Functional requirements | 8.12% |
| Test definition or execution | 2.76% |
| System, software architecture | 1.74% |
| Unspecified | 4.71% |

- **Most errors are local** - 85% of errors were correctable without touching more than one routine; when diagnosing, start from a single-routine hypothesis.
- **Many errors originate outside construction** - the three most common error sources were weak application-domain knowledge, unstable and conflicting requirements, and communication or coordination failure; fix those upstream rather than only in code.
- **Blame own code first** - roughly 95% of reported errors come from programmers, 2% from systems software (compiler, OS), 2% from other software, 1% from hardware; assume the OS, compiler, and database are fine until evidence says otherwise.
  - Systems software and tooling now have far broader user bases than in the 1970s and 1980s, so the programmer's share today is likely even larger than 95%.
- **Take typos seriously** - clerical mistakes accounted for 36% of construction errors in one study and 18% of all errors in a 3-million-line flight-dynamics study; 4% of all errors were spelling errors in messages.
  - Spell-check user-visible strings, including strings extracted from the built executable.
  - Three of the costliest software failures on record ($1.6 billion, $900 million, $245 million) came from changing a single character in previously correct code; attention to detail counts down to the single character.
- **Understand the design before coding** - 16% and 19% of errors in two studies came from misread or misunderstood design; spend the time to understand the design fully even though it shows no immediate output.
- **Error-fix effort distribution** - about 85% of errors are fixed in under a few hours, about 15% take a few hours to a few days, about 1% take longer; about 20% of errors consume about 80% of fix resources.
  - Prevent the expensive minority with upstream requirements and design reviews; optimize throughput for the numerous cheap errors.
- **Measure your own defect data** - organization-to-organization variation is large and some findings contradict intuition, so instrument the local development process instead of importing another organization's error profile.

### Construction's Share of Defects

- **Construction always produces a significant defect count** - never treat coding as a minor defect source, regardless of project size.
- **Small projects are construction-dominated** - on a 1000-line project, 75% of defects came from coding versus 15% design and 10% requirements; that split is representative of many small projects.
- **Floor of 35% at any size** - whatever the project's size, at least 35% of its defects trace to construction; some very large projects report proportions near 75%, and even the largest projects put 45-75% of all errors in construction.
  - The proportion of construction-caused errors falls as project size grows, but never to insignificance.
  - The better the application area is understood and the better the architecture, the more errors concentrate in detailed design and coding.
- **Cheaper per defect does not mean cheaper overall** - measured on two very large projects, fixing one construction defect ran at only 25-50% of the cost of fixing one design error, yet construction defects were numerous enough that their aggregate fix cost came to 1-2x that of design defects; reject the argument that construction defects are economically negligible.

### Expected Defect Rates by Process Quality

| Process | Defects per 1000 lines |
|---|---|
| Industry average, delivered software, mixed techniques | 1-25 |
| Microsoft Applications Division, in-house testing | 10-20 |
| Microsoft Applications Division, released product | 0.5 |
| Cleanroom development, in-house testing | 3 |
| Cleanroom development, released product | 0.1 |
| Team Software Process (TSP) | 0.06 |

- **Rates follow process, not luck** - pick the process that yields the target defect rate; results ten times better than the industry average are rare, and results ten times worse are seldom reported because such projects probably never finish.
- **Microsoft-level rates come from a combination** - to target the Microsoft Applications Division rates, combine code-reading techniques with independent testing.
- **Zero-defect results exist but require formal methods** - 0 defects in 500,000 lines (space-shuttle software) required formal development methods, peer reviews, and statistical testing together.
- **TSP prevents rather than removes** - TSP's mechanism is training developers not to inject defects at all.
- **Building high quality is cheaper than building then fixing** - a fully checked-out 80,000-line cleanroom project reached 740 lines of code per work-month against an industry average of 250-300 lines per work-month including all noncoding overhead; the gain comes from spending essentially no time debugging.

### Errors in the Tests Themselves

- **Suspect the test data** - a test case carries an equal or higher chance of being wrong than the code it exercises, and hunting these errors wastes time without improving the product; when the code reads correct, hand-calculations check out, and new cases pass, re-examine the test data before continuing to hunt in production code.
  - Root cause: tests get written ad hoc, treated as throwaway one-shot artifacts, and get care proportional to that expectation - especially when the code's author writes them.
- **Apply production standards to test code** - design, construct, and double-check tests as rigorously as shipped code; step test code through a debugger line by line and subject test data to walk-throughs and inspections.
- **Plan tests from the requirements stage** - begin test planning at requirements time or as soon as the assignment arrives, to avoid encoding mistaken assumptions into test cases.
- **Keep every test case** - retain tests for regression testing and the next version; never discard them.
- **Integrate unit tests into a framework immediately** - write the unit test first, then wire it into a systemwide framework (for example JUnit) as each test is finished; the framework is what structurally prevents discarding tests.

### Test Scaffolding

- **Scaffolding defined** - scaffolding is code built only to make exercising other code easy.
- **Use mock or stub objects for collaborators** - substitute a dummied-up class ("mock object", "stub object") or low-level "stub routine" for a real dependency, with realism tuned to the veracity actually needed. A stub can:
  - return immediately doing nothing;
  - validate the data passed to it;
  - print a diagnostic or echo its parameters, or log to a file;
  - take return values from interactive input;
  - return one fixed answer for all inputs;
  - consume the clock cycles budgeted for the real component;
  - behave as a slower, larger, simpler, or less accurate stand-in for the real component.
- **Use a driver or test harness to call the code under test** - a driver ("test harness") is a fake caller that can:
  - invoke the object with a fixed input set;
  - prompt interactively and invoke with the entered input;
  - take command-line arguments and invoke with them, where the OS supports it;
  - read arguments from a file and invoke with them;
  - iterate predefined input sets across multiple invocations.
- **Use dummy files** - build a miniature file carrying the same component types as the real one; small size means its exact contents are known and it is credibly error-free, and it can be designed so any misuse is conspicuous.
- **Justify scaffolding by reuse and depth** - scaffolding pays back whenever a defect is later found in the class, isolates the class from interference by other classes, and is especially worthwhile for subtle algorithms and for code buried so deep that each test case otherwise takes minutes to run; minutes spent building it save hours of debugging.
- **Prefer an existing framework** - use JUnit, CppUnit, NUnit, or equivalent, and use available tools that automate mock-object creation.
  - Fallback when no framework supports the environment: add a `main()` scaffolding routine in the file that reads command-line arguments and calls the routine under test, so the routine can be exercised standalone before integration.
  - On integration, leave the scaffolding in place at the bottom of the file and deactivate it with preprocessor directives or comments; preprocessed-out scaffolding does not reach the executable, stays available for reuse, and costs nothing to keep.

### Other Test-Support Tools

- **Diff tools for regression comparison** - redirect program output to a file and compare it against a previously saved expected-output file with a file-comparison tool such as `diff`; any difference is a regression error.
- **Test-data generators** - write code that systematically exercises chosen parts of the program.
  - Randomize the inputs that matter (random content, random size 0K-500K, random password length 1-255) and verify by round-trip comparison against an untouched copy, byte by byte: generate two copies, transform one, reinitialize, reverse the transform, then compare.
  - On any mismatch, print everything needed to reproduce the failure.
  - Expect this to pay off fast and then to earn confidence at volume: about 100 generated cases exposed two real defects that lay in special cases unlikely to appear in practice, after which weeks of running over 100,000 files error-free justified asserting the code correct across the tested ranges of content, length, and password.
