- **False: certain operations are "probably" faster or smaller than others** - there is no "probably" in performance. Always measure to learn whether a change helped or hurt.
  - The outcome changes with language, compiler, compiler version, library, library version, processor, and available memory; what holds on one machine with one toolchain can be false on another.
  - Consequences that argue against code tuning: a technique that speeds one environment can slow another, breaking portability; a compiler upgrade may perform your hand optimization automatically, wasting the work; hand tuning can defeat stronger compiler optimizations designed to operate on straightforward code.
  - **Reprofiling obligation** - tuning code commits you to re-profiling every optimization after any change of compiler brand, compiler version, or library version; skipping this lets a former win become a loss.
- **False: optimize as you go** - "premature optimization is the root of all evil"; small efficiencies should be ignored roughly 97 percent of the time. Micro-optimizing routine by routine hides the global optimizations.
  - Bottlenecks are nearly impossible to identify before the program works completely; programmers guess badly, so optimize-as-you-go spends on average 96 percent of its optimization time on code that does not need it, leaving little for the 4 percent that does.
  - Even when a bottleneck is guessed right, it gets overkilled while others become critical, reducing performance. Post-completion optimization exposes each problem area and its relative importance so effort can be allocated.
  - Early optimization crowds out correctness, information hiding, and readability, which are harder to retrofit than performance. Post hoc performance work usually touches under 5 percent of the code, whereas readability work touches 100 percent.
  - Spending the time saved by writing the simplest program on optimizing the working program always outperforms indiscriminate optimization during development.
  - **Name the core defect - lack of perspective** - premature optimization sacrifices final code speed, the performance attributes that outrank code speed, program quality, and the users themselves.
  - **Exception - if you must optimize before completion, build in perspective**: specify size and speed goals per feature and optimize only to meet those goals as you go.
  - **When post hoc tuning is insufficient** and the completed code needs major change, the defect is inadequate architecture, not inadequate code quality; localized optimizations would not have delivered the needed gains either.
- **False: a fast program is as important as a correct one** - correctness precedes speed almost always. An incorrect program can be made arbitrarily fast, which makes its speed meaningless.
  - **Exception** - a minority class of projects (smaller than commonly assumed and shrinking) does have speed or size as a major concern; for those, address the performance risks in up-front design. For all others, early optimization threatens overall software quality, performance included.

### When to Tune

- **Jackson's Rules of Optimization** - Rule 1: do not do it. Rule 2 (experts only): do not do it yet, meaning not until a completely clear, unoptimized solution exists.
- **Ordered procedure for reaching the point where tuning is allowed** - work these steps in order:
  1. Use a high-quality design.
  2. Make the program correct.
  3. Make it modular and easily modifiable so later work is cheap.
  4. When it is complete and correct, measure performance.
  5. Only if it is too slow or too large, make it fast and small.
- **Never optimize before you know you need to** - the need is established by measurement, not by prediction.
- **Reject "rewrite the whole code base in assembler" as a response to a slow program** - schedule the hot few percent for tuning near the end of the project instead. One graphing program taking 45 minutes per graph dropped to under 30 seconds from a small number of code-tuning changes found in a day's work; under 1 percent of the code accounted for 90 percent of run time, and later tuning brought the same graph to a little over 1 second.

### Compiler Optimizations

- **Assume modern optimizers are stronger than expected** - a compiler can optimize a nested loop as well as a hand rewrite in a supposedly more efficient style.
- **Benchmark candidate compilers on your own program** - compilers differ in strengths and weaknesses, and some suit a given program far better than others; the same applies across JVMs.
- **Write straightforward code so the optimizer can work** - optimizers handle straightforward code better than tricky code; playing games with loop indexes makes the compiler's job harder and hurts the program. A straightforward version compiled 11 percent faster than comparable "tricky" code.
- **Calibration - compiler gain vs hand-tuning gain** - a good optimizing compiler can improve speed 40 percent or more across the board, while many manual code-tuning techniques yield only 15-30 percent. Default to clear code plus the optimizer.
- **Verify your own toolchain's optimizer gain** - the effect is highly uneven. Insertion-sort routine, optimizations off vs on:

  | Language / Runtime | Time Without Optimizations | Time With Optimizations | Time Savings | Performance Ratio |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | C++ compiler 1 | 2.21 | 1.05 | 52% | 2:1 |
  | C++ compiler 2 | 2.78 | 1.15 | 59% | 2.5:1 |
  | C++ compiler 3 | 2.43 | 1.25 | 49% | 2:1 |
  | C# compiler | 1.55 | 1.55 | 0% | 1:1 |
  | Visual Basic | 1.78 | 1.78 | 0% | 1:1 |
  | Java VM 1 | 2.77 | 2.77 | 0% | 1:1 |
  | Java VM 2 | 1.39 | 1.38 | <1% | 1:1 |
  | Java VM 3 | 2.63 | 2.63 | 0% | 1:1 |

  - Some compilers optimize better than others; some are already better with optimizations off. Measure your own compiler, JVM, or both.
  - **Two figures stand side by side; apply each to its own condition** - the across-the-board 40-percent-or-more claim holds for toolchains whose optimizer does real work (the three C++ compilers above, 49 to 59 percent), while the C# compiler, Visual Basic, and all three JVMs measured 0 to under 1 percent. Never assume the optimizer buys anything on an unmeasured toolchain.

### Reading and Producing Benchmark Numbers

- **Compare only within one table row** - times are in seconds and carry meaning only for the variants sitting in the same row; they are not comparable between separate tests.
- **Run enough iterations** - benchmark figures should aggregate several thousand to many million executions of the fragment to smooth sample-to-sample noise.
- **Do not generalize across environments** - actual times vary with the compiler, the compiler options, and the run environment; brands and versions differ enough that they are not interchangeable.
- **Treat cross-language results as often meaningless** - compilers for different languages do not always offer comparable code-generation options, so a language-to-language comparison may carry no information.
- **Treat interpreted-language results as weaker evidence** - benchmark figures for interpreted languages such as PHP and Python are typically based on under 1 percent of the test runs used for the other languages, so do not weight them equally.
- **Expect rounding drift** - a stated savings percentage may not recompute exactly from the rounded straight-time and tuned-time entries.

### Kinds of Fat and Molasses - Common Sources of Inefficiency

- **Profile before believing anything is slow or large** - only profiling identifies the slow and fat parts with confidence; historically suspect operations are merely a starting list for investigation, never a substitute for measurement.
- **Eliminate unnecessary I/O first** - unnecessary input/output is one of the largest sources of inefficiency.
  - **Prefer an in-memory data structure** when the choice is between working with data in memory versus on disk, in a database, or across a network. **Exception**: choose the external medium when space is critical.
  - Random access to 100 in-memory array elements vs 100 records in a disk file - in-memory access is on the order of 1000 times faster; with one C++ compiler the in-memory time was below measurement resolution:

    | Language | External File Time | In-Memory Data Time | Time Savings | Performance Ratio |
    |---|---|---|---|---|
    | C++ | 6.04 | 0.000 | 100% | n/a |
    | C# | 12.8 | 0.010 | 100% | 1000:1 |

  - Sequential access shows the same direction (these runs used 13 times the data volume of the random-access runs, so the two tests are not comparable with each other):

    | Language | External File Time | In-Memory Data Time | Time Savings | Performance Ratio |
    |---|---|---|---|---|
    | C++ | 3.29 | 0.021 | 99% | 150:1 |
    | C# | 2.60 | 0.030 | 99% | 85:1 |

  - A slower external medium, such as a hard disk reached over a network, widens the gap further. Random access against a network location instead of the local machine:

    | Language | Local File Time | Network File Time | Time Savings |
    |---|---|---|---|
    | C++ | 6.04 | 6.64 | -10% |
    | C# | 12.8 | 14.1 | -10% |

  - Network results vary sharply with network speed, network load, distance to the networked drive, and the relative speed of the networked and local drives; measure in the target environment rather than reusing these figures.
  - **Keep the two ratios distinct** - the roughly 1000:1 figure compares in-memory access against file access; the roughly 10 percent penalty compares a local file against a network file. Neither figure substitutes for the other.
- **Treat I/O as a red flag in speed-critical code** - in-memory access is fast enough relative to I/O that any I/O inside a speed-critical path must be justified or removed.
- **Count page swaps as a first-order cost** - any operation that makes the operating system swap memory pages runs much slower than the same work confined to a single page, so keep hot working sets inside one page wherever the data layout allows it.
- **Traverse multidimensional arrays in memory-layout order** - iterate so the fastest-changing subscript is the one that stays within a memory page; a loop nest ordered against the layout can fault a page on every single element access.
  - When a single array element occupies about 4000 bytes on a system with 4K pages and the array has many rows, an inner loop over rows changes row on every access and therefore pages to disk on every access; swapping the nest so rows are the outer loop cuts row switches from `MAX_ROWS * MAX_COLUMNS` to `MAX_ROWS`.
  - Measured payoff varies wildly by available memory: about 1000x faster on a memory-limited machine, as little as 2x on a machine with more memory, and no measurable difference at all except at very large `MAX_ROWS` and `MAX_COLUMNS`. Never assume the win without measuring on the target machine.

    ```java
    // BAD - switches rows on every access
    for ( column = 0; column < MAX_COLUMNS; column++ ) {
        for ( row = 0; row < MAX_ROWS; row++ ) {
            table[ row ][ column ] = BlankTableElement();
        }
    }
    // GOOD - switches rows MAX_ROWS times
    for ( row = 0; row < MAX_ROWS; row++ ) {
        for ( column = 0; column < MAX_COLUMNS; column++ ) {
            table[ row ][ column ] = BlankTableElement();
        }
    }
    ```

- **Assume system calls are expensive and measure them** - calls into system routines are often costly because they frequently force a context switch (save program state, restore kernel state, then reverse). System routines include disk, keyboard, screen, printer and other device I/O, memory management, and some utility routines. If performance matters, find out the actual cost of your system calls before designing around them.
- **Three responses when system calls are the bottleneck** - apply only after measurement shows the calls are expensive:
  1. Write your own service from lower-level primitives when you need only a fraction of the system routine's functionality; the replacement can be faster, smaller and better fitted.
  2. Avoid calling into the system at all.
  3. Report the weak-performing call to the system vendor and work with them to speed it up.
- **Audit base-class constructors of high-volume objects for hidden system calls** - a constructor that queries the system on every instantiation multiplies into tens of thousands of system-level calls. Overriding such a constructor to initialize the field to a constant (for example a time field set to 0 when the real system time is irrelevant) can yield as much gain as every other tuning change combined.
- **Expect a large constant-factor penalty from interpreted languages** - an interpreter pays a significant cost per statement because it must digest each instruction of the language before it can produce and run the corresponding machine code. If speed is the binding constraint, choose a compiled or byte-code language.

  | Language | Type of Language | Execution Time Relative to C++ |
  |---|---|---|
  | C++ | Compiled | 1:1 |
  | Visual Basic | Compiled | 1:1 |
  | C# | Compiled | 1:1 |
  | Java | Byte code | 1.5:1 |
  | PHP | Interpreted | >100:1 |
  | Python | Interpreted | >100:1 |

- **Read the language table as an order-of-magnitude guide, not a per-snippet prediction** - C++, Visual Basic and C# are comparable; Java is close but tends to be slower; PHP and Python code tended to run 100x or more slower than C++, Visual Basic, C# and Java. For any specific piece of code, one of C++, Visual Basic, C# or Java may still be twice as fast or half as fast as the others.
- **Suspect defects before optimizing** - performance problems are often plain errors: debugging code left enabled (such as trace logging to a file), memory never deallocated, poorly designed database tables, polling nonexistent devices until they time out. Fix the error; do not tune around it.
  - Indexing a commonly used table improved some operations by a factor of 30. Defining that index is ordinary good practice, not optimization, so do not classify it as tuning or defer it to a tuning phase.
  - Do not accept folklore explanations for a slow operation; unexplained slowness that survives a release usually has a mundane, findable cause.

### Relative Performance Costs of Common Operations

- **Use cost tables only to form initial guesses** - never assume one operation is more expensive than another without measuring it; use the table to pick where to look first.
- **All speed tuning is replacing an expensive operation with a cheaper one** - every technique reduces to that substitution, so you need a cost model of the target machine to tune at all.
- **Build your own cost table when the published one does not match your environment** - the measurements are highly sensitive to local machine environment, compiler optimizations and the code a specific compiler generates. The C++ and Java columns are not directly comparable to each other.
- **Discard performance intuitions older than the current toolchain** - relative operation costs have shifted substantially over a decade; 10-year-old cost assumptions are invalid input to a tuning decision.

| Operation | Example | C++ | Java |
|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline (integer assignment) | `i = j` | 1 | 1 |
| Call routine with no parameters | `foo()` | 1 | n/a |
| Call private routine with no parameters | `this.foo()` | 1 | 0.5 |
| Call private routine with 1 parameter | `this.foo( i )` | 1.5 | 0.5 |
| Call private routine with 2 parameters | `this.foo( i, j )` | 2 | 0.5 |
| Object routine call | `bar.foo()` | 2 | 1 |
| Derived routine call | `derivedBar.foo()` | 2 | 1 |
| Polymorphic routine call | `abstractBar.foo()` | 2.5 | 2 |
| Level 1 object dereference | `i = obj.num` | 1 | 1 |
| Level 2 object dereference | `i = obj1.obj2.num` | 1 | 1 |
| Each additional dereference | `i = obj1.obj2.obj3...` | not measurable | not measurable |
| Integer assignment (local) | `i = j` | 1 | 1 |
| Integer assignment (inherited) | `i = j` | 1 | 1 |
| Integer addition | `i = j + k` | 1 | 1 |
| Integer subtraction | `i = j - k` | 1 | 1 |
| Integer multiplication | `i = j * k` | 1 | 1 |
| Integer division | `i = j / k` | 5 | 1.5 |
| Floating-point assignment | `x = y` | 1 | 1 |
| Floating-point addition | `x = y + z` | 1 | 1 |
| Floating-point subtraction | `x = y - z` | 1 | 1 |
| Floating-point multiplication | `x = y * z` | 1 | 1 |
| Floating-point division | `x = y / z` | 4 | 1 |
| Floating-point square root | `x = sqrt( y )` | 15 | 4 |
| Floating-point sine | `x = sin( y )` | 25 | 20 |
| Floating-point logarithm | `x = log( y )` | 25 | 20 |
| Floating-point e^y | `x = exp( y )` | 50 | 20 |
| Integer array, constant subscript | `i = a[ 5 ]` | 1 | 1 |
| Integer array, variable subscript | `i = a[ j ]` | 1 | 1 |
| 2-D integer array, constant subscripts | `i = a[ 3, 5 ]` | 1 | 1 |
| 2-D integer array, variable subscripts | `i = a[ j, k ]` | 1 | 1 |
| Floating-point array, constant subscript | `x = z[ 5 ]` | 1 | 1 |
| Floating-point array, integer-variable subscript | `x = z[ j ]` | 1 | 1 |
| 2-D floating-point array, constant subscripts | `x = z[ 3, 5 ]` | 1 | 1 |
| 2-D floating-point array, integer-variable subscripts | `x = z[ j, k ]` | 1 | 1 |

- **Do not tune the cheap operations** - routine calls, assignments, integer arithmetic, floating-point arithmetic and array accesses are all roughly equal in cost. Target transcendental math functions, which are extremely expensive, and integer/floating-point division. Polymorphic calls cost somewhat more than other call forms.
- **Do not chase object dereference depth** - additional levels of dereference beyond level 2 were not measurable in either C++ or Java, so removing them buys nothing.

### Measurement

- **Measure to locate hot spots, then measure again after tuning** - a small piece of a program usually accounts for a disproportionate slice of its run time; measure first to find those parts, and measure after each optimization to confirm the change improved rather than degraded the code.
- **Never trust intuition about performance** - many performance effects are counterintuitive; 10 lines of code can be both faster and smaller than one line. Certainty about an optimization's effect comes only from measurement.
- **Never trust experience as a substitute for measurement** - prior experience may come from a different machine, language or compiler; when any of those change, every prior assumption is void.
- **Never trade clarity for an unmeasured performance guess** - the only reliable result of an unmeasured optimization is harder-to-read code. If a change is not worth measuring, it is not worth the loss of clarity.
- **Assume the optimizer already did the obvious rewrite** - hand-converting array indexing to pointer arithmetic to eliminate index multiplications produced zero improvement at any matrix size because the compiler's optimizer was already converting array accesses to pointers. Inspect generated code or measure before hand-applying a transformation a compiler may perform.
  - The same pointer conversion is reported to have hurt performance by about 10 percent in one setting and improved it by more than 50 percent in another. The direction of the effect is environment-dependent, so it must be measured per environment.
- **No bottleneck can be predicted or analyzed without data** - expect the real hot spot to be somewhere other than where you think it is.

#### Measurements Need to Be Precise

- **Use precise instruments only** - a stopwatch or human counting is not measurement. Use profiling tools, or the system clock with routines that record elapsed times for computing operations.
- **Measure only the code under test** - whether using a third-party tool or your own harness, isolate the execution time of the code being tuned.
- **Count CPU clock ticks allocated to your program, not time of day** - wall-clock timing penalizes one of your routines for time the system spent running another program.
- **Factor out measurement overhead and program-startup overhead** - otherwise either the original code or the tuning attempt is unfairly penalized.

### Iteration

- **Keep tuning a confirmed bottleneck after the first success** - achieving the desired performance gain through code tuning usually takes multiple iterations: a single technique rarely yields a 10-fold improvement, but techniques combine effectively, so continue iterating past the first one that works and try more than one change per bottleneck.
- **Expect most attempts to fail** - two failure rates apply in different contexts, and both mean planning for a majority of discards and reverting every failure:
  - As general guidance for any tuning effort: typically over half of attempted tunings deliver a negligible gain or make performance worse.
  - In the aggressive DES case study specifically: at least two-thirds of the optimizations tried did not work, and some doubled the run time.
- **Accept that aggressive tuning destroys code quality** - as a rule, the more aggressive the tuning, the less readable and maintainable the result. Transforming the DES code within the high-level language left it barely readable; the assembler rewrite produced one 500-line routine.
- **Judge cumulative, not individual, improvement against the goal** - single techniques rarely suffice: no three or four of the optimizations in the sequence below would alone have hit the target, yet stacked they overshot it. A DES implementation fell from 21:40 to 0:22 (98% total reduction) against a goal of encrypting an 18K file in 37 seconds on an original IBM PC, via this sequence:

| Optimization | Benchmark Time | Improvement |
|---|---|---|
| Implement initially - straightforward | 21:40 | - |
| Convert from bit fields to arrays | 7:30 | 65% |
| Unroll innermost `for` loop | 6:00 | 20% |
| Remove final permutation | 5:24 | 10% |
| Combine two variables | 5:06 | 5% |
| Use a logical identity to combine the first two steps of the DES algorithm | 4:30 | 12% |
| Make two variables share the same memory to reduce data shuttling in inner loop | 3:36 | 20% |
| Make two variables share the same memory to reduce data shuttling in outer loop | 3:09 | 13% |
| Unfold all loops and use literal array subscripts | 1:36 | 49% |
| Remove routine calls and inline all the code | 0:45 | 53% |
| Rewrite the whole routine in assembler | 0:22 | 51% |
| Final | 0:22 | 98% |

### Summary of the Approach to Code Tuning

- **Ordered procedure for deciding whether code tuning can improve a program's performance** - follow this order exactly:
  1. Develop the software with well-designed code that is easy to understand and modify.
  2. If performance is poor:
     a. Save a working version so you can return to the last known good state.
     b. Measure the system to find hot spots.
     c. Diagnose the source: is the slowness caused by a weak design, wrong data types, or a wrong algorithm, and is code tuning the appropriate remedy at all? If it is not appropriate, return to step 1.
     d. Tune only the bottleneck diagnosed in step (c).
     e. Measure each improvement one at a time.
     f. Roll the change back to the version stored in step (a) whenever it fails to improve the code; expect this often, since over half of attempted tunings typically deliver a negligible gain or worsen performance. Never keep a change that costs clarity for an unproven gain.
  3. Repeat from step 2.

### Code Tuning Versus Refactoring

- **Scope code tuning to small-scale changes** - code tuning means small-scale changes, not larger-scale design changes.
- **Do not expect size reductions from code tuning** - performance covers both speed and size, but size reductions come mainly from redesigning classes and data rather than tuning code.
- **Treat tuning changes as anti-refactorings** - refactorings improve a program's internal structure; code tunings degrade internal structure in exchange for performance. Never mislabel a tuning as a refactoring or apply one where structure is the goal.
- **Adapt tuning techniques rather than copying them** - few tunings are general enough to paste into another program; treat each as a pattern to fit to the measured situation.

## Code Complete: Ch26 Code-Tuning Techniques

### Ground rules for every technique in this chapter

- **Treat every code tuning as a degradation of internal structure** - by definition an optimization degrades internal structure; if a change did not degrade internal structure it would not be an optimization, it would be standard coding practice used by default.
- **Code tunings are heuristics, not rules of thumb** - the "rules of thumb" concept applies poorly to code tuning. Treat this catalog as "things to try," many of which will not work in your environment and some of which will work very well.
- **The only reliable rule of thumb is to measure the effect of each tuning in your environment** - results of optimizations vary widely with different languages, compilers, and environments, so you must measure the effect of each specific optimization to be sure of its effect, no exceptions. Without measuring a specific optimization you will have no idea whether it will help or hurt your program.
- **Never follow optimization advice blindly** - specific compiler implementations significantly affect results; the same tuning helps dramatically in one language and hurts in another.
- **Expect the examples in this chapter to violate good-programming rules** - readability and maintenance are usually more important than execution speed or size; these techniques are shown as performance tradeoffs against the other objectives, and several are practices not recommended as general coding practice.
- **Do not stop after one successful optimization** - the first optimization is often not the best; even after you find a good one, keep looking for one that is better. A first tuning may earn 30-40 percent while a second or third earns 90+ percent on the same code.
- **When one optimization fails, try a seemingly similar one** - many times when one optimization does not produce the desired results, a seemingly similar optimization will work as expected.

#### How to read the benchmark numbers in this chapter

- **Times are in seconds and are meaningful only for comparisons across rows of the same table.** Actual times vary with the compiler, the compiler options used, and the environment of each test run.
- **Benchmark results are made up of several thousand to many million executions of each fragment** to smooth out sample-to-sample fluctuations.
- **Specific brands and versions of compilers are not indicated** - performance characteristics vary significantly from brand to brand and version to version.
- **Comparisons among results from different languages are not always meaningful** because compilers for different languages do not always offer comparable code-generation options.
- **Results for interpreted languages (PHP and Python) are typically based on less than 1 percent of the test runs used for the other languages.**
- **Some "time savings" percentages are not exactly reproducible from the table data** due to rounding of the "straight time" and "code-tuned time" entries.

### 26.1 Logic

#### Stop Testing When You Know the Answer

- **Stop evaluating a test as soon as the answer is known** - once you determine that x is not greater than 5 in `if ( 5 < x ) and ( x < 10 )`, do not perform the second half of the test. Improves speed only.
- **Rely on short-circuit evaluation where the language has it** - short-circuit evaluation means the compiler generates code that automatically stops testing as soon as it knows the answer. It is part of C++'s standard operators and Java's "conditional" operators.
- **If your language does not support short-circuit evaluation natively, avoid `and` and `or` and add logic instead** - convert the compound test into nested tests:

```pseudocode
if ( 5 < x ) then
   if ( x < 10 ) then ...
```

- **Apply the same principle to search loops: exit as soon as the answer is known.**

```cpp
// BAD - keeps scanning after the answer is known
negativeInputFound = false;
for ( i = 0; i < count; i++ ) {
   if ( input[ i ] < 0 ) {
      negativeInputFound = true;
   }
}
```

  Any of these fixes solves it:
  - Add a `break` statement after the `negativeInputFound = true` line.
  - If your language has no `break`, emulate one with a `goto` to the first statement after the loop.
  - Change the `for` loop to a `while` loop and check for `negativeInputFound` as well as for incrementing the loop counter past `count`.
  - Change the `for` loop to a `while` loop, put a sentinel value in the first array element after the last value entry, and check only for a negative value in the `while` test; after the loop, see whether the position of the first found value is in the array or one past the end.
- **Expect the payoff to vary a great deal with how many values you have and how often you expect to find a hit.** Benchmark assumed an average of 100 values with a negative value found 50 percent of the time:

| Language | Straight Time | Code-Tuned Time | Time Savings |
|---|---|---|---|
| C++ | 4.27 | 3.68 | 14% |
| Java | 4.85 | 3.46 | 29% |

#### Order Tests by Frequency

- **Arrange tests so that the one that is fastest and most likely to be true is performed first** - it should be easy to drop through the normal case, and inefficiencies should be in processing the uncommon cases. This applies to `case` statements and to chains of if-then-elses. Improves speed only.
- **Do not order cases by ASCII/collation order when you know the input frequencies** - in a `case` statement the effect is often the same as a big set of if-then-elses, so an alphabetic input tested against math symbols, punctuation, digits and space first pays for all those tests. Put the most common cases first (alphabetic, then space, then punctuation, then digits, then math symbols).
- **`case`-statement results by frequency ordering** (input mix: 78 percent alphabetic characters, 17 percent spaces, 5 percent punctuation symbols):

| Language | Straight Time | Code-Tuned Time | Time Savings |
|---|---|---|---|
| C# | 0.220 | 0.260 | -18% |
| Java | 2.56 | 2.56 | 0% |
| Visual Basic | 0.280 | 0.260 | 7% |

  - C#/Java note: because each `switch-case` value must be enumerated individually rather than in ranges, the C# and Java code does not benefit from this optimization as the Visual Basic code does.
- **Same tests written as if-then-elses give a more consistent improvement:**

| Language | Straight Time | Code-Tuned Time | Time Savings |
|---|---|---|---|
| C# | 0.630 | 0.330 | 48% |
| Java | 0.922 | 0.460 | 50% |
| Visual Basic | 1.36 | 1.00 | 26% |

  - Visual Basic note: for the same number of tests the Visual Basic compiler takes about five times as long in the unoptimized if-then-else case and four times as long in the optimized case as with `case`, so the compiler generates different code for the two approaches. Do not assume `case` and if-then-else compile to similar code.
  - **Treat the more consistent if-then-else improvement as a mixed blessing** - in C# and Visual Basic both versions of the `case` approach are faster than both versions of the if-then-else approach, whereas in Java both `case` versions are slower. A more consistent percentage improvement does not mean the structure is the faster one.

#### Compare Performance of Similar Logic Structures

- **Measure `case` against if-then-else in your environment rather than reasoning about which should win** - the same tests can be written either way and either may be better depending on environment. Improves speed only.

| Language | case | if-then-else | Time Savings | Performance Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C# | 0.260 | 0.330 | -27% | 1:1 |
| Java | 2.56 | 0.460 | 82% | 6:1 |
| Visual Basic | 0.260 | 1.00 | -258% | 1:4 |

  - These results defy any logical explanation: in one language `case` is dramatically superior, in another if-then-else is dramatically superior, in the third the difference is relatively small. C# and Java share similar `case` syntax yet their results are opposite each other. There is simply no reliable substitute for measuring results.

#### Substitute Table Lookups for Complicated Expressions

- **Replace a complicated chain of logic with a table lookup when the chain's purpose is to categorize something and act on the category** - in some circumstances a table lookup is quicker, and it is more modifiable. Improves both speed and size.

```cpp
// BAD
if ( ( a && !c ) || ( a && b && c ) )      { category = 1; }
else if ( ( b && !a ) || ( a && c && !b ) ) { category = 2; }
else if ( c && !a && !b )                   { category = 3; }
else                                        { category = 0; }

// GOOD
static int categoryTable[ 2 ][ 2 ][ 2 ] = {
   // !b!c  !bc  b!c  bc
        0,   3,   2,   2,   // !a
        1,   2,   1,   1    // a
};
category = categoryTable[ a ][ b ][ c ];
```

- **Comment table definitions heavily** - a table definition is somewhat difficult to understand; any commenting that makes it readable helps. Well documented, it is no harder to read than the complicated logic chain, and if the definition changes it is much easier to maintain.

| Language | Straight Time | Code-Tuned Time | Time Savings | Performance Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C++ | 5.04 | 3.39 | 33% | 1.5:1 |
| Visual Basic | 5.21 | 2.60 | 50% | 2:1 |

#### Use Lazy Evaluation

- **Avoid doing any work until the work is needed** - lazy evaluation is similar to just-in-time strategies that do the work closest to when it is needed. Improves speed only.
- **Do not build a whole table at startup when only a small percentage of its entries are used** - for a table of 5000 values generated at startup, computing entries as they are needed can make more sense. Once an entry is computed it can still be stored for future reference ("cached").

### 26.2 Loops

- **Look for hot spots inside loops** - because loops are executed many times, the hot spots in a program are often inside loops.

#### Unswitching

- **Unswitch a loop: move a decision that does not change during the loop outside the loop** - switching means making a decision inside a loop every time it is executed. Usually this requires turning the loop inside out, putting loops inside the conditional rather than the conditional inside the loop. Applies to a loop that contains an if test. Improves speed only.

```cpp
// BAD
for ( i = 0; i < count; i++ ) {
   if ( sumType == SUMTYPE_NET ) { netSum = netSum + amount[ i ]; }
   else                          { grossSum = grossSum + amount[ i ]; }
}

// GOOD
if ( sumType == SUMTYPE_NET ) {
   for ( i = 0; i < count; i++ ) { netSum = netSum + amount[ i ]; }
}
else {
   for ( i = 0; i < count; i++ ) { grossSum = grossSum + amount[ i ]; }
}
```

- **Hazard distinct to unswitching: the two loops must be maintained in parallel** - if `count` changes to `clientCount` you must remember to change it in both places, a maintenance headache for anyone else working with the code.
- **Worth about a 20 percent time savings, but not everywhere:**

| Language | Straight Time | Code-Tuned Time | Time Savings |
|---|---|---|---|
| C++ | 2.81 | 2.27 | 19% |
| Java | 3.97 | 3.12 | 21% |
| Visual Basic | 2.78 | 2.77 | <1% |
| Python | 8.14 | 5.87 | 28% |

  - In that specific version of Visual Basic this optimization produces less maintainable code with no offsetting gain in performance.

#### Jamming

- **Jam ("fusion") two loops that operate on the same set of elements into one** - the gain is cutting loop overhead from two loops to one. Improves both speed and size.
- **Precondition: the loop counters usually have to be the same** - two loops that both run from `0` to `employeeCount - 1` can be jammed.

```vb
' BAD
For i = 0 to employeeCount - 1 : employeeName( i ) = ""     : Next
For i = 0 to employeeCount - 1 : employeeEarnings( i ) = 0  : Next

' GOOD
For i = 0 to employeeCount - 1
   employeeName( i ) = ""
   employeeEarnings( i ) = 0
Next
```

- **Two main hazards of loop jamming:**
  - The indexes for the two jammed parts might change so that they are no longer compatible.
  - You might not be able to combine the loops easily; before combining, make sure they will still be in the right order with respect to the rest of the code.

| Language | Straight Time | Code-Tuned Time | Time Savings |
|---|---|---|---|
| C++ | 3.68 | 2.65 | 28% |
| PHP | 3.97 | 2.42 | 32% |
| Visual Basic | 3.75 | 3.56 | 4% |

  Benchmarked with `employeeCount` equal to 100.

#### Unrolling

- **Unroll a loop to reduce loop housekeeping.** Improves speed only.
- **Complete unrolling works well only for a small, known number of elements** - it is not practical when you have a large number of elements or do not know in advance how many elements you will have. (Completely unrolling one loop so that all 10 array accesses were done individually made 10 lines of code faster than 3.)
- **Partially unroll by handling two or more cases per pass; this hurts readability but does not hurt the generality of the loop.**
- **To unroll, convert a `for` loop to a `while` loop.**

```java
// BAD (straight)
i = 0;
while ( i < count ) { a[ i ] = i; i = i + 1; }

// GOOD (unrolled once)
i = 0;
while ( i < count - 1 ) {
   a[ i ] = i;
   a[ i + 1 ] = i + 1;
   i = i + 2;
}
if ( i == count - 1) { a[ count - 1 ] = count - 1; }   // odd count leftover
```

- **Always add the trailing code that picks up the case that would fall through the cracks** - the extra code after the `while` loop is needed when `count` is odd and one iteration remains after the loop terminates.
- **Main hazard of loop unrolling: an off-by-one error in the code after the loop that picks up the last case.**
- **Accept the quality cost consciously** - five lines of straightforward code expanding to nine lines of tricky code is harder to read and maintain; except for the gain in speed its quality is poor. Part of any design discipline is making necessary tradeoffs, so a technique that generally represents poor coding practice may still be the best one in specific circumstances.
- **Unrolled once (gain of 16 to 43 percent, but watch for hurting performance as Python shows):**

| Language | Straight Time | Code-Tuned Time | Time Savings |
|---|---|---|---|
| C++ | 1.75 | 1.15 | 34% |
| Java | 1.01 | 0.581 | 43% |
| PHP | 5.33 | 4.49 | 16% |
| Python | 2.51 | 3.21 | -27% |

- **Unrolling twice can yield further savings, but not necessarily** - Java showed no further gain. Two leftover tests are then required (`if ( i <= count - 1 )` and `if ( i == count - 2 )`). The main concern is how Byzantine the code becomes.

| Language | Straight Time | Double Unrolled Time | Time Savings |
|---|---|---|---|
| C++ | 1.75 | 1.01 | 42% |
| Java | 1.01 | 0.581 | 43% |
| PHP | 5.33 | 3.70 | 31% |
| Python | 2.51 | 2.79 | -12% |

  Both unrolling tables benchmarked for `count` equal to 100.

#### Minimizing the Work Inside Loops

- **Minimize the work done inside a loop: if you can evaluate a statement or part of a statement outside the loop so that only the result is used inside, do so** - it is good programming practice and in some cases it improves readability. Improves speed only.
- **Hoist a complicated pointer expression into a well-named variable outside the loop** - this improves readability and often improves performance, and it saves the pointer from being dereferenced three times per pass.

```cpp
// BAD
for ( i = 0; i < rateCount; i++ ) {
   netRate[ i ] = baseRate[ i ] * rates->discounts->factors->net;
}

// GOOD
quantityDiscount = rates->discounts->factors->net;
for ( i = 0; i < rateCount; i++ ) {
   netRate[ i ] = baseRate[ i ] * quantityDiscount;
}
```

| Language | Straight Time | Code-Tuned Time | Time Savings |
|---|---|---|---|
| C++ | 3.69 | 2.97 | 19% |
| C# | 2.27 | 1.97 | 13% |
| Java | 4.13 | 2.35 | 43% |

  Benchmarked for `rateCount` equal to 100. Except for the Java compiler the savings are unimpressive, implying that during initial coding you can use whichever technique is more readable without worrying about speed until later.

#### Sentinel Values

- **Simplify a compound loop test with a sentinel value** - a sentinel is a value you put just past the end of the search range that is guaranteed to terminate the search. Use sentinels in search loops. Improves speed only.
- **In a search loop that tests both "found" and "not run out of values," collapse three tests per iteration into one** - the classic compound test `while ( ( !found ) && ( i < count ) )` plus the inner `item[ i ] == testValue` test is three tests per iteration.

```csharp
// GOOD
initialValue = item[ count ];   // preserve the original value
item[ count ] = testValue;      // set sentinel
i = 0;
while ( item[ i ] != testValue ) { i++; }
if ( i < count ) { ... }        // value really was found
```

- **Remember to allow space for the sentinel value at the end of the array when you declare it.**
- **Applicable to virtually any linear search, on linked lists as well as arrays.** The only caveats: you must choose the sentinel value carefully, and you must be careful about how you put the sentinel value into the data structure.
- **Savings depend on the element type** - integers:

| Language | Straight Time | Code-Tuned Time | Time Savings | Performance Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C# | 0.771 | 0.590 | 23% | 1.3:1 |
| Java | 1.63 | 0.912 | 44% | 2:1 |
| Visual Basic | 1.34 | 0.470 | 65% | 3:1 |

  Search of a 100-element array of integers.

  Single-precision (4-byte) floating point:

| Language | Straight Time | Code-Tuned Time | Time Savings |
|---|---|---|---|
| C# | 1.351 | 1.021 | 24% |
| Java | 1.923 | 1.282 | 33% |
| Visual Basic | 1.752 | 1.011 | 42% |

#### Putting the Busiest Loop on the Inside

- **In nested loops, put the busiest loop on the inside** - each loop execution must initialize the index, increment it each pass, and check it after each pass. Improves speed only.
  - `for column 0..99 { for row 0..4 }` costs 100 outer plus 100 * 5 = 500 inner, total 600 iterations. Swapping gives 5 outer plus 5 * 100 = 500 inner, total 505 iterations. Analytically you expect (600 - 505) / 600 = 16 percent savings.

| Language | Straight Time | Code-Tuned Time | Time Savings |
|---|---|---|---|
| C++ | 4.75 | 3.19 | 33% |
| Java | 5.39 | 3.56 | 34% |
| PHP | 4.16 | 3.65 | 12% |
| Python | 3.48 | 3.33 | 4% |

#### Strength Reduction (in loops)

- **Reduce strength: replace an expensive operation such as multiplication with a cheaper one such as addition** - addition is usually faster than multiplication, so if you can compute the same number by adding an amount on each iteration rather than by multiplying, the code typically runs faster. Improves speed only.
- **Precondition: the original multiplication has to depend on the loop index** - when the loop index is the only part of the expression that varies, the expression can be recoded more economically.

```vb
' BAD
For i = 0 to saleCount - 1
   commission( i ) = (i + 1) * revenue * baseCommission * discount
Next

' GOOD
incrementalCommission = revenue * baseCommission * discount
cumulativeCommission = incrementalCommission
For i = 0 to saleCount - 1
   commission( i ) = cumulativeCommission
   cumulativeCommission = cumulativeCommission + incrementalCommission
Next
```

| Language | Straight Time | Code-Tuned Time | Time Savings |
|---|---|---|---|
| C++ | 4.33 | 3.80 | 12% |
| Visual Basic | 3.54 | 1.80 | 49% |

  Benchmarked with `saleCount` equal to 20; all computed variables floating point.

### 26.3 Data Transformations

- **Use data-type changes as a powerful aid in reducing program size and improving execution speed** - modest changes in the implementation of a specific data type can improve performance even though data-structure design is a separate topic.

#### Use Integers Rather Than Floating-Point Numbers

- **Prefer integers to floating point for addition and multiplication; change a floating-point loop index to an integer.** Improves both speed and size.

```vb
' BAD
Dim x As Single
For x = 0 to 99 : a( x ) = 0 : Next

' GOOD
Dim i As Integer
For i = 0 to 99 : a( i ) = 0 : Next
```

| Language | Straight Time | Code-Tuned Time | Time Savings | Performance Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C++ | 2.80 | 0.801 | 71% | 3.5:1 |
| PHP | 5.01 | 4.65 | 7% | 1:1 |
| Visual Basic | 6.84 | 0.280 | 96% | 25:1 |

#### Use the Fewest Array Dimensions Possible

- **Restructure data into a one-dimensional array instead of two or three dimensions where you can** - conventional wisdom maintains that multiple dimensions on arrays are expensive. Improves speed only.
  - A 50-row by 20-column two-dimensional initialization took twice as long with the author's then-current Java compiler as the one-dimensional restructuring `for ( entry = 0; entry < numRows * numColumns; entry++ ) matrix[ entry ] = 0;`.

| Language | Straight Time | Code-Tuned Time | Time Savings | Performance Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C++ | 8.75 | 7.82 | 11% | 1:1 |
| C# | 3.28 | 2.99 | 9% | 1:1 |
| Java | 7.78 | 4.14 | 47% | 2:1 |
| PHP | 6.24 | 4.10 | 34% | 1.5:1 |
| Python | 3.31 | 2.23 | 32% | 1.5:1 |
| Visual Basic | 9.43 | 3.22 | 66% | 3:1 |

  Times for Python and PHP are not directly comparable to the other languages because they were run <1 percent as many iterations. Results are excellent in Visual Basic and Java, good in PHP and Python, mediocre in C++ and C# (the C# unoptimized time was the best of the group).

#### Minimize Array References

- **Minimize array accesses generally, not just accesses to doubly or triply dimensioned arrays** - a loop that repeatedly uses one element of an array is a good candidate. Improves speed only.
- **Hoist an inner-loop array reference that does not vary with the inner index out to the outer loop** - one array access per outer-loop execution instead of one per inner-loop execution.

```cpp
// BAD
for ( discountType = 0; discountType < typeCount; discountType++ ) {
   for ( discountLevel = 0; discountLevel < levelCount; discountLevel++ ) {
      rate[ discountLevel ] = rate[ discountLevel ] * discount[ discountType ];
   }
}

// GOOD
for ( discountType = 0; discountType < typeCount; discountType++ ) {
   thisDiscount = discount[ discountType ];
   for ( discountLevel = 0; discountLevel < levelCount; discountLevel++ ) {
      rate[ discountLevel ] = rate[ discountLevel ] * thisDiscount;
   }
}
```

| Language | Straight Time | Code-Tuned Time | Time Savings |
|---|---|---|---|
| C++ | 32.1 | 34.5 | -7% |
| C# | 18.3 | 17.0 | 7% |
| Visual Basic | 23.2 | 18.4 | 20% |

  Benchmarked with `typeCount` equal to 10 and `levelCount` equal to 100.

#### Use Supplementary Indexes

- **Add related data that makes accessing a data type more efficient** - either add it to the main data type or store it in a parallel structure. Improves speed only.
- **String-length index: keep track of the length of a variable-length data type rather than computing the length each time you need it.**
  - C note: strings are terminated by a byte set to 0, so a program must start at the beginning and count each byte until it finds the 0 byte.
  - Visual Basic note: a length byte hidden at the beginning of each string indicates the length, so the program just looks at the length byte. This is augmenting a data type with an index to make an operation faster.
- **Independent, parallel index structure: manipulate an index to a data type instead of the data type itself when items are big or hard to move** - sorting and searching index references is faster than working with the data directly.
  - If each data item is large, create an auxiliary structure of key values plus pointers to the detailed information.
  - If the size difference between the data-structure item and the auxiliary-structure item is great enough, you can sometimes store the key item in memory even when the data item must be stored externally: all searching and sorting is done in memory and you access the disk only once, when you know the exact location of the item you want.

#### Use Caching

- **Cache: save a few values so that the most commonly used values are retrieved more easily than the less commonly used values** - for random disk reads, check the cache first and return from memory rather than disk when the record is present. Improves speed only.
- **Cache the results of time-consuming computations, especially when the parameters to the calculation are simple and the same values tend to be requested repeatedly.**

```java
// GOOD - cache guarded by the exact parameters
private double cachedHypotenuse = 0;
private double cachedSideA = 0;
private double cachedSideB = 0;
public double Hypotenuse( double sideA, double sideB ) {
   if ( ( sideA == cachedSideA ) && ( sideB == cachedSideB ) ) {
      return cachedHypotenuse;
   }
   cachedHypotenuse = Math.sqrt( ( sideA * sideA ) + ( sideB * sideB ) );
   cachedSideA = sideA;
   cachedSideB = sideB;
   return cachedHypotenuse;
}
```

- **Require speed to be at a premium before caching** - the cached version is more complicated and takes up more space; many caching schemes cache more than one element and so have even more overhead. Caching adds complexity and tends to be error-prone.
- **Judge cache value by these factors:** the relative costs of accessing a cached element, creating an uncached element, and saving a new element in the cache; how often the cached information is requested; and in some cases caching done by the hardware. The more it costs to generate a new element and the more times the same information is requested, the more valuable a cache is. The cheaper it is to access a cached element and to save new elements, the more valuable a cache is.
- **Field data point:** in a Microsoft Windows font-proofing program the bottleneck was retrieving each character's width as it was displayed; caching the most recently used character width roughly doubled the display speed.

| Language | Straight Time | Code-Tuned Time | Time Savings | Performance Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C++ | 4.06 | 1.05 | 74% | 4:1 |
| Java | 2.54 | 1.40 | 45% | 2:1 |
| Python | 8.16 | 4.17 | 49% | 2:1 |
| Visual Basic | 24.0 | 12.9 | 47% | 2:1 |

  Results assume the cache is hit twice for each time it is set.

### 26.4 Expressions

#### Exploit Algebraic Identities

- **Use algebraic identities to replace costly operations with cheaper ones** - `not a and not b` is equivalent to `not (a or b)`, saving a `not`. The savings from avoiding a single `not` are probably inconsequential, but the general principle is powerful. Improves speed only.
- **Replace `sqrt(x) < sqrt(y)` with `x < y`** - `sqrt(x)` is less than `sqrt(y)` only when x is less than y, and the savings are dramatic given the cost of `sqrt()`.

| Language | Straight Time | Code-Tuned Time | Time Savings | Performance Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C++ | 7.43 | 0.010 | 99.9% | 750:1 |
| Visual Basic | 4.59 | 0.220 | 95% | 20:1 |
| Python | 4.21 | 0.401 | 90% | 10:1 |

#### Use Strength Reduction

- **Reduce strength in logical and mathematical expressions: substitute cheaper operations for expensive ones** - improves speed only. Substitutions to use:
  - Replace multiplication with addition.
  - Replace exponentiation with multiplication.
  - Replace trigonometric routines with their trigonometric identities.
  - Replace longlong integers with longs or ints, but watch for performance issues associated with using native-length vs. non-native-length integers.
  - Replace floating-point numbers with fixed-point numbers or integers.
  - Replace double-precision floating points with single-precision numbers.
  - Replace integer multiplication-by-two and division-by-two with shift operations.
- **Polynomial evaluation, first reduction: replace exponentiation with a multiplication accumulated each pass.**

```vb
' BAD
value = coefficient( 0 )
For power = 1 To order
   value = value + coefficient( power ) * x^power
Next

' GOOD
value = coefficient( 0 )
powerOfX = x
For power = 1 to order
   value = value + coefficient( power ) * powerOfX
   powerOfX = powerOfX * x
Next
```

  - Noticeable advantage only for second-order polynomials (highest-power term squared) or higher-order polynomials.

| Language | Straight Time | Code-Tuned Time | Time Savings | Performance Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Python | 3.24 | 2.60 | 20% | 1:1 |
| Visual Basic | 6.26 | 0.160 | 97% | 40:1 |

- **A second, theoretically stronger reduction can be slower - measure it.** Accumulating powers via `value = ( value + coefficient( power ) ) * x` counting down from `order` to 1 eliminates `powerOfX` and replaces the two multiplications per pass with one, yet:

| Language | Straight Time | First Optimization | Second Optimization | Savings over First Optimization |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Python | 3.24 | 2.60 | 2.53 | 3% |
| Visual Basic | 6.26 | 0.16 | 0.31 | -94% |

  - This is theory not holding up to practice. One possibility is that decrementing a loop by 1 instead of incrementing it by 1 in Visual Basic hurts performance, but you would have to measure that hypothesis to be sure.

#### Initialize at Compile Time

- **Treat a named constant or magic number used as the sole argument to a routine call as a clue to precompute the number, put it into a constant, and avoid the routine call** - the same principle applies to multiplications, divisions, additions, and other operations. Improves both speed and size.

```cpp
// BAD
unsigned int Log2( unsigned int x ) { return (unsigned int) ( log( x ) / log( 2 ) ); }

// GOOD
const double LOG2 = 0.69314718;
unsigned int Log2( unsigned int x ) { return (unsigned int) ( log( x ) / LOG2 ); }
```

| Language | Straight Time | Code-Tuned Time | Time Savings |
|---|---|---|---|
| C++ | 9.66 | 5.97 | 38% |
| Java | 17.0 | 12.3 | 28% |
| PHP | 2.45 | 1.50 | 39% |

  - `log()` is much more expensive than type conversions or division, so cutting the calls to `log()` by half cut the routine's time by roughly the predicted 50 percent.

#### Be Wary of System Routines

- **Be wary of system routines: they are expensive and provide accuracy that is often wasted** - typical system math routines are designed to put an astronaut on the moon within +/-2 feet of the target; if you do not need that degree of accuracy you do not need to spend the time to compute it. Improves speed only.
- **Most so-called "transcendental" functions are designed for the worst case and convert to double-precision floating point internally even when given an integer argument** - if you find one in a tight section of code and do not need that much accuracy, give it your immediate attention.
- **Replace a floating-point computation that returns an integer result with integer operations** - a chain of integer comparisons (`if ( x < 2 ) return 0; if ( x < 4 ) return 1; ... if ( x < 2147483648 ) return 30; return 31;`) is perfectly accurate for an integer log2, never converts to floating point, and blows the doors off both floating-point versions:

| Language | Straight Time | Code-Tuned Time | Time Savings | Performance Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C++ | 9.66 | 0.662 | 93% | 15:1 |
| Java | 17.0 | 0.882 | 95% | 20:1 |
| PHP | 2.45 | 3.45 | -41% | 2:3 |

- **A right-shift alternative trades speed for portability** - the number of times you can divide a number by two and still have a nonzero value equals log2 of that number:

```cpp
unsigned int Log2( unsigned int x ) {
   unsigned int i = 0;
   while ( ( x = ( x >> 1 ) ) != 0 ) { i++; }
   return i ;
}
```

  - This routine takes about 350 percent longer than the integer-comparison version, executing in 2.4 seconds rather than 0.66 seconds, but it is faster than the original `log( x ) / log( 2 )` version and adapts easily to 32-bit, 64-bit, and other environments.
  - The complicated expression in the `while` condition is particularly hard to read for non-C++ programmers and is a coding practice you should avoid unless you have a good reason to use it.

#### Use the Correct Type of Constants

- **Use named constants and literals that are the same type as the variables they are assigned to** - when a constant and its related variable are different types the compiler has to do a type conversion. A good compiler does the conversion at compile time so run-time performance is unaffected; a less advanced compiler or an interpreter generates code for a run-time conversion, so you might be stuck. Improves both speed and size.
  - Requires conversion: `x = 5` and `i = 3.14` where x is floating point and i is integer.
  - Requires no conversion: `x = 3.14` and `i = 5`.

| Language | Straight Time | Code-Tuned Time | Time Savings | Performance Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C++ | 1.11 | 0.000 | 100% | not measurable |
| C# | 1.49 | 1.48 | <1% | 1:1 |
| Java | 1.66 | 1.11 | 33% | 1.5:1 |
| Visual Basic | 0.721 | 0.000 | 100% | not measurable |
| PHP | 0.872 | 0.847 | 3% | 1:1 |

#### Precompute Results

- **When results are used many times, compute them once, save them, and look them up the rest of the time** - the choice manifests as computing part of an expression outside a loop, computing a lookup table once at program start, or storing results in a data file or embedding them in a program. Improves both speed and size.
- **Restrict the table's index variables to the ones with few distinct values, and recompute the wide-ranging part each time** - in a loan-payment routine, `interestRate` from 5 percent through 20 percent by quarter points is only 61 distinct rates and `months` from 12 through 72 is only 61 distinct periods, whereas `loanAmount` from $1000 through $100,000 is more entries than you would generally want in a lookup table. Since most of the computation does not depend on `loanAmount`, put the expensive denominator of the payment formula into a table indexed by `interestRate` and `months` and recompute the `loanAmount` part each time.
  - Field data point: in a space-wars video game the expensive gravity-coefficient computation affected performance, but the program recognized relatively few distinct distances from the sun, so precomputing the coefficients into a 10-element array was much faster than the computation.

```java
// BAD - the whole formula is recomputed on every call
payment = loanAmount /
   ( ( 1.0 - Math.pow( ( 1.0 + ( interestRate / 12.0 ) ), -months ) ) / ( interestRate / 12.0 ) );

// GOOD - denominator precomputed into loanDivisor, indexed by rate and term
interestIndex = Math.round( ( interestRate - LOWEST_RATE ) * GRANULARITY * 100.00 );
payment = loanAmount / loanDivisor[ interestIndex ][ months ];
```

| Language | Straight Time | Code-Tuned Time | Time Savings | Performance Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Java | 2.97 | 0.251 | 92% | 10:1 |
| Python | 3.86 | 4.63 | -20% | 1:1 |

- **You do not have to create a table to gain from precomputation: hoist the complicated part of the expression outside the loop and use it inside** - computing that denominator once into `divisor` outside a loop over many loan amounts and using `payment = loanAmount / divisor` inside gives:

| Language | Straight Time | Code-Tuned Time | Time Savings | Performance Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Java | 7.43 | 0.24 | 97% | 30:1 |
| Python | 5.00 | 1.69 | 66% | 3:1 |

  - Python improved here but not with the precomputed table, illustrating that a seemingly similar optimization may work when the first does not.
- **Precomputation can take several forms:**
  - Computing results before the program executes, and wiring them into constants that are assigned at compile time.
  - Computing results before the program executes, and hard-coding them into variables used at run time.
  - Computing results before the program executes, and putting them into a file that is loaded at run time.
  - Computing results once, at program startup, and then referencing them each time they are needed.
  - Computing as much as possible before a loop begins, minimizing the work done inside the loop.
  - Computing results the first time they are needed, and storing them so that you can retrieve them when they are needed again.
- **Populate a precomputed table by initialization at program start, by reading it from a disk file, or by initializing to 0 and computing each element on first request** - the last is a form of caching.

#### Eliminate Common Subexpressions

- **If an expression is repeated several times, assign it to a variable and refer to the variable rather than recomputing it** - with a well-chosen variable name this improves readability at the same time as performance (`monthlyInterest = interestRate / 12.0;` used twice instead of computing `interestRate / 12.0` twice). Improves both speed and size.

| Language | Straight Time | Code-Tuned Time | Time Savings |
|---|---|---|---|
| Java | 2.94 | 2.83 | 4% |
| Python | 3.91 | 3.94 | -1% |

  - The savings are unimpressive here because `Math.pow()` is so costly that it overshadows them, or possibly because the compiler already eliminates the subexpression. If the subexpression were a bigger part of the whole expression's cost, or the compiler optimizer were less effective, the optimization might have more impact.

### 26.5 Routines

- **Treat good routine decomposition as one of the most powerful tools in code tuning** - small, well-defined routines save space because they take the place of doing jobs separately in multiple places; they make a program easy to optimize because refactoring code in one routine improves every routine that calls it; and they are relatively easy to rewrite in a low-level language, whereas long, tortuous routines are impossible in a language like assembler.

#### Rewrite Routines Inline

- **Expect no reliable speed gain from rewriting routines inline** - modern machines, and "modern" means any machine you are ever likely to work on, impose virtually no penalty for calling a routine. You are as likely to degrade performance by keeping code inline as to optimize it. In some cases you might be able to save a few nanoseconds.
  - Historical reason the advice existed: some early machines imposed prohibitive penalties, having to swap out the program, swap in a directory of routines, swap in the particular routine, execute it, swap it out, and swap the calling routine back in.
  - Mechanisms if you do it: a language feature like C++'s `inline` keyword, or a macro via a macro preprocessor when the language has no `inline`, switching it in and out as needed.
  - Conflicting guidance retained: rewriting routines inline is classified as a technique that improves speed only. Apply it only where measurement in your environment shows a gain; the measurement here shows Java degrading by 10 percent.

| Language | Routine Time | Inline-Code Time | Time Savings |
|---|---|---|---|
| C++ | 0.471 | 0.431 | 8% |
| Java | 13.1 | 14.4 | -10% |

### 26.6 Recoding in a Low-Level Language

- **Recoding a bottleneck in a low-level language tends to improve both speed and code size** - for C++ the low-level language might be assembler; for Python it might be C.
- **Typical approach to optimizing with a low-level language, in order:**
  1. Write 100 percent of an application in a high-level language.
  2. Fully test the application, and verify that it is correct.
  3. If performance improvements are needed after that, profile the application to identify hot spots. Since about 5 percent of a program usually accounts for about 50 percent of the running time, you can usually identify small pieces of the program as hot spots.
  4. Recode a few small pieces in a low-level language to improve overall performance.
- **Base the decision to follow this path on how comfortable you are with low-level languages, how well-suited the problem is to low-level languages, and your level of desperation.** On a Data Encryption Standard program that remained twice as slow as the speed goal after every other known optimization, a straight novice-level translation to assembler still yielded a 50 percent improvement.
- **Target code whose work is a poor fit for the high-level language** - heavy bit manipulation is not Delphi's forte but is assembler's forte, making a bit-twiddling routine that converts binary data to uppercase ASCII characters a good candidate.
- **Expect less gain when the high-level language is already suited to the operation** - C++ starts stronger at bit manipulation than Delphi, and after recoding both look virtually identical, so the assembler code minimized the initial performance difference between them:

| Language | High-Level Time | Assembler Time | Time Savings |
|---|---|---|---|
| C++ | 4.25 | 3.02 | 29% |
| Delphi | 5.18 | 3.04 | 41% |

- **Rewriting in assembler does not have to produce a huge, ugly routine** - such routines are often quite modest, and sometimes assembler code is almost as compact as its high-level-language equivalent.
- **Effective strategy for recoding in assembler:**
  1. Start with a compiler that generates assembler listings as a byproduct of compilation.
  2. Extract the assembler code for the routine you need to tune and save it in a separate source file.
  3. Using the compiler's assembler code as a base, hand-optimize the code, checking for correctness and measuring improvements at each step.
  4. If your compiler intersperses the high-level-language statements as comments in the assembler code, keep them there as documentation.

### 26.7 The More Things Change, the More They Stay the Same

- **Assume this level of optimization is irrelevant for many common kinds of programs** - computers are dramatically faster and memory more plentiful; where the first edition ran most tests 10,000 to 50,000 times to get meaningful, measurable results, this edition had to run most tests 1 million to 100 million times. When you must run a test 100 million times to get measurable results, ask whether anyone will ever notice the impact in a real program.
- **Still apply these techniques for embedded systems, real-time systems, and other systems with strict speed or space restrictions** - people writing desktop applications may not need this information.
- **The need to measure the impact of each and every attempt at code tuning has been a constant since 1971.**
- **The effect of any specific optimization is less predictable now than it was 10 years ago** - it is affected by the programming language, compiler, compiler version, code libraries, library versions, and compiler settings, among other things.
- **Accept that code tuning invariably trades complexity, readability, simplicity, and maintainability against performance, and adds high maintenance overhead because of all the reprofiling required.**
- **Insist on measurable improvement as the gate** - it resists premature optimization and enforces a bias toward clear, straightforward code.
  - If an optimization is important enough to haul out the profiler and measure its effect, it is probably important enough to allow, as long as it works.
  - If an optimization is not important enough to haul out the profiling machinery, it is not important enough to degrade readability, maintainability, and other code characteristics.
  - The impact of unmeasured code tuning on performance is speculative at best, whereas the impact on readability is as certain as it is detrimental.

### Key Points

- **Code tuning is a controversial, emotional topic** - some people think it is so detrimental to reliability and maintainability that they will not do it at all; others think that with proper safeguards it is beneficial. If you decide to use these techniques, apply them with care.

## Code Complete: Ch27 How Program Size Affects Construction

### 27.1 Communication and Size

- **Do not assume scaling up is taking a small project and making each part bigger** - a 250,000-line program that is 10 times as large as a 25,000-line, 20-staff-month predecessor takes about 30 times the effort, not 10 times.
- **Expect errors to grow superlinearly with size** - a program 10 times as large as one with 500 field-testing errors will have about 15 times as many errors, or more.
- **Match formality to project size in both directions** - a first medium-to-large project can rage riotously out of control if you are accustomed to small projects, and approaches that are too formal will topple a small project under the weight of its own overhead if you are accustomed to large ones.
- **Treat communication paths as growing with the square of team size** - the count does not increase additively as people are added; it increases multiplicatively, proportionally to the square of the number of people.
  - 2-person project: 1 communication path.
  - 5-person project: 10 paths.
  - 10-person project: 45 paths, assuming every person talks to every other person.
  - The 10 percent of projects that have 50 or more programmers have at least 1,200 potential paths.
- **Expect more communication time and more communication mistakes as paths multiply** - the more communication paths you have, the more time you spend communicating and the more opportunities are created for communication errors.
- **On larger projects, adopt organizational techniques that streamline communication or limit it in a sensible way** - the typical approach is to formalize communication in documents (text or graphic, paper or electronic) so that N people read and write documents instead of talking in every conceivable combination. As project size increases, communication must be supported: the point of most methodologies is to reduce communication problems, and a methodology should live or die on its merits as a communication facilitator.

### 27.2 Range of Project Sizes

- **Never assume a single project size is typical** - the range of project sizes is wide enough that no size can be treated as the norm.
- **Distinguish percentage of projects from percentage of programmers** - larger projects use more programmers each, so they employ a large percentage of all programmers even though they are a minority of projects.

| Team Size | Approximate Percentage of Projects |
|---|---|
| 1-3 | 25% |
| 4-10 | 30% |
| 11-25 | 20% |
| 26-50 | 15% |
| 50+ | 10% |

| Team Size | Approximate Percentage of Programmers |
|---|---|
| 1-3 | 5% |
| 4-10 | 10% |
| 11-25 | 15% |
| 26-50 | 20% |
| 50+ | 50% |

### 27.3 Effect of Project Size on Errors

- **Expect project size to change both the quantity and the type of errors** - as project size increases, a larger percentage of errors can usually be attributed to mistakes in requirements and design.
- **On small projects, target construction quality first** - construction errors make up about 75 percent of all errors found; methodology has less influence on code quality, and the biggest influence on program quality is often the skill of the individual writing the program.
- **On larger projects, expect construction errors to taper to about 50 percent of total errors** - requirements and architecture errors make up the difference, presumably because more requirements development and architectural design are required, so the opportunity for errors from those activities is proportionally larger.
- **Do not assume large size always shifts errors away from construction** - in some very large projects the proportion of construction errors remains high; sometimes even with 500,000 lines of code, up to 75 percent of the errors can be attributed to construction. Both statements hold: the general trend is a shift toward requirements and design errors, but specific very large projects remain construction-dominated.
- **Expect defect density, not just defect count, to rise with size** - all other things being equal, a large project will have more errors per thousand lines of code than a small one; the number of defects per 1000 lines of code increases, so a product twice as large is likely to have more than twice as many errors.

| Project Size (in Lines of Code) | Typical Error Density |
|---|---|
| Smaller than 2K | 0-25 errors per thousand lines of code (KLOC) |
| 2K-16K | 0-40 errors per KLOC |
| 16K-64K | 0.5-50 errors per KLOC |
| 64K-512K | 2-70 errors per KLOC |
| 512K or more | 4-100 errors per KLOC |

- **Plan extra quality effort on a large project to reach the same error rate as a small one** - very large projects have up to four times as many errors per thousand lines of code as small projects, so a large project must work harder to achieve the same error rate.
- **Treat the error-density ranges as industry averages, not as a target floor** - the data was derived from specific projects and may bear little resemblance to your own; a handful of organizations have reported better error rates than the minimums shown.

### 27.4 Effect of Project Size on Productivity

- **At small sizes (2000 lines of code or smaller), treat individual programmer skill as the single biggest influence on productivity** - as project size increases, team size and organization become greater influences.
- **Expect team size to affect productivity at very small thresholds** - smaller teams completed their projects with 39 percent higher productivity than larger teams, where "small" was two people and "large" was three.
- **Expect large-project productivity to be lower** - all other things being equal, productivity will be lower on a large project than on a small one; productivity on small projects can be 2-3 times as high as productivity on large projects, and productivity can vary by a factor of 5-10 from the smallest projects to the largest.

| Project Size (in Lines of Code) | Lines of Code per Staff-Year (Cocomo II Nominal in Parentheses) |
|---|---|
| 1K | 2,500-25,000 (4,000) |
| 10K | 2,000-25,000 (3,200) |
| 100K | 1,000-20,000 (2,600) |
| 1,000K | 700-10,000 (2,000) |
| 10,000K | 300-5,000 (1,600) |

- **Do not read the lines-of-code-per-staff-year figures as precise** - productivity is substantially determined by kind of software, personnel quality, programming language, methodology, product complexity, programming environment, tool support, how "lines of code" are counted, and how nonprogrammer support effort is factored into the "lines of code per staff-year" figure, and many other factors, so specific figures vary dramatically; only the general trend is significant.

### 27.5 Effect of Project Size on Development Activities

- **Recognize the shift in what determines success** - on a one-person project the biggest influence on success or failure is you; on a 25-person project your organization is the more likely dominant influence.

#### Activity Proportions and Size

- **Expect the mix of activities to change dramatically with size** - as project size and the need for formal communication increase, the kinds of activities a project needs change.
- **On a small project, expect construction to dominate** - taking up as much as 65 percent of total development time.
- **On a medium-size project, expect construction to remain dominant** - its share of the total effort falls to about 50 percent.
- **On very large projects, expect architecture, integration, and system testing to take up more time and construction to become less dominant** - as project size increases, construction becomes a smaller part of the total effort, so the activities that are taken for granted on small projects must be carefully planned on larger ones.
- **Expect construction effort to scale near-linearly with size while other activities scale faster** - the construction activities (detailed design, coding, debugging, and unit testing) scale up proportionately, a near-linear function of project size, while many other activities scale up faster and nonlinearly.
- **Do not scale requirements effort by program size** - requirements effort is not as directly a function of program size as other activities are.
- **Only transfer practices between projects of similar size** - projects that are close in size will perform similar activities, but as sizes diverge the kinds of activities will diverge too.
- **Expect nonlinear multipliers when size grows tenfold** - a product 10 times the size of its predecessor needs 25 times more construction effort, 25-50 times the planning effort, 30 times the integration effort, and 40 times the architecture and system testing.
- **Scale architecture and requirements spending to project size** - spending about five percent of total project costs on architecture and requirements produced the lowest cost for projects in the 10,000-lines-of-code range, but for projects in the 100,000-lines-of-code range, spending 15-20 percent of project effort on architecture and requirements produced the best results.
- **Treat these activities as growing at a more-than-linear rate as project size increases:**
  - Communication
  - Planning
  - Management
  - Requirements development
  - System functional design
  - Interface design and specification
  - Architecture
  - Integration
  - Defect removal
  - System testing
  - Document production
- **Apply these techniques regardless of project size** - disciplined coding practices, design and code inspections by other developers, good tool support, and use of high-level languages. They are valuable on small projects and invaluable on large ones.

#### Programs, Products, Systems, and System Products

- **Treat quality and complexity of the final software as a size influence** - lines of code and team size are not the only influences on a project's size.
- **Classify the software as a program, product, system, or system product and use the matching cost multiple when estimating:**

| Kind | Definition | Cost relative to a simple program |
|---|---|---|
| Program | The simplest software: a single program used by itself by the person who developed it or, informally, by a few others. | 1x |
| Product | A program intended for use by people other than the original developer; used in environments differing from where it was created; extensively tested before release, documented, and capable of being maintained by others. | About 3x |
| System | A group of programs that work together; more complicated because of the complexity of developing interfaces among the pieces and the care needed to integrate them. | About 3x |
| System product | Has the polish of a product and the multiple parts of a system. | About 9x |

- **Do not estimate a system product from experience building a program** - failure to appreciate the differences in polish and complexity among programs, products, systems, and system products is a common cause of estimation errors; programmers who do this can underestimate by a factor of almost 10.
- **Do not estimate a whole program from raw coding time** - writing 2K lines of code does not take as long as creating a whole program that contains 2K lines of code. A 2K estimate based only on construction experience is only 65 percent of the total time actually needed, so development will take 50 percent more time than you estimate.
- **Expect estimation error from construction experience to grow with target size** - using your own 2K construction experience to estimate a 32K program yields an estimate that is only 50 percent of the total time required; development would take 100 percent more time than estimated.
- **Compound the correction when the target is a product rather than a mere program** - if you also fail to account for the extra degree of polish a product requires, the error could easily increase by a factor of three or more.

#### Methodology and Size

- **Accept that every project uses a methodology** - on small projects methodologies tend to be casual and instinctive; on large projects they tend to be rigorous and carefully planned.
