Any approach to programming constitutes a methodology no matter how unconscious or primitive; the programmer who insists on avoiding methodologies is only avoiding choosing one explicitly.
- **Choose strategies for large projects explicitly** - greater complexity requires greater conscious attention to methodology, and unconscious choices are inadequate on large projects.
- **Do not apply a formal approach that does not fit the project** - formal approaches that are misapplied have overhead that gobbles up their other savings.
- **Expect paperwork share to rise with size** - a project of 1,000 lines of code will average about 7 percent of its effort on paperwork, whereas a 100,000-lines-of-code project will average about 26 percent.
- **Scale formal documentation to the number of people being coordinated** - the paperwork is a direct result of communication-path growth: the more people's brains you have to coordinate, the more formal documentation you need to coordinate them.
- **Write documentation to force thinking and to communicate, never for its own sake** - the point of writing a configuration-management plan is to force careful thought about configuration management and to explain the plan to everyone else; documentation is a tangible side effect of the real planning and construction work. If you feel as though you are going through the motions and writing generic documents, something is wrong.
- **Start your methods small and scale them up rather than paring down an all-inclusive method** - "More" is not better as far as methodologies are concerned; scaling up a lightweight methodology for a large project usually works better than starting with an all-inclusive method and paring it down for a small project.
- **Aim for a "right-weight" methodology** - this is the most effective approach of all: instead of arguing "lightweight" versus "heavyweight," consider your project's specific size and type and then find the methodology that fits it.

## Code Complete: Ch28 Managing Construction

### 28.1 Encouraging Good Coding

- **Let quality goals and program size drive how the project is managed** - both significantly affect how a specific software project should be managed, as does the difference between traditional sequential approaches to development and modern iterative approaches.
- **Do not mandate strict technical standards from the management position** - in general this isn't a good idea; if there are going to be programming standards, the programmers must buy into them.
- **Have a respected architect define standards, not the manager** - software projects operate as much on an "expertise hierarchy" as on an "authority hierarchy"; the team will generally follow standards set by the project's recognized thought leader.
  - Verify the architect really is respected. A senior person who has been around too long and is out of touch with production coding issues will be resented for defining standards out of touch with the work.
- **Offer weaker forms when a group resists strict standards** - use flexible guidelines, a collection of suggestions rather than guidelines, or a set of examples that embody the best practices. Standards are more useful in some organizations than others; some developers welcome them because they reduce arbitrary variance. Good coding practices can be achieved either through enforced standards or through more light-handed approaches.
- **Assign two people to every part of the project** - if two people work on each line of code, at least two people think it works and is readable. Mechanisms range from pair programming to mentor-trainee pairs to buddy-system reviews.
- **Review every line of code** - a code review typically involves the programmer and at least two reviewers, so at least three people read every line.
  - Reviews provide a safety net if the original programmer leaves the project.
  - Reviews improve quality because the programmer knows others will read the code ("peer pressure").
  - Even with no explicit coding standards, reviews move the group toward a group coding standard: decisions are made by the group during reviews and over time the group derives its own standards.
- **Require code sign-offs** - before code is considered complete, senior technical personnel must sign the code listing, meaning that to the best of their knowledge the code is technically competent and error-free.
- **Route good code examples for review** - circulate good code or post it for public display to communicate the quality you're aiming for. A coding-standards manual can consist mainly of a set of "best code listings"; identifying certain listings as "best" sets an example, is easier to update than a prose standards manual, and conveys subtleties of coding style that prose cannot capture point by point.
- **Emphasize that code listings are public assets, not private property** - code is part of the project and should be freely available to anyone on the project who needs it, and must be seen by others during reviews and maintenance even if at no other time.
  - Supporting data: one of the most successful projects ever reported developed 83,000 lines of code in 11 work-years, with only one error causing system failure detected in the first 13 months of operation, completed in the late 1960s without online compilation or interactive debugging; productivity was 7500 lines of code per work-year. The chief programmer reported that a key to success was identifying all computer runs (erroneous and otherwise) as public rather than private assets. The idea extends to Open Source Software and Extreme Programming's collective ownership.
- **Reward good code, with these constraints**:
  - The reward must be something the programmer wants. Many programmers find "attaboy" rewards distasteful, especially from nontechnical managers.
  - Code receiving an award must be exceptionally good. Awarding a programmer everyone knows does bad work destroys credibility; a cooperative attitude or punctuality does not matter.
  - If you are not technically skilled enough to make the good-code judgment, don't - make no award at all, or let the team choose the recipient.
- **One easy standard** - if you manage a programming project and have a programming background, state "I must be able to read and understand any code written for the project." A manager who isn't the hottest technical hotshot is an advantage here: it discourages "clever" or tricky code.
- **Never use a good-practices book as a set of rigid standards** - use it as a basis for discussion, a sourcebook of good practices, and for identifying practices that could benefit your environment.

### 28.2 Configuration Management

- **Assume the project is dynamic** - the code changes, the design changes, and the requirements change; changes in the requirements lead to more changes in the design, and changes in the design lead to even more changes in the code and test cases. Configuration management was not invented by programmers, but because programming projects are so volatile it is especially useful to them.
- **Definition** - configuration management is the practice of identifying project artifacts and handling changes systematically so a system can maintain its integrity over time; also called "change control." It includes techniques for evaluating proposed changes, tracking changes, and keeping copies of the system as it existed at various points in time. Applied to software it is called software configuration management (SCM) and focuses on a program's requirements, source code, documentation, and test data.
- **Control changes to requirements** - otherwise you write code for parts of the system that are eventually eliminated, or code incompatible with new parts, with incompatibilities undetected until integration time when nobody knows what's going on.
- **Control changes to code** - otherwise you may change a routine someone else is changing simultaneously and combining the changes becomes problematic; uncontrolled changes make code seem more tested than it is (the tested version is the old unchanged one); and after finding new errors you cannot back up to the old, working routine.
- **Handle changes systematically or you are thrashing** - unsystematic change means taking random steps in the fog rather than moving directly toward a clear destination, and time goes to thrashing rather than to developing code; configuration management is what makes the time effective.
- **Treat overcontrol as the systemic problem with SCM** - plan SCM carefully so it is an asset rather than an albatross: design the plan to help programmers and to minimize overhead, and check that the approach avoids overcontrolling the project. Properly applied, configuration management makes programmers' jobs easier, and this especially includes change control. Stopping all development would control changes but is a terrible way to develop software.
- **Scale SCM formality to project size**:
  - Small, one-person project: no SCM beyond planning for informal periodic backups is probably adequate, though configuration management is still useful.
  - Large, 50-person project: a full-blown SCM scheme, including fairly formal backup procedures, change control for requirements and design, and control over documents, source code, content, test cases, and other artifacts.
  - Neither very large nor very small: settle on a degree of formality between the two extremes.
- **Adoption data** - a survey more than 20 years ago found over a third of programmers were not even familiar with the idea of configuration management, with little indication that has changed; a more recent Software Engineering Institute study found that of organizations using informal software-development practices, less than 20 percent had adequate configuration management.

#### Requirements and Design Changes

- **Do not implement each improvement idea as it occurs to you** - you end up on a software treadmill: the system changes constantly without moving closer to completion.
- **Follow a systematic change-control procedure** - it makes clear that changes will be considered in the context of what's best for the project overall.
- **Handle change requests in groups** - write down all ideas and suggestions no matter how easy they would be to implement, save them, then view them as a group and choose the most beneficial. Group them either informally, such as through a list of pending changes, or systematically, such as through a change-control board.
  - Failure mode of one-at-a-time handling: a simple change thought of 25 percent through the project while on schedule gets made; another thought of 50 percent through while behind does not. At the end you cannot make any nonessential changes even if the second change is 10 times as good as the first. The best changes slip through the cracks merely because you thought of them later.
- **Systematically estimate the cost, schedule, and quality impact of each proposed change** - estimate the time to make the change including review of the changed code and retesting the whole system, plus time for the ripple effect through requirements, design, code, test, and user documentation. Tell all interested parties that software is intricately interwoven so estimation is necessary even when the change appears small.
  - Refrain from giving an off-the-cuff estimate regardless of how optimistic you feel when the change is first suggested: such estimates are often mistaken by a factor of 2 or more.
- **Treat a high volume of change requests, or any major change, as a key warning sign** - it indicates requirements development isn't yet complete: requirements, architecture, or top-level design weren't done well enough to support effective construction. Backing up to work on requirements or architecture seems expensive but is far cheaper than constructing the software more than once or throwing away code for features you didn't need.
- **Establish a change-control board or its equivalent** - its job is to separate the wheat from the chaff in change requests. Anyone proposing a change submits a change request; the board meets periodically and approves, disapproves, or defers each one.
  - "Change request" means any request that would change the software: an idea for a new feature, a change to an existing feature, an "error report" that might or might not report a real error, and so on.
  - Change-control boards are considered a best practice for prioritizing and controlling requirements changes; however, they are still fairly uncommon in commercial settings.
- **Watch for bureaucracy, but never let fear of bureaucracy preclude effective change control** - lack of disciplined change control is one of the biggest management problems facing the software industry. A significant percentage of projects perceived as late would be on time if they accounted for the impact of untracked but agreed-upon changes. Poor change control lets changes accumulate off the books, undermining status visibility, long-range predictability, project planning, risk management specifically, and project management generally. Ham-handed change control is seen occasionally; no meaningful change control at all is seen 10 times as often.
- **Streamline the mechanism, but keep the substance** - acceptable lightweight forms: a simple "ChangeBoard" e-mail alias people mail requests to; change proposals presented interactively at a board meeting; logging change requests as defects in your defect-tracking software (classified as "requirements defects" or as changes rather than defects). Implement the board formally, or as a Product Planning Group or War Council carrying the traditional responsibilities, or as a single Change Czar - but whatever you call it, do it.

#### Software Code Changes

- **Use version-control software** - use it to facilitate configuration management and to reduce the coordination problems of working in teams; it is indispensable on team projects and works so easily you barely notice you're using it.
  - Locking style: you check a file out; if someone else has it checked out you're notified you can't; you work as you would without version control and then check it in.
  - Merging style: multiple people work on files simultaneously and the tool handles merging changes at check-in.
  - Either way, on check-in the tool asks why you changed the file and you type in a reason.
- **Benefits to expect from version control**:
  - You don't step on anyone's toes by working on a file someone else is working on, or at least you know about it if you do.
  - You can update your copies of all project files to current versions, usually with a single command.
  - You can backtrack to any version of any file ever checked in.
  - You can get a list of the changes made to any version of any file.
  - You don't have to worry about personal backups; the version-control copy is a safety net.
- **Integrate version control, defect tracking, and change management** - version control becomes even more powerful; Microsoft's applications division found its proprietary version-control tool to be a "major competitive advantage."
- **Use version history to diagnose errors** - when a new error surfaces that seems unrelated to your change, compare the new version of the code to the old, and to older versions if needed.

#### Tool Versions

- **Put tools under version control when the exact build environment must be reproducible** - for some kinds of projects you must be able to reconstruct the exact environment used to create each specific version of the software, including compilers, linkers, and code libraries.

#### Machine Configurations

- **Standardize development machine configurations** - create a disk image of a standard developer workstation including all common developer tools and office applications and load it onto each developer's machine. This avoids problems from slightly different configuration settings and different tool versions, and greatly streamlines setting up new machines compared with installing each piece of software individually.

#### Backup Plan

- **Back up work periodically and transfer backups to off-site storage periodically** - guard against disk failure, accidental deletion of key files, sabotage by an angry employee, and loss of a machine to theft, flood, or fire.
- **Back up all important project materials** - documents, graphics, and important notes in addition to source code.
- **Test the backup procedure** - do a restore at some point to confirm the backup contains everything you need and that recovery works. This is the often-overlooked part of devising a backup plan.
- **Make a project archive when a project finishes** - save a copy of everything needed to re-create the product: source code, compilers, tools, requirements, design, documentation. Keep it in a safe place.

### 28.3 Estimating a Construction Schedule

- **Baseline overrun data** - the average large software project is one year late and 100 percent over budget. Surveys of estimated vs. actual schedules find developers' estimates tend to have an optimism factor of 20 to 30 percent, which has as much to do with poor size and effort estimates as with poor development efforts.

#### Estimation Approaches

- **Choose among these ways to estimate project size and effort**:
  - Use estimating software.
  - Use an algorithmic approach such as Cocomo II, Barry Boehm's estimation model.
  - Have outside estimation experts estimate the project.
  - Have a walk-through meeting for estimates.
  - Estimate pieces of the project, then add the pieces together.
  - Have people estimate their own tasks, then add the task estimates together.
  - Refer to experience on previous projects.
  - Keep previous estimates, see how accurate they were, and use them to adjust new estimates.
- **Follow this approach to estimating a project, in order** - good software estimation is a significant challenge; the keys to success are using multiple approaches, tightening down your estimates as you work your way into the project, and making use of data to create the estimates.

1. **Establish objectives** - why do you need an estimate; what are you estimating; only construction activities or all of development; only project effort or project plus vacations, holidays, training, and other nonproject activities; how accurate must the estimate be to meet your objectives; what degree of certainty must be associated with it; would an optimistic or a pessimistic estimate produce substantially different results.
2. **Allow time for the estimate, and plan it** - rushed estimates are inaccurate estimates. For a large project, treat estimation as a miniproject and miniplan it so you can do it well.
3. **Spell out software requirements before estimating** - you cannot reliably estimate a "pretty big" software project any more than an architect can estimate a "pretty big" house. Define requirements or plan a preliminary exploration phase before making an estimate.
4. **Estimate at a low level of detail** - depending on the objectives you identified, base the estimate on a detailed examination of project activities; in general the more detailed the examination, the more accurate the estimate. The Law of Large Numbers: a 10 percent error on one big piece is 10 percent high or 10 percent low; across 50 small pieces some 10 percent errors will be high and some low, and they tend to cancel out.
5. **Use several different estimation techniques and compare the results** - they won't all produce the same results; study the differences, which can be illuminating. No approach is best in all circumstances.
   - Worked illustration: an eyeball estimate of 250-300 pages vs. an in-depth estimate of 873 pages vs. a completely different technique giving 828 pages. Because the two detailed estimates agreed within about five percent, the true value was much closer to 850 than to 250.
6. **Reestimate periodically** - factors change after the initial estimate. Estimate accuracy improves as you move toward completion; variation in project scope estimates (effort, cost, or features) narrows over time through the range 0.25x, 0.67x, 0.8x, 1.0x, 1.25x, 1.5x, 2x, 4x. From time to time compare actual results to estimated results and use the evaluation to refine estimates for the remainder of the project.

#### Estimating the Amount of Construction

- **Base the construction share on activity proportions until you have your own data** - construction means detailed design, coding and debugging, and unit testing; its proportion of a project varies by project size. Until your company has project-history data of its own, published activity proportions are a good place to start.
- **Keep records of your organization's project experience** - the proportion devoted to construction varies from project to project and organization to organization; use your own records to estimate the time future projects will take.

#### Influences on Schedule

- **Size is the largest influence** - the size of the program to be produced is the largest single influence on a software project's schedule, but many other factors also influence it.
- **Quantified effort factors** (percentage change in project effort; negative = helpful, positive = harmful):

| Factor | Potential Helpful Influence | Potential Harmful Influence |
|---|---|---|
| Co-located vs. multisite development | -14% | 22% |
| Database size | -10% | 28% |
| Documentation match to project needs | -19% | 23% |
| Flexibility allowed in interpreting requirements | -9% | 10% |
| How actively risks are addressed | -12% | 14% |
| Language and tools experience | -16% | 20% |
| Personnel continuity (turnover) | -19% | 29% |
| Platform volatility | -13% | 30% |
| Process maturity | -13% | 15% |
| Product complexity | -27% | 74% |
| Programmer capability | -24% | 34% |
| Reliability required | -18% | 26% |
| Requirements analyst capability | -29% | 42% |
| Reuse requirements | -5% | 24% |
| State-of-the-art application | -11% | 12% |
| Storage constraint (how much of available storage will be consumed) | 0% | 46% |
| Team cohesion | -10% | 11% |
| Team's experience in the applications area | -19% | 22% |
| Team's experience on the technology platform | -15% | 19% |
| Time constraint (of the application itself) | 0% | 63% |
| Use of software tools | -22% | 17% |

- **Also consider these less easily quantified factors** - requirements developer experience and capability; programmer experience and capability; team motivation; management quality; amount of code reused; personnel turnover; requirements volatility; quality of relationship with customer; user participation in requirements; customer experience with the type of application; extent to which programmers participate in requirements development; classified security environment for computer, programs, and data; amount of documentation; project objectives (schedule vs. quality vs. usability vs. the many other possible objectives). Each can be significant; consider them alongside the quantified table.

#### Estimation vs. Control

- **Prioritize control over prediction** - once you have a delivery date and a product specification, the main problem is controlling the expenditure of human and technical resources for on-time delivery. The accuracy of the initial estimate is much less important than subsequent success at controlling resources to meet the schedule.

#### What to Do If You're Behind

- **Add time if you can** - the average project overruns its planned schedule by about 100 percent; when behind, increasing the amount of time usually isn't an option, but if it is, do it. Otherwise try one or more of the following.
- **Never rely on hoping you'll catch up** - the rationalization that time lost in requirements will be made up during coding and testing is hardly ever the case. One survey of over 300 software projects concluded that delays and overruns generally increase toward the end of a project: projects don't make up lost time later, they fall further behind.
- **Expanding the team is usually harmful (Brooks's law)** - adding people to a late software project makes it later. New people need time to familiarize themselves with the project before becoming productive; their training consumes the time of already-trained people; and more people increase the complexity and amount of project communication. One woman having a baby in nine months does not imply nine women can have a baby in one month. Developing software isn't like riveting sheet metal: more workers working doesn't necessarily mean more work gets done.
  - Exception: adding people does not help when tasks can't be divided and performed independently, but if a project's tasks are partitionable you can divide them further and assign them to different people, even people added late in the project. Other researchers have formally identified circumstances under which you can add people to a late project without making it later.
- **Reduce the scope of the project** - a powerful technique that is often overlooked. Eliminating a feature eliminates its design, coding, debugging, testing, documentation, and its interface to other features.
  - Partition the product's capabilities into "must haves," "nice to haves," and "optionals" when planning initially. If you fall behind, prioritize the "optionals" and "nice to haves" and drop the least important.
  - Short of dropping a feature, provide a cheaper version of the same functionality: a version that is on time but not tuned for performance; a version in which the least important functionality is implemented crudely; back off a speed requirement because a slow version is much easier to provide; back off a space requirement because a memory-intensive version is easier.
  - Reestimate development time for the least important features: ask what functionality you can provide in two hours, two days, or two weeks, and what you gain by building the two-week version rather than the two-day version, or the two-day rather than the two-hour.

### 28.4 Measurement

- **For any project attribute, measuring it in some way is superior to not measuring it at all** - the measurement might be imprecise, difficult to make, and need refinement over time, but it gives you a handle on your development process that you don't have without it. Measurement is a key to successful construction management, and accurate measurement is a key to accurate scheduling, to quality control, and to improving your development process.
- **Quantify data used to evaluate methods** - if data is to be used in a scientific experiment it must be quantified. "This new method seems more productive" isn't good enough, just as a scientist could not ban a food product because rats "just seemed to get sicker" than another group; demand a quantified reason such as "rats that ate the new food product were sick 3.7 more days per month than rats that didn't."
- **Do not argue against all measurement because some measurements are inconclusive** - that is arguing against windows because some are cloudy. To argue against measurement is to argue that it's better not to know what's really happening on your project.
- **Be aware of measurement side effects** - what gets measured, gets done. Measurement has a motivational effect: people pay attention to whatever is measured, assuming it's used to evaluate them, and tend to focus on measured work and ignore unmeasured work. Choose what you measure carefully.
- **Useful software-development measurements**:

| Category | Measurements |
|---|---|
| Size | Total lines of code written; total comment lines; total number of classes or routines; total data declarations; total blank lines |
| Overall Quality | Total number of defects; number of defects in each class or routine; average defects per thousand lines of code; mean time between failures; compiler-detected errors |
| Defect Tracking | Severity of each defect; location of each defect (class or routine); origin of each defect (requirements, design, construction, test); way in which each defect is corrected; person responsible for each defect; number of lines affected by each defect correction; work hours spent correcting each defect; average time required to find a defect; average time required to fix a defect; number of attempts made to correct each defect; number of new errors resulting from defect correction |
| Maintainability | Number of public routines on each class; number of parameters passed to each routine; number of private routines and/or variables on each class; number of local variables used by each routine; number of routines called by each class or routine; number of decision points in each routine; control-flow complexity in each routine; lines of code in each class or routine; lines of comments in each class or routine; number of data declarations in each class or routine; number of blank lines in each class or routine; number of gotos in each class or routine; number of input or output statements in each class or routine |
| Productivity | Work-hours spent on the project; work-hours spent on each class or routine; number of times each class or routine changed; dollars spent on project; dollars spent per line of code; dollars spent per defect |

- **Use these measurements to find outliers, not fine distinctions** - most of them are not useful for making fine distinctions among programs, classes, and routines. They are useful mainly for identifying routines that are "outliers"; an abnormal measurement in a routine is a warning sign to reexamine that routine, checking for unusually low quality. Most can be collected with currently available software tools.
- **Don't start by collecting data on all possible measurements** - you'll bury yourself in data so complex you can't figure out what any of it means. Start with a simple set such as number of defects, number of work-months, total dollars, and total lines of code. Standardize the measurements across your projects, then refine and add to them as your understanding of what you want to measure improves.
- **Collect data for a reason** - set goals, determine the questions you need to ask to meet the goals, then measure to answer the questions. Ask for only as much information as is feasible to obtain, and keep in mind that data collection will always take a back seat to deadlines.

### 28.5 Treating Programmers as People

- **Treat programmers and managers as people; they work best when treated as such** - offset the abstractness of programming with a natural office environment and rich coworker contact. The most successful technical companies combine elements of high-tech and high-touch: parklike campuses, organic organizational structures, comfortable offices and other "high-touch" features.

#### How Do Programmers Spend Their Time?

- **Time-and-motion data (1964 Bell Laboratories study of 70 programmers)** - the data is old and proportions vary among programmers, but the pattern has not visibly changed.
  - Totals by source category: Source Code 35%, Business 29%, Personal 13%, Meetings 7%, Training 6%, Mail/Misc. Documents 5%, Technical Manuals 2%, Operating Procedures/Misc. 2%, Program Test 1%.
  - Totals by activity: Talk or listen 32%; Talk with manager 1%; Telephone 3%; Read 18%; Write/record 14%; Away or out 15%; Walking 6%; Miscellaneous 11%.
  - About 30 percent of a programmer's time goes to nontechnical activities that don't directly help the project: walking, personal business, and so on.
  - Walking is 6 percent of time: about 2.5 hours a week, about 125 hours a year - as much time as is spent in training, three times as much as reading technical manuals, six times as much as talking with managers.

#### Variation in Performance and Quality

- **Expect order-of-magnitude differences among programmers** - many studies have shown order-of-magnitude differences in the quality of the programs written, the sizes of the programs written, and the productivity of programmers.
- **The top 20 percent produce about 50 percent of the output** - one study across writing, football, invention, police work, and aircraft piloting found this, based on productivity data such as touchdowns, patents, and solved cases. Because people making no tangible contribution were excluded, the data probably understates actual variation.
- **Individual variation figures** - the original study of professional programmers averaging 7 years' experience found the ratio between best and worst of about 20 to 1 for initial coding time, over 25 to 1 for debugging time, 5 to 1 for program size, and about 10 to 1 for program execution speed. It found no relationship between a programmer's amount of experience and code quality or productivity.
  - Treat specific ratios such as 25 to 1 as not particularly meaningful; the general statement "There are order-of-magnitude differences among programmers" is meaningful and has been confirmed by many other studies of professional programmers.
- **Team variation figures**:
  - Good programmers tend to cluster, as do bad programmers - confirmed by a study of 166 professional programmers from 18 organizations.
  - In one study of seven identical projects, efforts expended varied by a factor of 3.4 to 1 and program sizes by a factor of 3 to 1, even though all participants were professional programmers with several years of experience enrolled in a computer-science graduate program; a less homogeneous group would likely show even greater differences.
  - An earlier study of programming teams observed a 5-to-1 difference in program size and a 2.6-to-1 variation in time required for a team to complete the same project.
  - After reviewing more than 20 years of data for Cocomo II, researchers concluded that developing a program with a team in the 15th percentile of programmers ranked by ability typically requires about 3.5 times as many work-months as with a team in the 90th percentile. 80 percent of the contribution comes from 20 percent of the contributors.
- **Pay more to hire top programmers** - if you must pay more to get a top-10-percent programmer rather than a bottom-10-percent programmer, jump at the chance. You get an immediate payoff in that programmer's quality and productivity, plus a residual effect in the quality and productivity of the other programmers your organization can then retain, because good programmers tend to cluster.

#### Religious Issues

- **Treat these as matters of religion, reflecting personal style** - requiring compliance invites programmers' ire: programming language; indentation style; placing of braces; choice of IDE; commenting style; efficiency vs. readability tradeoffs; choice of methodology (for example Scrum vs. Extreme Programming vs. evolutionary delivery); programming utilities; naming conventions; use of gotos; use of global variables; measurements, especially productivity measures such as lines of code per day.
- **Sound out the programmer on each emotional topic before jumping in with both feet** - be aware you're dealing with a sensitive area.
- **Prefer "suggestions" and "guidelines" over rigid "rules" and "standards" for matters of religion** - when you address a religious issue such as indentation style, brace placement, commenting style, naming conventions, or productivity measurement, express the expectation as a suggestion or guideline and do not set a rigid rule or standard.
- **Finesse issues by sidestepping explicit mandates** - to finesse indentation style or brace placement, require source code to be run through a pretty-printer formatter before it's declared finished and let the pretty printer do the formatting. To finesse commenting style, require that all code be reviewed and that unclear code be modified until it's clear.
- **Have programmers develop their own standards** - the details of a specific standard are often less important than the fact that some standard exists. Don't set standards for your programmers, but do insist they standardize in the areas important to you.
- **Choose battles by project impact** - conformity in minor matters of style probably won't produce enough benefit to offset lower morale, and the biggest battles, over nuances of coding style, can be avoided with no loss to the project. But if you find indiscriminate use of gotos or global variables, unreadable styles, or other practices affecting whole projects, be prepared to put up with some friction to improve code quality; with conscientious programmers this is rarely a problem.

#### Physical Environment

- **Physical environment makes a big difference in productivity** - a farm has over $100,000 in equipment per worker; a programming shop has under $25,000 per employee (desk, chair, a few books, a computer).
- **Office-space differences between best and worst performers** (166 programmers from 35 organizations; most rated their workplaces as not acceptable):

| Environmental Factor | Top 25% | Bottom 25% |
|---|---|---|
| Dedicated floor space | 78 sq. ft. | 46 sq. ft. |
| Acceptably quiet workspace | 57% yes | 29% yes |
| Acceptably private workspace | 62% yes | 19% yes |
| Ability to silence phone | 52% yes | 10% yes |
| Ability to divert calls | 76% yes | 19% yes |
| Frequent needless interruptions | 38% yes | 76% yes |
| Workspace that makes programmer feel appreciated | 57% yes | 29% yes |

- **Productivity correlates strongly with workplace quality** - programmers in the top 25 percent were 2.6 times more productive than those in the bottom 25 percent. The explanation is not that better programmers were promoted into better offices: programmers from the same organizations had similar facilities regardless of differences in their performance.
- **Capital investment in offices pays back** - Xerox, TRW, IBM, and Bell Labs reported significantly improved productivity from a $10,000 to $30,000 capital investment per person, more than recaptured in improved productivity. With "productivity offices," self-reported estimates ranged from 39 to 47 percent improvement.
- **Expected gains** - moving a bottom-25-percent environment to a top-25-percent environment can yield about a 100 percent productivity improvement; moving an average workplace to a top-25-percent environment can still yield 40 percent or more.

### 28.6 Managing Your Manager

- **Recognize the situation** - nontechnical managers are common, as are managers with technical experience who are 10 years behind the times; technically competent, technically current managers are rare. If you work for one, do whatever you can to keep your job.
- **"Managing your manager" means telling your manager what to do rather than the other way around** - the trick is to do it in a way that allows your manager to continue believing you are the one being managed. Approaches:
  - Plant ideas for what you want to do, then wait for your manager to have a brainstorm (your idea) about doing what you want to do.
  - Educate your manager about the right way to do things - this is the best long-term solution, though it is not always easy, and it is an ongoing job because managers are often promoted, transferred, or fired.
  - Focus on your manager's interests, doing what he or she really wants you to do, and don't distract your manager with unnecessary implementation details ("encapsulation" of your job).
  - Refuse to do what your manager tells you, and insist on doing your job the right way.
  - Find another job.

## Code Complete: Ch29 Integration

### Integration as a First-Class Activity

- **Treat integration as its own activity** - Do not classify integration as testing work; it runs after developer testing and in conjunction with system testing, yet it is complex enough that it must be treated as an independent activity.
- **Software must be sound at every construction step, not only when finished** - A build order that would produce a correct final product is still wrong if intermediate states cannot stand on their own; the wrong order makes code harder to write, harder to test and harder to debug.
- **Never accept an order where nothing works until everything works** - Such a project can seem as though it will never finish and can collapse under its own weight: a bug count that looks insurmountable, progress that is invisible, complexity that is overwhelming, all of it possible even though the finished product would have worked.
- **Expected payoff of a careful integration approach** - Optimize integration order for these outcomes:
  - Easier defect diagnosis.
  - Fewer defects.
  - Less scaffolding required.
  - Shorter time to a first working product.
  - Shorter overall development schedule.
  - Better customer relations.
  - Higher morale.
  - Higher chance the project completes at all.
  - More reliable schedule estimates and more accurate status reporting.
  - Better code quality.
  - Less documentation.
  - Less testing effort.

### Integration Frequency - Phased or Incremental?

- **Choose one of exactly two frequencies** - Every program is integrated either phased (all at once) or incrementally (a piece at a time); decide deliberately rather than by default. Unless the project is trivial, every variety of incremental integration is better than phased integration.

### Phased Integration

- **Definition - phased integration procedure** - Its three phases, in order:
  1. Design, code, test and debug each class independently ("unit development").
  2. Combine all classes into one whole system at once ("system integration").
  3. Test and debug the entire assembled system ("system dis-integration").
- **Expect every class to be suspect on first combination** - When classes meet for the first time, new defects appear and the cause may lie in a weakly tested class, in an interface between two classes, or in an interaction between two classes; localization is unavailable.
- **Expect defects to interact and mask each other** - All problems surface simultaneously, so diagnosis must cope with inter-class problems plus interference between the problems themselves. Hence the alternate name "big bang integration."
- **Known amplifiers of big-bang failure** - Expect big-bang integration to fail harder when any of these is present: poorly documented interfaces, weak encapsulation, divergent error-handling assumptions between components, global variables.
- **Phased integration cannot start until late** - It is blocked until every class is developer-tested, so defects arrive in bulk at the end of the schedule and drive panic debugging instead of methodical detection and correction.
- **Exception - tiny programs only** - At two or three classes, phased integration might save time, and only with luck; for anything larger another approach is better.

### Incremental Integration

- **Definition - incremental integration procedure** - Write and test in small pieces and combine them one at a time:
  1. Build one small functional part of the system, chosen as the smallest such part, the hardest one, a key one, or any mix of those, and test and debug it thoroughly. It becomes the skeleton every later part hangs on.
  2. Design, code, test and debug one class.
  3. Integrate that class with the skeleton and test/debug the combination. Do not add another class until the current combination works. Repeat from step 2 while work remains.
- **Unit of integration may exceed one class** - Integrating a whole component still counts as incremental if that component was thoroughly tested and its classes were themselves mini-integrated.
- **Momentum compounds** - Each added piece makes the system larger and faster-moving; incremental integration supports and encourages other incremental strategies.

### Benefits of Incremental Integration

- **Errors localize to the new piece** - Any new failure implicates the class just added: either its interface to the rest of the program or its interaction with an already-integrated class. Fewer simultaneous defects also cuts the risk of defects interacting or masking one another.
  - The more interface errors a project tends to produce, the larger this benefit; one project's defect accounting attributed 39 percent of errors to inter-module interface errors.
  - Debugging consumes up to 50 percent of developer time on many projects, so maximizing debugging effectiveness by making errors easy to locate converts directly into quality and productivity.
  - Contrast: with phased integration a failure may sit in any component or in any connection between components.
- **The system succeeds early** - Once code is integrated and running, even if not yet usable, viability is visible; developers see results from their work early and morale holds.
- **Progress monitoring improves** - Frequent integration makes present versus absent features obvious. 50 percent of capability demonstrably working is better status information than a claim that coding is "99 percent complete."
- **Customer relations improve** - Incremental builds supply frequent, visible signs of progress.
- **Units get exercised more** - Each class is integrated as it is finished, so every class runs as part of the whole system far more often than under one end-of-project integration binge. Classes are developer-tested either way; only the system-level exercise differs.
- **Calendar schedule shortens** - With careful integration planning, one part can be designed while another is coded. Total work-hours for design plus code do not drop; some work simply runs in parallel, which is an advantage when calendar time is at a premium.

### Incremental Integration Strategies

- **Plan construction order to serve integration order** - Construction sequence and integration approach govern the order in which classes are designed, coded and tested, so settle both before scheduling class-level work. Phased integration needs no order plan because everything joins at once and any build order works provided all components are ready on the day. Incremental integration requires some components to be integrated before others, so construction sequencing must be planned to match, with each class finished by the time integration needs it.
- **No strategy is universally best** - Select or synthesize the integration order that fits the specific project's demands; know the standard strategies as reference points, not as prescriptions. Before accepting an integration plan, confirm that the strategy names the optimal order for integrating subsystems, classes and routines, makes defect diagnosis easy, holds scaffolding to a minimum, and is better than the alternative approaches.

### Top-Down Integration

- **Definition** - Write and integrate the class at the top of the hierarchy first, then work downward, replacing stub classes with real ones as each level is integrated.
  - "Top" means the main window, the application control loop, the object holding `main()` in Java, `WinMain()` in Microsoft Windows programming, or the equivalent entry point.
  - Stubs must be written to exercise the top class.
- **Verify interface specifications before integrating** - Before integrating, confirm that the interfaces between classes and components are well specified; specifying interfaces is not itself an integration task, but confirming that they were specified well is. The hardest defects to debug come from subtle interactions between classes, not from single classes.
- **Advantage - control logic is validated early** - Top-of-hierarchy classes get heavy exercise, so large conceptual and design defects surface quickly.
- **Advantage - a partially working system arrives early** - If the user-interface parts are at the top, a basic interface can run early with detail filled in later, which sustains both user and developer morale.
- **Advantage - coding can start before low-level design is finished** - Once the design is driven to a fairly low level of detail across all areas, higher-level classes may be implemented and integrated without completing every remaining detail.
- **Hazard - tricky system interfaces are exercised last** - Pure top-down defers the awkward system interfaces to the end; buggy or slow system interfaces normally need to be reached long before a project's end.
  - A low-level problem can bubble upward, forcing high-level changes and destroying the value of earlier integration work.
  - Mitigate the bubbling problem by developer-testing early and carefully, and by analyzing performance, for whichever classes drive the system interfaces.
- **Hazard - stub explosion** - Integrating downward requires very many stubs while low-level classes remain unintegrated. Stubs are test code and are likelier to contain defects than production code; a defective stub supporting a new class destroys the single-new-class error localization that incremental integration exists to provide.
- **Pure top-down integration is effectively unimplementable** - By the book it requires integrating every class at Level 2 before any class at Level 3, and so on; that rigidity is arbitrary. Use a hybrid, such as top-down within sections.
- **Precondition - a top must exist** - Top-down integration is unusable when the class collection has no top. In interactive systems the location of the top is subjective: sometimes the user interface, sometimes `main()`.
- **Good alternative - vertical-slice integration** - Implement top-down in sections, completing one area of functionality at a time and then moving to the next. The pure top-down benefits and hazards still apply to looser top-down approaches like vertical slices, less visibly; keep them in mind.
- **Do not conflate with top-down design** - Top-down integration and top-down design share a name only.

### Bottom-Up Integration

- **Definition** - Start with the bottom-of-hierarchy classes and work upward; what makes the strategy incremental is adding those low-level classes singly instead of in one batch.
  - Write test drivers to exercise the low-level classes; extend the test-driver scaffolding as classes are developed and replace driver classes with real higher-level classes as those arrive.
- **Advantages are a limited subset of incremental benefits** - Error sources are restricted to the one class being integrated so defects are easy to locate; integration can start early; and potentially troublesome system interfaces get exercised early, which matters because system limitations often decide whether the system's goals are reachable at all.
- **Hazard - major high-level interfaces are integrated last** - Conceptual design defects at higher levels are not found by construction until all detailed work is done; if the design then must change significantly, low-level work may have to be thrown away.
- **Precondition - finish the whole system's design before starting bottom-up integration** - Otherwise assumptions that should never have governed the design become embedded in low-level code, forcing high-level classes to be designed around low-level problems. Letting low-level details drive higher-level design violates information hiding and object-oriented design principles.
  - Weigh the tradeoff correctly: the cost of integrating higher-level classes late is trivial next to the cost of starting low-level coding before high-level class design is complete.
- **Pure bottom-up integration is rare** - Use a hybrid, such as integrating bottom-up in sections; that variant blurs into feature-oriented integration.

### Sandwich Integration

- **Definition** - Sandwich integration answers the drawbacks of both pure top-down and pure bottom-up: start with top-of-hierarchy, high-level business-object classes; next take bottom-level device-interface classes plus utility classes that are used widely; defer all middle-level classes to the end.
- **Why sandwich integration is practical** - Prefer it over pure top-down or pure bottom-up when either extreme is too rigid: it puts the error-prone classes in first and tends to need the least scaffolding. Treat it as the realistic, practical default among the pure orderings.

### Risk-Oriented Integration

- **Definition** - Risk-oriented integration, also called "hard part first integration", ranks every class by implementation risk and integrates the riskiest first; the easy remainder waits until last.
- **Relation to sandwich integration** - Like sandwich integration, it seeks to avoid the problems inherent in pure top-down and pure bottom-up integration, and it also usually ends up integrating top and bottom classes first and middle-level classes last, but for a different reason: risk ranking, not layer position.
- **Default risk list** - Treat top-level interfaces as risky and system interfaces (typically the bottom of the hierarchy) as risky; both normally head the risk list.
- **Middle-level risk** - Also pull a middle-level class in early when it is known to be hard, for example when it implements a poorly understood algorithm or must hit aggressive performance targets.
- **Accept residual surprise** - Expect some of the code deferred as "easy" to turn out harder than estimated; that is unavoidable and is not a reason to abandon risk ordering.

### Feature-Oriented Integration

- **Definition** - Integrate one feature at a time, where a feature is any identifiable function of the system (for example, on-screen underlining or automatic document reformatting), not something elaborate.
- **Increment size tradeoff** - When a feature spans more than one class, the integration increment is larger than one class, which weakens certainty about where a new error came from; that loss is small only if every class implementing the feature was thoroughly tested before integration.
- **Recursive use** - Apply the incremental integration strategies recursively: integrate small pieces into features, then integrate features into the system.
- **Start from a supporting skeleton** - Integrate first the skeleton feature chosen for its ability to carry the others; in an interactive system that is typically the interactive menu system, and the remaining features hang off it.
- **Feature trees** - Add components as "feature trees" - hierarchical groups of classes making up one feature.
- **Keep features independent** - Integration is easier when features are relatively independent: shared calls down into the same low-level library code are fine, but avoid features sharing calls into common middle-level code.
- **Advantage 1, scaffolding** - It removes scaffolding for essentially everything except low-level library classes, because each self-contained feature carries its own support code; the skeleton may still need a little scaffolding, or parts of it may stay non-operational until specific features land.
- **Advantage 2, visible functionality** - Each integrated feature adds functionality, giving evidence of steady progress and producing working software that can go to customers for evaluation or ship earlier with less functionality than originally planned.
- **Advantage 3, object-oriented fit** - Objects map well onto features, so this strategy is a natural fit for object-oriented systems.
- **Purity is as hard as the other pure forms** - Pursuing feature-oriented integration in pure form is as difficult as pure top-down or pure bottom-up, because significant features usually cannot land until some low-level code is already integrated; run it as a mixed strategy.

### T-Shaped Integration

- **Definition** - "T-shaped integration" attacks the same top-down and bottom-up defects as sandwich and risk-oriented ordering: select one vertical slice for early development and integration, where the slice exercises the system end to end and can expose major flaws in the design assumptions.
- **Order** - Build and integrate the deep slice first and fix every problem it reveals; only then develop the breadth of the system (for example, a desktop application's menu system), which then frames development of the remaining functionality.
- **Combine it** - Pair it with risk ordering or feature ordering rather than running it alone.

### Summary of Integration Approaches

- **Treat strategies as heuristics** - Bottom-up, top-down, sandwich, risk-oriented, feature-oriented and T-shaped are heuristics, not algorithms; none is a robust step-by-step procedure that terminates in a declared "done".
- **Tailor, do not follow dogmatically** - Compose a unique strategy fitted to the specific project instead of applying any named procedure by rote; the best approach for a given project is usually a combination of top-down, bottom-up, risk-oriented and other approaches, and T-shaped integration and vertical-slice integration are two that often work well.

### Daily Build and Smoke Test

- **The practice** - Whatever integration strategy is chosen, compile, link and combine every file into an executable each day, then run a "smoke test" - a relatively simple check that the running product does not "smoke". Daily builds reduce integration problems, improve developer morale, and provide useful project-management information.
- **Benefit, low-quality risk** - The risk of low quality is bound to the risk of failed or troubled integration, so smoke-test all code daily to stop quality problems from taking control: reach a known good state, then hold it there instead of letting decay reach the point where fixing quality costs real time.
- **Benefit, defect diagnosis** - Daily build plus test localizes breakage in time: a product healthy on one day and broken the next was broken by something between those two builds.
- **Benefit, morale** - A visibly working product raises morale regardless of how little it does, and a bit more works each day.
- **Benefit, surfacing hidden work** - Frequent integration exposes work that would otherwise pile up invisibly and appear as an end-of-project tar pit costing weeks or months.
- **Do not misread the slowdown** - Teams new to daily builds often perceive them as slowing progress to a crawl; in fact the builds spread the same work evenly across the project and reveal the team's true historical pace.
- **Build daily** - The "daily" part is fundamental; treat the build as the project's heartbeat and as its sync pulse. Developers' code may drift out of sync between pulses but must realign at every pulse, and close pulses prevent anyone from drifting out of sync entirely. No heartbeat means the project is dead.
  - **Weekly cadence is the failure case** - Building only once a week means a single broken build can leave the project without a good one for several weeks, and that outcome forfeits virtually all the benefit of frequent building.
- **Check for broken builds** - If the built software is not usable, declare the build broken and make fixing it the top priority.
- **Define "breaking the build" per project** - Set a standard strict enough to exclude showstopper defects and lenient enough to ignore trivial defects, since attention to trivia paralyzes progress.
- **Minimum bar for a good build** - A good build must clear all three:
  1. Every source file, library and component compiles clean.
  2. Every source file, library and component links clean.
  3. No showstopper bug blocks launch or makes the program hazardous to operate - that is, it passes the smoke test.
- **Smoke test daily** - Exercise the whole system end to end; the test need not be exhaustive but must expose major problems and must be thorough enough that passing it justifies assuming the build is stable enough for deeper testing.
- **Never build without smoke testing** - The daily build has little value alone; the smoke test is the sentry against quality decay and creeping integration problems, and without it the build degenerates into a daily clean-compile ritual that wastes time.
- **Keep the smoke test current** - Grow the test as the system grows; it may start as a "Hello, World" level check running in seconds and expand to 10 minutes, an hour, or more. A stale smoke test turns the daily build into self-deception, where a fractional test set manufactures false confidence.
- **Automate build and smoke test** - Automate both; tending them by hand consumes too much time and daily build-and-smoke-test is not practical without automation.
- **Establish a build group** - On most projects, tending the build and updating the smoke test grows large enough to be written into someone's job explicitly; on large projects it fills more than one full-time role. Microsoft Windows NT staffed four people full time on builds for its first release.
- **Add revisions only when they form a consistent chunk** - Individual developers rarely produce a meaningful daily increment; work on a chunk and integrate it once the collection of code is in a consistent state, usually every few days.
- **But never delay a check-in too long** - Check in frequently, going no more than a day or two between check-ins. Infrequent check-ins undermine the daily build: a developer buried in revisions that touch nearly every file loses the benefit the rest of the team still gets. Once a developer has passed roughly two days with no changes checked in, classify that work as at risk.
- **Split features across episodes when needed** - Frequent integration sometimes splits one feature's construction into several separate episodes; accept that overhead as the price of lower integration risk, clearer status visibility, better testability and the other gains of frequent integration.
- **Require pre-integration smoke testing by the author** - Developers must test their own code before adding it to the build, either by making a private build on a personal machine and testing it, or by handing the private build to a "testing buddy" tester focused on that developer's code. Either way, new code must pass the smoke test before it can affect the rest of the system.
- **Create a holding area for incoming code** - The process only works if good and bad builds are distinguishable, and a developer testing new code needs a known good system underneath it. Route candidate code into a holding area, build with it, and migrate it into the primary sources only if that build is acceptable.
  - **Small and medium projects** - A version-control system can serve as the holding area: developers check code in, and anyone needing a known good build sets a date option in version control to fetch files as of the last known good build.
  - **Large projects or weak version-control tools** - Run the holding area by hand: the author mails the build group the location of the new files, or the group hosts a staging directory on a shared file server for new source versions; the build group then owns the check-in into version control, only after confirming the code does not break the build.
- **Create a penalty for breaking the build** - Make build health an explicit top project priority and a broken build the exception, not the rule; require any developer who broke the build to stop all other work until it is fixed. A build broken too often makes the whole obligation unenforceable.
  - Light penalties can carry the message: a lollipop taped to the offender's door until the fix lands, goat horns, or $5 into a morale fund.
  - Harsher penalties exist: developers on high-profile Microsoft projects such as Windows 2000 and Microsoft Office carried beepers late in the project and were called in to fix a break even at 3 a.m.
- **Release builds in the morning** - Prefer building overnight, smoke testing early in the morning, and releasing the build in the morning rather than the afternoon.
  - Morning release lets testers test a fresh build the same day; afternoon release pressures testers to launch automated tests before leaving, and a delayed build then forces them to stay late through no fault of their own, which demoralizes them.
  - Morning completion gives more reliable access to developers when the build has problems, since they are down the hall during the day and anywhere at night; beepers do not reliably locate them.
  - Late-day smoke testing with middle-of-the-night callouts is harder on the team, wastes time, and loses more than it gains.
- **Build and smoke test even under pressure** - Never drop the daily build when schedule pressure spikes, even though maintaining it then looks like extravagant overhead; the reverse holds. Under stress, developers lose discipline, take construction shortcuts they would otherwise refuse, and give their own code weaker review and testing, so entropy accelerates. Daily builds impose the discipline that brings that decay to heel each day, though the underlying tendency remains.

### What Kinds of Projects Can Use the Daily Build Process

- **Size is not an exemption** - Reject "too large to build daily". Microsoft Windows 2000 shipped at roughly 50 million lines of code across tens of thousands of source files, with a complete build taking up to 19 hours across several machines, and still built every day; the team credited much of its success to those daily builds.
- **Scale increases the need** - Incremental integration matters more as project size grows, not less.
- **Adoption baseline** - A review of 104 projects across the U.S., India, Japan and Europe found only 20-25 percent used daily builds at the beginning or middle of the project, leaving substantial room for improvement.

### Continuous Integration

- **Read "continuous" as "at least daily"** - Most published recommendations for continuous integration use "continuous" to mean at least daily, which is the reasonable reading.
- **Do not integrate literally continuously** - Merging each change into the newest build on a two-hour rhythm is excessive for most projects; polled top technical executives at companies including Amazon.com, Boeing, Expedia, Microsoft and Nordstrom unanimously rated continuous integration no better than daily integration.
- **Value of short desynchronization** - Brief drift out of sync is useful on medium and large projects, since larger-scale changes routinely desynchronize a developer who then resynchronizes soon after; a daily build already supplies rendezvous points often enough, so syncing every day removes any need for continuous rendezvous.

### Programming Tools

- **Invest in the tool set** - Modern tooling shortens construction time; a leading-edge tool set combined with real fluency in those tools can lift productivity by 50 percent or more, and good tools also strip out tedious detail work.
- **Close tool gaps** - 20 percent of tools account for 80 percent of tool usage, so a missing helpful tool is a heavily used capability forgone. Years of programming can pass without encountering some of the most valuable tools, so periodically survey what exists and check for overlooked ones.
- **Scope of tool selection** - Restrict attention to construction tools rather than requirements-specification, management or end-to-end-development tools, and reason about kinds of tools rather than specific brands, since versions, products and vendors change faster than any recorded recommendation stays valid.

## Code Complete: Ch30 Programming Tools

### Design Tools

- **Use graphical design tools for notation, not just drawing** - When expressing a design, use a tool that supports the target notation (UML, architecture block diagrams, hierarchy charts, entity-relationship diagrams, class diagrams); some tools support one notation only, others several.
  - Design tools are often bundled inside a computer-aided software engineering (CASE) tool with wider scope; some vendors label a standalone design tool a CASE tool.
- **Justify a design tool by capabilities a drawing package lacks** - Anything a design tool draws can be drawn with a generic graphics package or paper, so pick a design tool only for the extra capabilities: automatic rearrangement of remaining nodes, connecting arrows and dependent lower-level nodes when a node is added or deleted; navigation between levels of abstraction; consistency checking of the design; and in some tools, code generation from the design.

### Source-Code Tools: Editing

- **Expect richer, more mature tooling for source code than for design** - Source-code tooling outclasses design tooling in both breadth and maturity, so budget design-phase effort accordingly.
- **Invest in the best available IDE** - Editing consumes as much as 40 percent of some programmers' time, so paying extra for the strongest IDE pays back; several editors already provide every required capability, so do not settle for a primitive editor.
- **Require these IDE capabilities beyond basic word processing** - Treat the following as the selection checklist:
  - Compile and detect errors without leaving the editor.
  - Integration with version control, build, test, and debugging tools, plus other useful functions.
  - Compressed or outline views showing class names only, or logical structure without bodies ("folding").
  - Jump to the definition of a class, routine, or variable.
  - Jump to every use site of a class, routine, or variable.
  - Formatting driven by the rules of the language in use.
  - Interactive language help while editing.
  - Match braces, or begin-end pairs.
  - Templates for common constructs, with the editor completing a structure such as a `for` loop from the keyword.
  - Smart indenting, including cheap re-indentation of a whole statement block when logic changes.
  - Automated code transforms and refactorings.
  - Macros written in a programming language already familiar to the team.
  - A history of search strings so common ones need not be retyped.
  - Search and replace driven by regular expressions.
  - Search and replace spanning a group of files.
  - Edit several files at once.
  - Compare two files side by side.
  - Undo across many levels, not just the last action.
- **Add a standalone multi-file search tool if the editor lacks one** - Use it to locate every occurrence of a class or routine name, and, after finding one defect, to hunt the same mistake in other files.
- **Match search strength to the task: exact, case-insensitive, or regular expression** - Regular expressions carry the most power because they match complex patterns; sharpen the pattern to narrow results.
  - To find array subscripts holding magic numbers, match `[`, then zero or more spaces, then one or more digits, then zero or more spaces, then `]`. With grep:

```sh
grep "\[ *[0-9]+ *\]" *.cpp
```

- **Keep multi-file renaming frictionless** - Renaming a routine, constant, or global variable may touch several files; use tools that change strings across files (Perl, AWK, sed) so nothing obstructs choosing excellent class, routine, and constant names.
- **Use a diff tool to answer "what changed"** - Compare original against modified files to strip failed correction attempts; compare current code against the last version worked on to see other people's changes; compare current against an older version to locate the change that introduced a newly discovered defect. This function is frequently built into revision-control tools.
- **Treat merge tools as critical under concurrent-edit version control** - One revision-control style locks a file so only one person edits it at a time; the other permits simultaneous edits and merges at check-in. Under the second style, merge tools are critical: they resolve simple merges automatically and prompt the user for conflicting or complicated merges.
- **Know which class of beautifier you are running** - Beautifiers make source look consistent: highlighting class and routine names, standardizing indentation, formatting comments uniformly, and optionally emitting one routine per web or printed page. Most allow customization.
  - Class 1 reads source and emits better-looking output while leaving the source unchanged.
  - Class 2 rewrites the source itself, standardizing indentation, parameter-list formatting, and similar. Use this class on large legacy code bases to absorb the tedious formatting work of conforming legacy code to the project's style conventions.
- **Extract interface documentation from tagged source** - Mark text with clues such as `@tag` fields so an interface documentation tool (Javadoc is the prominent example) can extract and format the programmer-interface documentation.
- **Use templates to make repeated keyboarding consistent** - Build a skeleton with correct syntax and slots for every required item (for example a standard comment prolog), store it in a file or keyboard macro, and insert it when creating the entity. Apply the technique to large entities (classes, files) and small ones (loops).
  - On a group project, publish templates to the whole team at project start; adoption follows because templates reduce work, and style and documentation consistency arrives as a side effect.
- **Generate cross-reference listings** - A cross-reference tool lists variables and routines with every place they are used, typically as web pages.
- **Generate class hierarchies for structure analysis** - A class-hierarchy generator reports inheritance trees; occasionally useful in debugging, but its main use is analyzing program structure and splitting a program into packages or subsystems. Some IDEs already provide it.

### Source-Code Tools: Analyzing Code Quality

- **Run a picky syntax and semantics checker on top of the compiler** - The compiler may check only rudimentary syntax; a picky checker exploits language nuances to flag constructs that are legal but almost certainly unintended.
  - C/C++: Lint is the picky checker in many environments. It warns about uninitialized variables, variables never used at all, variables assigned but never read, routine parameters passed out without being assigned, suspicious pointer operations, suspicious logical comparisons, unreachable code, and other common problems. Equivalent tools exist for other languages.
  - C++: assignment inside a condition compiles cleanly but is usually a typo for comparison.

```cpp
// BAD - legal, but assigns and tests the result
while ( i = 0 ) ...
// GOOD
while ( i == 0 ) ...
```

- **Use metrics reporters to target review effort** - Obtain per-routine complexity reports and aim extra review, testing, or redesign at the most complicated routines.
  - Metrics tools also count code lines, declarations of data, comment lines, and blank lines, either per program or per routine; track defects and tie them to the programmers who introduced them, the corrective changes, and the programmers who corrected them; count modifications; and identify the routines modified most often.
  - Complexity analysis tools have been measured at roughly a 20 percent positive impact on maintenance productivity.

### Source-Code Tools: Refactoring Source Code

- **Prefer a refactoring tool over hand-editing for mechanical refactorings** - Do not perform a mechanical refactoring by hand when a tool can do it. A refactoring program, standalone or embedded in an IDE, renames a class across an entire code base and extracts a routine from highlighted code given a new name and an ordered parameter list. It makes code changes faster and less error-prone. Available for Java and Smalltalk, appearing for other languages.
- **Use a restructurer to remove gotos, but do not expect it to fix bad logic** - Restructuring tools convert goto-laden spaghetti into better-structured goto-free code, and in maintenance environments have been reported to lift maintenance productivity by 25-30 percent.
  - A restructurer must assume a great deal during conversion: terrible logic in the input stays terrible in the output.
  - For a manual conversion, run the restructurer over the general cases and hand-tune the hard cases; alternatively use its output only as input to the hand conversion.
- **Reach for a code translator when moving a large code base to another environment** - Some tools translate source from one language to another; that migration case is where a translator pays.
  - Hazard: bad input code is translated as-is, leaving the same bad code expressed in a language the team knows less well.

### Source-Code Tools: Version Control

- **Control proliferating versions with version-control tools across four axes** - Put every project artifact under version control, not just code: content, requirements, designs, project plans, and the rest.
  - Source-code control.
  - Dependency control, of the kind the UNIX `make` utility provides.
  - Versioning of project documentation.
  - Traceability links among project artifacts (requirements, code, test cases) so a requirement change reveals the affected code and tests.

### Source-Code Tools: Data Dictionaries

- **Maintain a data dictionary for significant project data** - A data dictionary is a database describing all significant data in a project; it frequently centers on database schemas. For each data item (database table or class) store the item's name and description, and optionally notes on how it is used.
- **Use the data dictionary to prevent naming clashes on large projects** - On large projects it also tracks hundreds or thousands of class definitions; on a very large project, keep a data dictionary or another central repository holding authoritative descriptions of every class used in the system. Guard against the direct syntactic clash of the same name used twice, and against the subtler clash or gap where different names denote the same thing or one name denotes subtly different things.

### Executable-Code Tools: Code Creation

- **Expect executable-code tooling to be as rich as source-code tooling** - Look for a tool before hand-rolling any step of code creation, packaging, or installation.
- **Know the compiler's role** - A compiler turns source into executable code; the normal expectation is compilation, though interpretation is still in use for some programs.
- **Let the linker handle cross-language integration** - A standard linker joins compiler-produced object files with the standard code needed for an executable, and typically links objects from multiple languages. Exploit this to pick the most appropriate language per program part instead of hand-managing integration.
- **Use an overlay linker when the program exceeds available memory** - It builds an executable that keeps only a portion of itself resident, holding the remainder on disk until needed, so the program runs in less memory than its total size.
- **Use a build tool to rebuild only what changed** - Use dependency-control software so programs build efficiently and reliably: declare, per target file, the source files it depends on and how to make it. Common tools: the UNIX `make` utility, and `ant` for Java.
  - Dependency semantics: if target `userface.obj` is made by compiling `userface.cpp`, and `userface.cpp` depends on `userface.h`, `stdlib.h`, and `project.h`, then a change to any of those headers requires recompiling `userface.cpp`.
  - The tool walks the declared dependencies and recompiles exactly the affected files: with 5 of 250 source files depending on data definitions in a changed `userface.h`, those 5 are recompiled and the other 245 are not.
  - Build tools also eliminate inconsistent-source errors by forcing all sources to a consistent state; the alternatives (recompiling all 250 files, or recompiling by hand, missing one, and hitting out-of-synch errors) are worse. Net effect is substantially better time and reliability in the average compile-link-run cycle.
- **Consider full rebuilds instead of dependency checking when sources are optimized** - Rebuilding every source file can beat extensive dependency checking provided the source files themselves (header file contents and so on) are optimized. Under that approach the Microsoft Word project rebuilt its entire executable, several million lines, in about 13 minutes on an average developer machine.
