- **Buy or adopt an open source library before writing code yourself** - The fastest route to high-quality code in little time is not writing it; write custom code only when no adequate library exists. Proven libraries cover at least:
  - Container classes.
  - Credit card transaction services (e-commerce services).
  - Cross-platform development tools, allowing code to run on Microsoft Windows, Apple Macintosh, and the X Window System by recompiling per environment.
  - Data compression tools.
  - Data types and algorithms.
  - Database operations and data-file manipulation tools.
  - Diagramming, graphing, and charting tools.
  - Imaging tools.
  - License managers.
  - Mathematical operations.
  - Networking and internet communications tools.
  - Report generators and report query builders.
  - Security and encryption tools.
  - Spreadsheet and grid tools.
  - Text and spelling tools.
  - Voice, phone, and fax tools.
- **Use code-generation wizards where handcrafted code is not required** - Generators, frequently integrated into IDEs, tend to target database applications; commonly available ones emit code for databases, user interfaces, and compilers. Generated code is rarely as good as a human programmer's, but for some users 10 working applications outrank one exceptional one.
- **Use a code generator for prototypes and design experiments** - A generator can produce in a few hours a prototype demonstrating key user-interface aspects or comparing design approaches that would take weeks to hand-code; when only experimenting, take the cheapest path.
- **Weigh the readability cost before generating code that must be maintained** - Generators commonly emit nearly unreadable code; if the output will have to be maintained, hand-writing it instead is usually the better trade.
- **Use setup-creation tools for installation packaging** - Vendor tools build setup programs producing disks, CDs, or DVDs, or installing over the web, and check for pre-existing common library files and library versions on the target machine.

### Executable-Code Tools: Preprocessors

- **Use preprocessor macros to swap development-only code out of production builds** - Insert a macro call (for example a memory-fragmentation check at the start of each routine) during development, then redefine the macro to expand to nothing for the production build so the checks are not shipped.
- **Use preprocessor macros for multi-environment compilation** - The same mechanism targets one code base at multiple environments, for example Windows and Linux.
- **Emulate structured control flow in primitive languages** - When the language offers only primitive control constructs (assembler), write a control-flow preprocessor that supplies `if-then-else` and `while` equivalents rather than hand-coding jump logic.
- **Preprocess outside the language when needed** - If the language has no built-in preprocessor, run a standalone preprocessor (for example M4) as a step in the build process.

### Debugging Tools

- **Keep a debugging toolset available** - Rely on these, not on guesswork:
  - Compiler warning messages.
  - Test scaffolding.
  - Diff tools for comparing source-file versions.
  - Execution profilers.
  - Trace monitors.
  - Interactive debuggers, both software and hardware; make active use of one rather than relying on inspection alone.
- **Treat debugging and testing tools as one family** - Testing tools overlap debugging tools; select them together.

### Testing Tools

- **Equip the test environment with all of these capabilities** - Absence of any of them is a gap to close:
  - Automated test frameworks (JUnit, NUnit, CppUnit, and equivalents).
  - Automated test generators.
  - Test-case record and playback utilities.
  - Coverage monitors (logic analyzers and execution profilers).
  - Symbolic debuggers.
  - System perturbers: memory fillers, memory shakers, selective memory failers, memory-access checkers.
  - Diff tools covering data files, captured output, and screen images.
  - Scaffolding.
  - Defect-injection tools.
  - Defect-tracking software.

### Code-Tuning Tools

- **Profile before tuning** - Use an execution profiler to measure how many times each statement runs, or how much time is spent per statement or execution path, and target tuning only at the measured hot spots.
- **Read the generated assembler when high-level behavior is unexplained** - Obtain an assembler listing from the compiler, or reconstruct it with a disassembler from the machine code, to see how efficiently the compiler translates the source. This explains high-level code that looks fast but runs slowly, and it explains counterintuitive benchmark results.
  - Comparing each high-level statement against the instructions the compiler emits is also the most direct way to learn assembly.
  - Compilers routinely emit considerably more instructions than the operation requires; expect that when reading listings.
  - Conversely, some environments force the compiler to emit extremely complex code; read that output as a measure of how much hand work a lower-level language would cost, not as compiler waste. Both readings are legitimate, so judge per environment.

### Tool-Oriented Environments

- **Prefer environments built from small composable tools** - UNIX-style toolsets (grep, diff, sort, make, crypt, tar, lint, ctags, sed, awk, vi) are better suited to tool-oriented programming because the parts combine.
- **Compose small functions into larger ones** - C and C++, closely coupled to UNIX, embody the same small-composable-parts philosophy; the standard C++ library is built from small functions that combine into larger ones precisely because they work well together.
- **Carry the toolset across platforms instead of abandoning it** - Use UNIX work-alike tool suites (for example cygwin on Windows) to keep composable tooling in non-UNIX environments.

### Building Your Own Programming Tools

- **Build the tool rather than doing the job by hand** - Given a five-hour manual task, spending nearly all of that budget building a tool that then finishes the job in 15 minutes is the correct default choice; doing it by hand is right roughly one time in a million. Tool building is a normal part of programming, not a detour.
- **Treat the standard tool categories as buildable** - Editors, analyzers, debuggers, test harnesses and the rest carry no insurmountable technical barrier to writing yourself; the only real question is cost-effectiveness, and building is often not cost-effective. Buy or reuse when an adequate general-purpose tool already exists; build the special-purpose tool yourself when none exists, because many of them are within reach.
- **Expect large organizations to run tool groups** - Nearly every organization above 1000 programmers has in-house tool and support groups, and many own proprietary requirements and design tools better than anything sold commercially.

#### Project-Specific Tools

- **Plan and budget project-specific tools up front** - Most medium and large projects need unique tools, especially tools that automate repetitive tasks; include identifying them and allocating build time in project planning, not as an afterthought.
- **Build tools that isolate one source of error from another** - When both new data and new code could be at fault, write a checker for the data so failures can be attributed correctly (as with validating new font data files separately from new font-display code).
- **Build tools for independent verification of computed results** - When accuracy is essential and hand-checking is slow, write a separate single-case calculator so results from the main system can be verified in seconds instead of minutes.
- **Build custom analysis tools for recorded runtime data** - When the system's behavior is captured by a recorder (for example an in-flight data recorder), write custom analysis tools and run them after each run to verify the primary system.
- **Other standing needs that justify a custom tool** - Build a custom tool as well when the project needs to generate special kinds of test data, verify the quality of data files, or emulate hardware that does not exist yet.

#### Scripts

- **Automate every repetitive chore with a script** - A script (also called a batch file or macro) automates repetition; the most useful ones are often the simplest to write.
- **Scripting threshold** - Anything longer than about five characters typed more than a few times a day is a candidate for a script or batch file. Typical candidates: compile/link sequences, backup commands, any command with many parameters.
- **Scripts buy correctness, not just typing speed** - Use them to guarantee that every required step runs and runs in the right order, eliminating mistyped parameters and skipped steps.
- **Never embed secrets in a script** - Pass passwords and other credentials as invocation parameters (`%1` in a Windows batch file); keep them out of the script body.

```bat
crypto c:\word\journal.* %1 /d /Es /s
word c:\word\journal.doc
crypto c:\word\journal.* %1 /Es /s
```

### Tool Fantasyland

- **Never accept a claim that a tool eliminates programming** - Vendor and pundit predictions of programming's elimination have failed for decades, starting with Fortran ("Formula Translation Language"), which let scientists and engineers write programs but is itself a comparatively low-level language today. Discount any such claim outright.
- **Do not extrapolate incremental tool gains to infinity** - Each innovation ships with defects; removing those accidental difficulties recovers the "one step back" of "two steps forward, one step back" and does not by itself raise productivity beyond the tool's original concept.
  - What tooling legitimately removes is tedium: arranging source statements, the manual edit-compile-link-run cycle, hunting mismatched braces, the step count for routine constructs such as standard message boxes. Good tools make work substantially easier, but they cannot remove the need for programming and will keep reshaping what programming means. Claim only that much.
- **Judge each tool wave by its incremental gain only** - Third-generation languages, fourth-generation languages, automatic programming, CASE tools, and visual programming each produced valuable incremental improvements, collectively transforming programming, and none eliminated it.
- **Assume the hard part stays hard** - Programming is fundamentally hard regardless of tooling: messy real-world domains, rigorous reasoning about sequences, dependencies, and exceptions, undecided end users, ill-defined interfaces to other software and hardware, plus regulations, business rules, and other externally sourced complexity.
- **Expect the bridging role to remain** - Someone must always connect the real-world problem to the machine that is meant to solve it. That role is programming, whether the thing being manipulated is an assembler register or a Microsoft Visual Basic dialog box; as long as computers exist, someone must tell them what to do.
- **Tool availability tracks environment maturity** - How much tooling exists depends partly on the maturity of the technical environment.

### Programming Tools Checklist

- **Assess overall tool support** - Treat inadequate environment-wide tool support as a defect to fix.

### Key Points

- **Actively survey available tools** - Powerful tools are commonly overlooked for years before being discovered; go looking rather than waiting.
- **Adopt tooling in every one of these areas** - Ready-made tools already exist for each: editing, code tuning, testing, debugging, version control, refactoring, and analysis of code quality.

## Code Complete: Ch31 Layout and Style

### 31.1 Layout Fundamentals

- **Treat layout as a maintainability decision, not a performance one** - Layout does not affect execution speed, memory use, or any externally visible behavior; it affects how easily code is read, understood, reviewed, and revised months later, by the author and by successors.
- **Treat formatting minutiae as quality-bearing** - Across a project's life, attention to small layout and formatting details changes both the code's initial quality and its ultimate maintainability; do not dismiss them as cosmetic.
- **Do layout during initial construction** - These details are too integral to coding to be retrofitted effectively later; if they are to be done at all, do them while writing the code.
- **Agree a team layout style before coding starts** - On a team project, settle the formatting style up front rather than reconciling styles afterward.
- **Fundamental Theorem of Formatting** - Good visual layout shows the logical structure of a program. Showing structure is the primary purpose of layout; making code look pretty is worth something, but worth less.
- **Structure beats beauty** - If one technique shows the structure better and another looks better, use the one that shows the structure better. Many formatting styles look good but misrepresent the code's logical organization.
- **Do not chase uniform prettiness** - Techniques that make good code look good and bad code look bad are more useful than techniques that make all code look good. Prioritizing logical representation usually does not create ugly code unless the logic itself is ugly. Looking good is secondary to accuracy, consistency, readability, and maintainability - a distant second; if those criteria are met and the underlying code is good, the layout will look fine anyway.
- **White space is only for humans** - The computer interprets any layout with equal ease; white space exists solely to make the code readable by people. The larger part of programming is writing so other humans can read it.
- **Bad layout cancels good comments and good names** - Two versions of the same routine can be identical in code and comments and differ only in white space, and still sit at opposite ends of the bad-to-good layout scale. Thorough comments, good variable names, and clear logic are not helpful when the layout is so poor that it gives no clue to the routine's logical organization.
- **Layout must tell the human the same story it tells the compiler** - Do not let indentation imply a structure the compiler does not see.
  - Missing braces under a loop: indentation says three statements repeat, the compiler repeats only the first.

```java
// BAD - human sees a 3-statement body; compiler loops only the first line
for ( i = 0; i < MAX_ELEMENTS; i++ )
    leftElement = left[ i ];
    left[ i ] = right[ i ];
    right[ i ] = leftElement;
```

  - Spacing that fakes precedence: `x = 3+4 * 2+7;` reads to a human as (3+4) * (2+7) = 63; the computer ignores white space and evaluates 3 + (4*2) + 7 = 18.
- **Consistency outranks the specific convention** - Structuring code is important for its own sake. The details of a specific method of structuring a program are much less important than the fact that the program is structured consistently. A convention followed inconsistently can actually hurt readability.
- **Expect expectation effects** - Programmers hold strong expectations that others follow discourse rules; when the rules are violated in seemingly innocuous ways, comprehension performance drops drastically and the utility of those built-up expectations is nullified. Layout different from the reader's own scheme may harm even an expert's ability to read a program.
- **Empirical basis** - When program statements were arranged in a sensible order, experts remembered them better than novices; when statements were shuffled, the experts' superiority was reduced. The same pattern holds for chess positions: experts recall game-like arrangements far better than novices but recall randomly arranged pieces no better than novices, because expertise is a knowledge structure that only helps when new information corresponds to it. The basic concept has also been confirmed in Go, bridge, electronics, music, and physics. Structure helps experts perceive, comprehend, and remember important features of programs.
- **Stay open-minded about layout** - Accept practices proven better than the ones you are used to even if adjusting causes initial discomfort. Debates about formatting often sound like religious wars; separate objective preferences from subjective ones by stating explicit criteria.
- **Objectives of a good layout scheme** - The first priority of visual layout is to illuminate the logical organization of the code; assess whether that priority is achieved using accuracy, consistency, readability, and maintainability. A layout scheme must:
  - **Accurately represent the logical structure of the code** - typically via indentation and other white space.
  - **Consistently represent the logical structure of the code** - reject styles whose rules have so many exceptions that they cannot be followed consistently; a good style applies to most cases.
  - **Improve readability** - an indentation strategy that is logical but makes code harder to read is useless; spaces only where the compiler requires them is logical but not readable.
  - **Withstand modifications** - modifying one line of code should not require modifying several others.
  - **Optionally, minimize lines** - minimizing the number of lines needed for a simple statement or block is sometimes also considered (for example when screen space is scarce), but weighting it differently changes conclusions.

### 31.2 Layout Techniques

- **Use white space to enhance readability** - Spaces, tabs, line breaks, and blank lines are the main tools for showing program structure. Program information is denser than book text, so a program should give more organizational clues than a book, not fewer.
- **Group related statements** - A paragraph of code should contain only statements that accomplish a single task and that are related to each other.
- **Separate unrelated statements with blank lines** - Start each new paragraph of code with a blank line. Use blank lines to divide groups of related statements, to separate routines from one another, and to highlight comments.
- **Blank-line ratio** - The optimal number of blank lines in a program is about 8 to 16 percent. Above 16 percent, debug time increases dramatically. This particular statistic may be hard to put to work directly.
- **Indent subordinate statements** - As a rule, indent statements under the statement to which they are logically subordinate.
- **Use two-to-four-space indentation** - Subjects scored 20 to 30 percent higher on comprehension tests with a two-to-four-space indentation scheme than with no indentation at all. Lowest comprehension scores came from no indentation; second lowest from six-space indentation; two-to-four spaces was optimal. Six-space indentation looks pleasing and many subjects felt it was easier to use, but it is less readable. Neither underemphasize nor overemphasize the logical structure.
- **Use more parentheses than you think you need** - Add parentheses to clarify any expression involving more than two terms. They may not be needed, they add clarity, and they cost nothing. Use parentheses whenever there is any doubt about how an expression is evaluated; even experienced programmers cannot confidently evaluate `12 + 4 % 3 * 7 / 8` (C++) or `12 + 4 mod 3 * 7 / 8` (Visual Basic) without checking a reference.

### 31.3 Layout Styles

- **Block, defined** - A block is a group of statements below a control statement, enclosed between braces or keywords (`{` and `}` in C++ and Java, if-then-endif in Visual Basic, equivalent structures elsewhere). Most layout issues concern blocks. The four general styles are pure blocks, emulating pure blocks, using begin-end pairs (braces) as block boundaries, and endline layout.
- **Pure blocks** - In a well-designed language each control construct has its own terminator and cannot be used without it, so code is blocked naturally and indenting the inside is uncontroversial.
  - **Visual Basic** has pure blocks: `If-Then ... End If`, `While ... Wend`, `Select Case ... End Select`. The alignment of the opening and closing statements provides solid visual closure.
- **Emulating pure blocks** - In languages without pure blocks, view the `begin`/`end` keywords (or `{`/`}` tokens) as extensions of the control construct: put the opening brace at the end of the control statement and the closing brace alone on the closing line. This looks good, applies consistently, is maintainable, and supports the Fundamental Theorem of Formatting. It is standard in Java and common in C++.

```cpp
// GOOD - pure-block emulation
if ( pixelColor == Color_Red ) {
   statement1;
   statement2;
}
```

- **Using begin-end pairs as block boundaries** - Alternatively, treat `begin`/`end` as statements that follow the control construct: put the opening brace at the start of the block, indented one level, and the closing brace at the end of the block, aligned with it. This works well and exposes the logical structure.
  - **Limitation** - It cannot be applied literally to switch/case statements in C++ and Java: `break` substitutes for the closing brace, but there is no equivalent to the opening brace.

```cpp
// GOOD - begin-end as block boundaries
if ( pixelColor == Color_Red )
   {
   statement1;
   statement2;
   }
```

- **Endline layout** - Any strategy that indents code to the middle or end of the line: aligning a block under the keyword that began it, aligning subsequent parameters under the first parameter, aligning cases in a case statement.
  - It works acceptably in a few cases, for example a short `If/Else/End If` where the aligned keywords and aligned code produce a clear logical structure.
  - **Do not adopt it as a general style** - Overall, endline layout is inaccurate, hard to apply consistently, and hard to maintain. As conditional expressions become more complicated, it gives useless or misleading clues about logical structure (nested `Else` clauses indented under their keywords do not clarify anything), and changing the length of the first line forces reindenting every corresponding statement. Pure block, pure-block emulation, and begin-end block boundaries do not have this maintenance problem. Numerous textbooks from the mid-1970s through 2003 have recommended it anyway.
- **Which style is best** - Language-specific:
  - **Visual Basic** - use pure-block indentation; the IDE makes it hard not to.
  - **Java** - use pure-block indentation, which is standard practice in Java.
  - **C++** - choose the style you like or the one the majority of your team prefers; either pure-block emulation or begin-end block boundaries work equally well. The only study comparing the two found no statistically significant difference in understandability.
  - Neither style is foolproof; each requires an occasional reasonable and obvious compromise. Once you have chosen a style, you reap the most benefit by applying it consistently.

### 31.4 Laying Out Control Structures

- **Treat control-structure layout as a practical priority** - Unlike the layout of some program elements, which is primarily aesthetic, layout of control structures affects readability and comprehensibility. Indentation of blocks is the major issue.
- **Avoid unindented begin-end pairs** - Avoid aligning the braces with the control structure and then indenting the enclosed statements under the brace. It looks fine but violates the Fundamental Theorem of Formatting: the braces are neither part of the control construct nor part of the statements after it, so the enclosed statements look neither part of nor subordinate to the control statement. If you have used this approach, change to pure-block emulation or begin-end block boundaries so that formatting is more consistent.
- **Avoid double indentation with begin and end** - This is a corollary to the rule against unindented begin-end pairs: avoid indenting the braces one level and the statements they enclose a second level. One study showed no difference in comprehension between singly indented and doubly indented programs, but this style does not accurately show the logical structure: the enclosed calls are shown as if they were logically subordinate to the begin-end pair, and they are not.
  - It also exaggerates the complexity of the logical structure: nesting two or three levels yields four or six levels of indentation, so the layout looks more complicated than the code is.
  - Fix it by using pure-block emulation, or by using begin and end as block boundaries and aligning begin and end with the statements they enclose.
- **Use blank lines between paragraphs** - A logical block, a group of statements that belong together, should be treated the way paragraphs are in English and separated from other blocks by blank lines. Applies even to blocks not demarcated by begin-end pairs.
  - Lumping order-independent statements together tempts you to skip organizing them; the discipline of inserting blank lines makes you think harder about which statements really belong together and which need a specific order.
  - Blank lines also open natural spaces for a comment above each block.
  - **Do not use the aligned-equals-signs trick to group statements** - together with missing blank lines it makes statements look more related than they are.
- **Format single-statement blocks consistently** - For a single statement following a control structure, braces are not needed for correct compilation. Three options exist:

```java
Style 1  if ( expression )
             one-statement;

Style 2a if ( expression ) {
             one-statement;
         }

Style 2b if ( expression )
             {
             one-statement;
             }

Style 3  if ( expression ) one-statement;
```

  - Style 1 is consistent with the block indentation scheme.
  - Style 2 (2a or 2b) is also consistent, and the begin-end pair reduces the chance that you add statements after the `if` test and forget to add braces - a particularly subtle error because the indentation says everything is OK while the compiler interprets it differently.
  - Style 3's advantage over Style 2 is that it is easier to type; over Style 1, that copying it elsewhere is more likely to be copied correctly. Its disadvantage is that a line-oriented debugger treats it as one line and does not show whether the statement after the `if` executed.
  - Style 1 has repeatedly caused incorrect modification. Style 3 is an exception to the indentation strategy and should be avoided altogether. On a group project, favor either variation of Style 2 for consistency and safe modifiability.
  - Regardless of the style chosen, use it consistently and use the same style for `if` tests and all loops.
- **For complicated expressions, put separate conditions on separate lines** - Put each part of a complicated expression on its own line, using indentation, spacing, number-line ordering, and making each incomplete line obvious. A minor error such as `z` where `Z` was intended becomes obvious in code formatted this way and stays hidden with less careful formatting.

```java
// GOOD
if ( ( ( '0' <= inChar ) && ( inChar <= '9' ) ) ||
   ( ( 'a' <= inChar ) && ( inChar <= 'z' ) ) ||
   ( ( 'A' <= inChar ) && ( inChar <= 'Z' ) ) )
```

- **Avoid gotos** - The pressing problem for most programmers is not provability but that gotos make code hard to format: there is no good answer to whether to indent code between the goto and its label, or how to indent multiple gotos to the same label. Avoiding gotos sidesteps the formatting problem altogether. When an expert programmer conscientiously decides a goto is the best design choice, format it this way:
  1. Use a name in all caps for the label the code goes to, to make the label obvious.
  2. Put the statement containing the goto on a line by itself, to make the goto obvious.
  3. Put the label the goto goes to on a line by itself, surrounded by blank lines, and outdent the label line to the left margin to make it as obvious as possible.
- **No endline exception for case statements** - Do not indent cases to the right of the case description (putting the action on the same line as `case X:` and aligning actions in a column). It is a maintenance headache: adding a case with a longer name forces shifting out all cases and their code, and the large initial indentation makes it awkward to accommodate any further logic. Use your standard indentation increment instead - if you indent statements in a loop three spaces, indent cases the same three spaces. Many people prefer the looks of the endline version, but the standard-indentation version wins hands down for accommodating longer lines, consistency, and maintainability.
  - **Exception, with a warning** - If all the cases are exactly parallel and all the actions are short, you could consider putting case and action on the same line, but in most instances you will live to regret it: the formatting is a pain initially, breaks under modification, and it is hard to keep all cases parallel as short actions become longer.

### 31.5 Laying Out Individual Statements

#### Statement Length

- **Limit statement line length to about 80 characters** - This common rule is somewhat outdated. Its reasons: lines longer than 80 characters are hard to read; the limit discourages deep nesting; longer lines often will not fit on 8.5" x 11" paper, especially when code is printed "2 up" (2 pages of code per physical page).
- **Exceed 80 columns occasionally rather than breaking badly** - With larger screens, narrow typefaces, and landscape mode the 80-character limit is increasingly arbitrary. A single 90-character line is usually more readable than one broken in two just to avoid spilling over the 80th column. With modern technology it is probably all right to exceed 80 columns occasionally.

#### Using Spaces for Clarity

- **Use spaces to make logical expressions readable** - As a rule, separate identifiers from other identifiers with spaces. Adding further spaces to emphasize logical structure is fine. Extra spaces hardly ever hurt, so be generous with them.
- **Use spaces to make array references readable** - Put spaces around each index in an array reference: `grossRate[ census[ groupId ].gender, census[ groupId ].ageGroup ]`.
- **Use spaces to make routine arguments readable** - Space out argument lists so a specific argument position can be found quickly. Argument positions are significant in all major procedural languages, and it is common to compare each formal parameter against each actual parameter side by side on screen.

#### Formatting Continuation Lines

- **Scope** - Apply these continuation-line rules consistently; they are a sensible, consistent approach and are particularly useful in Java, C, C++, Visual Basic, and other languages that encourage long variable names.
- **Make the incompleteness of a statement obvious** - Break a statement across lines only when it is longer than programming standards allow or too absurdly long for one line, and then break it so that the part on the first line is blatantly incorrect syntactically if it stands alone: leave the trailing `&&`, `+`, or `,` at the end of the first line. This also prevents incorrect modification - if the continuation is deleted, the first line clearly needs something more rather than looking like a missing parenthesis or semicolon.
- **Alternative: put the continuation operator at the beginning of the continuation line** - This also works well. It will not induce a syntax error from a hanging `&&` or `+`, but it makes it easier to scan for operators at the aligned left edge than at the ragged right edge, and it illuminates the structure of long chains of operations.

```java
// GOOD - operator-leading style illuminates the structure
totalBill = totalBill
   + customerPurchases[ customerID ]
   + CitySalesTax( customerPurchases[ customerID ] )
   - SalesTaxExemption( customerPurchases[ customerID ] );
```

- **Keep closely related elements together** - When you break a line, keep together things that belong together: array references, arguments to a routine, and so on. Breaking in the middle of `LateCharge( paymentHistory[ customerID ] )` satisfies the obvious-incompleteness guideline but makes the statement unnecessarily hard to read; break before `LateCharge(` instead.
- **Indent routine-call continuation lines the standard amount** - If you normally indent three spaces for statements in a loop or conditional, indent routine-call continuation lines three spaces.
  - **Alternative rejected: aligning continuation lines under the first argument** - It looks ragged and is difficult to maintain as routine names and argument names change. Most programmers gravitate toward standard indentation over time.
  - **Alternative for finding the end of a call: one argument per line, closing `);` on its own line** - It takes up a lot of real estate, but when arguments are long object-field references or pointer names it improves readability substantially, the `);` makes the end of the call clear, and adding a parameter requires no reformatting, just a new line.
  - In practice usually only a few routines need to be broken into multiple lines. Any of the three multiple-line options works all right if used consistently.
- **Indent control-statement continuation lines the standard amount** - If you run out of room in a `for`, `while`, or `if`, indent the continuation by the same amount you indent statements inside the construct. This is logical (always indented under the statement it continues), consistent, readable, and maintainable. You might improve readability by fine-tuning indentation or spacing in some cases, but keep the maintainability tradeoff in mind.
- **Do not align right sides of assignment statements** - Aligning the right sides (or the equals signs) may look attractive but becomes a headache: alignment must be maintained as variable names change, tools substitute tabs for spaces and spaces for tabs, and lines move among parts of the program with different indentation levels. Treat groups of statements containing assignments just as you would treat other statements.
- **Indent assignment-statement continuation lines the standard amount** - Indent the continuation of an assignment statement by the standard indentation amount, for general readability and maintainability.

#### Using Only One Statement Per Line

- **Use only one statement per line** - Limit yourself to one statement per line even in languages such as C++ and Java that allow several, so do not write `i = 0; j = 0; k = 0; DestroyBadLoopNames( i, j, k );`. The arguments for multiple statements per line (fewer lines of screen or paper, grouping related statements, supposed optimization clues) are good reasons, but these reasons are more compelling:
  - One statement per line provides an accurate view of a program's complexity: complex statements look complex, easy ones look easy.
  - Multiple statements per line does not provide optimization clues to modern compilers; today's optimizing compilers do not depend on formatting clues.
  - The code reads top to bottom instead of top to bottom and left to right; your eye can follow the left margin instead of dipping into each line.
  - Syntax errors are easy to find when the compiler gives only line numbers; with multiple statements per line the line number does not identify the failing statement.
  - Line-oriented debuggers can step statement by statement; otherwise the debugger executes them all at once and you must switch to assembler.
  - Editing individual statements (deleting a line, commenting out a line) is easy instead of requiring surgery between other statements.
- **In C++, avoid using multiple operations per line (side effects)** - A side effect is a consequence of a statement other than its main consequence: `++` on a line containing other operations, or assigning a value to a variable and using the left side of that assignment in a conditional. Side effects make code difficult to read, so write each statement without side effects.
  - `PrintMessage( ++n, n + 2 );` with n equal to 4 is undefined in practice: the first argument `++n` is 5, but C++ does not define the order in which terms in an expression or arguments to a routine are evaluated, so the second argument may be 6 or 7 depending on the compiler. Put the side effect on its own line: `++n; PrintMessage( n, n + 2 );` on separate lines.
  - Cramming operations onto one line hides bugs by inviting recognition instead of reading. `while ( *++t = *++s ) ;` is recognized as `strcpy()` and its defect goes unseen; expanded into separate `++t; ++s; *t = *s;` statements it is obvious that t and s are incremented before the copy, so the first character is missed. This is exactly the situation you are in when debugging: the code you overlook because you recognize it rather than read it can contain the error.
  - **Performance does not justify it** - Profiling the two logically equivalent `strcpy()` versions, the "clever" one-line version took 4.81 seconds to copy 5,000,000 strings and the expanded version took 4.35 seconds: an 11 percent speed penalty for the clever version. Results vary from compiler to compiler, but until you have measured performance gains, strive for clarity and correctness first, performance second.
  - Even if you read side effects easily, most good programmers need to think twice to understand expressions with side effects; do not spend readers' effort on syntactic details.

#### Laying Out Data Declarations

- **Use only one data declaration per line** - Give each declaration its own line, complete with the variable type. It is easier to comment each declaration, easier to modify because each declaration is self-contained, easier to find a specific variable by scanning a single column, and easier to find and fix syntax errors because the compiler's line number has only one declaration on it.
  - This costs screen space (20 lines instead of three for the same declarations) and no study shows it leads to fewer bugs or greater comprehension, but crowded declarations make both the variable and its type hard to find and are grounds for rejecting code in review.
- **Declare variables close to where they're first used** - Declare each variable near its first use rather than declaring all variables in one big block; this reduces "span" and "live time" and facilitates refactoring code into smaller routines when necessary.
- **Order declarations sensibly** - Grouping by type is usually sensible since variables of the same type tend to be used in related operations. Alphabetical ordering by variable name is an alternative with many advocates, but it is too much work for what it is worth; if your list of variables is so long that alphabetical ordering helps, the routine is probably too big - break it up into smaller routines with fewer variables.
- **In C++, put the asterisk next to the variable name in pointer declarations, or declare pointer types** - Putting the asterisk next to the type name (`EmployeeList* employees;`) is wrong when more than one declaration is on a line, because the asterisk applies only to the first variable even though the visual formatting suggests it applies to all. Writing `EmployeeList *employees;` avoids that but wrongly suggests the asterisk is part of the variable name, which it is not; the variable can be used either with or without the asterisk.
  - **Best approach** - Declare a pointer type and use it: `EmployeeListPointer employees;`. Solve the problem either by requiring all pointers to be declared using pointer types or by requiring no more than one variable declaration per line. Be sure to choose at least one of these solutions.

### 31.6 Laying Out Comments

- **Indent a comment with its corresponding code** - Comments flush-left inside indented code completely obscure the visual indentation and destroy the reader's clue to the logical structure. One study of commenting effectiveness found the benefit of having comments was not conclusive, and the author speculated it was because comments "disrupt visual scanning of the program"; the style of commenting strongly influences whether comments are disruptive.
- **Set off each comment with at least one blank line** - The most effective way to get an overview of a program is to read the comments without the code, and blank lines help a reader scan. Using a blank line both before and after a comment costs more display space; unless display space is at a premium, one versus two is a purely aesthetic judgment - the fact that a convention exists is more important than its specific details.
- **Keep the commenting style easy to maintain** - Choose a commenting layout that stays correct as the code changes, and reject one that is not easy to maintain.

### 31.7 Laying Out Routines

- **Use blank lines to separate parts of a routine** - Put blank lines between the routine header, its data and named-constant declarations (if any), and its body.
- **Use standard indentation for routine arguments** - Put the opening parenthesis at the end of the routine name line, each parameter on its own line indented one standard increment, and the closing parenthesis on its own line, so that each argument is easy to read, modify, and comment. Standard indentation does better than no conscious layout or endline layout in accuracy, consistency, readability, and modifiability.
  - **No conscious layout** (parameters jammed together with no spaces) is purely utilitarian and troublesome for humans.
  - **Endline layout** (parameters aligned under the first parameter) is neat and aesthetically appealing but takes a lot of work to maintain, and styles that are hard to maintain are not maintained: renaming the routine throws the alignment off and forces reformatting every remaining parameter line, and the elements are already so far right that you run out of space.
  - Standard indentation holds up under modification: renaming the routine affects no parameter, and adding or deleting a parameter changes only one line plus or minus a comma. The visual cues match the indentation scheme for a loop or an `if`, so the reader always knows where the information is.
  - **Visual Basic** - the same style applies but requires the `_` line-continuation character at the end of each continued line.

### 31.8 Laying Out Classes

- **Order class interface members this way**:
  1. Header comment that describes the class and provides any notes about the overall usage of the class
  2. Constructors and destructors
  3. Public routines
  4. Protected routines
  5. Private routines and member data
- **Order class implementations this way**:
  1. Header comment that describes the contents of the file the class is in
  2. Class data
  3. Public routines
  4. Protected routines
  5. Private routines
- **If you have more than one class in a file, identify each class clearly** - Group related routines together into classes and separate each class from its neighbors with several blank lines plus the class name in a header comment, the way a book starts each chapter on a new page with the title in big print.
  - This advice applies only when your language restricts the number of files you can use. In C++, Java, Visual Basic, or other languages supporting multiple source files, put only one class in each file unless you have a compelling reason to do otherwise (such as a few small classes that make up a single pattern). Within a single class you may still group subgroups of routines using these techniques.
- **Avoid overemphasizing comments within classes** - If you mark every routine and comment with a row of asterisks, nothing is really emphasized and you have no device left to mark the start of a new class; the program becomes a dense forest of asterisks. In formatting, less is more.
- **If you must separate parts of a program with long lines of special characters, use a hierarchy of characters from densest to lightest** - For example, asterisks for class divisions, dashes for routine divisions, and blank lines for important comments. The lighter line visually reinforces that the routine is subordinate to the class. Refrain from putting two rows of asterisks or dashes together.
- **Put one class in one file** - A file is not just a bucket holding some code; if your language allows it, a file should hold a collection of routines supporting one and only one purpose, reinforcing that those routines are in the same class. The class may be one the program recognizes as such or just a logical entity you created as part of your design.
  - Classes are a semantic language concept; files are a physical operating-system concept. The correspondence is coincidental and continues to weaken as more environments support putting code into databases or otherwise obscuring the relationship between routines, classes, and files.
- **Give the file a name related to the class name** - Most projects have a one-to-one correspondence: class `CustomerAccount` in files `CustomerAccount.cpp` and `CustomerAccount.h`.
- **Separate routines within a file clearly** - Separate each routine from other routines with at least two blank lines; use two or three so the separation between routines is more noticeable than blank lines inside a routine. Blank lines are as effective as big rows of asterisks or dashes and are far easier to type and maintain.
- **Sequence routines alphabetically** - Use alphabetical order only in lieu of a stronger organizing principle: when you cannot break a program up into classes, or your editor does not let you find functions easily, alphabetical order can save search time. Otherwise group related routines in a file.
- **In C++, order the source file carefully** - Typical order of source-file contents:
  1. File-description comment
  2. `#include` files
  3. Constant definitions that apply to more than one class (if more than one class in the file)
  4. Enums that apply to more than one class (if more than one class in the file)
  5. Macro function definitions
  6. Type definitions that apply to more than one class (if more than one class in the file)
  7. Global variables and functions imported
  8. Global variables and functions exported
  9. Variables and functions that are private to the file
  10. Classes, including constant definitions, enums, and type definitions within each class

## Code Complete: Ch32 Self-Documenting Code

### External Documentation Artifacts

- **Unit development folder (UDF)** - Maintain an informal per-unit folder, also called a software-development folder (SDF), holding construction-time notes; treat a "unit" loosely as a class, and optionally a package or component.
  - Its primary job is to record design decisions that are documented nowhere else.
  - Typical mandated minimum content: relevant requirements, the slice of top-level design the unit realizes, the applicable development standards, a current code listing, and the developer's design notes.
  - A UDF may be a customer deliverable or internal-only; check the project standard before assuming.
- **Detailed-design document** - Record low-level design at class and routine level, including alternatives considered and the reason the chosen approach won.
  - It may exist as a formal document (then detailed design is treated as separate from construction), as developer notes collected in a UDF, or - most often - only in the code itself.

### Programming Style as Documentation

- **Internal over external documentation** - Internal documentation lives in the program listing at source-statement level; it is the most detailed kind and the kind most likely to stay correct as code changes, so put documentation there first.
- **Style carries the documentation load, not comments** - Treat programming style as the primary code-level documentation. Its constituents: sound structure; obvious rather than ingenious approaches; informative variable names; informative routine names; named constants replacing literals; clean layout; low control-flow complexity; low data-structure complexity. Comments are the final layer on top, never the substitute.
- **Cryptic code is badly documented even with zero comments** - Diagnose unreadability as a style defect (uninformative names, crude layout) before reaching for comments; adding comments to cryptic code is the wrong fix.
- **Aim for self-documenting code** - Target code whose meaning is clear at first glance and whose loop and block boundaries are evident without counting braces.
- **Add a clarifying variable when it makes an operation legible** - Introducing a variable purely to name an intermediate quantity is a legitimate documentation technique; add extra variables wherever they buy clarity.

```java
// BAD
for ( i = 2; i <= num / 2; i++ ) {
  j = i + i;
  while ( j <= num ) { meetsCriteria[ j ] = false; j = j + i; }
}

// GOOD
for ( int factor = 2; factor < ( num / 2 ); factor++ ) {
  int factorableNumber = factor + factor;
  while ( factorableNumber <= num ) {
    isPrime[ factorableNumber ] = false;
    factorableNumber = factorableNumber + factor;
  }
}
```

### Self-Documenting Code Checklist

- **Classes** - Enforce all of these on every class.
  - Present one consistent abstraction through the interface.
  - Name the class well, so the name states its central purpose.
  - Make correct usage obvious from the interface alone.
  - Keep the interface abstract enough that callers need not reason about implementation; the class must be usable as a black box.
- **Routines** - Enforce all of these on every routine.
  - Make the name describe exactly what the routine does.
  - Give each routine one well-defined task.
  - Extract every part of a routine that would benefit from being its own routine.
  - Keep the interface obvious and clear.
- **Data names** - Enforce all of these on declarations.
  - Make type names descriptive enough to document the declarations that use them.
  - Name variables well, and use each variable only for the purpose its name states.
  - Give loop counters names more informative than `i`, `j`, `k`.
  - Use well-named enumerated types in place of improvised flags or boolean variables.
  - Use named constants in place of magic numbers and magic strings.
  - Make the naming convention itself signal which category an identifier belongs to: type, enumerated type, named constant, local, class variable, global.
- **Data organization** - Enforce all of these.
  - Keep references to a variable close together.
  - Keep data types simple to minimize complexity.
  - Access complicated data through abstract access routines (abstract data types).
- **Control** - Enforce all of these.
  - Keep the nominal path through the code clear.
  - Group related statements together.
  - Package relatively independent statement groups into their own routines.
  - Put the normal case in the `if` branch, not the `else`.
  - Keep control structures simple to minimize complexity.
  - Make each loop perform exactly one function, as a well-defined routine would.
  - Minimize nesting.
  - Simplify boolean expressions with additional boolean variables, boolean functions, and decision tables.
- **Layout** - Make the layout expose the program's logical structure.
- **Design** - Enforce all of these.
  - Keep code straightforward; avoid cleverness.
  - Hide implementation details as much as possible.
  - Express the program in problem-domain vocabulary wherever possible; fall back to computer-science or programming-language constructs only where the domain offers no expression.

### To Comment or Not to Comment

- **Assume comments are easier to do badly than well** - Bad commenting does more damage than no commenting, so hold every comment to a standard rather than counting them.
- **Comments must clarify intent, never restate code** - Write comments one level of abstraction above the code, stating what is being attempted; a comment that repeats the code adds only reading volume.
- **Comments are a scanning index** - Their function is to let a maintainer locate the section to change the way headings or a table of contents work: reading one sentence of prose is faster than parsing 20 lines of code. Once located, the maintainer reads the code.
- **"Self-documenting code needs no comments" is false in part** - Code states what the compiler needs; it does not state what is meant to happen. Refactoring does remove most comments, and a refactored stretch of 20 to 30 routine calls can need none, but intent that cannot be deduced from the code must still be written down.
- **Volume itself is a cost** - Every added comment is more text a maintainer must read, so heavily commented code can read harder than sparse code; that cost is only repaid by comments carrying information the code lacks.
- **Comments lose precision, and that is the point** - A programming language is more precise than prose; the value of the comment is the higher level of abstraction, not precision.
- **Never treat a comment as authoritative over the code** - A disagreement between comment and code usually means both are wrong. Comment rot is a real cost, but it does not make commenting itself wrong.
- **Diagnose refusal to comment** - A developer who will not comment is usually in one of five states: overrating the clarity of the code; overrating how interested other developers are in it; overrating how smart they are; laziness; fear that someone else will understand the code.
- **Use code reviews to enforce comment quality** - Peer questions of the form "what is this code trying to do" are the mechanism that produces useful comments and calibrates the team on which comments actually help. When another developer's code is hard to understand, tell that developer specifically how to make it clearer.
- **Commenting is a comprehension check** - If a comment is hard to write, either the code is bad or it is not understood well enough; in both cases the time goes into work that was required anyway, so it is not wasted.
- **Read your own code months later** - Use that as the test of whether commenting and code-reading ability are adequate; the two skills are additive, not a choice.

### Keys to Effective Comments

- **Poor comments are worse than none** - An inaccurate comment sends a maintainer confidently in the wrong direction; a comment that merely paraphrases the code earns nothing. Delete such comments rather than keep them.
- **A correct comment survives poor style** - Where code is mediocre but the comment is accurate and names the technique in use, the comment is the only thing carrying the meaning.

```java
// BAD - comment is wrong; code computes Fibonacci numbers
// write out the sums 1..n for all n from 1 to num
sum = current + previous;

// BAD - comment is accurate but only a verbose echo of the code
// loop from 2 to "num"
for ( int i = 2; i <= num; i++ ) {

// GOOD - names the algorithm, which the code does not state
// compute the square root of Num using the Newton-Raphson approximation
r = num / 2;
```

#### Kinds of Comments

- **Classify every comment by kind** - Six kinds exist; decide which kind a comment is before deciding whether it may stay.
- **Repeat of the code** - Restates the code in other words; supplies no information. Never ship.
- **Explanation of the code** - Explains complicated, tricky, or sensitive code. Useful only because the code is confusing; when code needs explaining, almost always improve the code and then replace the explanation with a summary or intent comment.
- **Marker in the code** - A note that work is unfinished, not intended to survive. Rules:
  - Standardize on one marker style across the project; mixed conventions (`******`, `!!!!!!`, `TBD`, ad hoc) make mechanical search for unfinished code error-prone or impossible.
  - Some deliberately use a syntactically invalid marker so the compiler flags it; others use a comment-safe token so it can be searched.
  - Make a mechanical search for the marker a step in the release checklist; shipping defective code is bad, and shipping code already known to be defective is worse.
  - Use editor "to do" tag navigation where available.
- **Summary of the code** - Distills several lines into one or two sentences. More valuable than repetition because it can be scanned faster than the code; especially valuable to someone other than the original author.
- **Description of the code's intent** - Explains purpose, phrased at the level of the problem rather than the solution. `-- get current employee information` is intent; `-- update employeeRecord object` is a summary in solution terms. A six-month IBM study found maintenance programmers most often named understanding the original programmer's intent as their hardest problem. The intent/summary boundary is fuzzy and the distinction usually does not matter.
- **Information that cannot be expressed in code** - Some facts belong in the source yet cannot be encoded in it: legal notices (copyright, confidentiality), version numbers and similar housekeeping, design notes, optimization notes, links out to requirements or architecture documents, links to online material, and tool-mandated comments such as those consumed by Javadoc and Doxygen.
- **Only three kinds may remain in completed code** - Intent comments, summary comments, and information the code cannot express. Strip everything else before the code is called done.

#### Commenting Efficiently

- **Excess and shortage cost the same** - Over-commenting is as damaging as under-commenting; the economical middle ground is reachable, and effective commenting is not time-consuming.
- **Abandon any commenting style that creates busy work** - A style that is tedious to maintain will not be maintained, and the comments will drift into inaccuracy and become worse than no comments.
  - Drop decorative leader dots aligning names to descriptions; the list works without them.
  - C++: drop right-hand columns of asterisks in block comments; keep the top and bottom asterisk rules only, so text edits do not force realignment on both sides.
  - Visual Basic: drop dashed underlines terminated by an aligned `+`; the rule must be re-measured on every comment edit, and a comment that wraps to two lines leaves no defensible alignment at all. Applying such a style consistently multiplies the problem.
  - If the editor can insert neat aligned decoration with one keystroke, decoration is acceptable; the defect is the manual upkeep, not the asterisks.
  - If underlining is needed for emphasis, use a fixed-length rule independent of comment length, insertable by a text-editor macro; time spent adding and deleting dashes to line up punctuation is not programming.
  - Any style that is too fancy is annoying to maintain: measure a commenting style by its upkeep cost, and replace it when the upkeep is busy work.
- **Prefer accurate comments over good-looking comments** - When the two conflict, and they usually do, accuracy wins.
  - Java/C++: use `//` for single-line comments and `/* ... */` for longer ones; hand-maintaining long columns of `//` and manual line breaking is unrewarding work.

```cpp
// BAD - every text edit forces realigning the right-hand asterisks
/**********************************************************
 * class: GigaTron (GIGATRON.CPP)                         *
 * author: Dwight K. Coder                               *
 **********************************************************/

// GOOD - looks nearly as good, costs nothing to edit
/**********************************************************
  class: GigaTron (GIGATRON.CPP)
  author: Dwight K. Coder
 **********************************************************/
```

- **Use the Pseudocode Programming Process to cut commenting time** - Design each routine in pseudocode and outline the code in comments before writing it, then fill in the code between the comments: the comments are finished when the code is, no separate commenting effort is needed, and the high-level design benefits come along with it. This only works if the resulting comments do not merely repeat the code.
- **Integrate commenting into the development flow; never defer it to the end** - Deferred commenting becomes a task of its own, feels larger, costs more because the code must be re-derived instead of transcribed from current thinking, and is less accurate because assumptions and design subtleties are forgotten.
- **Treat "commenting breaks my concentration" as a warning sign** - Code that demands that much concentration should be designed in pseudocode first and the pseudocode converted to comments; if the design is hard to code, simplify the design before worrying about code or comments.
- **Performance never justifies omitting comments** - Interpreted or over-the-wire environments where comments cost measurable runtime (1980s Basic on the original IBM PC, 1990s `.asp` pages, 2000s JavaScript and other network-shipped code) are solved by producing a release version distinct from the development version, typically by stripping comments with a build-process tool.

#### Optimum Number of Comments

- **Peak clarity sits near one comment per 10 statements** - IBM studies reported by Capers Jones found clarity peaked at roughly one comment every 10 statements; fewer comments made code hard to understand, and more comments also reduced understandability.
- **Never convert a comment density into a rule** - Never adopt a standard of the form "one comment every x lines"; a standard such as "at least one comment every five lines" treats the symptom of unclear code and ignores the cause. Encourage commenting without being naive about it.
- **Let the count be a side effect** - Using the Pseudocode Programming Process well tends to land at a comment every few lines on its own. Judge each comment's efficiency, not the total; if comments explain why the code was written and meet the other criteria here, the quantity is sufficient.

### Commenting Techniques

- **Match the technique to the level** - Choose the commenting approach according to scope: program, file, routine, paragraph, or individual line.

#### Commenting Individual Lines

- **Comment a single line only for one of two reasons** - The line is complicated enough to require explanation, or the line once contained an error and a record of that error is wanted. In good code this need is rare.
- **Never write self-indulgent comments** - A comment must relate to why the code is what it is. A private joke or personal reference attached to a value (`MOV AX, 723h ; R. I. P. L. V. B.`, encoding Beethoven's death year in hex) tells a maintainer nothing about why the value is needed and wastes debugging time.

#### Endline Comments and Their Problems

- **Know the systemic defects of endline comments** - Comments trailing a line of code are useful in a few situations only; the following defects apply otherwise.
  - Alignment: they need a clean right-hand column or the listing looks mangled, and aligning them burns time that yields no understanding of the code.
  - Fragility: growing one line of code shoves its comment right, and every neighbor must move to match; a style this costly stops being maintained, so the commenting rots as the code changes instead of improving.
  - Crypticness: the margin is narrow and the comment must stay on one line, so effort shifts to brevity at the expense of clarity.
- **Avoid endline comments on single lines** - A meaningful comment for one line of code is rarely writable, so such comments almost always echo the line and do net harm.

```cpp
// BAD - each comment restates its line
memoryToInitialize = MemoryAvailable();      // get amount of memory available
pointer = GetMemory( memoryToInitialize );   // get a ptr to the available memory
ZeroMemory( pointer, memoryToInitialize );   // set memory to 0
```

- **Avoid endline comments meant to cover multiple lines** - The formatting cannot show scope, so the reader must read both comment and code to learn whether the comment applies to one statement or to the whole block; the content may be fine and the placement still wrong.

```vb
' BAD - does the comment cover the loop or only the first statement?
For rateIdx = 1 to rateCount            ' Compute discounted rates
  LookupRegularRate( rateIdx, regularRate )
  rate( rateIdx ) = regularRate * discount( rateIdx )
Next
```

#### When to Use Endline Comments

- **Exception 1: annotating data declarations** - Endline comments are useful on declarations, which do not suffer the systemic problems, provided the line width allows it; at 132 columns a meaningful comment fits beside each declaration.

```java
// GOOD
int boundary = 0;              // upper index of sorted part of array
String insertVal = BLANK;      // data elmt to insert in sorted part of array
int insertPos = 0;             // position to insert elmt in sorted part of array
```

- **Exception 2: marking where a long block ends** - Tagging the closing line of a long `while` loop or a long `if` statement with an endline comment is a legitimate use.
- **Never use endline comments for maintenance notes** - Dates, programmer initials, and error-report numbers (`-- fixed error #A423 10/1/05 (scm)`) have no place in production code; version-control software handles that history. Comments must explain why the code works now, not why it once failed.
- **Default position** - Aside from those special cases, avoid endline comments: they carry conceptual problems, tend to appear on code that is too complicated, and are hard to format and maintain.

#### Commenting Paragraphs of Code

- **Default form** - Write most comments as a single sentence, or a pair of sentences, describing one paragraph of code; in a well-documented program those make up the bulk of the comments.
- **Write at the level of intent** - State the problem-level purpose of the block that follows, not its mechanics. Intent-level comments survive code changes, including bug fixes inside the block; comments written below the level of intent are harder to maintain. Code good enough to read at close to the level of intent makes the comment somewhat redundant, a condition few programs ever reach.

```java
// GOOD - states intent, survives a fix to the swap logic
// swap the roots
oldRoot = root[0];
root[0] = root[1];
root[1] = oldRoot;
```

- **Escalate a comment until it adds information the code cannot** - Rank candidates and pick the one carrying knowledge absent from the listing.
  1. Restating the loop mechanics ("check each character until a dollar sign is found or all characters have been checked") repeats the code and gives no insight.
  2. Naming the goal (`// find '$' in inputString`) is better but does not say why.
  3. Naming the domain meaning (`// find the command-word terminator ($)`) is genuinely helpful because the fact that `$` terminates a command word cannot be deduced from the code.
- **Test a paragraph comment by the routine-name substitution** - Ask what a routine doing the same work would be named. If the paragraph has a single purpose the name comes easily; `FindCommandWordTerminator()` is decent, while `Find$InInputString()` and `CheckEachCharacterInInputStrUntilADollarSignIsFoundOrAllCharactersHaveBeenChecked()` are poor or invalid. Write that description out unshortened and unabbreviated - that text is the comment, and it will be at the level of intent.
- **Fix the code before writing the comment** - The code is always the first documentation to check.
  - Replace literals such as `'$'` with a named constant (`COMMAND_WORD_TERMINATOR`).
  - Rename variables so they reveal what is happening (`done` to `foundTheTerminator`, `maxLen` to `commandStringLength`, `i` to `testCharPosition`).
  - Add a variable to hold the search result (`terminatorPosition`) so the loop index and the loop's result are clearly distinct.
  - Java: for a task like searching a string, call the built-in string library instead of hand-coding the loop; know the language's existing capabilities before writing code that duplicates them.
- **Prefer extraction over explanation** - When a comment summarizes a block, move the block into a routine named after the comment (for example `FindCommandWordTerminator()`); a routine name is less likely than a comment to drift out of date as the software evolves.
- **Why, not how** - Comments that state how an operation is performed sit at programming-language level, are usually redundant, and cannot convey intent; state why instead.

```java
// BAD - restates the code
// if account flag is zero
if ( accountFlag == 0 ) ...

// GOOD - states intent, then fix the code too
// if establishing a new account
if ( accountType == AccountType.NewAccount ) ...
```

- **Re-question a comment after improving the code** - Once enumerated types and meaningful names make the comment redundant, delete it; alternatively repurpose it as a section-heading summary comment for the whole block of code that follows.
- **Comments prepare the reader** - A reader scanning only the comments must get a correct idea of what the code does and where a specific activity lives.
  - Corollary: a comment always precedes the code it describes - a long-standing convention in commercial practice, whether or not it was taught.
- **Make every comment count** - Excessive commenting obscures the code it is meant to clarify; spend surplus effort on making the code more readable rather than on writing more comments.
- **Document surprises** - Anything not obvious from the code goes into a comment.
  - When a tricky technique replaces a straightforward one for performance, name the straightforward technique and quantify the gain; example: right shift instead of divide-by-two, cutting loop time by 75%.
  - Document even "common knowledge" tricks, because the point is that the code does not use the technique best suited to its purpose.
  - Caveat: most compilers already optimize integer divide-by-two into a right shift, so the lost clarity is usually pointless; complaints that such code is needlessly clever are usually justified, which is exactly why a genuine measured exception must be documented.

```cpp
for ( element = 0; element < elementCount; element++ ) {
   // Use right shift to divide by two. Substituting the
   // right-shift operation cuts the loop time by 75%.
   elementList[ element ] = elementList[ element ] >> 1;
}
```

- **Avoid abbreviations in comments** - Comments must be unambiguous and readable without decoding; allow only the most common abbreviations. The temptation arises mainly with endline comments, which are already a discredited technique.
- **Differentiating major from minor comments** - When a detailed comment is subordinate to a broader one, mark the relationship, but choose the mechanism carefully.
  - Underlining major comments is not recommended: once one comment is underlined, every following non-underlined comment reads as subordinate to it, so the next non-subordinate comment must be underlined too, cascading into over-underlining or inconsistent underlining.
  - All-caps major comments have the same defect, substituting too many all-caps comments for too many underlined ones.
  - Initial-cap-for-major, lowercase-for-minor is too subtle a visual cue and is easily missed.
  - Acceptable mechanism: prefix each minor comment with an ellipsis (`// ... determine number of strings in the table`).
  - Often best: move the major-comment operation into its own routine. Routines must be logically flat, with all activities at about the same logical level; a routine that distinguishes major from minor activities is not flat, and splitting yields two flat routines instead of one lumpy one.
  - Scope exception: this does not apply to indented code inside loops and conditionals, where indentation already carries the logical organization. It applies only to sequential paragraphs of code where several paragraphs form one operation and some are subordinate.
- **Comment every workaround for a language or environment defect or undocumented feature** - A defect is probably undocumented, and re-documenting it in the code costs nothing; an undocumented feature is by definition documented nowhere else.
  - Replace the magic value with a named constant while documenting the workaround.

```java
blockSize = optimalBlockSize( numItems, sizePerItem );
/* Works around a defect in WriteData() that appears only when the
   third parameter equals 500. */
if ( blockSize == WRITEDATA_BROKEN_SIZE ) {
   blockSize = WRITEDATA_WORKAROUND_SIZE;
}
```

- **Justify deliberate violations of good style** - Explain the reason, so a well-intentioned programmer does not "improve" the style and break the code, and so the deviation reads as intentional rather than sloppy.
- **Never comment tricky code; rewrite it** - Comments cannot rescue difficult code, so never document bad code, rewrite it. Reject the widespread and hazardous belief that especially tricky or sensitive sections should be flagged by comment so readers tread carefully.
  - Empirical calibration: source areas carrying the most comments also tended to carry the most defects and to consume the most development effort, consistent with programmers commenting difficult code heavily.
  - Treat "this is really tricky code" as a report that the code is bad; what seems mildly tricky to the author is incomprehensible to others. Having to ask whether something is tricky settles it: it is, and a non-tricky rewrite always exists.
  - Standard: make the code good enough to need no comments, then comment it to make it better still.
  - Exception: this applies mainly to first-time authorship. While maintaining a program with no latitude to rewrite bad code, commenting the tricky parts is good practice.

### Commenting Data Declarations

- **Document data at least as carefully as process** - Variable comments must describe what the name cannot; one company that studied its own practice concluded annotations on data matter even more than annotations on the processes using the data.
- **Comment the units of numeric data** - State inches vs feet vs meters vs kilometers, elapsed seconds since 1-1-1980 vs milliseconds since program start, latitude/longitude/altitude in radians vs degrees, coordinate system and origin. Never assume units are obvious; they are not obvious to a new programmer, to someone from another part of the system, or after substantial modification.
  - Often better: embed units in the variable names instead of comments. `distanceToSurface = marsLanderAltitude` looks plausible; `distanceToSurfaceInMeters = marsLanderAltitudeInFeet` exposes the defect.
- **Comment the allowable range of numeric values** - Document the expected range (for example dollars between $1 and $100, voltage between 105v and 125v).
  - Ada could restrict a numeric variable's allowable values in the language itself; most languages cannot, so use a comment.
  - Stronger technique: assert the expected range at the beginning and end of the routine.
- **Comment coded meanings** - Where the language has enumerated types (C++, Visual Basic), express coded meanings with them; otherwise comment what each value means and use a named constant, never a literal, for each value (for example 1 = alternating current, 2 = direct current, 3 = undefined).

```vb
Dim cursorX As Integer           ' horizontal cursor position; ranges from 1..MaxCols
Dim antennaLength As Long        ' length of antenna in meters; range is >= 2
Dim characterAttribute As Integer ' 0=Plain; 1=Italic; 2=Bold; 3=BoldItalic
```

- **Comment limitations on input data** - Apply the same rules to routine input parameters as to any other data, whatever the source (parameter, file, direct user input); document both expected and unexpected values, including data a routine must never receive. Assertions document valid ranges too and additionally make the code self-checking.
- **Document flags to the bit level** - For a bit-field variable, document the meaning of every bit from MSB to LSB, including reserved and unused bits and their required value.
  - C++ note: use bit-field syntax so the bit meanings are self-documenting instead of comment-documented.
- **Stamp variable-related comments with the variable name** - A comment referring to a specific variable must be updated whenever the variable is; including the name makes string searches for the variable find the comment too.
- **Document global data at its declaration** - State its purpose and why it must be global; at every use site make its global status evident. A naming convention is the first choice for signaling globalness; comments fill the gap only when no convention exists.

### Commenting Control Structures

- **Comment before each control structure** - The space before an `if`, `case`, loop, or block of statements is the natural comment site, and these constructs usually need explanation.
  - For `if` and `case`: give the reason for the decision and a summary of the outcome.
  - For a loop: state its purpose.
  - Place a setup comment so its position makes clear which variable is being prepared for the loop.
- **Comment the end of each control structure with what ended** - For example `} // for clientIndex - process record for each client`.
  - Especially valuable at the end of long loops and to disambiguate loop nesting; it supplements the indentation's visual cue about logical structure.
  - Not needed for short, non-nested loops; it pays off when nesting is deep or loops are long.
- **Treat an end-of-loop comment as a complexity warning** - A loop complicated enough to need one may need simplification; the same applies to complicated `if` tests and `case` statements. End-of-loop comments do give useful clues to logical structure, but writing and then maintaining them turns tedious, and the best escape is often to rewrite whatever code is complicated enough to demand tedious documentation.

### Commenting Routines

- **Never impose a monolithic, kitchen-sink routine prolog** - Do not require every routine, regardless of size or complexity, to carry a stack of Name / Purpose / Algorithm / Inputs / Outputs / Interface Assumptions / Modification History / Author / date / contact fields.
  - Such a header is out of proportion for a trivial routine, and Purpose and Algorithm entries become strained when the only honest descriptions are "copy a string" or the code itself.
  - Boilerplate fields like Interface Assumptions: None and Modification History: None only consume listing space.
  - Author names duplicate information the revision-control system holds more accurately.
  - Mandating all ingredients for every routine produces inaccurate comments and maintenance failure.
  - Heavy headers also discourage good factoring: high per-routine overhead pushes programmers toward fewer, larger routines. Coding conventions must encourage good practices, not penalize them.
- **Principle of Proximity** - Put comments as close as possible to the code they describe; comments kept far from their code are not maintained with it, drift into disagreement with it, and become worthless.
- **Use a prolog template as an optional menu** - Create a boilerplate documentation prolog for convenience, fill out only the parts that matter for the routine at hand, and delete the rest.
- **Summarize each routine in one or two sentences at its top** - Inability to describe the routine in a short sentence or two signals a weak design; return to design and try again.
  - Required in virtually all routines; exception: simple Get and Set accessors.
- **Document parameters where they are declared** - Place a comment next to each parameter declaration stating its role and legal range.
  - This is an explicit, sanctioned exception to the rule against endline comments.
